name: Wenfeng Pagoda
lede: A pagoda that is wider at the top than at the bottom. From the first storey to the fifth each is slightly broader than the one below—about a metre's difference over five storeys—so the whole reads like an opened umbrella, almost without parallel among Chinese pagodas. Built in 952 (Guangshun 2 of the Later Zhou), it is octagonal, five storeys high, brick-bodied with timber eaves, 38.65 m tall; above the fifth storey sits a small stupa-shaped tower, a pagoda on a pagoda. Originally the Tianning Temple Pagoda, it took the name Wenfeng ('Literary Peak') after Huang Bangning, prefect of Zhangde under the Qianlong emperor, inscribed 'Wenfeng rises in beauty' over its door.
facts: Form: An octagonal five-storey brick-and-timber pagoda with dense eaves, 38.65 m tall, 40 m around the base, standing on a round lotus pedestal of seven tiers of petals; the first and fifth storeys differ in width by about 1 m. The eight faces of the first storey carry brick reliefs of the life of the Buddha and the eight round corner columns each bear two dragons; one door is real and three are blind, their lintels carved with twin dragons chasing a pearl. The finial is a Tibetan-style stupa added in the Qing.

Dating: Tianning Temple was founded in the Renshou era of the Sui; the pagoda was built in 952 (Guangshun 2 of the Later Zhou) and repaired under the Song, Yuan, Ming and Qing. In 1772 (Qianlong 37) prefect Huang Bangning of Zhangde enlarged the temple and inscribed 'Wenfeng rises in beauty' over the pagoda door, giving it its present name; the most recent restoration was in 2015.

Significance: The base and first storey weigh close to 3,000 tonnes, storeys two to five plus the finial about 2,500—heavy below, light above—so the 'upside-down' pagoda rode out the 1966 Xingtai earthquake undamaged. Liang Sicheng noted in his History of Chinese Architecture that its form 'has many unusual points', and Zhao Puchu, climbing it, wrote of 'a layered umbrella holding a stupa aloft'.

name: Iron Lion of Cangzhou
sub: Original iron lion surviving at the old city (damage retained)
yearNote: The enlarged replica made in 2011 for Lion City Park is not used; the real damage, the lotus basin on its back and the necessary supports follow photographs.
lede: Cast in 953 under the Later Zhou, 6.26 m long, 5.47 m tall and 32 tonnes, the Cangzhou Iron Lion (Cangzhou Tie Shizi) is the largest surviving ancient cast-iron object. Its body is inscribed 'made by Li Yun of Shandong', it carries a lotus basin on its back and seems to bear the Diamond Sutra inside its belly, which makes it look more like the mount of Manjusri in a temple than the legendary 'Sea-Quelling Roar'. Over a thousand years it has been blown over, hacked, filled with sulphur and had its legs packed; today its four feet bear no load and a steel frame holds it up. The plate follows the original, breaks and props included.
facts: Form: 6.264 m long, 2.981 m wide and 5.47 m tall, hollow-bellied, weighing 32 tonnes against an estimated original of over 40; cast in sections with stacked clay moulds, about 500 in all. Head raised and mouth open, with straps across chest and haunches and a huge iron lotus basin on its back.

Inscriptions: 'cast in the 3rd year of Guangshun of the Great Zhou' on the right of the neck and along the teeth, 'made by Li Yun of Shandong' on the left flank, 'Lion King' on the head and under the neck, and what appears to be the Diamond Sutra inside the belly. Three explanations of its purpose, town guardian, sea-quelling image or the mount of Manjusri in a temple, remain unsettled.

Repairs: blown over by a gale in 1803 and righted in 1893; moved 8 m north in 1983, then damaged further by a sulphur compound poured in 1987 and by leg fillings in 1994-1995, so that the legs no longer bear weight and the lion stands only on external steel supports.

name: Zhakou White Pagoda
era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms · Wuyue
lede: Liang Sicheng said it was less a building than a piece of sculpture, a model. The White Pagoda at Zhakou takes sixty-one blocks of white Taihu stone and carves, to scale, the columns, lintels, bracket sets, balconies and eaves of an eight-sided, nine-storey timber pavilion pagoda, reaching only 14.4 m in all. It stands by the Qiantang River at the lock where the Grand Canal met the river; heritage authorities date it to the late Wuyue period of the Five Dynasties. One scholar, working from Southern Song sources, identifies it as the Anwu Pagoda of the Anwu Pagoda Cloister built by Qian Hongchu in 957; 'White Pagoda' was a later nickname, given after its protective building was lost.
facts: Form: an octagonal nine-storey stone pagoda imitating a timber pavilion, 14.4 m tall, assembled from sixty-one white stone blocks and tapering storey by storey; the base is carved with peaks and waves below a Sumeru pedestal, the 'nine mountains and eight seas', and the waist carries sutra text. Each storey has a body, eaves and a balcony; two jamb columns divide each face into three bays, the central bays of four faces open as arched doorways, and the lintels are carved with the 'seven red, eight white' pattern. 133 carved figures survive; the finial's rings are lost.

Dating: heritage authorities place it in the late Wuyue period without a fixed year. Research based on the Xianchun Lin'an Gazetteer and other Southern Song records holds that in 957 Qian Hongchu built the Anwu Pagoda Cloister at the southern foot of Longshan, and that this is its pagoda; the name 'White Pagoda' first appears in the early Southern Song, probably after the protective building was destroyed and the stone weathered pale. It was listed as a Major National Historical and Cultural Site in 1988.

Significance: the reign of Qian Hongchu was the peak of pagoda building in Wuyue, and its structural techniques were later absorbed into the Yingzao Fashi. Surveying it in the 1930s, Liang Sicheng found that 'in style and rule it is almost identical to the twin pagodas of Lingyin' and wrote 'The White Pagoda at Zhakou and the Twin Stone Pagodas of Lingyin Monastery', finished in 1937 but, because of the war, not published until 1986.

name: Yunyan Temple Pagoda, Tiger Hill
era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms · Wuyue
lede: Its top is more than two metres off the vertical and it leans nearly four degrees, yet it has stood for over a thousand years: the Yunyan Temple Pagoda on Tiger Hill is one of the most steeply leaning old pagodas in China. Begun in 959, the sixth year of Xiande of the Later Zhou, and completed in 961, the second year of Jianlong of the Northern Song, it has seven storeys and eight sides and rises 47.7 m, its brick body imitating a timber pavilion with engaged columns, lintels and bracket sets. The lean was already noticed when the seventh storey was rebuilt in the late Ming, and a dated stone casket was found inside during the foundation works of 1957.
facts: Form: a seven-storey octagonal brick pagoda in pavilion style imitating timber, surviving to 47.7 m; the brick body carries engaged columns, lintels, bracket sets and balconies, the timber eaves of each storey are long gone and only brick eaves remain. The foundation sits half on rock and half on fill, the root of the lean.

Dating: built from 959 to 961, from the sixth year of Xiande to the second year of Jianlong; during reinforcement in 1957 a stone casket was found between the first and second storeys holding a sutra chest inscribed with the seventeenth day of the twelfth month of the second year of Jianlong (961), matching the completion date. A repair in 1638, the eleventh year of Chongzhen, already found the tower leaning northeast, and the seventh storey was rebuilt with its centre shifted south.

Lean: the top leans about 2.3 m to the north-northeast, with a maximum tilt of 3 degrees 59 minutes; the lean began in the Ming. In 1957 grout was pumped into the foundation and the movement has since been held. Finds from inside the tower, including a Yue-ware celadon lotus bowl of the Five Dynasties, are now in Suzhou Museum.

name: Relic Pagoda of Qixia Temple
era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms · Southern Tang
lede: Dense-eaved pagodas are rare in the Jiangnan region to begin with, and this one is carved entirely in stone. The Sarira Pagoda of Qixia Temple is octagonal and five-storeyed, about 15 m high: a band of the Eight Scenes of the Buddha's life wraps the waist of the Sumeru base, the tall first storey rises above it with Heavenly Kings and guardians flanking the doors, and five tiers of stone eaves press down in close succession, each face between them holding two niches with a seated Buddha. The wooden pagoda built in 601 to house relics distributed by the Sui emperor is long gone; the present tower is a Southern Tang rebuilding, restored in 1929 to a design by Liu Dunzhen.
facts: Form: an octagonal five-storey stone pagoda with dense eaves, about 15 m in total height; a Sumeru base and three tiers of upturned lotus petals support the body, whose eight corners are carved as engaged columns, with doors on the south and north and Heavenly Kings and guardians on the other faces; the five stone eaves project far, each face between them opens two niches with a seated Buddha, and apsaras and worshipping deities are carved beneath the eaves.

Dating: tradition holds that in 601, the first year of Renshou, Emperor Wen of Sui distributed relics to the prefectures for pagodas, and the wooden pagoda at Qixia was one of them, later destroyed; the present stone pagoda was built in the Southern Tang (937-975) by Gao Yue and Lin Renzhao. In 1929 it was restored with funds from Robert Ho Tung and his wife, designed by Liu Dunzhen and directed by Ye Gongchuo; the finial is also a modern replacement.

Carving: the eight faces of the base's waist show the Eight Scenes of Shakyamuni, running clockwise from the descent on an elephant to the cremation after nirvana, and a band of waves, fish and shrimp, the 'Ocean of the Huayan Treasury', runs below. It is the largest surviving stone sarira pagoda in China and is regarded as a representative work of Jiangnan stone carving between Tang and Song; in 1993 eight fallen stone pieces were set back in place.

name: Stone Pagodas and Dharani Pillars of Lingyin Temple, Hangzhou
lede: The halls of Lingyin Monastery today are all rebuilt from the Qing onward; the only truly old pieces are the two stone pagodas before the Mahavira Hall and the two sutra pillars before the Hall of the Heavenly Kings. The pagodas are octagonal, nine storeys and 11 m tall, solid, copying a timber pagoda's balconies, bodies and eaves storey by storey into stone, with four-tier bracket sets under the balconies and five-tier sets under the eaves, as the Yingzao Fashi describes; they were built in 960, the first year of Jianlong of the Northern Song, while the region was still under the Qian family. The sutra pillars date from 969, the second year of Kaibao, and stood originally at Fengxian Monastery, the Qian ancestral temple, until they were moved here in 1035. The plate sets one of each side by side.
facts: Stone pagodas: the pair are 11 m tall, octagonal and nine-storeyed, solid, standing 42 m apart east and west; the base is carved with the 'nine mountains and eight seas', and the eight faces of the waist carry the full Great Usnisa Dharani Sutra. On four faces of each storey jamb columns divide the wall into three bays with an arched door in the middle, carved with door studs and knocker masks; the other four faces bear reliefs of Buddhas, bodhisattvas and Buddhist stories. The balconies rest on four-tier bracket sets, the eaves on five-tier sets; the finials are lost.

Sutra pillars: the pair are carved from Taihu stone and stand 74 m apart, the east pillar 9.46 m and the west 13.2 m in surviving height; the three tiers of the Sumeru pedestal carry four dragons, sixteen niches of bodhisattvas, and eight niches each with a Buddha, two disciples and two bodhisattvas. The eight-sided shaft bears sutra text on seven faces and a dedication on the eighth, and the two pillars carry different sutras. Qian Hongchu erected them at Fengxian Monastery in 969, and they were moved here in 1035.

Significance: Lingyin is said to have been founded in 326; under Qian Hongchu it grew to 1,300 bays of halls, yet every surviving building is a rebuild of the Qing or later, so the two pagodas and two pillars are the oldest objects in the monastery. After surveying them in the 1930s, Liang Sicheng observed that the Lingyin pagodas and the White Pagoda at Zhakou are almost identical in rule and were very probably made by the same craftsmen.

name: Zhenguo Temple, Pingyao
yearNote: Dated to the 7th year of Tianhui of the Northern Han. Although 963 already falls within the Northern Song reckoning, this part of Shanxi still belonged to the Northern Han, so the hall is not reassigned as a Song structure.
lede: The Northern Han lasted only twenty-eight years, and this hall is the one building it left above ground. The Wanfo Hall of 963, the seventh year of Tianhui, is three bays square; its eave columns are only 3.4 m tall, yet the bracket sets on them rise 1.7 m, seven-puzuo clusters with two arms and two cantilevers that push the eaves out nearly two metres. The brackets take up almost sixty per cent of the column height, the last enlargement of the Tang manner of big brackets on a small hall. Eleven Five Dynasties statues inside are as old as the building.
facts: Form: three bays wide and three deep, nearly square at 11.58 by 10.78 m and 8.8 m high, under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof; twelve eave columns 3.42 m tall, no plate, the architrave not projecting at the corners. Capital sets are seven-puzuo with two projecting arms and two downward cantilevers, intermediate sets five-puzuo with two arms; the brackets are 1.74 m high and the eaves project 1.94 m.

Date: an inscription under the ridge purlin records construction in 963, the seventh year of Tianhui of the Northern Han, a date confirmed by a stele of 1819; the temple, originally Jingcheng Temple, was renamed Zhenguo Temple in 1540, and steles record repairs in the Jin, Ming and Qing.

Significance: the only surviving building of the Northern Han and one of the earliest Five Dynasties to early Song timber structures; the eleven figures on the altar, a Buddha, two disciples, two bodhisattvas, two attendants, two heavenly kings and two offering boys, are original Five Dynasties work, the only hall sculpture of that era outside the Mogao Caves. Inscribed as World Heritage with the Ancient City of Pingyao and Shuanglin Temple in 1997.

name: Hualin Temple, Fuzhou
era: 2nd year of Qiande, Northern Song · Built under Wuyue
place: Fujian · Fuzhou · Gulou District · Southern foot of Mount Ping
lede: The oldest surviving timber building south of the Yangtze, and a small hall built with 'first-grade timber': only three bays wide, yet its brackets use the largest module that the Yingzao Fashi reserves for halls of nine to eleven bays; the cap-blocks are huge, and the roof is carried almost entirely by the bracket sets over the columns. In 964 Fuzhou still belonged to Wuyue, and the prefect Bao Xiurang built this Yueshan Jixiang Chan Cloister from the dismantled timbers of the Min kingdom's palaces, so the hall is at once early Northern Song and late Five Dynasties. During the 1980s dismantling repair the whole hall was also moved more than ten metres east.
facts: Form: three bays (15.84 m) wide and four bays (14.70 m) deep under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof; an eight-rafter frame with front and rear rufu beams on four columns. Only 18 columns in all (14 eave columns, 4 interior), column-top bracket sets of seven tiers with two huagong and three downward ang, very large timber module, and an open ceiling.

Dating: the Chunxi Sanshan Zhi records the founding in 964; samples taken during the 1980s repair were carbon-dated to generally over a thousand years old. Enlarged to seven bays with double eaves in the Jiaqing-Daoguang era, the hall was dismantled and rebuilt in 1984-1989 to its early three-bay single-eave form, on a site 14.6 m east of the original.

Comparison: by date it follows the Tang and Five Dynasties timber halls of Shanxi such as Nanchan and Foguang temples, making it the oldest timber building south of the Yangtze, about half a century earlier than the main hall of Baoguo Temple in Ningbo; Chinese and Japanese scholars widely see its entasis columns and oversized brackets as a source for Kamakura-period architecture in Japan.

name: Chongming Temple, Gaoping
place: Shanxi · Gaoping · Hexi Town · Guojiazhuang Village
lede: The Middle Buddha Hall at the eastern foot of Shengfo Mountain was finished in 971, the fourth year of Kaibao of the Northern Song, a hundred and thirty years before the Yingzao fashi was issued, yet it is still built the Tang way: seven-puzuo capital sets with two arms and two cantilevers match those of the East Hall of Foguang Temple almost exactly, the brackets stand nearly as tall as the columns, and there is no plate, the architrave not projecting at the corners. Not one interior column stands inside; look up and the main load-bearing beam turns out to be two short timbers butted end to end, held under the joint by a longitudinal tie, the so-called 'broken beam', a unique case of making big use of small timber.
facts: Form: three bays wide and six rafters deep under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof with a shallow pitch and deep eaves; capital sets are seven-puzuo with two arms and two downward cantilevers, the bracket height close to the column height in a ratio near 1:1, column tops gently rounded, no plate, architrave not projecting. There are no interior columns, the roof load passes through the bracket layer to the eave columns, and the beams are comparatively slender.

Date: a stele of 991, the Record of the Founding of the Imperially Named Chongming Temple on Shengfo Mountain, says the temple was founded in the Kaibao years; in the Taiping Xingguo years the founding monk Xingyong went to the capital and Emperor Taizong bestowed the name. The Middle Hall is dated to 971; major repairs followed in 1591 and 1826. The temple was originally called Langgu Temple.

Significance: the main load-bearing beam of the double-beam system is made of two short timbers of equal diameter and length butted together, carried under the joint by a longitudinal tie and resting at both ends on the tails of the front and rear eave brackets, the 'broken beam', unique among surviving ancient buildings; its bracket sets are one of nine surviving examples of this type predating the Yingzao fashi, hence the phrase 'Song structure in Tang manner'.

name: Longxing Temple
sub: Moni Hall · Hall of Great Compassion · Revolving Sutra Cabinet
lede: In 971 Emperor Taizu of Song ordered the Longzang Monastery enlarged and a bronze Guanyin seven zhang three chi tall cast; from this Longxing Temple (Longxing Si) became the most complete surviving ensemble of Northern Song official architecture. The Moni Hall of 1052 has a cruciform plan with a gabled porch on each of its four sides, gable ends facing outward, which Liang Sicheng called 'common in Song painting but never before found in a surviving building'. The 21.3 m Thousand-armed Guanyin in the Dabei Pavilion and the seven-metre revolving sutra repository in its own hall are, respectively, the largest surviving ancient bronze Guanyin and the earliest surviving revolving repository.
facts: Moni Hall: seven bays by seven on a near-square body, with a hip-and-gable porch projecting from the centre of each side, gable forward, forming a cross-shaped plan; a double-eave hip-and-gable roof over thick walls, with doors and windows only in the porch fronts, a form close to the buildings seen in surviving Song paintings.

Dates: founded in 586 as Longzang Monastery, with the Longzang Temple stele of that year still on site; enlarged by imperial order in 971, when the Guanyin was cast; the Moni Hall was built in 1052, and the name Longxing Si was conferred in 1710 under Kangxi.

Song superlatives: the bronze Thousand-armed Guanyin in the Dabei Pavilion is 21.3 m tall with forty-two arms, the largest surviving ancient bronze Guanyin; the revolving sutra repository is about 7 m across, carried on eight-tier bracket sets with five projecting arms, and is the earliest surviving example. The present Dabei Pavilion was rebuilt around 1940.

name: Jidu Temple
sub: A Song-dynasty Sleeping Hall at the source of the Ji River
yearNote: Based on the date of the timber Sleeping Hall; the Sui founding history of Jidu Temple is not applied to the Song hall.
lede: The Ji River has long since vanished, yet of the temples to the Four Great Rivers only the Jidu Temple still stands intact. Its oldest hall is the Qingong, the 'sleeping palace': built in 973 (Kaibao 6 of the Northern Song), five bays wide under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof, with short, stout eave columns, huge widely spaced bracket sets and a gently sloping roof—Liu Dunzhen saw it in 1936 and called it the earliest timber building he knew of in Henan. The plate shows the front elevation of this hall; the Yuande Hall that once stood before it burned in the Tongzhi era of the Qing, leaving only its platform.
facts: Form: The Qingong is five bays wide and four rafters deep under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof; the eave columns are short and thick, carrying massive, widely spaced bracket sets, and the roof pitch is gentle. A covered passage once joined it to the Yuande Hall in front, forming an I-shaped plan—the typical Song layout of 'hall in front, sleeping quarters behind'.

Dating: The Qingong was built in 973 (Kaibao 6 of the Northern Song) and is the oldest surviving timber building in Henan, one of only two Song timber halls left in the province (the other is the main hall of Chuzu'an at Shaolin). The Yuande Hall was burned by Nian rebels in the Tongzhi era of the Qing; column bases 60 cm across remain on its platform.

Significance: The temple was founded in 582 (Kaihuang 2 of the Sui), and in 796 (Zhenyuan 12 of the Tang) a shrine to the North Sea was added, making this the state's place of sacrifice to both the Ji River and the North Sea. Twenty-three buildings from Song to Qing survive on 86,000 square metres, the only complete temple of the Four Great Rivers; Luo Zhewen called it 'the surviving treasure of the Four Rivers'.

name: Fan Pagoda, Kaifeng
sub: Surviving three-story main body and small pagoda
yearNote: 974 is the year the Song main body was built; the small pagoda on top and the repaired details are not dated by this year.
siteCoordinateSource: Commons塔内实拍File:Inside the Brahma Pagoda - panoramio.jpg公布相机点34.770613,114.358728；因在塔内拍摄，可作繁塔单体近似定位，非测绘中轴。https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Inside_the_Brahma_Pagoda_-_panoramio.jpg
lede: 'The Iron Pagoda is tall, the Iron Pagoda is tall, but it only reaches the Fan Pagoda's waist'—so goes the Kaifeng rhyme, because the Fan Pagoda was once a hexagonal tower of nine storeys, begun in 974 (Kaibao 7 of the Northern Song) as the city's first Buddhist pagoda. Only three stout storeys remain today, but a small pagoda added in the early Qing sits on top, so that from afar it looks like a bronze bell. It is 36.68 m tall, and inside and out every brick bears a Buddha—close to seven thousand of them. The plate shows the surviving three-storey body with the small tower on top; the former nine storeys are not reconstructed.
facts: Form: A hexagonal brick pagoda in the storeyed-pavilion style, three storeys surviving, 36.68 m tall overall on a base of 501.6 square metres, with a six-tier small pagoda built on the truncated top. Inside and out the walls are faced with image bricks—Buddhas, bodhisattvas, musicians and more, over 110 types and nearly 7,000 figures; more than 200 inscribed stones survive inside, including 184 Song sutra tablets, most in the hand of Zhao Anren.

Dating: Begun in 974 (Kaibao 7 of the Northern Song) as the Xingci Pagoda, also called the Tianqing Temple Pagoda after the monastery it stood in, it was built as donations came in and finished around or after 990 (Chunhua 1). In 1527 Li Mengyang's record of the rebuilding of Guoxiang Temple states that 'at the founding of the dynasty the royal aura was razed; of the pagoda's seven storeys four were removed'; in the early Qing a monk capped the stump with the small pagoda.

Significance: It is the oldest standing building in Kaifeng, climbed by a route that threads through the walls and circles the exterior balconies. Its shape is still debated: the traditional view holds that it was cut down in the early Ming, while Song Xixin argues that the present form is the Song original and that the 'nine storeys' always meant a three-storey tower crowned by a six-tier spire.

name: Longhua Pagoda
sub: Eight-sided, seven stories · Brick-and-timber pavilion-style pagoda
era: 2nd year of Taiping Xingguo · Rebuilt by Qian Chu of Wuyue
yearNote: The main body of the surviving pagoda is placed by its rebuilding by Qian Chu of Wuyue in the 2nd year of Taiping Xingguo (977); the national listing dates it to the Song. The timber eaves, railings and other parts have been repaired over the centuries, and the legend of a founding in the Three Kingdoms period is not taken as the date of the surviving pagoda.
lede: Seven octagonal storeys narrow upwards above Shanghai’s streets, with timber eaves and balconies giving Longhua Pagoda a slender profile. Its surviving core is dated to Qian Chu’s rebuilding in 977; a Three Kingdoms origin remains a tradition. Old brickwork and repeatedly renewed outer timber together reveal accumulated layers of time.
facts: The octagonal, seven-storey brick-and-timber pagoda is about forty metres tall. From the second storey, height and area decrease upwards; openings, timber eaves and balconies give the brick body a tower-like articulation.
Xuhui archival material dates the surviving structure to rebuilding by Qian Chu in 977. The claimed Three Kingdoms foundation is traditional, and does not date the present pagoda to that period.
The old brick core and repaired eaves and balustrades are not all of one age. Before modern high-rises, the pagoda long provided a prominent height marker in the local landscape.

name: Twin Pagodas and Main Hall Ruins of Luohan Monastery, Suzhou
sub: Seven-tiered, eight-sided twin pagodas · Song stone columns
era: Begun in the 7th year of Taiping Xingguo
lede: Two identical brick pagodas stand shoulder to shoulder, each topped by a slender iron spire that takes up nearly a quarter of its height, the earliest large iron pagoda finials known. They were donated in 982, the seventh year of Taiping Xingguo of the Northern Song, by Wang Wenhan and his brothers; octagonal and seven storeys, they rise to a total height of 33.3 m. Except on the second storey the inner chambers are square, each turned 45 degrees from the one below while the exterior stays octagonal. Twenty-one metres north stands the site of the main hall, burnt in 1860, with sixteen carved stone columns still in place.
facts: Form: the two pagodas are identical in size and structure, octagonal seven-storey brick pagodas in pavilion style, 33.3 m in total height with a ground storey 5.5 m to a side; each storey has doors on four faces and blind lattice windows on the other four, with eaves corbelled out in brick; the chambers are square on every storey but the octagonal second, each rotated 45 degrees from the last, and the iron finial is about 8 m tall.

Dating: the temple began as the Banruo Cloister in the Xiantong era of the Tang and was renamed Luohan Cloister under Wuyue; in 982 the three Wang Wenhan brothers built the twin pagodas, named the Sarira Pagoda and the Merit Sarira Pagoda; in 1860, the tenth year of Xianfeng, the main hall was destroyed in war and only its remains survive.

Hall site: the platform lies 21 m north of the pagodas, square in plan, three bays wide and deep; sixteen stone columns about 4 m tall survive, in three types, carved round, melon-fluted and octagonal, together with thirty basin-shaped column bases, and the six front-eave columns are carved all over with peonies, lotus, okra flowers and playing children, among the finest Song architectural stone carving.
captions: Twin Pagodas of Luohan Monastery · Remains of stone columns
Northern Song · Begun in the 7th year of Taiping Xingguo

name: Youxian Temple, Gaoping
era: Chunhua era, Northern Song · Vairocana Hall
yearNote: Local culture and tourism accounts give 990, but no inscription recording a founding at that time has been found for the front hall; the period 990–994 is used as an approximate placement, without claiming a precise completion year.
place: Shanxi · Gaoping · Mount Niu, Zaili Village, Hexi Town
lede: On Niushan hill, a stele records that the temple was founded in 990, the first year of Chunhua of the Northern Song, and the Vairocana Hall is dated to the Chunhua years. Three bays wide, six rafters deep and nearly square, its thick walls wrap the eave columns inside, and the deep eaves press down on the wall mass; the capital sets are five-puzuo with one arm and one cantilever, the cantilever and the head both cut in the sharp 'split-bamboo' profile, and neither plate nor architrave projects at the corners. The frame inside is left open to view, and the hip rafter beam is simply a naturally bent log sawn to shape, the offhand ingenuity of local craftsmen.
facts: Form: three bays wide and six rafters deep, nearly square in plan, under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof of flat and cylinder tiles with carved-brick ridge ornaments; capital sets are five-puzuo with one arm and one cantilever, open-heart construction, one five-puzuo intermediate set with two arms in each bay, the heads shaped as split-bamboo cantilevers; plate and architrave both stop at the corners. The frame uses a four-rafter beam against a rear two-rafter beam on three columns, exposed without a ceiling.

Date: according to steles in the temple it was founded in 990, originally named Cijiao Cloister, and repaired in the Jin, Yuan, Ming and Qing. The Vairocana Hall is identified as original Northern Song work, placed approximately in the Chunhua years (990–994) since no inscription of its own has been found; the Three Buddhas Hall is a Jin structure and the rest Ming and Qing.

Significance: the hip rafter beam is sawn from a naturally curved timber, preserving the local Song-period practice of southeastern Shanxi; the Song Sumeru-style altar inside, carved with waist panels, cusped openings and flowers, is one of the few surviving original Song altars. The temple is noted locally for its many steles and for the scene of 'the dawn bell of Youxian'.

name: Yanqing Temple Pagoda, Songyang
lede: The body leans 2.38 degrees to the north-east and the finial is 1.76 m off plumb; Qing county gazetteers already recorded the lean, and during the major repair of the 1980s the expert panel finally decided not to straighten it, only to stabilise it. The Yanqing Temple Pagoda is the best-preserved Northern Song pavilion-style brick-and-timber pagoda in south-western Zhejiang: begun in 999, the second year of Xianping, to house relics brought back by the monk Xingda, and completed in 1002, it is hexagonal, seven storeys, 38.32 m tall, with an added ring of lower eaves around the ground storey, so that eight tiers of eaves can be counted from outside, and from the second storey up every level has a balcony gallery one can walk around.
facts: Form: a hexagonal seven-storey pavilion-style pagoda of brick and timber, 38.32 m tall; the ground storey has a surrounding lower eave, storeys two to seven have balcony galleries outside the walls, and arched doors on each face allow ascent storey by storey. All 126 bracket sets are five-tier with open-ended arms, the eaves spread gently; the iron finial consists of an inverted bowl, jewel, dew plate, seven-stage sleeve with rings, and a gourd.

Dating: the Songyang County Gazetteer and the Northern Song writer Zhu Lin's Record of the Yanqing Temple Pagoda relate that the monk Xingda travelled west, obtained forty-nine relics, and on his return built pagodas at Songyang and Yongjia; this one was begun in 999 and finished in 1002. Bricks in the body bear the inscription 'fifth year of Chunhua' (994). The walls keep red-painted flying apsaras, ink-painted arhats and visitors' inscriptions from the Song, Yuan and Ming.

Repairs: by the 1980s the timber had rotted and the tiles were falling; in 1983 Zhejiang Province ordered emergency repairs, completed in 1991. Whether to right the pagoda was debated between a 'sinking-well' straightening scheme and a 'static-pressure pile' reinforcement; in the end the lean was kept, the foundation reinforced with pressed piles and the eaves and galleries restored. The pagoda takes its name from Yanqing Temple, founded in the Dabao era of the Liang, which once stood beside it.

name: Yuanqi Temple, Lucheng
era: Founded in the 6th year of Tianbao, Tang · Surviving Song structures
place: Shanxi · Lucheng · Bank of the Zhuozhang River · Xin'an Village
lede: The temple sits on the summit of Fenghuang Hill on the west bank of the Zhuozhang River, barely twenty-two metres north to south and thirty-three east to west, and was founded in 747, the sixth year of Tianbao of the Tang. Its surviving main hall and Azure Dragon Pagoda are both Song: a three-bay, four-rafter hall under a hip-and-gable roof with plain brackets, and west of it an octagonal seven-storey brick pagoda about seventeen metres high, carved-brick brackets under each tier of eaves and a vase-shaped finial tied by eight iron chains to eight iron figures at the corners. Hall and pagoda stand side by side on the cliff top; from the valley the pagoda catches the eye first.
facts: Form: the main hall is three bays wide and four rafters deep under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof, plain in form with simple brackets; the Azure Dragon Pagoda west of the hall is an octagonal seven-storey brick pagoda about 17 m high, with eaves on every storey, carved-brick imitation brackets beneath them and a vase-shaped finial, each of the eight corners anchored by an iron figure holding an iron chain.

Date: the temple was founded in 747; the main hall and pagoda are Song buildings, the pagoda by one account of 1087, the second year of Yuanyou of the Northern Song; the offering pavilion and side halls are Ming and Qing. The heritage authorities date the complex as a whole to the Song.

Significance: the site measures only 22.3 m north-south by 32.7 m east-west, 729 square metres, yet hall and pagoda side by side on the lone peak make a complete composition, the pagoda set west of the hall rather than on the axis; with Dayun Monastery and Tiantai Hermitage a little downstream it forms the Song link in the sequence of early buildings along the Zhuozhang valley.

name: Mahavira Hall of Mei'an, Zhaoqing
sub: Song timber frame · Present flush gable roof
yearNote: Mei'an was founded in 996; 1000 is only an approximate ordering point for the Song structure, without asserting that every component of the surviving hall was completed in the same year. The Mahavira Hall retains features of Song timber construction; its roof was changed to a flush gable roof in later repairs, and the plate follows the present state.
lede: Mei’an’s Mahavira Hall preserves Song-period building characteristics in a five-bay timber body, while its roof was later changed from hip-and-gable to gabled with flush end walls. Early framing and a later roof therefore coexist. Although the monastery was founded under the Northern Song, repeated repairs prevent one year from dating every part. Brackets and beams beneath the eaves reveal its construction history more clearly than the roof alone.
facts: The hall is five bays wide and three deep, with the present roof ending flush with its gable walls. Column-top brackets project outward in successive layers. The body and framing preserve Song characteristics, including slightly inward-inclined eaves columns.

Mei’an was founded in 996, under the Northern Song. The hall retains Song fabric and underwent repeated Ming, Qing and modern repairs. Its original hip-and-gable roof was later changed, so the foundation year cannot date all present components.

Bracket pins and plates beneath the blocks provide evidence for Song timber practice surviving in Lingnan. The coexistence of older framing and an altered roof also illustrates the continuing adaptation of historic buildings in use.

name: Ruiguang Pagoda, Suzhou
era: Built from the 1st year of Jingde to the 8th year of Tiansheng
lede: In 1978 some boys climbing the tower for fun stumbled on a wooden casket in the 'heavenly chamber' at the core of the third storey; inside was a reliquary shrine set with more than forty thousand pearls, and the Ruiguang Pagoda has been famous ever since. It stands inside Pan Gate, seven storeys and eight sides, a brick body with timber eaves and galleries, about 43 m high; dated inscriptions on bricks, caskets and stone Buddhas place the construction of the present body between 1004 and 1030, from the first year of Jingde to the eighth year of Tiansheng of the Northern Song. The temple's claimed origin under the Eastern Wu is tradition only.
facts: Form: a seven-storey octagonal pagoda in pavilion style of brick and timber, about 43 m high; the brick body carries the load, with timber intermediate eaves and balustraded galleries added outside, and simple Buddhist carvings at the base. The temple halls have long since vanished and only the pagoda remains within Pan Gate.

Dating: dated inscriptions found in the tower on the reliquary casket, sutras, stone Buddhas, stone bases and bricks, together with its plan and structure, date the present pagoda to 1004-1030, from the first year of Jingde to the eighth year of Tiansheng, when the temple was called Ruiguang Chan Cloister; the inner wall of the wooden casket holding the shrine is inscribed in ink with the eighteenth day of the fourth month of the sixth year of Dazhong Xiangfu (1013). It was repaired repeatedly from the Chunxi era of the Southern Song onward, and in 1860 the temple burnt while the pagoda survived.

Heavenly chamber: in April 1978 a group of objects from the Five Dynasties and early Northern Song was found in the chamber of the third storey, the finest being the Pearl Sarira Shrine: 122.6 cm tall, framed in nanmu wood, in three parts of Sumeru base, Buddha hall and spire, combining wood carving, gold tracery, jade carving and gold and silver work, set with more than forty thousand pearls, now in Suzhou Museum.

name: Baoguo Temple, Ningbo
lede: The Main Hall of the 6th year of Dazhong Xiangfu in the Northern Song (1013) is the earliest surviving timber building south of the Yangtze. It was originally a three-bay hall with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; in the Qing a peristyle was added all around, producing the five-bay, double-eaved hall seen today — the central three bays are still Song construction from a thousand years ago.
facts: The plan is deeper than it is wide, and three caisson ceilings in the front bay of the interior hide the beam frame, which is why it is popularly called the “Beamless Hall.”

The melon-ribbed columns are each assembled from four smaller pieces into one large column, the earliest surviving example of composite columns in China; the bracket sets are seven-puzuo, with two projecting arms and two descending cantilevers.
“Birds do not roost, insects do not bore, spiders spin no webs and no dust settles on the beams” — legend credits the timber, but in fact it is the cross-draft through the hall.
No Buddha images are enshrined in the temple; it is now a museum of ancient architecture.

name: Chongqing Temple, Zhangzi
era: 9th year of Dazhong Xiangfu, Northern Song · Thousand-Buddha Hall
place: Shanxi · Zhangzi · Mount Ziyun, Ju Village, Setou Town
lede: The Thousand-Buddha Hall of Chongqing Temple sits on the slope of Mount Ziyun, its wide eaves covering three plain bays of thick walls. The Northern Song timber structure stands next to the temple's Song painted clay arhats, so the different dates of architecture and sculpture can be read side by side in one small temple.
facts: Song structure of 1016: The Thousand-Buddha Hall dates from the 9th year of Dazhong Xiangfu in the Northern Song; it is three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, and the surviving main structure is recorded as Song.

Wide eaves, thick walls: The walls lie close to the plane of the eave columns; the central timber door and the vertical-bar windows on either side are tucked under the great eaves, and the bracket sets beneath the eaves are sturdy and clear.
Song sculpture next door: The temple's Dashi Hall and its eighteen arhats bear a date of 1079, and the walls and other halls have later repairs; this drawing depicts only the Thousand-Buddha Hall.

name: Xiude Temple Pagoda
sub: Surviving brick pagoda combining pavilion and flower-pagoda forms
yearNote: The county gazetteer says the pagoda was completed in 1020; the provincial cultural heritage bureau dates it only to the Song and records six tiers with no surviving finial. Later photographs were checked against the surviving tiers, and the common seven-story account is not used to reconstruct it.
lede: Below, a plain storeyed body; in the middle it suddenly swells into a 'flower pagoda' tier studded with miniature stupa niches; above, it returns to storeyed form. Two pagoda types joined in one, the 32 m brick Xiude Temple Pagoda (Xiudesi Ta) at Quyang is a rare variant of the flower pagoda. A tablet set in the body records that 'on the 8th day of the 4th month of Tianxi 3 of the Great Song (1019) the villagers of Shuidouyan and other villages together repaired one tier of the relic pagoda'; the county gazetteer says the pagoda was finished the following year (1020), while the stone casket in the crypt dates the original relic pagoda to 601. In 1953 a large hoard of white-marble Buddhist statues from the Northern Dynasties to the Tang was unearthed beneath the base, now divided between the Palace Museum and the Hebei Provincial Museum.
facts: Form: an octagonal brick pagoda 32 m high. The second storey is exceptionally tall and ringed with 110 small stupa niches in the flower-pagoda manner; the tiers below and above are storeyed in form. Usually counted as seven storeys, though the provincial heritage bureau records six; the finial is lost.

Dates: a tablet in the body reads 'Tianxi 3 (1019), 4th month, 8th day ... together repaired one tier of the relic pagoda', and the gazetteer records completion in 1020; the crypt casket inscription puts the first relic pagoda in 601 (Sui). Xiude Temple, founded north of the pagoda in the Yuanyou era (1086-1093), no longer exists.

Finds: in 1953 white-marble statues from the Northern Wei to the Tang were excavated under the base, including 48 of the Sui Daye era and 33 of the Northern Qi Tianbao era, now in the Palace Museum and the Hebei Provincial Museum; the crypt itself was found in 1994.

name: Jiwang Temple, Wanrong
place: Shanxi · Wanrong · Nanzhang Township · Taizhao Village
lede: A low, spreading hipped roof covers a five-bay facade, and a deep gallery encloses the ritual space within. The temple is dedicated to Houji, the ancestor of agriculture, and its main hall, framed without full-length great beams, preserves a distinctive Northern Song structural solution.
facts: Northern Song structure: Official sources date the main hall to the Northern Song and record that the temple was founded no later than the 1st year of Tiansheng (1023).
Five-bay hipped hall: The main hall is five bays wide with a single-eaved hipped roof, and bracket sets on the column heads and between the columns carry the deep eaves.

“Beamless Hall”: The popular name comes from the absence of full-length great beams inside; it still has a timber beam frame and is not a masonry beamless hall. It was listed in the 5th batch of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level in 2001.

name: Ashoka Pagoda of Haiqing Temple
place: Jiangsu · Lianyungang · Foot of Huaguo Mountain
lede: The Tancheng earthquake of 1668 measured magnitude 8.5, with its epicentre not far to the north, yet this tower did not tilt. The Ashoka Pagoda of Haiqing Temple stands by Dacun Reservoir at the foot of Huaguo Mountain, octagonal and nine storeys, 40.58 m high, the tallest and oldest surviving pagoda in northern Jiangsu. Begun in the first year of Tiansheng of the Northern Song and finished in the ninth (1023-1031), it was built to enshrine a bodily relic of the Buddha and a 'tooth of King Ashoka'; a stone set into its inner wall records that a Tang pagoda once stood here, said to rank second in the realm. The temple is long gone and the pagoda stands alone.
facts: Form: an octagonal nine-storey brick pagoda in pavilion style, 40.58 m high; arched doors open on the east, west, south and north faces, the brick eaves are corbelled out tier by tier, and the interior can be climbed. It is the tallest old pagoda surviving in northern Jiangsu.

Dating: completed between 1023 and 1031, the first to ninth years of Tiansheng of the Northern Song; according to an inscription set into the inner wall when it was built, an earlier pagoda stood here that was called the second in the realm in the Tang, and the present tower was rebuilt on the old site. It became a Jiangsu provincial protected site in 1956 and a national key protected site in 2006.

Name: Haiqing Temple once stood beside it as a subsidiary of the Sanyuan Palace, the main temple of Huaguo Mountain; the temple perished and the pagoda survived, locally called the Dacun Pagoda, and it is named the Ashoka Pagoda because it enshrined a bodily relic of the Buddha and a relic tooth. In the Ming it figured as the scene 'Ancient Pagoda Piercing the Clouds' and in the Qing as 'The Pagoda's Shadow Rounding Full' among the sights of Yuntai Mountain.

name: Zhaozhou Dharani Pillar
yearNote: Uses the date of the subject drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
siteCoordinateSource: 维基百科《赵州陀罗尼经幢》坐标37°44′50.6″N,114°46′07.3″E。https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/赵州陀罗尼经幢 ；OSM塔体way949954413旁证37.74741,114.76864：https://mapcarta.com/W949954413
lede: At 16.44 m the tallest surviving sutra pillar, the Zhaozhou Dharani Pillar (Zhaozhou Tuoluoni Jingchuang) stands where two main streets of Zhaoxian meet, like a stone pagoda built up from scripture and carving. It was erected in 1038 under prefect Wang Decheng; each of the seven tiers of the shaft is cut from a single block, and between them canopies, upturned lotus, an octagonal walled city and straining strongmen appear in turn. The third-tier eave carries the Prince Siddhartha leaving the city by its four gates; on the fifth tier eight strongmen hold up the tier above with hands or heads. The original Kaiyuan Temple is long gone, but the pillar still stands in place; lightning wrecked tiers three to five in 1983 and they were restored in 1990.
facts: Form: 16.44 m tall overall, facing south. A square podium 1.9 m high and 7.35 m on a side carries a two-tier octagonal Sumeru pedestal; the shaft has seven tiers, each carved from one stone and stepping inward, topped by a peach-shaped bronze flaming jewel.

Inscriptions: the south face of the first tier bears in seal script 'Reverently made for all living beings on land and water of the great earth, the Usnisa-vijaya Dharani Pillar'; the tiers carry dharani texts and donor names, and the sixth tier records a repair in the ninth month of Longqing 5 (1571).

Carving: the third-tier eave is an octagonal walled city whose four cardinal faces form 'Prince Siddhartha at the Four Gates'; each of the eight faces of the fifth tier has a strongman supporting the eave; the podium has strongmen at the corners and 'women closing doors' reliefs on three sides. Struck by lightning in 1983, restored in 1990 with a protective pool added.

name: Lingxiao Pagoda of Tianning Temple
era: Founded in the Tang · Rebuilt in the 5th year of Qingli, Song
lede: The lower four storeys are Song brick, the upper five Jin timber: two dynasties stacked in one pagoda, and no rebuilding ever started from scratch. At the centre of the fourth storey rises a central mast bound from nine round logs and running to the top; Luo Zhewen called this structure unique among surviving buildings. The inscription on the crypt casket records that the Lingxiao Pagoda (Lingxiao Ta) of Tianning Temple was first built in the reign of Tang Daizong; it was rebuilt on the Tang ruins in 1045 (Northern Song) and its upper part rebuilt in 1141 (Jin). The 1966 Xingtai earthquake wrecked everything above the seventh storey, and repairs began in 1981.
facts: Form: octagonal, nine storeys of pavilion type, about 41 m high; storeys one to four are brick, five and above timber. A central mast of nine bundled logs rises from the fourth storey to the top; the central-mast system was the main way of building pagodas before the Tang, and this is the only surviving example.

Dates: a crypt found beneath the base in 1982 held a casket inscribed 'pagoda built in the reign of Daizong', placing the foundation between 756 and 779; rebuilt in 1045 (Qingli 5 of Northern Song) and the upper part rebuilt in 1141 (Huangtong 1 of Jin). Its original name was Huiguang Pagoda.

Repairs: in the Northern Song the monk Huaibing replaced the rotten central mast, and the tale behind the idiom 'steal the beam, change the pillar' has attached itself to the pagoda; the 1966 Xingtai earthquake badly damaged the storeys above the seventh, and Hebei's heritage authorities rebuilt them after a full survey begun in 1981.

name: Iron Pagoda, Kaifeng
yearNote: Uses the date of the subject drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
lede: It is not made of iron. Its brown glazed bricks look like rust from a distance, and since the Yuan the people of Kaifeng have called it the Iron Pagoda. In 1049 (Huangyou 1 of the Northern Song) Emperor Renzong had a brick pagoda raised on the site of the Lingan timber pagoda that lightning had burned down: octagonal, thirteen storeys, 55.88 m tall, the earliest and tallest glazed-brick pagoda surviving in China. Its surface is laid entirely in patterned bricks—standing Buddhas, apsaras, qilin, musicians, more than fifty designs—and in over nine centuries of dozens of earthquakes and repeated Yellow River floods it has not fallen. The plate shows the full elevation.
facts: Form: A regular octagonal brick pagoda of thirteen storeys in the storeyed-pavilion style, 55.88 m tall, each face of the ground storey 4.16 m wide and narrowing storey by storey; the exterior is faced with red, brown, blue and green glazed bricks in more than fifty patterns, with wind-bells under the eaves. The balcony at each level doubles as drainage, sparing the body from rain.

Dating: The site first held the Lingan timber pagoda of Kaibao Temple, built by the Wuyue master craftsman Yu Hao, which lightning destroyed in 1044 (Qingli 4). Renzong ordered it rebuilt in brick and stone; the new pagoda was completed in 1049 (Huangyou 1), first called the Kaibao Temple Pagoda and renamed Youguo Temple Pagoda with the temple in the Ming. It was shelled by Japanese troops during the war and reopened after repairs in 1956.

Significance: This was the first use of glazed brick for a pagoda, and the name 'Iron Pagoda' has been current since the Yuan. It has withstood dozens of earthquakes and many Yellow River floods; when the river broke its banks in 1847 and destroyed Youguo Temple, the pagoda alone survived. In 1961 it was listed in the first batch of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level.

name: Fotou Temple, Pingshun
place: Shanxi · Pingshun · South bank of the Zhuozhang River · Chedang Village
lede: On the slope above Chedang village, on the south bank of the Zhuozhang River, a small temple has been reduced to a single hall of a hundred and thirty-one square metres. Three bays and four rafters under a hip-and-gable roof, five-puzuo sets with two cantilevers at both capitals and intermediate positions, a three-rafter beam meeting a rear single-rafter tie inside, a short post carrying the collar beam: the State Council's list dates it Song. The four walls inside carry murals of the Twenty-four Devas from a different age than the timber frame, two periods' handiwork layered in one hall.
facts: Form: the hall faces south, three bays wide and four rafters deep, with a floor area of 131 square metres, under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof with glazed ridge ornaments; capital and intermediate sets are both five-puzuo with two downward cantilevers; the frame sets a three-rafter beam against a rear single-rafter tie on three columns, and a short post carries the collar beam.

Date: the temple takes its name from the hill behind, shaped like a Buddha's head; its founding date is unknown. The surviving hall is dated Song in the list published by the State Council in 2006; the murals are said to be Yuan, while a local newspaper calls the building 'Jin structure, Ming painting', so both dates are disputed. This entry follows the official list and gives Northern Song.

Significance: the Twenty-four Devas painted on the four walls are rare Yuan (or, by one account, Ming) murals in the Zhuozhang valley; with Chunhua Temple and the Jiutian Shengmu Temple it belongs to the small Song and Jin shrines of Pingshun county, and though modest in size its frame and brackets are complete, a Song three-bay hall that can be read at a glance.

name: Baosheng Temple
yearNote: 1050 is only an approximate Northern Song placement on the timeline, not an exact date of sculpting; the original 1961 national listing gives Northern Song, and the traditional attribution to Yang Huizhi of the Tang is not treated as settled authorship.
lede: The wall is not a backdrop but a mountain: the arhats are set into a rolling sculpted wall where rocks, clouds, grottoes and figures are modelled together out of the surface, nine of them each in their own place. This half-hall of arhats at Baosheng Temple was stumbled on by Gu Jiegang in the small town of Luzhi in 1918, and the Japanese scholar Omura Seigai came specially to see it, calling it the 'marvel of Wu'. Tradition attributed the figures to the Tang 'sage of sculpture' Yang Huizhi; the 1961 heritage register dated them to the Northern Song. When half the hall collapsed in 1928 only nine of the eighteen survived, and they now live in the antiquities hall built for them in the early 1930s. The plate shows one of them.
facts: Sculpted wall: nine arhats survive, attached to a single sculpted landscape wall where rocks, clouds and grottoes interweave; the figures differ in pose and expression, with broad drapery folds and lean faces. There were originally eighteen; nine were lost when half the hall collapsed in 1928. The plate shows one figure.

Dating: the temple was founded in 503, the second year of Tianjian of the Liang, and rebuilt in 1013, the sixth year of Dazhong Xiangfu of the Northern Song; the statues were traditionally attributed to Yang Huizhi of the Tang, a view already held in the Qing text Wumen Biaoyin, but the first national list of key protected sites in 1961 dated them to the Northern Song, and the attribution remains open.

Rescue: in 1922 Gu Jiegang published an appeal to save 'a thousand-year-old work of art', and Omura Seigai published Remnants of the Marvellous Sculpted Wall of Wu in 1926; in 1929 Cai Yuanpei and others formed a preservation society for the Tang arhats, and an antiquities hall designed by Fan Wenzhao was completed in the early 1930s to house the survivors. Liang Sicheng called them 'among the most precious of our country's works of art'.

name: Puli Temple Pagoda
sub: Square seven-story body and balcony eaves
yearNote: The provincial cultural heritage bureau clearly gives the 3rd year of Huangyou; the surviving seven stories are kept, and other pagodas of the same name are not confused with it.
siteCoordinateSource: 维基百科《普利寺塔》37°26′16″N,114°30′06″E，公开塔址近似坐标：https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/普利寺塔 。
lede: A Northern Song pagoda on a square plan, the only one preserved in China: after the Tang most brick pagodas went octagonal, but the Puli Temple Pagoda (Pulisi Ta) at Lincheng kept the square. It is 33 m tall, its outer walls studded with thousand-Buddha brick reliefs, a balcony ringing it beneath the second storey, and the eaves above tightly stacked. Storey counts disagree: the provincial heritage bureau says seven, the national register eight, the local gazetteer nine, the difference being whether the balcony eave counts as a storey. The Hebei Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau dates it to 1051; the temple is long gone and the pagoda stands alone on its high terrace.
facts: Form: a square brick pagoda 33 m high in the timber-imitating dense-eave style. The outer walls carry 974 brick-relief Buddhas and the inner walls 40, hence the alternative name Ten-Thousand-Buddha Pagoda; a tall body below the second storey projects a balcony, and above it the eaves are closely stacked and taper upward.

Date: the Hebei Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau records construction in 1051 (Huangyou 3 of Northern Song); the national register of protected sites gives 1052 (Huangyou 4), and the local gazetteer claims supervision by Emperor Huizong. Puli Temple was founded in the Northern Dynasties and only the pagoda remains.

Storeys: counts of seven, eight and nine exist depending on whether the balcony eave is included; this entry follows the provincial bureau's seven. Iron bells once hung at the four corners of every storey and rang in the evening wind, the 'Puli evening bells' of old.

name: Kaiyuan Temple Pagoda, Dingzhou
era: Begun in the 4th year of Xianping · Completed in the 2nd year of Zhihe
lede: At 83.7 m, the tallest surviving brick pagoda in China. Work on the Kaiyuan Temple Pagoda of Dingzhou (Kaiyuansi Ta, the Liaodi Pagoda) began in 1001 under Emperor Zhenzong of Song and was not finished until 1055 under Renzong, fifty-four years in all, leaving the local saying 'they felled every tree on Jiashan to raise the Dingzhou pagoda'. Dingzhou was a military stronghold on the Song-Liao frontier, and from the top one could watch for Khitan movements, hence the name Liaodi, 'gauging the enemy'. Eleven storeys taper upward; inside, a corridor runs between an inner core and the outer shell, a pagoda within a pagoda. In 1884 the north-east face collapsed from top to bottom, and the gash stayed open for over a century until it was closed early this century.
facts: Form: an octagonal brick pagoda of eleven storeys in pavilion style, 83.7 m high and tapering storey by storey; it combines a through-core with a ring corridor in a double inner-and-outer structure, with stairs to climb inside, the only pagoda in north China built on the through-core system. Doors open on four faces, and the top carries a honeysuckle-carved inverted bowl and a bronze finial.

Date: in 1001 the monk Huineng of Kaiyuan Temple returned from India with relics and Emperor Zhenzong ordered the pagoda built; it was completed in 1055 after more than fifty years. During the Song-Liao standoff it served as a lookout for enemy movements, hence its other name, Liaodi Pagoda.

Repairs: in the sixth month of 1884 the north-east face of the body collapsed from top to bottom and remained broken for over a hundred years; large-scale restoration by the national heritage authorities began in 1986 and the pagoda reopened in 2002, ending the 'beauty of imperfection' of the ruined silhouette.

name: Pizhi Pagoda of Lingyan Temple, Jinan
sub: Octagonal, nine stories · Brick pagoda with twelve eaves
era: Rebuilt from the 5th year of Chunhua · Completed in the Jiayou era
yearNote: The pagoda inscription records rebuilding in the 5th year of Chunhua (994); image inscriptions of 1057–1058 provide the basis for completion in the Jiayou era, and 1057 is used as an approximate placement on the timeline.
lede: The Pizhi Pagoda stands amid the mountain scenery of Lingyan Temple, its octagonal body tapering story by story. The lower three stories each have two brick eaves and the upper six one each, so the nine-story body shows twelve tiers of eaves; an iron finial and fine chains close the outline at the top.
facts: The surviving pagoda is a Northern Song rebuilding. The pagoda inscription records that work began in the 5th year of Chunhua (994), and image inscriptions of the Jiayou era provide the basis for its completion date.
Octagonal with nine stories, double eaves on the lower three and single eaves on the upper six, twelve eaves in all; the brick eaves organize the outline with timber-style details.

The plate is drawn from daytime photographs of the surviving pagoda, keeping the gray-brown brick and stone, the dark eaves and some ochre-red door and window frames; it is not a reconstruction of historical paintwork.

name: Iron Pagoda of Yuquan Temple
sub: Northern Song iron pagoda · Octagonal, thirteen tiers
yearNote: The iron body is dated by its casting in the 6th year of Jiayou in the Northern Song (1061), while the finial on top is a later Qing-dynasty replacement; the drawing distinguishes the components of the two periods and does not date the modern temple buildings to the Song along with it.
lede: Yuquan Temple’s iron pagoda tapers through thirteen octagonal levels. Cast columns, brackets and eaves carefully imitate a timber pavilion tower. Its body and base are principally dated to Northern Song casting, while the copper finial was added in the Qing period and modern conservation has also shaped its appearance. Buddhist images, reliefs and inscriptions make it evidence for devotion, casting techniques and Song architectural forms.
facts: The octagonal, thirteen-level pavilion-style pagoda tapers upward, with projecting platforms and brackets supporting each eave above a Sumeru pedestal. Columns, corner beams and reliefs are cast in metal but retain detailed timber-like forms.

Inscriptions date the body’s casting to Jiayou 6 of the Northern Song, or 1061. The finial was replaced in copper during the Qing Daoguang reign. Modern protective treatments add another phase; the body and crown were not produced at the same time.

Buddhist images, reliefs and construction inscriptions connect worship with craftsmen’s skill. Seeing how cast-iron brackets translate timber construction helps explain the relationship between Song metalcasting and architectural traditions.

name: Guanyin Pagoda of Xiangshan Temple
era: Northern Song · Rebuilt in the 1st year of Xining
yearNote: Takes the rebuilding in the 1st year of Xining in the Song recorded by the municipal culture and tourism bureau; the original founding date of the temple and pagoda is unknown, and repairs continued in later periods.
lede: Before the pagoda stands a stele, composed by Jiang Zhiqi and written out by Cai Jing, telling how Miaoshan, third daughter of King Zhuang of Chu, attained enlightenment here as Guanyin—the earliest physical record of the sinicised Guanyin legend stands at the foot of this tower. The pagoda itself is an octagonal nine-storey brick tower with dense eaves, rebuilt by imperial decree of Emperor Shenzong in 1068 (Xining 1 of the Northern Song): the ground storey is laid in red stone, the second and third storeys are pierced by hundreds of small niches, and above them the body tapers into an octagonal cone. The plate draws the body as it can now be seen, leaving blank the lower part hidden by the neighbouring hall.
facts: Form: An octagonal nine-storey brick-and-stone pagoda of the storeyed-pavilion type with dense eaves; the ground storey, 8 m high, is built entirely of red stone, storeys two to nine of grey brick, each shorter than the last so that the body forms an octagonal cone. Hundreds of niches line the second and third storeys, the fourth has cusped doorways and the sixth to ninth arched ones; every storey has corbelled eaves with a balcony above. The finial is an inverted basin, jewel and rings.

Dating: Rebuilt by decree in 1068 (Xining 1 of the Northern Song), with the fifth storey repaired in 1071 (Xining 4); in 1571 (Longqing 5 of the Ming) steps and railings were added, in 1630 (Chongzhen 3) the body was repaired, and in 1907 (Guangxu 33 of the Qing) the mast was replaced and the rings renewed. The most recent full restoration ran from 2020 to 2023.

Significance: The stele of the Life of the Great Compassionate Bodhisattva of Xiangshan at Ruzhou, composed by Jiang Zhiqi and written by Cai Jing, was cut in the Song and recut in the Yuan; 2.66 m tall, it is the earliest object in China recording the legend of the sinicised Guanyin (Miaoshan). Behind the pagoda stands the 1185 (Dading 25 of the Jin) stele on the rebuilding of the Guanyin Chan Cloister. The temple keeps more than a dozen Song-to-Qing steles in all.

name: Kaihua Temple, Gaoping
era: 6th year of Xining, Northern Song · Mahavira Hall
place: Shanxi · Gaoping · Mount Sheli, Wang Village, Chenqu Town
lede: The Mahavira Hall of Kaihua Temple is a hall where three kinds of Song work can be seen at once: the timber frame of 1073, the sixth year of Xining; Song 'full polychrome' painting on beams and brackets; and eighty-eight square metres of Northern Song murals on the east, west and north walls, dated by the painters' own labels to 1096, the third year of Shaosheng, with fishermen, farmers, pavilions and boats woven into the sutra stories, earning the name 'Qingming Scroll of mural painting'. A three-bay, six-rafter hall under a hip-and-gable roof, with square eave columns in the central bay.
facts: Form: three bays wide and six rafters deep, nearly square in plan, under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof with glazed ridge ornaments; the front and rear eave columns of the central bay are square, carrying architrave and plate; capital sets are five-puzuo with one arm and one cantilever, cantilever and head both cut in the sharp split-bamboo profile, with doubled arms in full-heart construction. The frame sets a four-rafter beam against a rear two-rafter beam on three columns, left exposed.

Date: an eave column bears the inscription 'Xining 6 of the Song', and the hall is dated to 1073; the murals are dated by the painters' labels to 1096 and are recorded separately from the timber frame. The temple was first called Qingliang Temple, its steles tracing it to the reign of Emperor Zhaozong in the late Tang, and in 1030 it was renamed Kaihua Chan Cloister.

Significance: the east, west and north walls are covered with Song murals totalling 88.68 square metres, the west wall illustrating the Sutra of the Great Skilful Means of Repaying Kindness and the east wall the Avatamsaka Sutra, the largest Northern Song temple murals in existence; the Song polychromy on beams and brackets is of the highest 'full polychrome' grade, its patterns close to those in the Yingzao fashi, the most complete Song architectural painting surviving.

name: Relic Pagoda of Kaifu Temple
yearNote: The provincial bureau gives 1079 alongside the 3rd year of Yuanfeng, a clerical error in the date; it should be the 2nd year of Yuanfeng. 1079 is used, with the source checked against the stele record.
lede: The Cangzhou lion, Zhaozhou Bridge, the Zhengding bodhisattva and the Jingzhou Pagoda: among Hebei's 'four ancient treasures' the Jingzhou Pagoda (Kaifu Temple Relic Pagoda, Kaifusi Shelita) is the only tall tower. Octagonal, thirteen storeys and 63.85 m high, it is crowned by a finial of five stacked bronze gourds inside an iron cage 3.3 m tall, with iron plaques on four sides, three of them cast 'repaired under Qi and Sui'. The present body dates to a rebuilding in 1079 (Northern Song), on the evidence of a stele inside the first storey; inscriptions found in the finial record further repairs in 1139 (Jin) and 1517 (Ming).
facts: Form: an octagonal thirteen-storey brick-and-stone pagoda of pavilion type, 63.85 m tall, with a base 50.5 m in circumference; the foundation is paved with huge bluestone blocks and the body is brick, with arched doorways on the four cardinal faces of each storey, vaulted galleries from the second storey up, and a brick stair through the core to the top.

Date: a stele in the first storey records rebuilding in 1079 (Yuanfeng 2 of Northern Song); the provincial register's 'Yuanfeng 3' beside 1079 is a slip. Iron plaques on the pagoda read 'repaired under Qi and Sui', and inscriptions in the finial record repairs in 1139 and 1517; the foundation may go back to the Northern Wei.

Finial: five bronze gourds of different sizes stacked 2.05 m high inside an iron cage 3.3 m tall; during repairs in 1973 nine volumes of Ming woodblock sutras and a bronze reclining Buddha were found inside it. Kaifu Temple was built beside the pagoda in 1407, giving it its present official name.

name: Pagoda of Xingshengjiao Temple, Songjiang
sub: Square Pagoda Park · Nine-story square pagoda
yearNote: Uses the construction range of 1068–1093 recorded in the Songjiang Yearbook 2019; 1080 is used only as an approximate placement on the timeline, not as a confirmed completion year. The temple's founding in 949 is recorded separately from the Northern Song construction of the pagoda.
lede: On the square body, nine tiers of timber eaves spread like layered wings. Xingshengjiao Temple no longer has its original extent, but this Northern Song brick-and-timber pagoda still stands with slender proportions in the old town of Songjiang, where locals simply call it the “Square Pagoda.”
facts: Xingshengjiao Temple was founded in the 2nd year of Qianyou in the Later Han of the Five Dynasties (949), while the pagoda was built in the Xining and Yuanyou eras of the Northern Song (1068–1093); the two are not conflated as one date.

The pagoda is square in plan and of brick-and-timber construction, a nine-story pavilion-style pagoda about 42.65 m tall overall; the brick walls are divided into three bays by timber-style columns, with a cusped kunmen opening in the middle.

Each story has timber waist eaves, a balcony platform and railings, and an iron finial stands at the top. It has been repaired through the Yuan, Ming, Qing and modern times, and the plate shows its surviving form.
captions: Square, nine stories · Brick-and-timber pagoda
Northern Song · Xining and Yuanyou eras

name: Qinglian Temple, Jincheng
sub: Sakyamuni Hall of the Upper Temple
lede: On the slopes of Mount Xiashi beside the Dan River, Qinglian Temple is divided into upper and lower compounds. Stone inscriptions in the Sakyamuni Hall of the Upper Temple record the 4th year of Yuanyou in the Northern Song; the small three-bay hall stands on a high platform, its stone columns carrying deep eaves. Farther down the mountain, the Lower Temple still preserves Tang painted sculptures.
facts: The Sakyamuni Hall is three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; an inscription on the stone door frame provides the basis for dating it to the 4th year of Yuanyou in the Northern Song (1089).

Square chamfered stone columns carry five-puzuo bracket sets with one projecting arm and one descending cantilever, and there are no intercolumnar sets; the central bay has a door and the two side bays have vertical-bar windows.

The Sakyamuni Hall of the Upper Temple holds four Song sculptures, and the Maitreya Hall of the Lower Temple six Tang sculptures. In one temple, upper and lower, timber structures and painted sculptures each preserve the appearance of different dynasties.

name: Wubian Temple, Taigu
sub: White Pagoda · Ancient City of Taigu
lede: The tallest thing in the old town of Taigu is a Song pagoda. When the temple was renovated in 1090, the fifth year of Yuanyou, this octagonal White Pagoda went up: seven storeys outside but nine within, with brick purlins, brackets and balconies imitating a timber tower storey by storey, forty-three metres high, gently tapering, with a wooden stair inside. A fire in the Tongzhi years of the Qing burned the temple to the ground and left only this pagoda standing in the smoke; the halls rebuilt in the Guangxu years grew back around it.
facts: Form: an octagonal hollow brick pagoda of the storeyed type, seven storeys outside and nine inside, 43 m high overall; each storey has eaves with carved-brick imitation brackets beneath, giving a doubled-eave effect, the body tapers gently, and a wooden stair inside allows the ascent. The pagoda stands in the second courtyard and is the visual centre of the whole temple.

Date: the Guangxu-era Taigu County Gazetteer records the temple's founding in 272, the eighth year of Taishi of the Western Jin; after a Northern Song rebuilding it was called Puci Temple, and in 1090 it was renovated and the pagoda built. After the Tongzhi fire only the White Pagoda survived; the halls were rebuilt in 1904–06 and the name Wubian Temple restored. The pagoda is dated by the year 1090, not by the legend of the temple's founding.

Significance: the surviving temple covers 3,960 square metres in three courtyards, with gate and rear-facing stage, Siming Pavilion, White Pagoda, Heavenly Kings Hall and Mahavira Hall in sequence on the axis, preserving the early layout with a pagoda at the centre; the State Council's list dates the temple Song to Qing, and the pagoda is its only Song structure. The plate shows the pagoda alone.

name: Chongfa Temple Pagoda
sub: A Song pagoda raised on tiers of balcony platforms and lotus petals
yearNote: Dated by the pagoda's completion in 1098; a foundation's materials give 1093 for the building of the underground crypt and 1095 for the start of the body. Some secondary sources wrongly equate 1093 with the 1st year of Shaosheng; this erroneous conversion is not adopted.
lede: Under every storey's eaves runs a ring of upturned lotus petals, so that the nine storeys rise like nine lotus flowers opening one above another. This brick pagoda in the old town of Yongcheng is octagonal, nine storeys and 34.6 m tall; its crypt was begun in 1093 (Yuanyou 8 of the Northern Song), the body in 1095 (Shaosheng 2), and the whole was finished in 1098 (Shaosheng 5)—a stone casket in the crypt and five inscribed tablets inside record the sequence. The stair threads through the core on the first two storeys and gains a gallery on the third; scholars read it as a meeting of northern and southern pagoda-building methods. Chongfa Temple itself disappeared long ago.
facts: Form: An octagonal nine-storey brick pagoda in the storeyed-pavilion style, 34.6 m tall, the ground storey 7.7 m across and 5 m high; each storey opens doors on four sides and rests on a ring of upturned lotus petals under the eaves, the balconies once carried token railings, and stone dragon heads at the corners hang iron bells. The finial of inverted bowl, rings, canopy and vase is chained to the roof.

Dating: The crypt was built in 1093 (Yuanyou 8), the body begun in 1095 (Shaosheng 2) and the pagoda completed in 1098 (Shaosheng 5); five inscribed tablets inside are dated 1095 and the inscription on the crypt's stone casket records the whole undertaking. It was repaired in the 1950s and 1980s, and Song coins were found when the crypt was cleared.

Significance: The inner walls hold 651 yellow-and-green glazed image bricks, each showing a Buddha with two attendants; the stair is of the 'through-the-core' type on the first two storeys, gains a gallery on the third and turns within the walls above—several schemes combined in one tower. Li Junshan, director of the Yongcheng Museum, sees in it a fusion of northern and southern pagoda art; 'the pagoda wreathed in cloud' was one of the Eight Views of old Yongcheng.

name: Anyue Rock Carvings
lede: Right leg drawn up and resting on a lotus leaf, left foot hanging down to touch a flower, left hand braced on the leaf, right hand on the knee, the torso turned slightly to one side: this Guanyin, about 3 m high, sits at ease, as if resting by the water. At Pilu Cave she is called the Purple Bamboo Guanyin, though the subject is the Water-Moon Guanyin; carved in the Song, she is a rare masterpiece of Song stone sculpture. Pilu Cave was first cut in the Tianfu era of the Later Jin (Five Dynasties) and in the Northern Song was an important seat of Esoteric Buddhism in Sichuan; five niches with 465 figures survive. The plate shows this one figure only.
facts: Form: a high-relief seated figure about 3 m high on a curved lotus leaf; the right leg is bent and raised with the foot on the leaf, the left foot hangs over the lotus seat and lightly touches a flower, the left hand braces on the leaf, the right rests on the knee, the torso leans a little to the left, the feet are bare: the 'royal ease' posture favoured in the Song.

Dating: Pilu Cave was begun in the Tianfu era of the Later Jin and flourished in the Song, with further carving and repeated repainting down to the Qing; 5 niches, 465 figures and 32 inscriptions survive. The Guanyin is generally dated to the Northern Song, while the Sichuan Provincial Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology places the main carving in the Southern Song; both views stand.

Significance: Pilu Cave was one of the chief seats of Esoteric Buddhism in Northern Song Sichuan, and also holds the 'Ten Austerities' of Liu Benzun with more than three hundred small relief figures. The Water-Moon Guanyin, for her relaxed pose and lifelike drapery, has been called the 'Venus of the East' and is a rare Song masterpiece; the site was listed as a Major National Historical and Cultural Site in 2001.
captions: Anyue Rock Carvings · Water-Moon Guanyin of Pilu Cave
Song · Purple Bamboo Guanyin in royal ease
