name: Xiaoshang Bridge
era: Song main structure · Repairs over the centuries
yearNote: 1100 is only an approximate ordering point for the surviving Song main structure. The county gazetteer records the bridge as built in the 4th year of Kaihuang in the Sui; Mao Yisheng considered a founding in the early Sui credible but the form of the surviving bridge still open to study, and Luo Zhewen judged the style and carving of the surviving bridge body to be Song remains.
lede: A low, red-sandstone arch bridge with a small arch cut into each shoulder of the main span—the same 'open-spandrel' scheme as the Zhaozhou Bridge, yet the county gazetteer dates it to 584 (Kaihuang 4 of the Sui), earlier than Zhaozhou. Mao Yisheng accepted an early-Sui foundation as credible but left open whether the present structure is the original form; Luo Zhewen, visiting in 1992, judged the style and carving of the existing bridge to be Song. It is 20.87 m long and 6.67 m wide, with a clear main span of 11.6 m. The plate shows the side elevation: one main arch, two spandrel arches and the parapet above.
facts: Form: A single-span open-spandrel segmental stone bridge of red sandstone, running north–south across the Xiaoshang River (the old Ying River). It is 20.87 m long, 6.67 m wide and 4 m high; the main arch has a clear span of 11.6 m and a rise of 2.13 m, a ratio of 1:5, with iron cramps between the voussoirs; the two spandrel arches each span 2.13 m. The arch faces carry reliefs of heavenly horses, lions and lotus, and a dragon head projects from the crown.

Dating: The Linying County Gazetteer records 'built in Kaihuang 4 of the Sui, repaired in the Dade era of the Yuan', with further repairs in the Zhengde era of the Ming and in 1675 (Kangxi 14 of the Qing). After a three-man survey he dispatched in 1982, Mao Yisheng wrote that 'a Sui foundation is credible' but that the present form 'awaits further verification'; in 1992 Luo Zhewen judged the existing structure a Song survival. A state-funded restoration followed in 1994–95.

Significance: If the founding date holds, Xiaoshang is an open-spandrel segmental arch older than Zhaozhou, from which Mao Yisheng inferred that the type had already developed before Zhaozhou was built. Two hundred metres north of the bridge lies the tomb of Yang Zaixing, Yue Fei's officer, who fell here fighting the Jin in 1140 (Shaoxing 10 of the Southern Song).

name: Daqin Temple Pagoda, Zhouzhi
era: Surviving pagoda dated to the Song
yearNote: The 6th batch of the national listing places the surviving Daqin Temple Pagoda in the Song; 1100 is only an approximate Song ordering point. Discussions of the temple's origins or of the Church of the East do not prove that today's pagoda was built in the Tang.
lede: This seven-storey octagonal brick tower stands at the northern foot of the Zhongnan Mountains. Staggered openings, restrained eaves and a slight lean retain its repaired appearance. The name Daqin Temple invites associations with Tang Christianity, but a temple’s origins do not date the surviving tower. Heritage records classify its fabric as Song; the exact construction year remains unknown, making its structural evidence the best starting point.
facts: The hollow brick tower has seven octagonal storeys, with engaged corner columns, lintels and simple brackets. Openings in intermediate levels are staggered vertically. Corbelled brickwork and diagonally set bricks articulate the cornices.

Heritage records date the surviving tower to the Song period, and architectural research similarly favours a Song attribution based on its construction. The exact year is unresolved. Earlier temple history or Christian associations cannot establish the date of today’s fabric.

Brick columns, brackets and staggered openings offer physical evidence for comparison with other old towers. Separating architectural form from documentary associations helps distinguish the historical layers behind a place name rich in legend.

Song · Song dynasty · Exact year undetermined

name: Jinci Temple
era: Renovated in the 1st year of Chongning, Northern Song
lede: The Hall of the Holy Mother, built in the Tiansheng years of the Northern Song (1023–32) for Yi Jiang, mother of Tang Shuyu, and rebuilt in 1102, the first year of Chongning, is the oldest building at Jinci. Seven bays wide under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof, it is ringed by a gallery, and its front porch is two bays deep, unusually open; on each of the eight front columns coils a carved wooden dragon, the earliest wooden dragons in China. Inside, more than forty Song statues of attendant women stand to either side of the Holy Mother, each with her duty. The plate shows the front of the hall; the Fish Pond Flying Bridge is not included.
facts: Form: seven bays wide and six deep (eight rafters), under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof, about 19 m high and nearly square; a 'surrounding secondary eave' gallery runs round all four sides, the front porch two bays deep. Columns are omitted inside, leaving a single row; the eave columns lean inward and rise toward the corners, the upper-eave capitals are six-puzuo with two arms and one cantilever, the lower eave five-puzuo. Each of the eight front columns carries a coiled dragon, carved separately and fitted to the shaft with mortise and tenon.

Date: founded in the Tiansheng years (1023–32) and rebuilt in 1102; the varied dimensions of its members reflect several campaigns of building. The Offering Hall was added in front in 1168, the eighth year of Dading of the Jin, and the hall was dismantled and restored in 1993–96. Of the 43 painted statues inside, 41 are Song and 2 are Ming replacements.

Significance: the Hall of the Holy Mother, the Fish Pond Flying Bridge and the Offering Hall are the 'three treasures of Jinci', the cross-shaped bridge before the hall being the only surviving example of its type; the eight wooden dragons are the earliest extant; the Song attendant statues, the Zhou cypress and the Nanlao Spring are the 'three wonders'. Liang Sicheng recorded his survey in the Preliminary Report on Ancient Architecture of the Jin and Fen Valleys of 1934.

name: Faxing Temple, Zhangzi
era: Northern Song · Song sculpture of the 1st year of Zhenghe
yearNote: Takes 1111, the year the central Song sculpture of Sakyamuni drawn here was made, not the founding year of the temple or the 1081 enlargement of the Yuanjue Hall. The temple was moved to its present site in 1984–1996, and the painted sculptures have been repaired and redecorated over the centuries; the replica outer eaves of the present hall are not taken as original fabric of 1081.
place: Shanxi · Zhangzi · Mount Cuiyun, Cilin Town
lede: At the center of the Yuanjue Hall, the seated Sakyamuni sits cross-legged on a lotus throne, its drapery folds and gestures still keeping the composure of Song sculpture. The plate draws only the principal figure and its pedestal as they are now, recording this group of painted sculptures preserved through the temple's relocation.
facts: Date of the Song sculptures: The Song sculptures in the hall are dated 1111, and records name the sculptor Feng Zongben and the painters Chen Daorong and Lü Rong; this drawing takes only the central Sakyamuni.

Hall and figures dated separately: The Yuanjue Hall was dismantled and enlarged in 1081, before the Song sculptures were made. The hall, the sculptures and later redecoration each have their own dates.

Relocation and protection: The temple was moved to Mount Cuiyun in 1984–1996; the outer eaves of the Yuanjue Hall were reproduced conjecturally from surviving Northern Song structures, so today's entire exterior cannot be regarded as original Song fabric.

name: First Patriarch Hermitage of Shaolin Temple
sub: Front of the Main Hall of the First Patriarch Hermitage
yearNote: Uses the date of the subject drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
siteCoordinateSource: UNESCO《Historic monuments of Mount Songshan》申遗文本1305rev.pdf（中心坐标表，第8页）明确初祖庵34°30′32.37″N,112°55′46.57″E；此为初祖庵分项中心，不是少林寺常住院。https://whc.unesco.org/uploads/nominations/1305rev.pdf
lede: A small hall only three bays square, yet the best surviving textbook for the Yingzao fashi: built in 1125 (Xuanhe 7 of the Northern Song), some twenty years after that building manual was issued, its bracket sets, framing and ornament largely follow the rules in the book. The six stone columns of the front eave are carved all over with scrolling foliage and birds, the four interior stone columns with heavenly kings and coiling dragons, and the stone columns carry deep timber eaves and massive bracket sets. The cloister was built to commemorate Bodhidharma's wall-gazing, and its hall is among the earliest timber buildings left in Henan. The plate shows the front of the hall.
facts: Form: The hall is three bays wide and three deep under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof edged with green glazed tiles; the eaves project far and rest on massive bracket sets. The central bay has a pair of plank doors and the side bays vertical-mullion windows. Six stone columns carved with scrolling foliage and birds stand in the front eave, four stone columns inside bear heavenly kings and dragons, the framing is left exposed, and the three walls carry paintings.

Dating: Built in 1125 (Xuanhe 7 of the Northern Song) and repaired many times since, with the principal members still Song originals; the reliefs on the plinth stones, eave and interior columns and the waist of the altar's sumeru base were cut at the founding. More than twenty wall paintings of Chan patriarchs date from about the late Ming. The Thousand Buddha Pavilion in front is Ming, and the gate was rebuilt to its old form in 1986.

Significance: With the Qingong of the Jidu Temple it is one of only two Song timber buildings surviving in Henan; built close to the time the Yingzao fashi was compiled, its brackets, framing and carving largely match the manual's prescriptions, a key witness to Song official timber construction. The cloister commemorates Bodhidharma, first patriarch of Shaolin, and in 2010 it was inscribed with the Shaolin complex in the World Heritage 'Centre of Heaven and Earth'.

name: Liuhe Pagoda, Hangzhou
era: Rebuilt in the 26th year of Shaoxing, Southern Song
lede: The King of Wuyue built it in the 3rd year of Kaibao in the Northern Song (970) to subdue the tidal bore of the Qiantang River; the surviving brick body was rebuilt in the 26th year of Shaoxing in the Southern Song (1156) and completed in the 1st year of Longxing (1163). The thirteen tiers of timber eaves on the outside were added in the 25th year of Guangxu in the Qing (1899).
facts: Mixed brick and timber, octagonal, 59.89 m tall overall; the brick body has seven stories and the exterior thirteen tiers of eaves — “thirteen outside, seven inside” — with balcony railings around each story.

The brick carvings of flowers, birds and beasts on the Sumeru plinths inside the pagoda match the patterns recorded in the Yingzao Fashi (Treatise on Architectural Methods), making them physical evidence for the study of Song architecture.
In 1934 Liang Sicheng drew up a “slimming” plan for the pagoda, removing the Guangxu-era timber eaves to restore the original appearance of the Song pagoda; it was never carried out.

name: Sanqing Hall of Xuanmiao Temple
sub: Suzhou · Nine-bay Southern Song main hall
lede: A hall nine bays and forty-five metres wide stands on Guanqian Street, the busiest street in Suzhou; rebuilt in 1179, the sixth year of Chunxi of the Southern Song, it is one of the few large Southern Song timber halls left in the Jiangnan region. The Sanqing Hall has a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof under black tiles, with a cast-iron 'three halberds' finial at the centre of the ridge and brick-carved dragon heads at its ends. The stone balustrade in front, the so-called 'nailed balustrade', is a Five Dynasties survival, and the west wall inside holds a Song recut of the Laozi portrait stele painted by Wu Daozi and inscribed by Yan Zhenqing. The plate shows the Sanqing Hall alone, without the gate or the incense pavilion.
facts: Form: facing south, nine bays and 45 m wide, six bays and 25 m deep, with a floor area of about 1,100 square metres; the double-eaved hip-and-gable roof is covered in black tube tiles, the ridge carries a cast-iron 'three halberds' finial at centre and brick-carved dragon heads at the ends, and a stone balustrade surviving from the Five Dynasties surrounds the front.

Dating: the temple was founded in 276, the second year of Xianning of the Western Jin, as the Zhenqing Daoist Cloister; destroyed in war in the Southern Song, the Sanqing Hall was rebuilt in 1179, the name Xuanmiao Guan was adopted in 1295, the first year of Yuanzhen of the Yuan, and under Kangxi it was briefly renamed Yuanmiao Guan to avoid the emperor's taboo name. Repairs in 1999 uncovered a Five Dynasties well on the axis in front of the hall.

Stele and damage: the west wall inside holds a Laozi portrait stele, painted by Wu Daozi, inscribed by Yan Zhenqing and eulogised by Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, recut in the Song; during the Cultural Revolution the head of the Yuqing statue was hacked off, the hall was turned into an exhibition venue and the side halls became shops, warehouses and a market. It was listed as a national key protected site in 1982.

name: Dazu Rock Carvings
era: Southern Song, Chunxi to Chunyou eras
lede: A serene Guanyin joins her hands at the centre, surrounded by arms radiating sideways and upwards. Their gestures and attributes turn the cliff into a spreading halo. Baodingshan’s niche 8 belongs to Southern Song construction, while gilding and colour underwent later renewal and modern conservation. This view focuses on the main figure and adjacent arms, revealing the contrast between quiet expression and intricate gestures.
facts: The principal figure sits cross-legged, with radiating arms around her sides and above her head, many holding ritual attributes. Extended, bent, frontal and sideways hands form an ordered field around the centre. This detail does not represent the whole niche.

Niche 8 was made during the Southern Song Chunxi–Chunyou period within the Baodingshan project led by Zhao Zhifeng. Existing gilding and paint include later renewal and modern restoration, rather than exclusively original Song surfaces.

The many hands and eyes express compassion and wisdom responding to varied suffering, while attributes make belief tangible. Carving, gilding and paint work together to reveal Song cave art and its continuing conservation.

name: Feilai Feng Grottoes
yearNote: 1200 is only an approximate timeline position for the traditional Southern Song dating, not the year of carving. The niche has no dated inscription, and some research proposes an early Yuan date; the year 966 is not used to impose a date.
lede: Beside Lengquan Creek, the Budai Maitreya laughs openly as he leans on his cloth sack, while the arhats in the rock niche each wear their own expression. Niche 68 brings Buddhist sculpture into vivid human moods and is the most familiar face of Feilai Feng.
facts: One niche, many figures: The complete Niche 68 centers on the Budai Maitreya, with nine arhats ranged on each side; this plate shows only the principal figure and the four nearest arhats.

Sack and prayer beads: The principal figure, chest and belly bare, rests his right hand on the sack and holds prayer beads in his left, expressing devotion to Maitreya through the image of the monk Budai.

Disputed date: Popular accounts adopt a Southern Song date, while some research argues for the early Yuan; the niche bears no exact dated inscription, and no single year can stand for the carvings of the whole hill.

name: Zijin'an Temple
yearNote: 1200 is only an approximate timeline placement within the Song tradition of arhat art, not an exact year of sculpting; the heritage listing dates the statues to the Song–Ming, and Lei Chao and his wife are the traditionally attributed sculptors.
lede: Sixteen arhats sit along the two sides of the hall, each little more than a metre tall, yet they read like sixteen people with tempers of their own: one lowers his eyes, one tilts an ear, one rests his fingers lightly together. The arhats of Zijin'an are traditionally the work of Lei Chao and his wife in the Southern Song, and the heritage register dates them to Song to Ming; the hall holds more than fifty statues in all, including the Buddhas of the Three Ages, Guanyin, the Twenty Devas and the Four Heavenly Kings, while the building itself is a Ming-Qing rebuilding. The plate takes the upper body of the arhat Panthaka.
facts: Statues: the main hall holds more than fifty statues, including the Buddhas of the Three Ages, Guanyin, sixteen arhats, the Twenty Devas and the Four Heavenly Kings; the sixteen arhats line the two sides, about 1.13 m tall, differing in pose, drapery and expression. The plate shows the upper body of the arhat Panthaka among them.

Dating: the hermitage is said to date either from the Southern Dynasties or from the Tang; the surviving main hall, Jingyin Hall, Tingsong Hall and Baiyun Lodge are all Ming or Qing. The arhats are recorded as the work of Lei Chao and his wife in the Southern Song, but the attribution is not settled, and when the site was listed as a national key protected site in 2006 the period was given as Song to Ming.

Comparison: Wuzhong in Suzhou has two famous sets of Song arhats: Baosheng Temple at Luzhi keeps only nine, set into a sculpted landscape wall, while Zijin'an keeps the full sixteen, seated independently, their colouring and repairs bearing traces of different periods, a complete sample for observing Jiangnan arhat sculpture from the Song onward.

name: Feiying Pagoda
lede: Feiying Pagoda contains an independent stone pagoda inside a seven-storey outer tower, creating its unusual pagoda-within-a-pagoda arrangement. Brick walls and timber eaves taper upwards around the carved Buddhist images of the inner monument. The present outer form largely follows a Southern Song rebuilding, with Yuan, Ming, Qing and modern repairs. The two towers have separate building histories; their complete appearance does not make them fabric of a single period.
facts: Form: the seven-storey outer tower combines brick walls with timber eaves. A separate stone pagoda stands inside; these are not simply two walls of one structure. The outer pavilion encloses and protects the stone reliquary pagoda.

Dating: accounts place the Southern Song rebuilding in either the Jiatai era or the early Duanping era, without establishing one certain year. The reported formation of the nested arrangement in the Northern Song Kaibao era is a separate event.

Significance: stone carving and brick-and-timber construction coexist here, demonstrating a distinctive combination of materials in Jiangnan Buddhist pagodas. Successive repairs preserved the arrangement while leaving evidence of different building phases.

name: Renshou Pagoda of Kaiyuan Temple, Quanzhou
sub: West pagoda · Octagonal five-story stone pagoda
era: 1st year of Shaoding to 1st year of Jiaxi
yearNote: The surviving stone pagoda was built in 1228–1237, and the completion year 1237 is used; the Five Dynasties timber pagoda was its predecessor and is not used as the date of the surviving structure.
place: Fujian · Quanzhou · West Pagoda Court of Kaiyuan Temple
lede: The west tower was finished more than a decade before the east tower and is slightly lower, at 45.06 m, rebuilt from brick to stone between 1228 and 1237. The two pagodas are almost identical in form and workmanship, but a closer look finds three differences: on the third, fourth and fifth storeys of the west tower there is only one intercolumnar bracket set per bay; the eighty figures on the outer walls are not ranked by stage of attainment but are Buddhist figures treated as equals; and the Sumeru base is carved with flowers and beasts rather than sutra stories. The fourth storey also carries an Indian-style male Avalokitesvara and a monkey pilgrim with the Peacock King Sutra tied at his waist.
facts: Form: a five-storey octagonal pavilion-style granite pagoda, 45.06 m high, with a ground-floor area of 270 square metres; its design and construction match the east tower, with a through core pillar, an outer shell tied storey by storey, an eaves gallery with stone balustrade on each level, and 16 carved figures per storey, 80 in all, on the outer walls.

Dating: first built in 916, under the Later Liang of the Five Dynasties, as a seven-storey timber pagoda named Wuliangshou; converted to brick and given its present name in the Chunxi era of the Southern Song; the surviving stone pagoda was built between 1228 and 1237, begun ten years and completed thirteen years before the east tower. The date used is 1237, the completion of the stone pagoda.

Differences: compared with the east tower, the west tower has only one intercolumnar bracket set on storeys three to five; its 80 figures are Buddhist personages expressing the equal Buddha-nature of all beings rather than a five-tier hierarchy; and its Sumeru base carries flower-and-beast reliefs. The Indian male Avalokitesvara and the monkey pilgrim carrying the Peacock King Sutra on the fourth storey show foreign religious imagery taking root in Quanzhou.

name: Zhenguo Pagoda of Kaiyuan Temple, Quanzhou
sub: East pagoda · Octagonal five-story stone pagoda
era: 2nd year of Jiaxi to 10th year of Chunyou
yearNote: The year used is 1250, the completion of the surviving granite pagoda; 865 marks the founding of the timber pagoda, and the brick pagoda of 1227 is not the surviving five-story stone pagoda.
place: Fujian · Quanzhou · East Pagoda Court of Kaiyuan Temple
lede: The east tower of the tallest surviving pair of Song-dynasty stone pagodas in China, 48.27 m high. Here granite imitates a timber pavilion in every detail: each wall face is carved with columns, lintels and bracket sets, every storey has an eaves gallery with a stone balustrade, and the brackets run one set over each column and two between, storey after storey. The core is an octagonal granite pillar about four metres across rising from base to top, to which the two-metre-thick outer shell is tied by beams and floors; it was this structure that kept the tower standing through the great Quanzhou earthquake of 1604.
facts: Form: a five-storey octagonal pavilion-style stone pagoda, 48.27 m high, with a ground-floor area of 255 square metres; the octagonal core pillar about 4 m in diameter runs the full height, the outer shell is about 2 m thick, and each storey is tied across by beams, brackets and floors, leaving climbable chambers; the ground storey opens doors on four sides, the doors and niches are staggered storey by storey above, and 16 Buddhist figures are carved on each storey's outer wall, 80 in all.

Dating: first built as a five-storey timber pagoda in 865, converted to a seven-storey brick pagoda in 1227, and rebuilt as the present stone pagoda between 1238 and 1250; neither the magnitude-8 Quanzhou earthquake of 1604 nor centuries of typhoons toppled it. The date used here is 1250, the completion of the surviving stone pagoda.

Comparison: with the west tower it preserves a layout of twin pagoda courts flanking the central axis, rarely seen after the 14th century; the east tower has one bracket set over each column and two between on every storey, whereas the west tower has only one intercolumnar set on storeys three to five. The 80 figures rise from heavenly generals through arhats, eminent monks and bodhisattvas to Buddhas, and 37 of the 40 reliefs on the Sumeru base tell sutra stories.

name: Bazi Bridge
sub: Three streets, three rivers · Ancient stone-beam bridge
yearNote: 1256 is the rebuilding year recorded in local gazetteers, and there was a further repair in 1783; what is seen today includes repairs from many periods, and not every stone member is an original of 1256.
lede: Bazi Bridge turns a complex junction in Shaoxing into a sequence of stone steps. Its main span crosses the channel, while stairs descend in different directions to connect streets and riverbanks without closing the waterway. The name refers to the splayed arrangement resembling the Chinese character for eight. A Southern Song rebuilding in 1256 provides its chronological anchor; later repairs also form part of the surviving structure, a tangible record of urban land-and-water transport.
facts: Form: stone beams rest on piers, and the approaches turn towards streets and banks. The distinctive feature is the combination of stairs descending in several directions, rather than a single tall round arch.

Dating: local records and an inscription on a bridge pier identify a rebuilding in 1256, the fourth Baoyou year of the Southern Song. Qing and modern repairs followed; the date does not apply to every surviving stone.
Significance: bridge, streets and channels meet at one transport node. The stone beams and approaches make Shaoxing’s arrangement of waterside streets and bridge-linked lanes directly understandable.

name: Geyuan Temple, Laiyuan
lede: A three-bay Buddha hall built to the timber grade of a seven-bay great hall: the bracket members of the Manjusri Hall (Wenshu Dian) of Geyuan Temple are the same size as those of the great hall of Shanhua Temple in Datong and the Yingxian timber pagoda, grade two in the Yingzao Fashi, which is why it has stood through a thousand years of earthquakes and has never once been dismantled for repair. Nearly square, about 15 m on a side, with a single-eave hip-and-gable roof and deep eaves, it uses column reduction and displacement to leave only two interior columns. The conventional date is 966 (Liao), making it the earliest of the eight surviving Liao timber buildings; the latticed doors and windows of the facade still contain late Liao originals.
facts: Form: three bays by three on a near-square plan about 15 m on a side, about 12.5 m high overall; single-eave hip-and-gable roof, with five-tier column-top bracket sets of two projecting arms and diagonal corner arms; inside, columns are reduced and shifted, the frame being 'a four-rafter beam in front and a two-rafter beam behind on three columns'.

Date: the temple keeps a sutra pillar of 867 (Tang), another of 966 (Liao) and an iron bell of 1114 (Liao); the hall is conventionally dated 966. Lu Sheng's survey of 1959 confirmed it as Liao work, and Feng Bingqi and Shen Tian published it in Wenwu in 1960.

Joinery and murals: the latticed doors and windows of the three front bays combine Liao, Yuan, Ming, Qing and Republican members, and some of the lozenge lattices are late Liao, among the earliest surviving timber window joinery in China; Liao murals inside, plastered over in the Ming, came to light again in the 1960s when the statues were destroyed.

name: Dule Temple, Tianjin
lede: Guanyin Pavilion is organized around a towering eleven-headed Avalokiteshvara. Two rings of timber columns are joined by beams and brackets, while a concealed intermediate level makes the apparently two-storey building three levels inside. Broad eaves and galleries give its substantial form an open rhythm. The surviving pavilion was rebuilt in 984, separately from the monastery’s earlier origins. Architecture and sculpture let worshippers view the same image from different heights.
facts: The pavilion is five bays wide and four deep. Its two visible storeys conceal a third internal level. Beams and brackets connect inner and outer column rings around the central space occupied by the tall image.

The present pavilion was rebuilt in 984, the second Tonghe year of Liao. Together with the gate, it preserves Liao construction. Earlier monastic origins, later repairs and interior decoration should be distinguished from that rebuilding.

Columns, beams and brackets support eaves and floors while arranging worship around the image. The Liao clay sculpture and timber pavilion together preserve evidence of early northern Chinese multilevel Buddhist architecture and its use.

name: Nong'an Liao Pagoda
yearNote: 1000 is only a sorting point. Jilin local gazetteer sources give a range of 983–1030; the 1023 date, which has problems with mixed-up reign names, is not taken as the exact year of construction.
place: Jilin · Nong'an · Ancient City of Huanglong Prefecture
lede: Thirteen closely packed eaves rise above the grey-brick body at the former Huanglongfu city. Nongan’s Liao pagoda combines an octagonal solid structure with brick details resembling timber construction. The gazetteer gives a building range of 983–1030, while modern repairs also shape the surviving appearance.
facts: The octagonal solid-brick pagoda has thirteen dense-eave tiers, brick brackets, varied roof tiles and bells at its corners. The narrowing body differs structurally from a storeyed pagoda that can be entered floor by floor.
The provincial gazetteer gives 983–1030 rather than a single construction year. The structure can be understood within the Liao period, with modern restoration rather than wholly original materials.

Near the former Huanglongfu, the pagoda marks local history. Its proportions from body to eaves and finial reveal Liao dense-eave construction without borrowing the decorative scheme of another Liao pagoda.

name: Kaishan Temple, Gaobeidian
lede: The plainest of the eight surviving Liao timber buildings, yet it uses the full Liao repertoire: columns reduced and shifted so that a five-by-three-bay hall keeps only four interior columns and the worship space runs clear; huge bracket sets, deep eaves, and rear and side columns visibly leaning inward. The Mahavira Hall (Daxiong Baodian) of Kaishan Temple has a single-eave hip roof with a gently curving surface. Surveying it in 1936, Liu Dunzhen read the garbled date 'Song Chongqing 2' on a Ming stele as a corruption of the Liao era Chongxi and judged the hall Liao; the exact year is still unsettled, so this entry gives only 'Liao'.
facts: Form: five bays by three, about 30.4 by 18.5 m and about 12 m high, on a stone platform 1.11 m high with a terrace 27.6 by 11.4 m in front; single-eave hip roof, only four interior columns, and a post-and-lintel frame left exposed, with great diagonal braces at the hip ends.

Dating: in 1936 Liu Dunzhen inferred that 'Song Chongqing 2' in the 1551 Record of Repairing Kaishan Temple was a corruption of the Liao era Chongxi, and, noting construction akin to Dule Temple, judged the hall Liao; one view reads a date on an interior beam as 1033, and scholars still dispute the exact year.

Study and repair: Qi Yingtao published 'The Great Hall of Kaishan Temple, Xincheng County, Hebei' in 1957; repairs in 2001 uncovered a Liao stone Thousand-armed Guanyin inside the rear-eave cavity wall; in August 2023 floods submerged the temple, and the water in the hall drained after several days.

name: Fengguo Temple, Yi County
place: Liaoning · Jinzhou · Old town of Yi County
lede: A nine-bay roof shelters a row of seven Buddhas: Fengguo Temple’s Main Hall conveys its Liao-period scale both outside and within. Its broad, single-eaved hip roof rises above a high platform, while columns support a deep interior and painted beams draw the eye upward. The temple was founded in 1020, but later buildings remain around the hall; timber architecture, sculpture and painting form its central ensemble.
facts: The hall is nine bays wide and five deep, with a single-eaved hip roof on a high platform. Beneath the spreading roof, successive timber members give the immense building a clear and orderly system of support.

Fengguo Temple was founded in 1020, and the Main Hall survives from the Liao dynasty. Gates and other buildings have Qing-period or reconstruction histories; the entire present temple cannot be assigned to the same Liao campaign.

The painted sculptures of the Seven Past Buddhas and the architectural paintings belong with the timber hall as its principal sights. Its broad interior and decorated beams help shape the solemn atmosphere rather than merely enclosing the statues.

name: Liao Twin Pagodas of Zhuozhou
sub: Yunju Temple Pagoda · Zhidu Temple Pagoda
lede: The contrast between the two pagodas is immediate: six storeys in the north and five in the south, both with timber-like columns, windows and brackets in brick. The temples that once housed them have disappeared, but the Liao towers still face each other across old Zhuozhou. Their masonry preserves the organisation and circulation of a multistorey building. Differing dates proposed for the northern tower remind us to distinguish architectural form from chronology.
facts: Both are octagonal, timber-inspired brick pagodas: the six-storey Yunju Temple tower to the north and the five-storey Zhidu Temple tower to the south. Arched doors on the principal faces alternate with blind lattice windows, while brackets articulate the storeys.

The Zhidu tower dates to 1031, the eleventh year of the Liao Taiping era. Dates in the Chongxi and Da’an eras have been proposed for Yunju. Both are described here as eleventh-century remains, without treating the disputed northern date as settled.

Corridors between outer and inner walls and winding steps within the central core provide internal circulation. Although their temples are gone, these structures offer tangible evidence for understanding Liao multistorey construction.

name: Huayan Temple
sub: Bhagavat Sutra Repository Hall · Mahavira Hall
lede: The Khitan worshipped the sun, so the whole monastery faces east. The Bhagavat Sutra Repository Hall of the lower temple is a library hall of 1038, the seventh year of Chongxi of the Liao; thirty-eight bays of two-storey pavilion-style sutra cabinets line its walls, and over the rear window an arched bridge carries the 'heavenly palace pavilions' that Liang Sicheng called unique in China. The Mahavira Hall of the upper temple burned in the Liao-Jin war of 1122 and was rebuilt in 1140, the third year of Tianjuan of the Jin, on its Liao platform, nine bays wide, the largest ancient Buddhist hall standing. The plate shows the front of the Mahavira Hall.
facts: Form: the Mahavira Hall stands on a platform 4 m high under a single-eave hip roof, nine bays wide and ten rafters deep, 1,559 square metres in area, with eaves projecting 3.6 m at a height of 9.5 m; the glazed owl-tail ridge ornaments are 4.5 m tall, the largest on any surviving ancient building; brackets are five-puzuo with two arms, and twelve columns are omitted inside. The Bhagavat Hall has a single-eave hip-and-gable roof, five bays wide and eight rafters deep, on a platform 3 m high.

Date: an inscription on the underside of a rafter in the Bhagavat Hall reads 'built at noon on the fifteenth day of the ninth month of the seventh year of Chongxi, the wuyin year', that is 1038; the Mahavira Hall was first built in 1062, destroyed in 1122 when Jin troops took the city, rebuilt in 1140 and restored in 1997–2000. Early in the Wanli years of the Ming the monastery was divided into upper and lower temples.

Significance: the 38 bays of wall cabinets, the heavenly palace pavilions and the 29 statues in the Bhagavat Hall are all original Liao work, the cabinets being the only Liao architectural model in China, and the attendant bodhisattva 'with joined palms and bared teeth' is especially famous; the east-facing orientation is linked to the Khitan custom of 'revering spirits and worshipping the sun'; the Mahavira Hall is the largest ancient Buddhist hall surviving in China.

name: Qingzhou White Pagoda
sub: Liao city of Qingzhou · Sakyamuni Buddha Relic Pagoda
lede: Qingzhou White Pagoda rises in seven octagonal storeys above the grassland. Brick-carved brackets meet timber rafters, bringing intricate detail to its clear silhouette. Built from 1047 to 1049 in the north-west of Liao Qingzhou, this reliquary pagoda preserves religious life through sculpture and scriptures discovered during repair.
facts: The seven-storey octagonal brick-and-timber pagoda has carved brick brackets supporting wooden rafters and guardian figures beside its doors. Receding storeys and eave bands distinguish it from a plain brick tower.
The local government records construction from Chongxi 16 to 18, or 1047–1049. It stands in the north-west of Liao Qingzhou; these dates refer to the pagoda, rather than later reuse of the city.
Repairs in 1989 revealed concealed scriptures and small wooden reliquary towers. Sacred texts and objects inside complement the exterior figures, providing physical evidence of Liao Buddhist ritual.

name: Huanghuatan Pagoda
lede: On its hilltop, Huanghuatan Pagoda overlooks the Liao-period Jianzhou city site below. A long octagonal body rises from a weighty base beneath thirteen closely spaced, tapering brick eaves, while Buddhist carvings remain on its surfaces. It is attributed to the Liao dynasty, although its exact construction year is unknown. The local custom of circling the tower adds a living memory to the monument.
facts: This solid octagonal brick pagoda has thirteen close-set eaves. Platform, body and cornices form a vertical sequence. Masonry profiles and Buddhist carvings show how Liao builders translated timber forms and sacred imagery into brick.

The tower is attributed to the Liao dynasty, but its precise construction date remains unclear. Its hill is associated with nearby Jianzhou’s archaeological site; the city’s relocation date cannot automatically date the pagoda.

On the fifteenth day of the fourth lunar month, local festivities include circumambulation and communal prayers. The pagoda is consequently both a surviving Liao building and a focus of customs passed down among neighbouring communities.

name: Yingxian Wooden Pagoda
lede: A sixty-seven-metre tower built entirely of wood, raised in 1056, the second year of Qingning of the Liao, and still standing after nine hundred and seventy years. Five storeys and six tiers of eaves show outside, but four hidden storeys lie within, nine in all; more than fifty kinds of bracket sets carry it tier upon tier, earning it the name 'museum of dougong', and not one iron nail is used. It has ridden out repeated earthquakes, took more than two hundred shells in the warlord fighting of 1926, and in 1974 yielded Liao printed sutras and relics of the Buddha's teeth from inside its statues: the tallest and oldest wooden pagoda in the world.
facts: Form: an octagonal storeyed timber pagoda 67.31 m high, 30.27 m across at the base and weighing about 7,400 tonnes; five storeys and six eaves outside, with a hidden storey between each of the first four, nine levels in all; a secondary eave surrounds the ground storey and balconies with railings ring each level; the main timber is North China larch, the brackets elm, more than fifty bracket types in all, and an iron finial crowns the top.

Date: Ming gazetteers record construction in 1056 and repairs in the Mingchang years of the Jin; inscriptions on the plaques record further repairs in 1194, 1436 and 1471. The pagoda took more than two hundred shells in 1926; the removal of infill walls and diagonal braces in 1935 left the structure twisted; a reinforcement scheme was fixed in 2013 and work began in 2014.

Significance: the seated Shakyamuni in the ground-floor inner bay is about 10 m high; in 1966 and 1974 Liao printed and handwritten sutras and two tooth relics of the Buddha were found inside the statues. Certified by Guinness World Records in 2016 as the world's tallest wooden pagoda; the plaques 'Divine Craft Reaching the Heights' by the Yongle emperor and 'Wonder of the World' by the Zhengde emperor still hang on it.

name: Nan'an Temple Pagoda
yearNote: The provincial cultural heritage bureau presumes a Liao date from its form; 1100 serves only as an approximate Liao value for sorting. 1706 marks the Qing encasing of the base and repairs, and in 1986 eave corners partly damaged by shelling were repaired.
siteCoordinateSource: Commons Category:Pagoda of Nan'an Temple 公布39°50′13″N,114°33′51″E，塔址近似坐标：https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Pagoda_of_Nan%27an_Temple 。
lede: The proportions of Nan’an Temple Pagoda are defined by a tall first section, an upturned lotus base and thirteen tightly stacked brick eaves. Rising above old Yuzhou, the solid octagonal tower has no climbable interior storeys, despite the doors and windows modelled on its walls. Its form suggests a Liao date, but the exact founding year is unknown. Qing masonry around the base and repairs to shell-damaged eaves reveal successive stages of care.
facts: This solid octagonal pagoda has a tall first section on an upturned lotus pedestal, followed by thirteen tapering eave tiers. Door-shaped arches on four faces alternate with blind windows; these carvings do not correspond to usable interior rooms.

The Hebei heritage authority assigns a probable Liao origin from its form, without a precise founding year. The base was encased and the tower repaired in 1706; three eave tiers damaged by earlier shelling were repaired in 1986.

Brickwork reproduces timber brackets, door leaves and attached columns, with paired dragons around a pearl above the arches. The transition from lotus pedestal to timber-like details and close eaves shows how decoration concentrates in the lower tower.

name: White Pagoda of Jixian, Tianjin
yearNote: The national listing dates it to the Liao through Qing. 1100 is only an approximate timeline placement for the Liao form and does not represent the exact year of founding, rebuilding or making of all surviving members; the plate shows the present appearance after repairs over the centuries.
lede: Jizhou’s White Pagoda joins contrasting forms vertically. An octagonal lower section narrows through low, closely spaced eaves into a rounded stupa body and slender finial. Its brickwork suggests a pavilion without the open floors of a timber tower. Official heritage records date it from Liao through Qing, acknowledging later repairs. The transition from angular walls to rounded upper surfaces makes the combination of pagoda forms directly visible.
facts: An octagonal brick lower section supports several low eaves, a rounded stupa body and a ringed finial. Pavilion-like angular walls give way vertically to curved Buddhist forms, distinguishing it from a conventional closely eaved pagoda.

Tianjin’s heritage authority records Liao through Qing. Liao forms and later repairs make up its present appearance. The precise foundation year remains unconfirmed; the age of an inherited form does not date every present component.

Pavilion-like, closely eaved and rounded stupa forms coexist in one tower, offering an example for comparing northern pagodas. Repair phases also show why a building’s historical period differs from the date of its visible surfaces.

name: Liaoyang White Pagoda
yearNote: 1100 is only a sorting position for the traditional Liao dating, not an exact construction year; neither the founding legends nor the competing Liao and Jin theories are used to force a completion year.
lede: Buddhist niches, flying figures and timber-like brackets spread across the broad first storey of Liaoyang’s White Pagoda; above them, thirteen eaves become progressively tighter. Its octagonal mass rises from a high base and gives masonry the image of timber architecture. Form and carving support a Liao attribution, while the exact foundation year remains debated and successive repairs add further history.
facts: The octagonal tower stands on a stone platform and brick pedestal. Niches, attendants and flying figures decorate its first storey. Brick brackets support the initial eaves, while tapering cornices connect this ornate lower section to the simpler upper tower.

Various foundation dates have been proposed. Heritage specialists attribute it to the middle or late Liao period from its form, bricks and carving. Ming repair plaques record Yuan-period repairs, but do not establish an uncontested foundation year.

Niches, lotus petals and timber-like brackets weave Buddhist imagery and architectural form into one brick tower. Its whitewashed surfaces give it a distinctive urban outline, while individual details reveal a shared artistic vocabulary of northeastern Liao pagodas.

name: Twin Pagodas of Chongxing Temple
sub: West and east pagodas · Thirteen eaves each
yearNote: 1100 is an approximate sorting point for the late Liao; heritage sources conjecture the reigns of Emperors Daozong to Tianzuo, and this does not mean it was definitely built in 1100.
lede: Two octagonal brick pagodas stand east and west. Their similar thirteen-tier eaves first suggest symmetry, then reveal differences in carving and repair. Tall bodies carry increasingly close cornices above niches, flying figures and guardian figures; the later temple behind them supplied their shared name. Their form is attributed to the late Liao period, with no precise foundation year, while subsequent repairs remain visible.
facts: Both are solid octagonal brick pagodas with thirteen close-set eaves, facing one another but slightly differing in height. Lotus petals and supporting figures decorate their bases; niches, attendants and flying figures cover the bodies, with brick brackets imitating timber beneath the first eaves.

No explicit construction record fixes their date. Heritage specialists attribute them to the late Liao period from structure and carving. Chongxing Temple behind them has a separate Ming–Qing history, and repair inscriptions cannot date the towers’ initial construction.

Repairs from the Yuan and Ming periods replaced some sculptures, and Qing work strengthened the foundations. Reading the two towers together reveals both a closely related architectural scheme and differing histories of preservation.

name: Tianning Temple Pagoda, Beijing
lede: In 1935 Liang Sicheng wrote that the Tianning Temple Pagoda was 'absolutely, absolutely not the original pagoda of the Sui Hongye Temple' and must date from the late Liao; in 1991, when the finial was dismantled for repair, a Liao stele recording the construction was taken from its base: the ninth year of Tianqing, 1119. He had been right. The pagoda is octagonal with thirteen tiers of close-set eaves, solid brick, 57.8 m high: two Sumeru bases, a ring of bracketed balcony and three tiers of lotus petals lift the tall body, and above it thirteen eaves press down one upon the next, tightening as they rise. Liang said it had a musical rhythm, a new type created by Han craftsmen for their Khitan rulers.
facts: Form: a solid brick pagoda, octagonal with thirteen tiers of dense eaves, 57.8 m high, standing on a square platform; the base is a double Sumeru pedestal with cusped panels in its waist, topped by a balcony of brick-carved bracket sets and balustrade and three tiers of upturned lotus petals. The body has brick-carved false doors on the four cardinal faces and lattice windows on the four diagonal faces, with guardian figures beside them and bodhisattva reliefs above, and rising and descending dragons on the corner pilasters.

Dating: texts traditionally made it a relic pagoda built by Emperor Wen of Sui; Liang Sicheng and Lin Huiyin judged it late Liao on stylistic grounds in 1935, and during the major repair of 1991-1992 a Liao construction stele was taken from the finial base, fixing the date at 1119, the ninth year of Tianqing. In 1435, the tenth year of Xuande, the temple was rebuilt and renamed Tianning, and the pagoda was repaired repeatedly under Zhengde, Jiajing and Qianlong.

Eaves: all thirteen eaves rest on brick-carved double-arm bracket sets; under the first eave each face has one intermediate set with 45-degree diagonal arms, the upper tiers two intermediate sets each, and the spacing shortens tier by tier; rafters, flying rafters and hip rafters are timber, while the tiles and ridge beasts are glazed. The 1976 Tangshan earthquake shook off the finial, many reliefs were smashed in the Cultural Revolution, and after the 1992 restoration the construction stele was put back in place.

name: Huilong Temple
sub: Main hall · South bank of the Zhuozhang River
place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Houbi Village
lede: In Houbi Village on the south bank of the Zhuozhang River, all that remains of Huilong Temple is a three-bay main hall. Two octagonal stone columns stand in the front porch, and a low, gently pitched overhanging gable roof reaches out to either side; with no tall pagoda or multistory halls, the weight of early timber construction rests among the few bracket sets beneath the eaves.
facts: The main hall is three bays wide and four rafters deep, with a single-eaved overhanging gable roof; two octagonal stone columns stand in the central bay of the front eave, the supports at either side are enclosed in the walls, and behind are one door and two windows.
No plate beam (pupaifang) is laid over the column heads, and the architraves do not project beyond the corner columns, preserving archaic structural features.

The national listing gives the date as Jin; other accounts, citing form and scientific dating, give the late Northern Song to early Jin. There is as yet no exact construction date, and the timeline gives only an approximate placement at the Song–Jin transition.

name: Shanhua Temple
sub: Mahavira Hall · Hall of the Three Sages · Puxian Pavilion
lede: The Liao Mahavira Hall stands at the north, the Jin Three Sages Hall and gate line the axis, and the Puxian Pavilion rises on the west: the largest and most complete Liao-Jin monastery surviving. From 1128, the sixth year of Tianhui of the Jin, the monk Yuanman spent fourteen years rebuilding it, finishing in 1143. The Puxian Pavilion shown in the plate was built in 1154, the second year of Zhenyuan: two storeys outside with a hidden balcony storey between, a double-eave hip-and-gable roof, three bays square, one of the few surviving witnesses to Liao-Jin multi-storey halls.
facts: Form: the Puxian Pavilion is three bays wide and three deep under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof, two storeys outside with a balcony mezzanine between the two main floors; in the side bays of the upper eave the capital, intermediate and corner sets are joined into one by shared arms, a rare device. The Mahavira Hall is seven bays and 41.8 m wide, five bays and 26.18 m deep under a single-eave hip roof; the Three Sages Hall is five bays and 32.5 m wide, its six-puzuo sets with diagonal arms stacked like opening flowers.

Date: founded in the Kaiyuan years of the Tang, destroyed by fire in 1122, the second year of Baoda of the Liao; rebuilt by the monk Yuanman from 1128 to 1143, with the Puxian Pavilion added in 1154; named Shanhua Temple by imperial decree in 1445. The Mahavira Hall is Liao, the gate, Three Sages Hall and Puxian Pavilion Jin. The Three Sages Hall underwent major repair in 2007.

Significance: the Mahavira Hall is the third-largest ancient Buddhist hall standing, with a complete set of thirty-four Jin statues, the Five Buddhas and the Twenty-four Devas; the stele of 1176 in the Three Sages Hall, with a text by Zhu Bian recording the rebuilding, is the basis of the temple's history; Liang Sicheng said of the Three Sages Hall brackets that they 'amply express the vigour of an age still on the rise'.

name: Erxian Temple of Xixi, Lingchuan
sub: Rear hall · Cult of the Two Immortals
yearNote: 1142 is the year a stele records for the start of rebuilding, not the precise completion year of the rear hall; the surviving main structure is dated by its Jin style.
place: Shanxi · Lingchuan · West of Lingchang Village, Chongwen Town
lede: The rear hall is the oldest building in the temple: a three-bay, six-rafter hall under a hip-and-gable roof, raised on a stone-faced platform, with five-puzuo bracket sets carrying two down-cantilevers of the 'qin-face' profile and lattice doors filling all three front bays. A stele records an enlargement in 1142, the second year of Huangtong of the Jin; the hall itself is dated by its Jin-style structure, and 1142 marks only the start of rebuilding, not its completion. The temple honours the two Le sisters and is the earliest-founded and largest of the Erxian temples of southeastern Shanxi.
facts: Form: the rear hall stands on a stone-faced platform, three bays wide and six rafters deep under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof; the frame uses a four-rafter beam against a front two-rafter beam on three columns; the capital sets are five-puzuo with two qin-face down-cantilevers, two intermediate sets in the central bay and a tiaowo lever inside; the three front bays carry six-rail lattice doors, and most of the glazed ridge ornaments are Ming.

Date: steles say the temple was founded in the Qianyuan years of the Tang (another view places it in the mid-to-late Northern Song), was granted the title Zhenze Palace in the Chongning years and enlarged in 1142; the stele under the rear hall's porch, composed by the Jin examination laureate Zhao Anshi in 1165, is the earliest in the temple, with further repairs in 1247 and 1382.

Significance: the rear hall and the east and west Dressing Towers are identified as Jin structures (the west tower rebuilt in the Republican period); the two-storey, triple-eaved towers are early examples of storied halls. The temple's 16 buildings run from the Jin to the Ming and Qing, with 29 steles, including Yuan Haowen's poem stele of 1317 set into the back wall of the middle hall. The plate shows the front of the rear hall; the Dressing Towers are not included.

name: Chongfu Temple, Shuozhou
yearNote: The construction date of the surviving Amitabha Hall is used; the paintings and statues inside the hall and the later repairs belong to separate phases.
lede: A seven-bay hall on a terrace more than two metres high, 41 m across the front, the largest surviving Jin Buddhist hall after the Mahavira Hall of Huayan Monastery in Datong. Under the eaves the bracket sets are seven-puzuo with two arms and two down-cantilevers, with diagonal arms added in the central bay; inside, two of the front interior columns are omitted and two shifted, clearing a Buddha altar five bays wide. An ink inscription under a beam reads 'specially built ... in the third year of Huangtong (1143)', and the name board, lattice doors, glazed tiles, statues and murals are all still Jin originals.
facts: Form: seven bays wide and four bays (eight rafters) deep under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof, 21 m high, 41.32 m wide and 22.7 m deep; the front capital sets are seven-puzuo with two arms and two down-cantilevers, single-arm open-heart construction, with diagonal arms; two front interior columns omitted and two shifted, the altar spanning five bays; the five front bays carry lattice doors with as many as fifteen lattice patterns.

Date: a Jin ink inscription under the tie-beam of the central bay reads 'specially built ... in the third year of Huangtong (1143)', and a chalk inscription in the end bays dated the first year of Zhenyuan (1153) records the painting, so construction lasted more than ten years; the vertical name board in front, 4.2 m high, is an original of 1184; the hall was dismantled and restored in 1987–91, with statues and paintings repaired.

Significance: the Jin-period roof bricks laid directly on the flying rafters without boarding are the only such survival among Liao and Jin buildings; the ridge-end owl-tail ornaments are 3.2 m high, their back beasts with open mouths unique for the period; of the nine Jin statues on the altar, the Amitabha is 8 m high with a 14 m halo reaching the ridge purlin; the murals cover 327 square metres, and the Thousand-armed Guanyin on the south wall, 4.68 m high, is the tallest surviving mural of its subject.

name: Macun Brick-Carved Tombs
sub: Tomb No. 1 · Woman opening the door
yearNote: 1150 is only an approximate sorting point for the early Jin, not the exact burial year of any tomb; the cemetery as a whole spans the late Northern Song to the Jin.
place: Shanxi · Jishan · Macun Village, Jifeng Town
lede: Tomb No. 1 is the most finely carved of this underground compound: a brick courtyard house with a double tier of bracket sets above, a gallery running round the middle, and in the centre of the front gatehouse a door half open with a maid leaning out; on the rear wall a troupe performs a zaju play. The cemetery belonged to the Duan family of Jishan and, according to the 'Record of the Pre-built Tomb of Duan Ji', dates from before the Dading era of the Jin; as a whole it spans the late Northern Song to the early Jin, and no single tomb has a firm burial date. The plate shows only the 'woman opening the door' corner of Tomb No. 1.
facts: Form: the brick chambers imitate timber construction and model an above-ground courtyard house, with a square truncated-pyramid vault, typically about 2.5 m long, 2.1 m wide and 3.5–4 m high; the gatehouses have double-tier balustrades or carved warriors and guardian beasts, and the lower walls form a waisted Sumeru base carved with flying horses and running deer; Tomb No. 1 has a double tier of brackets above, a gallery in the middle, the woman opening the door in the centre of the front gatehouse and a theatrical scene at the rear.

Date: the cemetery measures 160 m east–west by 140 m north–south; 14 tombs have been found and 9 were cleared by the Shanxi Institute of Archaeology in 1978–79; on the evidence of the 'Record of the Pre-built Tomb of Duan Ji' and the tomb forms, it is a Duan family cemetery of before the Dading era, spanning the late Northern Song to the early Jin; coins of the Xining and Tiansheng eras were found. The Shanxi Jin Tomb Museum was founded on the site in 1996.

Significance: the woman opening the door is a tomb motif going back to the Han that peaked in the Song, Liao and Jin, and the Macun carvings are among its representatives; the zaju troupes and musicians, the 'kaifang banquet' and the Twenty-four Paragons of Filial Piety in the tombs carve the Duan family's creed of 'filial piety for the family, diet for health, drama for the spirit' into the grave, and the Jin zaju carvings push physical evidence for Chinese drama back before the Yuan. A brick also bears a tonic recipe with 'three qian of deer antler'; the Duan were a family of physicians.

name: Yuanjue Temple, Hunyuan
place: Shanxi · Datong · Old town of Hunyuan · Shiqiao North Lane
lede: The iron phoenix on the finial still turns its head with the wind, the only surviving wind-vane instrument on a Chinese pagoda. This octagonal, nine-storey brick pagoda with close-set eaves at Yuanjue Monastery was, according to the Shunzhi-era Gazetteer of Hunyuan, built by the monk Xuanzhen in 1158, the third year of Zhenglong of the Jin, and stands more than thirty metres: on a four-metre base with four tiers of brick carving, the first storey opens imitation timber doors and windows, above which seven tiers of eaves tighten in one sweep until the spacing opens again between the eighth and ninth, so the silhouette never turns rigid.
facts: Form: an octagonal nine-storey brick pagoda with close-set eaves, more than 30 m high, built throughout in brick imitating timber; the base is about 4 m high with four tiers of carving, from bottom to top lions and beast masks, lotus petals, musicians and dancers (with more than ten instruments including bell chimes, pipa, panpipes and waist drums) and imitation bracket sets; the first storey carves imitation doors and windows on all eight faces, the north door with a relief of a woman half opening it, and seven continuous tiers of eaves rise above.

Date: according to the Shunzhi-era Gazetteer of Hunyuan, the monastery was built in 1158 under the monk Xuanzhen, the pagoda being a Jin relic repaired in the Ming and Qing; no dated inscription has been found on the pagoda itself, so its date follows the monastery's foundation. It was listed as a Shanxi provincial protected site in 1986 and a national one in 2013, and the Shanxi provincial government has published its conservation plan.

Significance: it is the only Jin close-eaved pagoda in the Datong region; the iron phoenix on the finial turns with the wind to show its direction and is regarded as the only surviving ancient Chinese wind-vane instrument. The pagoda is the landmark of the old town of Hunyuan, where the monastery is called the 'small temple' beside Yong'an Monastery, the 'large temple'. Su Bai's 1951 survey report on Hunyuan's ancient architecture already focused on these two monasteries.

name: Chunhua Temple, Pingshun
era: Before the 9th year of Dading, Jin
place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Yanggao Village
lede: The two stone sutra pillars in front, dated 970, the third year of Kaibao of the Northern Song, are two centuries older than the hall. The main hall is three bays wide and six rafters deep under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof with deep overhangs; the capital sets are four-puzuo with one cantilever of the 'qin-face' profile and there are no intermediate sets. The frame uses a single six-rafter beam spanning from front to rear eaves, with no four-rafter beam above it, only dwarf posts and short ties carrying the purlins, a timber-saving solution rare among early buildings in southeastern Shanxi. The hall bears no inscription and is dated to the Jin on structural grounds.
facts: Form: three bays wide and six rafters deep under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof, with a plate on the columns; the capital sets are four-puzuo with one qin-face cantilever and chamfered end arms, and there are no intermediate sets. A single six-rafter beam spans front to rear eaves, with dwarf posts and short ties above it carrying the purlins, the frame left exposed; doors open front and rear, and the small porch at the rear door is a later addition.

Date: the monastery was founded in the Tianbao years of the Northern Qi as Longmen Chan Cloister, a dependency of Longmen Monastery; it was rebuilt in the Kaibao years of the Northern Song and took its present name in 991. The main hall has no building inscription and is dated to the Jin by its structure; a poem stele by the county magistrate Li Yan dated 1169, the ninth year of Dading, is set in the north wall, and the two sutra pillars bear the date 970. Repairs are recorded in the Yongzheng and Jiaqing reigns and the Republican period.

Significance: among surviving early buildings in Shanxi, those six rafters deep mostly use composite frames, and a single six-rafter beam spanning the whole depth is very rare, this hall being the representative; the two pillars carry the Diamond Sutra and the Usnisa Vijaya Dharani respectively. On the same outing Li Yan also left an inscription on a rear eave column of Longmen Monastery, the two corroborating each other; Li Yan has a biography in the History of Jin and later rose to Minister of Rites.

name: Hua Pagoda of Guanghui Temple
era: Founded in the Tang · Restored in the Dading era, Jin
lede: The most ornate of China's surviving flower pagodas: the lower three stories form an octagonal pavilion, each of its four corners embracing a small hexagonal pagoda, and the top story gathers into a “bouquet,” with lions, elephants, bodhisattvas and guardian warriors clustered tier upon tier around the finial.
facts: Founded in the Tang and restored in the Dading era of the Jin; 40.5 m tall overall (another account gives 33.35 m), with four stories of brick imitating timber.

At the four corners of the first story, hexagonal annex chambers connect to the main pagoda, each with an arched doorway and an inverted-bowl top; this combination of “one main and four subsidiary” pagodas is seen nowhere else.

The bouquet-shaped body of the fourth story: its eight faces are modeled with lions, elephants, Buddhist niches and guardian warriors in staggered rows, eight tiers in all, which give the Flower Pagoda its name.
Together with the Xumi Pagoda of Kaiyuan Temple, the Lingxiao Pagoda of Tianning Temple and the Chengling Pagoda of Linji Temple, it is known as one of the “Four Pagodas of Zhengding.”

name: Pingyao Confucian Temple
yearNote: The date used is that of the main structure drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
lede: Among all the Confucian temples of China, this is the only Hall of Great Achievement built in Jin timber: rebuilt in 1163, the third year of Dading, it keeps its original appearance. The hall is five bays wide under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof, and its bracket sets use the independent cantilever, a device rare in China; the terrace in front is railed in bluestone and the central ramp carved with two dragons playing with a pearl. The temple is said to have been founded early in the Zhenguan era of the Tang, and in 1997 it was inscribed as World Heritage together with the ancient city of Pingyao. The plate shows the front of the hall; later buildings in the compound are not included.
facts: Form: the Hall of Great Achievement is five bays wide under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof and stands on a terrace railed in carved bluestone, with a 'worship stone' carved with the character for longevity set in its centre and stone ramps in front and to either side, the front ramp carved with two dragons playing with a pearl; the bracket sets under the eaves use an independent cantilever structure, rare among surviving Chinese timber buildings.

Date: the Pingyao Confucian Temple was founded early in the Zhenguan era of the Tang; the hall was rebuilt in 1163 and is the only Jin-dynasty building in any Confucian temple in China. The name 'Hall of Great Achievement' dates from 1104, when a Northern Song edict renamed the Hall of King Wenxuan, barely sixty years before this rebuilding. In 1997 the temple was inscribed as World Heritage with the ancient city of Pingyao, Zhenguo Monastery and Shuanglin Monastery.

Significance: this is the earliest surviving hall in any Confucian temple in China; in the symmetrical plan of old Pingyao, 'Confucian temple on the left, temple of the god of war on the right, Daoist abbey east and Buddhist monastery west', the temple holds one end. The terrace and the two side galleries of nine bays each enclose the main court, the galleries housing the sages and worthies of the past, a well-preserved example of a county-level school-temple layout.

name: Yanshan Temple, Fanshi
lede: Outside, Wenshu Hall is a Jin Buddhist hall five bays wide. Inside, its murals unfold another scale: cities, palaces and everyday activities set Buddhist stories within a human world. Wang Kui and other painters completed them in 1167; the timber hall later underwent Yuan repairs. Its single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, substantial brackets and wall paintings survive together. The framing records building practice, while the paintings reveal architecture and society, each with its own dating evidence.
facts: Timber: the hall is five bays wide and six rafter spans deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof. Its four-puzuo bracket sets project once. The framing and eaves supports retain the scale of the Jin structure, giving its simple form considerable presence.

Inscriptions: the hall survives from the Jin, while an inscription beneath a four-rafter beam records rebuilding in 1315. The murals were completed in 1167. Painting, construction and subsequent repair should therefore be treated as separate events.

Murals: the west wall depicts the Buddha’s life, the east the story of Prince Xusheti, and the north temple compounds and a maritime disaster. Buildings, streets and human activity make these religious paintings evidence for Song–Jin architecture and social life.

name: Qiyun Pagoda of White Horse Temple
sub: White Horse Temple · Jin brick pagoda
yearNote: A Jin rebuilding stele states 1175 explicitly; this is not 68, the year White Horse Temple was founded.
place: Henan · Luoyang · East Pagoda Court of White Horse Temple
lede: The year of the White Horse Temple's founding, 68 CE (Yongping 11 of the Eastern Han), is often hung on the Qiyun Pagoda, but the tower in front of us is Jin: a Jin stele beside it, the Record of Rebuilding the Shakyamuni Relic Pagoda of the East White Horse Temple on Left Street of Henan Prefecture, gives the rebuilding year plainly as 1175 (Dading 15). A square brick pagoda of thirteen dense-eaved storeys, its outline a parabola narrowing step by step from the sixth storey, topped by a vase-shaped finial, it is the oldest standing building in the Luoyang area. Originally the Shakyamuni Relic Pagoda, it was renamed Qiyun ('level with the clouds') in the Kangxi era by the abbot Ruxiu, following the tradition that Emperor Ming had built the first tower. The plate shows the whole pagoda.
facts: Form: A square brick pagoda with thirteen storeys of corbelled dense eaves, about 25 m tall overall (35 m by another account); the base is a waisted sumeru pedestal 7.80 m on a side, 6.76 m at the waist. The body draws in storey by storey so that the outline forms a parabola, and a vase-shaped finial crowns the top.

Dating: Its predecessor, the Shakyamuni Relic Pagoda of the White Horse Temple, is said to date from the reign of Emperor Ming of the Eastern Han and was destroyed by Jin troops at the end of the Northern Song; the present pagoda was rebuilt in 1175 (Dading 15 of the Jin), as recorded on the Jin stele of the rebuilding. A Qing abbot, Ruxiu, renamed it Qiyun on the strength of the record that Emperor Ming had founded the tower.

Significance: The Qiyun Pagoda is the earliest Jin-period building still standing in the Luoyang area, and its parabolic profile preserves the look of Tang pagodas. The pagoda court lies about 200 m south-east of the temple gate; enlarged in 1990 to one hectare, it is the only Buddhist nunnery in Henan. The White Horse Temple itself was listed among the first national protected sites in 1961.

Rebuilt in the 15th year of Dading, Jin (1175)

name: Baolun Temple Pagoda
sub: Thirteen eaves drawn into a slender silhouette
yearNote: Entered according to the surviving pagoda rebuilt in the Jin; the founding date of the old Tang temple is not substituted for the date of the pagoda.
lede: Clap beneath the pagoda and it answers with a toad's croak—people in Shanzhou call it the Toad Pagoda, and it is counted with the Echo Wall of Beijing's Temple of Heaven and the Yingying Pagoda at Yongji among China's four great echoing buildings, the oldest of them. In 1177 (Dading 17 of the Jin) the monk Zhixiu rebuilt this brick tower on the site of a Sui timber pagoda: square in plan, thirteen storeys of corbelled dense eaves, 26.5 m tall, on a platform and pedestal, each storey opening an arched door, a niche or a window, with wind-bells under the corners. The old walled town of Shanzhou has long been abandoned; the pagoda stands alone on its terrace. The plate shows the south face.
facts: Form: A thirteen-storey brick pagoda with corbelled dense eaves, nearly square in plan, laid in grey-blue brick, 26.5 m tall (27.2 m by another account) and 21.6 m around the base, on a platform and pedestal; each storey opens a round-arched doorway, a Buddha niche or a window, the interior holds a chamber and a stair for climbing, and wind-bells hang beneath the corners of the eaves.

Dating: Its full name is the Three Sages Relic Pagoda of Baolun Temple. The temple pagoda is said to go back to 601 (Renshou 1 of the Sui), when the nun Daoxiu directed a timber tower; in 1177 (Dading 17 of the Jin) the monk Zhixiu rebuilt it in brick—the pagoda that stands today. It has survived more than ten earthquakes with only a slight lean.

Significance: The echo inside sounds like frogs, hence the nickname Toad Pagoda; with the Echo Wall of the Temple of Heaven, the Yingying Pagoda at Yongji and the stone 'qin' of Dafo Temple at Tongnan it is counted among China's four great echoing buildings, and is the earliest. Baolun Temple itself is gone; the pagoda now stands in the Pagoda Garden of Shanzhou Park, within the site of the old town.

name: Erlang Temple of Wangbao, Gaoping
sub: Jin opera stage · Gable facing forward
lede: The stage at Wangbao’s Erlang Temple turns the gable of its hip-and-gable roof towards the audience. Four corner columns and substantial brackets carry the roof over a small, square, single-bay stage. The load-bearing arrangement is unusually clear. An inscription on the stone pedestal gives the year 1183 and names its masons. Facing the temple’s main hall, the stage places performance and worship in the same courtyard and preserves architectural evidence of village theatrical life.
facts: Structure: a square stage one bay wide has round columns at its corners and a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof with its gable facing forward. Broad lintels and brackets carry the roof; two intercolumnar bracket sets on each side give the small building a complete structural hierarchy.

Dating: the pedestal inscription records the twenty-third year of Dading and the masons Zhao Xian and Zhao Zhi, dating the work to the Jin. Other temple buildings were largely rebuilt in the Ming and Qing; their dates do not replace that of the inscribed stage.

Performance: standing on the courtyard’s south side and facing the main hall, the stage links performance with ritual. It provides physical evidence for early temple-fair theatre, while its inscription ties the timber form to a recorded date rather than a foundation legend.

name: Jingtu Temple, Ying County
lede: Jingtu Temple’s Mahavira Hall rewards looking up: caissons and miniature celestial pavilions spread across its ceiling, their columns, rails, eaves and brackets reduced to intricate joinery. The Jin hall is only three bays square, yet its interior constructs another architectural world above the worshipper. The temple was founded in 1124 and repaired in 1184, with later renovations. Here the structural frame and ornamental woodwork express architecture at different scales.
facts: Space: three bays wide and deep, the hall has a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof. Caissons and miniature pavilions furnish its ceiling with tiny columns, rails and eaves. A restrained exterior contrasts with the intricate interior.

History: the Yingzhou gazetteer records foundation in 1124 and repair in 1184; the surviving hall is Jin. Major Ming repairs followed. Foundation, repairs and later decorative work should not be compressed into one date.

Joinery: the celestial pavilions are images of buildings attached to the ceiling, not rooms to enter. Their fine components give architectural form to Pure Land imagery and preserve evidence for Jin interior decoration and woodworking.

name: Fengxian Temple, Jiyuan
yearNote: The Jin date of the surviving Sanqing Hall is used, not the founding of the temple in the 1st year of Chuigong in the Tang.
lede: A hall five bays wide whose entire roof rests inside on just two rear hypostyle columns—one of the clearest examples in China of 'column reduction'. The Hall of the Three Pure Ones at Fengxian Abbey in Jiyuan was built in 1184 (Dading 24 of the Jin): five bays wide, seven rafters deep, under a single-eave overhanging-gable roof. The Qianlong-era Jiyuan county gazetteer says its beams are of chaste-tree and persimmon wood and its columns of mulberry and jujube, hence the nickname 'Chaste-Tree Beam Abbey'. Liu Dunzhen, who saw it, praised its 'bold handling and extraordinary conception'. The plate shows the front of the hall; the Ming Jade Emperor Hall and the Qing gate of the abbey are not drawn.
facts: Form: The hall is five bays wide and seven rafters deep under a single-eave overhanging-gable roof; the plan uses column reduction, with only two rear hypostyle columns inside carrying the roof frame—a textbook case of the technique. The Qianlong-era Jiyuan gazetteer records that 'the beams are of chaste-tree and persimmon, the columns of mulberry and jujube, each two or three spans around and some two zhang long'.

Dating: Fengxian Abbey was founded in 685 (Chuigong 1 of the Tang); the two Daoist masters Lu of the Tang and Helan Qizhen of the Song practised here. The present Hall of the Three Pure Ones dates from 1184 (Dading 24 of the Jin). Ten Jin, Ming and Qing buildings survive, among them the Ming Jade Emperor Hall, three bays wide with an overhanging-gable roof, and the Qing gate, also three bays under an overhanging-gable roof.

Significance: Because its beams and columns use four woods rarely chosen for structural timber—chaste-tree, persimmon, mulberry and jujube—locals call it the 'Chaste-Tree Beam Abbey', and Liu Dunzhen praised its 'bold handling and extraordinary conception'. It is the most important of Henan's surviving Jin timber buildings and is often set beside the Hall of the Three Sages at Shanhua Temple in Datong, Shanxi.

name: Chengling Pagoda of Linji Temple
yearNote: The date used is that of the main structure drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
lede: Chengling Pagoda concentrates elaborate brick carving around its base and tall first section, then draws the eye upward through tapering eaves to its finial. It commemorates Yixuan, founder of the Linji school, but its present form mainly follows a major Jin repair rather than surviving unchanged from its Tang foundation. Blind doors, windows and brackets translate timber decoration into brick and give the memorial its distinctive texture.
facts: The solid octagonal brick pagoda has nine tiers, a double Sumeru pedestal and an upturned lotus base. Door-shaped arches on four principal faces alternate with blind windows; close eaves above the first section reproduce elements of timber architecture.

The early tower commemorated Yixuan, founder of the Linji school. Its present appearance chiefly follows the major repair of 1185. Yuan, Ming and Qing repairs followed; an earthquake damaged the finial in 1966, and it was reinstalled in 1985.

Carved doors, balustrades and brackets preserve finely differentiated components useful for studying Jin decoration and joinery. Comparing them with the closely stacked upper eaves reveals how monumental mass and intricate craftsmanship work together.
