name: Lugou Bridge, Beijing
era: Completed in the Jin · Ming–Qing repairs
lede: Lions beyond counting: 281 balustrade posts, each capped by a large lion with cubs, plus those on the ornamental columns and at the bridgeheads, 498 by one count and 501 by another; even the tally is unsettled. Lugou Bridge was begun in 1189, the twenty-ninth year of Dading of the Jin, and finished in 1192, the third year of Mingchang: an eleven-arch stone bridge across the Yongding River, 268 m long and 9.4 m wide, its piers built with cutwaters on the upstream face and iron posts on the points to break the ice. The shots of 7 July 1937 rang out here; in 1967 it was turned into a road bridge, and only in 1987 was it returned to a stone bridge. The plate views it from a shallow angle, with all eleven arches open.
facts: Form: an eleven-arch stone bridge running east-west, 268 m long including the approaches (the bridge proper 212.75 m) and 9.4 m wide, the spans ranging from 11.4 to 13.45 m; the ten piers have cutwaters on the upstream face with triangular iron posts against ice. Along the deck stand 281 balustrade posts and 279 stone panels, the posts about 1.4 m high and topped with carved lions; a pair of ornamental columns stands at each end, with crouching lions at the east end and elephants at the west bracing the balustrade.

Dating: in 1189 Emperor Zhangzong of Jin ordered a stone bridge, completed in 1192 and first named Guangli Bridge; twelve recorded repairs followed in the Ming and Qing, and in 1751, the sixteenth year of Qianlong, the stele 'Moon over Lugou at Dawn' was set up. The foundations, parts of the structure and some of the carving remain Jin originals, while posts and panels have been replaced over the centuries.

Events and value: on 7 July 1937, after exercises north of the bridge, Japanese troops attacked Wanping and the bridge, and the Lugou Bridge Incident became the starting point of full-scale war against Japan; in 1967-1968 the deck was overlaid with reinforced concrete as a road bridge, and in 1987 the stone bridge was restored and closed to traffic. It is the oldest large multi-arch stone bridge surviving in Beijing, and 'Moon over Lugou at Dawn' is one of the Eight Views of Yanjing.

name: Hongfu Temple, Dingxiang
lede: Hongfu Temple’s main hall stands within fortified walls on a high platform. Its five-bay, overhanging-gable hall and enclosing walls work at different scales: fortress-like outside, Buddhist temple within. The surviving Mahavira Hall is identified as a Jin structure, without an inscription establishing an exact building year. Nine clay figures remain on a brick altar. Timber architecture, sculpture and successive repairs coexist here; their different dates should not be compressed into a single year for the whole temple.
facts: Form: the main hall is five bays wide, with seven purlins, a depth of six rafter spans and an overhanging-gable roof supported by brackets. The temple stands on a raised earthen platform within fortified walls, giving a religious courtyard a closed exterior.

Dating: the surviving hall belongs to the Jin, but its precise construction year is uncertain. Nor should the temple’s foundation be dated from legend. Repairs from later periods are separate events; a timeline placement does not date every timber component.

Sculpture: nine clay figures occupy a brick altar, arranged as principal figure, bodhisattvas, disciples and guardians. Local research describes them as Song sculpture. Their dating should be distinguished from that of the Jin timber hall.

name: Yanqing Temple, Wutai
lede: Yanqing Temple’s Great Buddha Hall is only three bays wide, but its deep eaves give the small grey-tiled hall an expansive profile. A central plank door, flanking lattice windows and bracket sets reveal the column grid. The hall is identified as Jin, with no known exact building year. A Song stone scripture pillar in the temple predates the timber hall. Reading them separately shows a village temple’s long continuity without using the date of one earlier object for all its buildings.
facts: Form: three bays wide and six rafter spans deep, the hall has a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof of grey tiles. A plank door occupies the centre, with vertical-lattice windows beside it. Lintels connect the columns and brackets carry the broad eaves.

Dating: the surviving hall is Jin, with an uncertain construction year. The courtyard’s scripture pillar dates to 1035 under the Northern Song. Its inscription does not date the hall; different objects preserve different historical evidence.

Timber: column brackets project with an arm and a descending strut, while intercolumnar sets include diagonal arms. The exposed interior framing allows the eaves supports and roof supports to be examined separately, revealing the structure in its details.

name: Taifu Temple, Fenyang
era: Jin · Hall of the Haotian Jade Emperor
yearNote: 1200 is an approximate sorting point for the period indicated by the altar record of the 5th year of Cheng'an; the main hall is dated to the Jin from its architecture and heritage sources, and the altar date is not forced on the hall as a precise completion year.
lede: Taifu Temple’s Haotian Hall places a three-bay-square plan beneath a hip-and-gable roof. A plank door and vertical-lattice windows articulate a compact setting for worship of the Jade Emperor. The main hall retains Jin timber forms, while sculpture and other buildings include Ming and Qing layers. An inscription of 1200 records establishing a ritual altar, not necessarily completion of the hall. Structure, inscription and decoration each carry dates, revealing the gradual making of a religious site.
facts: Plan: three bays wide and deep, the nearly square hall has a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof. A central plank door and flanking vertical-lattice windows organise the facade. Worship of the Jade Emperor gives this compact hall its religious purpose.

Inscription: the Cheng’an fifth-year record concerns establishment of an altar, while the surviving hall is identified as Jin through its timber form. Setting up an altar and building a hall are separate events; the inscription does not precisely date every component.

Layers: other halls are largely Ming, while sculpture and painting include Ming and Qing work and repairs. The Jin main hall stands with later images and subsidiary buildings, revealing a site accumulated through construction, repair and continued use.

name: Yongle Palace, Ruicheng
lede: The long eaves of the Sanqing Hall lift gently at both sides, and huge glazed dragon ridge-end ornaments guard either end of the main ridge. Inside, the mural Homage to the Primordial (Chaoyuan Tu) arrays hundreds of deities in a grand procession, so that Yuan timber architecture and murals reflect each other within a single space.
facts: Seven-bay hipped hall: The Sanqing Hall, also called the Wuji Hall, is the main hall of Yongle Palace, seven bays wide with a single-eaved hipped roof, and is dated to the 3rd year of Zhongtong (1262).
Chaoyuan Tu: The murals in the hall were completed in 1325 and are recorded separately from the construction date of the building.
Relocation for protection: For the Sanmenxia Reservoir project, the palace buildings and murals were moved to their present site in the 1960s, preserving the original halls and murals.

name: Dengfeng Observatory
sub: Front of the platform and stone scale
yearNote: The date used is that of the main structure drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
lede: Dengfeng Observatory turns a solar-shadow instrument into a brick-and-stone building. Its square platform narrows upward, with a northern slot aligned to a long stone measuring rule and stairs leading to the top. Yuan observations directed by Guo Shoujing left a tangible apparatus here: astronomy also measured midday shadows to determine seasons and the length of a year.
facts: The brick-and-stone platform narrows toward the top. A measuring slot cuts through its north side, while eastern and western stairs ascend the platform. The stone rule extends northward beneath the slot to receive measurable shadows.

Built in 1276, the thirteenth year of the Yuan Zhiyuan era, the observatory was associated with Guo Shoujing’s survey of the heavens. The nearby Duke of Zhou shadow platform is a separate monument with a different building history.

Channels and pools beside the stone rule helped establish a level measuring surface and reduce error. This union of instrument and architecture shows how traditional calendars depended on repeated observation as well as calculation.

name: White Pagoda of Miaoying Temple, Beijing
era: Built from the 8th to the 16th year of Zhiyuan
lede: One of the first things to rise in the new capital of Dadu: in 1271, the eighth year of Zhiyuan, Khubilai Khan engaged the Nepalese craftsman Anige to direct the building of a stupa, eighty-five men worked for eight years, and it was finished in 1279, the sixteenth year of Zhiyuan, the earliest and largest Tibetan-style stupa surviving in China. It is 51 m high: a three-tiered base on a cross-shaped plan carries an inverted-bowl body 18.4 m across, above which rise the thirteen 'heavens', a bronze canopy 9.7 m in diameter and a four-ton gilt-bronze miniature stupa as the finial. In 1368 lightning fire destroyed the whole of the Great Shengshou Wan'an Temple around it, and only the White Stupa was untouched. The plate shows the stupa alone, without the halls in front.
facts: Form: a Tibetan-style brick stupa 51 m high, white throughout, in five parts, base, body, rings, canopy and finial; the base has three tiers on a cross-shaped plan, 810 square metres in area and 9 m high; above a lotus pedestal wound with five 'vajra rings' sits the inverted-bowl body 18.4 m across, bound with seven iron hoops; the thirteen rings carry a canopy 9.7 m in diameter hung with 36 wind bells, and the finial is a gilt-bronze stupa 5 m high weighing 4 tons.

Dating: begun in 1271 under Anige and completed in 1279, with the Great Shengshou Wan'an Temple then built around it; in 1368, the twenty-eighth year of Zhizheng, the temple burnt after a lightning strike and only the stupa survived. It was repaired in 1433, the temple was renamed Miaoying in 1457, 108 iron lamp niches were set around the base in 1465, and further repairs followed under Kangxi, Qianlong and Jiaqing.

Repairs and finds: during repairs in 1978 the top yielded deposits placed in 1753, the eighteenth year of Qianlong, including 724 cases of the Longzang Tripitaka, sutras and mantras in Qianlong's own hand, Buddha images and relics; the major repair of 2013-2015 removed and replaced about eighty percent of the surface brick, adding nearly ten thousand bricks. The guardian deities, five-Buddha emblems and other carvings that once decorated the base and body have almost entirely weathered away.

name: Prayer Hall of the Phoenix Mosque
sub: Hangzhou · Yuan hall of brick vaults and domes
era: Rebuilt in the Yuan · Repaired over the centuries
lede: Fenghuang Mosque’s prayer hall presents three pointed roofs outside but brick arches and domes within. A taller central roof and two smaller side roofs combine a West Asian worship space with Jiangnan tiled roofs and raised corners. Its surviving core comes from a Yuan rebuilding funded by Ala al-Din, followed by Ming, Qing and modern repairs. The building records the long local history of Hangzhou’s Muslim community through its architectural language.
facts: Form: brick walls and arches divide the hall into three transverse spaces, each covered by a dome. Pointed tiled roofs sit outside them; the taller central roof has double eaves, so the inner and outer roof forms differ.

Dating: the prayer hall survives from the Yuan rebuilding funded by Ala al-Din and predates the mosque’s other surviving buildings. Repeated Ming, Qing and modern repairs mean that not every present roof ornament is Yuan fabric.

Significance: arches, domes and local tiled roofs unite different construction traditions. The hall is also a historic setting for Hangzhou’s Muslim worship, significant both as architecture and as a continuing community space.

name: Ji Family Residence, Gaoping
place: Shanxi · Gaoping · Zhongzhuang Village, Chenqu Town
lede: The Ji family residence has no monumental temple facade, only three shallow bays with a recessed central entrance forming a small porch. Its importance lies beside the door: a stone doorway pedestal bears the thirty-first year of Zhiyuan, giving an ordinary house a recorded date. Beneath a low overhanging-gable roof, rough brackets and naturally curved timber retain Yuan building practice; the square-lattice windows were altered later. The dated structure and changing fittings show a historic dwelling shaped by continued use.
facts: Plan: three bays wide and six rafter spans deep, the house has a gently pitched overhanging-gable roof. Its recessed central entrance creates a porch and a slightly concave plan. The low roof, shallow porch and small bays serve domestic needs rather than temple ceremony.

Dating: a stone doorway pedestal records the thirty-first year of Zhiyuan, a jiawu year, corresponding to 1294. This direct evidence agrees with the timber construction. It should not be confused with dates under other reigns bearing the name Zhiyuan.

Components: the front column brackets are four-puzuo sets, with some pieces made from naturally curved timber. The window lattices were later changed to square grids. Yuan structural timber and altered fittings reveal the layers of time in a long-used home.

name: Tianning Wanshou Temple, Yuzhou
sub: Three-bay Yuan Buddhist hall preserved on a school campus
yearNote: The date of the hall's rebuilding is used; it was later restored in the Ming and Qing and was dismantled and repaired in 2013. The main gate is Ming in style and is not the subject of this plate.
lede: The main hall of Yuzhou’s Tianning Wanshou Temple survives within an old school campus. A three-bay grey-tiled hip-and-gable roof rests on brick walls and stone columns; brackets support its eaves, while exposed beams retain the curves of natural timber. Rebuilt under the Yuan and repaired under the Ming, Qing and in modern times, this modest hall reveals the continuity of local construction. Accounts of the temple’s origins should be distinguished from the date of this hall.
facts: Three bays wide and deep, the hall has a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and four-tier brackets with one descending cantilever arm. Its exposed framing combines stone columns, brick walls and naturally curved timber.

The hall is dated to its rebuilding in 1299, the third year of the Yuan Dade era. It was repaired in the Ming Hongzhi and Jiajing eras and the Qing Daoguang era; the dismantling repair of 2013 was a conservation project.

The hall once served as school accommodation and survives alongside the temple gate. Its curved beams and regional techniques offer material evidence for comparing Song–Jin construction with later Ming–Qing buildings.

name: Temple of the Holy Mother of the Nine Heavens
era: Restored in the 1st year of Jianzhong Jingguo, Song · Yuan offering hall
place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Donghe Village
lede: The offering hall at Jiutian Shengmu Temple is open on all sides. Stone columns carry timber beams and a roof, exposing their connections. Between the stage and the main hall, it fits into a close sequence of buildings whose eaves interweave within a compact courtyard. The surviving offering hall is identified as Yuan, not dated directly from the temple’s Song repair record. Ritual spaces, inscriptions and buildings of different periods reveal a village temple formed through successive campaigns.
facts: Openness: stone columns support a timber hall three bays wide and five deep, without enclosing walls. Adjacent buildings remain visible between the columns, and framing and eaves supports can be examined directly, unlike in the enclosed main hall.

Dating: the offering hall is Yuan, the main hall Song and the dressing tower Ming, while other parts contain Qing layers. Their close arrangement does not mean that all were built in the year recorded for a Song repair campaign.

Courtyard: the axis links gate-stage, offering hall and main hall, with subsidiary halls and galleries beside them. Worship and performance share the courtyard. Successive building inscriptions allow its spatial layout and written history to be read together.

name: Huishan Temple, Dengfeng
sub: Front of the Yuan main hall
yearNote: The main subject drawn is dated to the Yuan; the numeric year is only an approximate sorting value.
lede: Huishan Temple’s five-bay main hall spreads a broad façade at the southern foot of Mount Song. Layered brackets carry its hip-and-gable roof, with central doors flanked by window bays. The temple’s history predates this Yuan timber building, while inscriptions and subsequent repairs add further layers. Its broad roof, reduced interior columns and exposed framing explain how a hall could provide an open space for worship.
facts: Five bays wide and three deep, the hall has a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof with five-tier double-cantilever brackets. Reducing the number of interior columns enlarges the worship space beneath the broad roof.

The temple was founded and repaired over several periods. The surviving timber hall is assigned to the Yuan, but its exact construction year remains uncertain; the timeline position around 1300 is approximate.

Inscriptions record Buddhist activity and repairs from different periods, complementing evidence in the framing. The site illustrates the distinction between a temple’s long history and the date of one surviving building.

name: Sakyamuni Temple
yearNote: Dated by the structure of the Yuan hall; the temple's other, Ming halls are not mixed into the main subject.
lede: A broad central bay lies beneath the modest three-bay roof of Shijia Temple’s central hall. Its low, single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and timber frame support a Yuan attribution. The temple later expanded, with neighbouring roofs arranged to echo the hall, while ridges and ceilings were repaired or added. The building therefore combines the core of a Yuan frame with a worship space repeatedly shaped in the Ming and Qing periods.
facts: The central hall, or Mahavira Hall, is three bays wide and three deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof on a brick terrace. Its broad middle bay creates a concentrated interior; three exterior bays do not necessarily mean a small chamber.

The provincial heritage authority identifies a Yuan structure from the frame and appearance; inscriptions also attest to a Yuan Shijia Chan Temple. Expansion followed in the Hongwu era, and parts of the roof and interior ceiling are later additions or repairs.

The neighbouring halls have gable roofs but add columns and extended eaves towards the central hall, creating similar front elevations. This visual dialogue organises the temple as a whole while showing that its buildings belong to different phases.

name: Jiangzhou Great Hall
sub: Main hall of the prefectural office · Seven bays, overhanging gable roof
era: Yuan · Main hall of the prefectural office
yearNote: 1300 is only an approximate timeline placement for a surviving Yuan structure, not an exact completion year.
place: Shanxi · Xinjiang County · Jiangzhou Prefectural Office
lede: Jiangzhou’s administrative hall stretches across seven bays and opens its interior through reduced columns and large longitudinal beams. Its official scale is expressed in the structure as much as the roof. The surviving core is identified as Yuan, though its exact foundation year is unknown, and Ming and Qing repairs followed. Substantial timbers and front brackets preserve the load-bearing logic of a local government building. A projecting porch has been lost; the broad hall still reveals a public space different from an ordinary dwelling.
facts: Form: seven bays wide and eight rafter spans deep, the hall has a single-eaved overhanging-gable roof and seventeen bracket sets along the front. Columns, lintels and beams organise a broad facade, with enclosed ends and central openings producing different degrees of openness.

History: the foundation date is uncertain. The surviving core is Yuan, with repairs under Hongwu, Qianlong and Guangxu. A three-bay projecting porch formerly stood at the front but is lost. The present building is not the complete state of any single building campaign.

Reduced columns: large longitudinal beams work with the transverse framing to carry the roof with fewer internal columns. This surviving government hall helps explain Yuan public architecture through the arrangement of structural timber rather than decoration alone.

name: Fusheng Temple, Xinjiang County
yearNote: 1300 serves only as an approximate sorting point for a surviving Yuan structure and does not claim completion in that year.
place: Shanxi · Xinjiang County · Guang Village, Zezhang Town
lede: Fusheng Temple in Guang Village unfolds tier upon tier with the terrain, and the Amitabha Hall organizes its inner and outer spaces with double eaves and a surrounding gallery. Its Yuan timber structure and the painted sculptures inside depend on each other, and the north elevation shows the layers of eaves, rear wall and gallery columns more clearly.
facts: Yuan hall: The Amitabha Hall preserves a Yuan timber structure and was restored in the Hongzhi era of the Ming; the temple's founding history cannot directly stand in for the date of the surviving hall.

Double eaves and gallery: The Amitabha Hall is five bays square, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof and a gallery all around; the ground level differs between the high platform to the south and the rear courtyard to the north.

Surviving painted sculpture: The hall preserves painted sculptures of Amitabha Buddha, attendant bodhisattvas, Guanyin Crossing the Sea and others, which have undergone various later repairs; this plate shows the north side of the hall.

name: Jade Emperor Temple, Zezhou
sub: Fucheng · Painted sculptures of the Twenty-Eight Mansions
era: Yuan · Painted sculptures of the Twenty-Eight Mansions
yearNote: 1300 is only an approximate sorting point for the Yuan painted sculptures. Official sources give no exact date of making for the single figure selected; 1076 relates to the rebuilding of the temple and cannot substitute for the date of the sculptures.
place: Shanxi · Zezhou · Fucheng Village, Jincun Town
lede: At Zezhou’s Yuhuang Temple, the Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions become clay figures with individual poses, robes and animal companions. Xu Ri Shu is one of them: human expression and rat imagery turn an abstract celestial name into an identifiable deity. Official material dates the group to the Yuan, but not this individual figure to a precise year. The temple’s Northern Song rebuilding does not date the sculpture. One figure’s details help explain how astronomy, religion and human character meet in the ensemble.
facts: Form: Xu Ri Shu combines a person with rat imagery; robe, gesture and expression give the stellar deity a character. It is one member of a twenty-eight-figure group, so its specific features should not be treated as a uniform design for every deity.

Dating: official material identifies the ensemble as Yuan. The individual figure’s exact production year is unconfirmed. The temple’s rebuilding during the Northern Song belongs to architectural history and should not be used as the statue’s date.

Cosmology: the lunar mansions belong to the Azure Dragon, White Tiger, Vermilion Bird and Black Tortoise groups. Human and animal forms make their names visible. Celestial order and varied expressions allow the ensemble to be read both as a stellar system and as individual figures.

name: Ciyun Pavilion
yearNote: Of the original Dabei Pavilion complex only this pavilion survives; it was rebuilt in the 10th year of Dade in the Yuan.
lede: Ciyun Pavilion is small, yet its two storeys are supported through a remarkably compact arrangement. Broad eaves surround a nearly square three-bay frame, with hanging posts and diagonal corner beams helping transfer loads. Once called Dabei Pavilion, the surviving building is a Yuan reconstruction; most surrounding temple structures have vanished. The isolated pavilion still shows how Yuan carpenters organised complex support within limited space.
facts: The pavilion is three bays wide and three deep, nearly square, and two storeys high. Projecting eaves contrast with the compact body; the levels are not simply repeated, and the exterior silhouette works with the internal support system.

Its former name, Dabei Pavilion, referred to the bronze image of the Great Compassion Buddha inside. The surviving building was reconstructed in 1306. Only the pavilion remains from the former complex, and later repairs do not replace its Yuan attribution.

Tails of upper-eave bracket arms support a transverse beam, while hanging posts and diagonal beams handle the corners. These connections, easily missed from a distance, offer evidence of Yuan structural planning and craftsmanship.

name: Yong'an Chan Temple, Hunyuan
sub: Hall of the Orthodox Transmission of the Dharma
place: Shanxi · Datong · Old town of Hunyuan
lede: Chuanfa Zhengzong Hall anchors Yong’an Temple with a five-bay facade and a single-eaved hipped roof. Central entrances, large characters on the end walls and broad eaves create a ceremonial scale; water-and-land ritual murals fill the interior. The temple was founded in the Jin, while Gao Pu funded this surviving main hall in 1315 under the Yuan. Temple foundation and hall construction are distinct events. Timber structure and later paintings together preserve a space shaped by religious activity and repair.
facts: Form: five bays wide and three deep, the hall has a single-eaved hipped roof on a raised terrace, approached by a platform and stone steps. Its broad body, facade and eaves establish the spatial rank of the main hall.

Construction: the temple began in the Jin and was rebuilt after fire during the Yuan. Gao Pu funded this hall in 1315. The surviving main hall is Yuan; other Ming and Qing buildings and later repairs belong to separate phases.

Murals: water-and-land ritual paintings cover the interior walls, including Confucian, Buddhist and Daoist figures. They survive within the timber hall, but painting, repainting and hall construction are different events. The structure’s date does not automatically date every painted surface.

name: Yanfu Temple, Wuyi
sub: Main hall · Yuan structure in Jiangnan
era: Yuan · Rebuilt in the 4th year of Yanyou
lede: Yanfusi’s main hall stands in a mountain village near Taoxi, Wuyi. Timber columns, curved beams and bracket sets support a spreading double-eaved hip-and-gable roof. Some Song components were retained in the Yuan rebuilding, combining a Yuan structure with earlier construction practices. The fourth Yanyou year marks the start of a project that took several years. Later repairs preserve a layered example of the continuity between Song and Yuan timber architecture in Jiangnan.
facts: Form: bracket sets support the spreading double-eaved hip-and-gable roof. Spindle-shaped columns and curved beams within create a light composition distinct from the heavier character of many northern halls.

Dating: monks Huaifa and Dehuan raised funds for a rebuilding beginning in 1317 and lasting seven years. Some columns survive from the Song, while inscriptions record repairs since the Qing; the hall contains fabric of several periods.

Significance: retained Song components within a Yuan frame document continuity in Jiangnan timber construction. Liang Sicheng and Lin Huiyin’s measured survey and photographs connect modern architectural scholarship with the hall’s preservation.

name: Tianning Temple, Jinhua
lede: Jinhua’s Tianning Temple hall preserves the detail of Song–Yuan timber construction within a compact three-by-three-bay building. Beams and brackets support its single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, while an ink inscription beneath a beam dates a Yuan rebuilding to 1318. The temple’s earlier foundation, reused Song components and later repairs are separate phases. Although only part of the old monastery remains, its timber and inscription still reveal the transmission of building practices.
facts: Form: three bays wide and three deep, the hall has a near-square plan and a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof. Integrated beams and bracket sets support a roof whose deep eaves extend beyond the compact body.

Dating: an ink inscription beneath a beam records rebuilding in 1318, the fifth Yanyou year. The Yuan work reused some Song components, and modern dismantling repairs followed; the inscription does not date every surviving material.

Significance: the dated inscription and surviving timberwork provide firm points for comparison. Song components within the Yuan rebuilding show how Jiangnan temples could retain earlier construction rather than replace everything during renewal.

name: Main Hall of Zhenru Temple
sub: Three bays, single-eaved hip-and-gable roof · Yuan timber structure
yearNote: 1320 corresponds to the construction inscription on the hall's timber frame; the present appearance was restored through repairs including those of 1963, which removed a later lower eave. lede: A broad gray-tiled roof rests on the three-bay timber hall, with ridge-end ornaments curling skyward at both ends. The main hall of Zhenru Temple preserves Yuan Jiangnan timber construction within today's city, and an inscription among its beams still records its construction in the 7th year of Yanyou.
facts: An inscription on an interior architrave records that the hall was erected in the 7th year of Yanyou in the Yuan (1320); the hall retains Yuan timber members and is an important Yuan architectural survival in Shanghai.
Three bays wide, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; four columns across the front frame central lattice doors with windows at the sides, and ridge-end ornaments stand at both ends of the roof.

Repairs in 1963 removed a lower eave added later, restoring its single-eaved appearance. The plate shows only the main hall; the new pagoda behind it and the later buildings on either side have dates of their own.

name: Xia Yu Shrine
place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Houbi Village
lede: On the Yuwang Hillock, the highest point of Houbi Village in the Zhuozhang River valley, a temple of a single courtyard packs Yuan, Ming and Qing timber buildings into 877 square metres: the gate is Ming, with a rear-facing stage on its upper floor looking straight at the Yuan main hall, while the side halls and wing rooms were added in the Qing. The plate shows the main hall, a surviving structure of 1336 (2nd year of Zhiyuan, Yuan), three bays wide under a gable roof with a two-rafter-deep front porch; its framing of four-rafter beam against front ru-beam on four columns is a ready textbook for Yuan village temples of southeastern Shanxi.
facts: Main hall: three bays wide and six rafters deep, single-eave gable (xuanshan) roof, with a two-rafter-deep front porch; column-top bracket sets are four-puzuo with one downward ang, the three intercolumnar sets were added in the Qing; framing is a four-rafter beam against a front ru-beam, with four columns across the depth.

Dating: the shrine was founded in 1336 (2nd year of Zhiyuan, Yuan) and repaired repeatedly in the Ming and Qing; the hall keeps one Ming and two Qing inscribed wall stones and three stone offering tables of the Wanli reign; the gate is Ming, the side halls and wings Qing.

Layout: a single courtyard of only 877 square metres; the three-bay, four-rafter gate carries a rear-facing stage on its upper floor facing the main hall, and the convex altar terrace before the hall is carved in relief on three sides; the National Cultural Heritage Administration registers the site as "Yuan to Qing", three dynasties of timber work in one yard.

name: Second Gate of Tiger Hill
sub: Suzhou · Duanliang Hall of Tiger Hill
era: Yuan · Rebuilt in the 4th year of Zhiyuan
lede: The main beam is 'broken': strictly, the ridge purlin is not a single timber but two round logs butted together at the middle, with the bracket sets and frames below spreading the load to either side, and it has held for more than six hundred years. The second gate of Tiger Hill is therefore called the Broken Beam Hall; rebuilt in 1338, the fourth year of the Zhiyuan era of the Yuan, it is three bays wide and two deep under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, with one round-arched doorway at the centre of the front. Built in the same year as the main hall of Xuanyuan Palace at Dongshan on Lake Tai, the two are Suzhou's firmly dated Yuan timber buildings.
facts: Form: three bays wide and two deep under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, with a round-arched doorway at the centre of the front. The ridge purlin is made of two round logs joined end to end rather than one piece, hence the name 'broken beam'; the hall is neither beamless nor left hanging after a fracture.

Dating: the present second gate was rebuilt in 1338, the same year as the main hall of Xuanyuan Palace at Dongshan; the temple on Tiger Hill rose and fell repeatedly from the Five Dynasties and Northern Song onward, most of its halls burnt in the Taiping war of 1860, and the second gate survived as the earliest building on the hill after the Five Dynasties Yunyan Temple Pagoda.

Value: the broken beam is often called a 'miracle' of carpentry, but it is in fact a splicing technique that lets the frames and bracket sets on either side share the load, reflecting the Jiangnan craftsman's habit of using timber as it came; together with the Yunyan Temple Pagoda completed in 959-961 on the summit, it forms Tiger Hill's sequence of early buildings from the Five Dynasties to the Yuan.

name: Shrine of Grand Master Dou, Taiyuan
sub: Offering pavilion and main hall · Shanglan Village
era: Rebuilt in the 3rd year of Zhizheng
yearNote: Placed by the Yuan rebuilding date, the 3rd year of Zhizheng, of the surviving offering pavilion and main hall; neither the Spring and Autumn date of the person venerated nor the earlier history of the shrine is used as the date of the timber structures.
siteCoordinateSource: Wikimedia Commons · Category:Dou Dafu Ancestral Temple / Wikidata Q15929110
lede: Stout timber columns hold up deep eaves, and the offering pavilion joins the main hall behind it. Among the gray-brown old timbers, dark green glazed tiles outline the ridges and eave-tile ends; the Shrine of Grand Master Dou gathers its ritual space into a tight group of timber buildings.
facts: The shrine is dedicated to Dou Chou, a grand master of the state of Jin, and is also called the Lieshi Shrine and the Yingji Shrine; the early history of the shrine and the dates of the surviving buildings are described separately.

The surviving gate, offering pavilion and main hall were rebuilt in the 3rd year of Zhizheng in the Yuan (1343). The plate selects the offering pavilion and main hall and does not count the Qing side buildings as Yuan structures.

The hip-and-gable roof of the offering pavilion links with the overhanging gable roof of the main hall behind, and thick columns and massive bracket sets create a striking contrast of scale; the colored plate follows the surviving old timber, gray tiles and glazed tiles, and is not a reconstruction of historical painted decoration.

name: Cloud Platform at Juyong Pass, Beijing
sub: Yuan base of a street-spanning stupa · Half-hexagonal arched passage
era: Built from the 2nd to the 5th year of Zhizheng
lede: A stupa base whose stupas are gone: the Cloud Platform at Juyong Pass was built in 1342-1345, the second to fifth years of Zhizheng of the Yuan, as a street-spanning stupa gateway; the three Tibetan-style white stupas on top were destroyed early in the Ming, the Buddha hall later built in their place burnt in 1702, the forty-first year of Kangxi, and only this white marble platform remains. It is about 10 m high, 26.84 m along the base and 24.04 m along the top, tapering upward; a single arched passage runs through the centre from north to south, its vault folded into a half-hexagon, and its inner walls are covered with the Four Heavenly Kings, a thousand Buddhas and mandalas, together with scriptures in six scripts, Sanskrit, Tibetan, Chinese, Phagspa, Uyghur and Tangut, a stone dictionary of the Yuan empire's many written languages.
facts: Form: a white marble platform, narrower above than below, about 10 m high, 26.84 m east-west and 17.57 m north-south at the base, 24.04 m and 14.73 m at the top; a connected arched gateway opens at the centre of the north and south faces, 7.27 m high and 6.32 m wide. Two tiers of stone slabs project on all four sides of the top, carved with cloud scrolls, beast masks and tasselled pendants, carrying a stone balustrade, with dragon-head spouts beneath the posts and at the corners to drain the top.

Dating: begun in 1342 under four Tibetan designers and supervisors appointed by Emperor Shun, and finished in 1345 with three Tibetan-style white stupas on top; the stupas perished early in the Ming and a five-bay Buddha hall replaced them, rebuilt in 1443-1448, the eighth to thirteenth years of Zhengtong; in 1702 everything on the platform burnt and nothing has stood there since. Restoration began in 1993 and the site opened in 1998.

Carving and scripts: the vault of the passage bears five mandalas, the sloping faces the Buddhas of the Ten Directions, and a thousand Buddhas fill the spaces between; each side wall carries two Heavenly Kings, and between the four kings are the Dharani Sutra in six scripts, Sanskrit, Tibetan, Chinese, Phagspa, Uyghur and Tangut, and the Record of the Merit of Building the Stupa in five; the outer faces of the arches show the garuda with the whale, dragon children, boys riding beasts and elephants of the 'six ornaments', all in Tibetan style.
captions: Cloud Platform at Juyong Pass · Surviving base of the street-spanning stupa

name: Beiyue Temple
sub: Front elevation of the Dening Hall (with gallery and platform)
yearNote: The provincial cultural heritage bureau lists the present hall under the 7th year of Zhizheng (1347); the county gazetteer records completion in the 7th year of Zhiyuan (1270), so both construction phases need to be recorded.
lede: Dening Hall spreads broadly through two hipped roof tiers and a surrounding gallery. A high terrace and central stair elevate the ritual space, while Yuan murals fill its walls with mountain deities. Beiyue Temple served remote worship of Hengshan. Records give differing construction phases for the surviving hall; its architecture, murals and inscriptions together preserve successive traces of imperial mountain worship.
facts: The complete hall is nine bays wide and six deep, with a double-eaved hipped roof, surrounding gallery and central approach to a high terrace. Hall, gallery and platform combine into an elevation that expresses ritual status.

The hall is registered as Yuan. The provincial authority records rebuilding in 1347, while local gazetteer material also gives construction in 1270. These may represent different phases; neither is replaced by the temple’s Northern Wei origins.

The temple worshipped Hengshan from afar. Yuan murals survive on the eastern and western interior walls, alongside inscriptions of successive dynasties in the grounds. Timber, painting and text make the mountain cult spatially legible.

name: Main Hall of Xuanyuan Palace
lede: A small hall at Yangwan on Dongshan by Lake Tai, three bays square, its hip-and-gable roof pressed low and its eaves reaching far out; it was once the Temple of King Xu, dedicated to Wu Zixu, and only in the Republican era was it rededicated to the Yellow Emperor and renamed Xuanyuan Palace. The main hall was built in 1338, the fourth year of the Zhiyuan era of the Yuan, the same year as the second gate of Tiger Hill; it is 13.74 m wide and 11.43 m deep, with a ridge more than ten metres high. A major repair under Shunzhi in the Qing means that the Yuan frame and the traces of Ming-Qing repairs share the same building.
facts: Form: the main hall is three bays and 13.74 m wide, three bays and nine purlins or 11.43 m deep, under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof with a ridge over 10 m high; the body is nearly square and the eaves are deep. The plate shows the front of the main hall.

Dating: the founding date is unknown; it was repaired and renamed the Temple of King Xu in the Shaoxing era of the Southern Song, and the main hall was built in 1338; a further major repair followed in 1649-1655, the sixth to twelfth years of Shunzhi, so what stands today is not an untouched Yuan original. It was listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

History: the site began as a shrine to Wu Zixu, who by tradition built the great city of Helü on the orders of the King of Wu; Suzhou's Xu Gate and Xukou take their names from him, and dragon-boat racing at the Duanwu festival in the Jiangsu-Zhejiang region is also seen as his commemoration. In the Republican era the temple was rededicated to the Yellow Emperor and first called Xuanyuan Palace.

name: Shisi Temple, Jingning
sub: Main hall · Yuan structure in a mountain village
lede: Shisi Temple’s main hall stands among the historic buildings of Daji village in Jingning. Its timber body and layered double-eaved hip-and-gable roof retain the character of a Jiangnan Yuan hall. It dates to 1356, separately from the later Sanqing Hall and repaired bell tower. The temple’s links with the Mei lineage’s ritual and village life make the building an entry point into local religious and family memory as well as an architectural survival.
facts: Form: a timber frame supports the two tiers of eaves beneath a hip-and-gable roof. The main hall stands between the bell tower and Sanqing Hall within a compound of buildings serving different functions.

Dating: the hall was built in 1356, the sixteenth Zhizheng year. Ming and Qing expansion followed; the bell tower was repaired in 1646 and Sanqing Hall is later. One hall’s date does not describe the entire compound.

Significance: the Yuan hall alongside later buildings demonstrates the temple’s gradual growth. Its relationship with the Mei lineage joins religious space with family ritual, preserving several layers of local social history.

name: Stone Halls of Jijian Temple
lede: A small hall built in stone on the pattern of timber: stone columns, stone beams, stone purlins, even the roof is of stone slabs, and the back wall sits directly against the rock face of Tianchi Mountain. The stone hall of Jijian Temple, formerly Xitian Temple, was built in 1357, the seventeenth year of Zhizheng of the Yuan; it is three bays and 7.64 m wide, two bays and 5.52 m deep, under a low, compact single-eaved hip-and-gable roof. To the east and west stand two small stone shrines built around Buddha niches, one inscribed 'Tushita Palace' and the other 'Garden of Bliss', and the standing images inside them are Yuan originals as well.
facts: Form: the stone hall faces south, three bays and 7.64 m wide, two bays and 5.52 m deep, under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; columns, beams, purlins and roof are all carved in stone in imitation of timber, and the back of the hall sits against the natural rock face. The plate shows the front of the stone hall.

Dating: the Jijian Hermitage was founded in 1357, and became a temple after the Ming; the surviving stone hall, niches and images all date from the Yuan, and the site was listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Attached shrines: east and west of the hall stand two stone shrines built around Buddha niches in the manner of timber porches, each one bay wide and half a span deep: the west one has a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof and a standing Amitabha in its niche, inscribed 'Garden of Bliss'; the east one has a single-eaved roof and a standing Maitreya, inscribed 'Tushita Palace'. Yuan stone halls imitating timber are rare in the Jiangnan region, and this is a complete surviving group.

name: Qinglong Temple, Jishan
era: Late Yuan–early Ming · Middle hall murals
yearNote: The subject drawn is the middle hall murals, using the dating range of Sun Bo cited by the Yuncheng Museum; 1360 is only a sorting coordinate. It is not 1289, the completion year of the timber structure, and scholarly opinions on the dating of the murals still differ.
place: Shanxi · Jishan · Macun Village, Jifeng Town
lede: The earliest surviving wall painting of a Water-and-Land ritual in China is in the Middle Hall (yaodian) of Qinglong Temple at Macun: deities of Buddhism, Daoism and Confucianism parade in tiers, the Buddhas of the Three Ages enthroned at the top, drawn from the same southern Shanxi pattern books as the Yongle Palace one ridge away, yet in a manner of its own. An ink inscription of 1289 (26th year of Zhiyuan) under the hall's beams names the master carpenters; for the murals themselves there are two views, contemporary with the timber frame or repainted in the late Yuan to early Ming, and the timeline follows the latter. The plate redraws the Buddhas of the Three Ages in the upper part of the west wall and does not stand for all the murals and sculpture of the hall.
facts: Panels: each "Deities of the Three Realms" panel in the Middle Hall measures 223 cm high by 773 cm wide, principal Buddhas in the top register and lesser deities ranked below, linked by clouds; the line work is mainly iron-wire and nail-head-rat-tail strokes, the colouring based on azurite and malachite with vermilion, yellow, white and red.

Dating: the temple was founded in 662 (2nd year of Longshuo, Tang) and repaired repeatedly in the Yuan and Ming; an ink inscription under the ridge-brick tie beam of the Middle Hall reads "Great Yuan, 26th year of Zhiyuan, mid-autumn ... master carpenters ... respectfully recorded", i.e. the timber frame was completed in 1289; since Sun Bo's 2010 thesis the murals are dated to the Yuan, with a late-Yuan-to-early-Ming view as well.

Significance: the temple holds 196.38 square metres of Yuan and Ming murals; the Middle Hall cycle is regarded as the earliest extant Water-and-Land painting, its three-teachings pantheon leading on to Ming examples such as Pilu Temple; with the Sanqing Hall of Yongle Palace and the Mingying Wang Hall of the Water God Temple it belongs to the group of Yuan murals of southern Shanxi.

name: Pingyao City Wall
sub: Yingxun Gate and adjoining wall sections
yearNote: 1370 is used for sorting by the phase of the wall's expansion; the gate tower and surviving wall faces include later repairs.
siteCoordinateSource: Commons 2025-06-06迎薰门实拍的门前相机点37.198185,112.181053，仅作南门附近近似定位，非城楼中心测绘点。https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:20250606_Yingxun_Men.jpg
lede: After the enlargement and brick facing of 1370 (3rd year of Hongwu, Ming), this circuit of wall at Pingyao, over six thousand metres round and about twelve metres high, was never pulled down: six gates, four corner towers, seventy-two bastions and more than three thousand merlons can still be counted. It is the most complete county-town wall in China and the core of the "one city, two temples" World Heritage property of 1997. The plate takes the south gate, Yingxun Gate, where the arched passage, gate platform and double-eave gate tower stack into one group and the battlemented wall runs off east and west; both tower and wall surfaces include later repairs.
facts: Wall: about 6.4 km in circuit and about 12 m high, rammed earth faced with grey brick, paved on top with a horse ramp inside; a bastion with an enemy tower projects roughly every 50 m, 72 in all, with over three thousand merlons; the moat outside is about 4 m wide and 4 m deep.

History: tradition dates the first wall to King Xuan of Zhou; the present wall was enlarged and brick-cased in 1370 (3rd year of Hongwu, Ming) on the old town, and dozens of later repairs kept the early-Ming scheme; part of the south wall collapsed in 2004 and was rebuilt in 2005.

Heritage: in 1997 the Ancient City of Pingyao, with Shuanglin and Zhenguo temples, was inscribed as World Heritage, the wall enclosing a 225-hectare property; nearly four thousand Ming and Qing shops and dwellings inside bear witness to the town's years as China's financial centre from the 19th to the early 20th century.

name: Dacheng Hall of Hancheng Confucian Temple
era: Rebuilt in the Hongwu era, maintained over the centuries
yearNote: 1371 is the recorded rebuilding of the Confucian Temple on its Yuan site; the Dacheng Hall retains Yuan building methods and has been maintained over the centuries, so not every surviving member can be assigned to 1371.
place: Shaanxi · Weinan · Old town of Hancheng
lede: Hancheng Confucian Temple’s Dacheng Hall presents three broad bays in its front porch but five in the main frame, balancing openness with finer subdivision. Rebuilt on a Yuan site in the Hongwu period, the single-eaved hip-and-gable hall retains earlier displaced-column techniques. Roof, porch columns and interior space reveal layers of Ming rebuilding and later repair rather than one construction date.
facts: The hall is five bays wide, with a three-bay front porch beneath a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof. Large lintels above the eaves columns support the upper structure. Broad open porch bays contrast with the more finely divided frame behind.

The provincial gazetteer cites earlier records for rebuilding the temple on its Yuan site in 1371, followed by repeated repairs. The hall retains Yuan building techniques; the rebuilding date does not establish the manufacture date of every surviving timber.

Some interior columns are displaced, freeing the principal space from an evenly divided column grid. As the main hall for Confucian worship, it combines ritual axial order with practical space. Timber details explain its construction more clearly than the roof alone.

name: Jade Emperor Pavilion of Yuzhou
era: Founded in the 10th year of Hongwu
place: Hebei · Yu County · North city wall
lede: Jingbian Tower places Jade Emperor worship on Yuzhou’s northern city wall, giving a two-storey pavilion three eave lines. An intermediate eave links roof and galleries in strong horizontal bands, combining a frontier presence with temple dignity. Founded in the early Ming and repaired later, the building is best understood by separating roof tiers from usable storeys.
facts: Also called Yuhuang Pavilion, it stands on the northern wall with two storeys and three eave tiers beneath a glazed hip-and-gable roof. Galleries wrap the body; an intermediate eave adds a line without creating a third usable floor.

The provincial authority records foundation in 1377. Brackets and timber proportions retain Ming characteristics, but later repairs must be distinguished from the founding phase; not every visible component is an original early Ming piece.

The pavilion forms a religious precinct with the Heavenly Kings Hall and bell and drum towers, while the city wall gives it a prominent urban position. Frontier defence and Jade Emperor worship meet in the setting implied by its name Jingbian.

name: Xi'an City Wall
sub: Arrow tower of Anding Gate · Ming rampart
lede: Anding Gate’s arrow tower has a broad face pierced by firing windows, while one arch concentrates movement into a single entrance. Xi’an’s western gate developed during the Hongwu expansion, with arrow tower, inner gate tower and barbican forming successive defences. Repaired through the Ming, Qing and modern periods, the brick-faced earthen walls make a defensive plan tangible.
facts: The arrow tower stands on a massive gate platform, its walls densely pierced by firing windows. A central arch passes below it. A barbican connects it to the inner gate tower; the passage is only one component of this layered defensive space.

Local records associate Anding Gate with the expansion of 1374–1378. Repeated Ming and Qing repairs followed, and the outer gate tower was lost in the late Qing. The surviving arrow and inner towers still include later repaired brickwork and timber.

Gate defences had to accommodate both movement and resistance. Raised towers, narrow passages and enclosed courts worked together. Tracing a route from outside to inside explains the city’s defence better than treating its walls as one continuous barrier.

name: Bell Tower and Drum Tower of Xi'an
era: Founded in the Hongwu era · Moved in the Wanli era
place: Shaanxi · Xi'an · Center of the prefectural city
lede: The Bell Tower’s roof converges above a square plan, while the Drum Tower spreads beneath a long ridge. Their bells and drums once made the city’s hours audible. The Drum Tower began in 1380; the Bell Tower followed four years later and moved to today’s street junction in 1582. Comparing bases, passages and eaves reveals a shared timekeeping purpose expressed through different proportions.
facts: The Bell Tower has a square base, intersecting arched passages and three eaves beneath a pyramidal roof. The Drum Tower has a rectangular base, seven-bay frontage and surrounding galleries; its hip-and-gable roof and lower eaves emphasise width.

The Drum Tower was founded in 1380, and the Bell Tower in 1384 before moving in 1582. A new base was built for the relocated Bell Tower. Later repairs mean the foundation dates cannot be assigned to every surviving component.

Both towers announced time, linking sound with the main streets. Square and rectangular platforms, and pyramidal and hip-and-gable roofs, give one civic purpose distinct forms. They are juxtaposed here but are not immediately adjacent in reality.

name: Beamless Hall of Linggu Temple
lede: Not a single piece of timber: the Beamless Hall of Linggu Temple is built entirely of brick, three barrel vaults running side by side from east to west carry the roof, the central one spanning eleven and a half metres and rising fourteen, and the front and rear walls are four metres thick. Built in 1381, the fourteenth year of Hongwu of the Ming, it originally housed the Buddha of Infinite Life, Wuliang, and 'Wuliang Hall' became 'Wuliang Hall', beamless, in speech; it is the largest brick hall of its kind in China. In the Xianfeng era the temple was all but levelled in war and only this brick hall stood; in 1931 it became the memorial hall of the cemetery for fallen soldiers of the National Revolutionary Army.
facts: Form: inside, five bays and 53.8 m from east to west, three bays and 37.85 m from north to south, with the roof 22 m high; a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof in grey glazed tile carries three white glazed lama stupas on the ridge, the central one hollow at the base and open to the ceiling coffer inside to admit light. Three vaults run side by side, the middle one spanning 11.5 m and 14 m high, the side ones 5 m and 7.4 m; front and rear walls each open three doors and are about 4 m thick.

Dating: Linggu Temple was moved here from Dulongfu in 1381 and the Beamless Hall was completed the same year; in the Zhengtong era it housed three great Buddhas with the Twenty-four Devas along the sides and served as a sutra store, and it was repaired repeatedly under Jiaqing and Daoguang; in the Xianfeng era most of the temple's halls burnt in the fighting between Qing and Taiping forces, and only this brick hall survived.

Memorial hall: in 1928 the Nationalist government built the cemetery for fallen soldiers of the National Revolutionary Army on the old temple site, and in 1931 the restored Beamless Hall became its memorial hall, the Hall of Righteous Spirit; 110 slabs of Taihu bluestone set into the walls list 33,224 soldiers who fell in the Northern Expedition and in the fighting against Japan at Shanghai and in north China; the Nanjing municipal government restored it again in 1981.

name: Chongshan Temple, Taiyuan
sub: Hall of Great Compassion · Early Ming official-style timber structure
era: Hongwu era, Ming · Hall of Great Compassion
yearNote: 1385 is only an approximate timeline placement within the Hongwu reign, not a precise completion year. Neither the temple's history nor its Qing main gate replaces the date of the Ming main subject drawn.
lede: In 1381 (14th year of Hongwu, Ming) Zhu Gang, Prince Gong of Jin, enlarged this temple for his late mother Empress Ma; at 140,000 square metres with six great halls on the axis it was once the largest in Shanxi. After a fire in 1864 (3rd year of Tongzhi, Qing) only the fifth hall on the axis, the Dabei Hall, was left. Seven bays wide under double eaves and nearly twenty metres high, together with its three Hongwu-era painted statues over eight metres tall, it is the most dependable specimen of an early-Ming official-style Buddhist hall in Taiyuan. The plate shows the front of the Dabei Hall.
facts: Dabei Hall: seven bays wide and four bays deep, double-eave hip-and-gable (xieshan) roof, nearly 20 m high overall; in the centre stands the Thousand-armed, Thousand-eyed, Eleven-headed Guanyin, flanked by the Thousand-bowl Manjusri and Samantabhadra, all three original Hongwu-period statues over 8 m tall.

History: according to the Daoguang-era Yangqu County Gazetteer the site was a travel palace of Emperor Yang of Sui and was called Baima Temple in the early Tang; the enlargement ran from 1381 to 1391 (14th to 24th years of Hongwu), and the present name dates from the Jiajing reign; after the fire of 1864, Zhang Zhidong in 1882 (8th year of Guangxu) turned the ruined front part into the Taiyuan Prefectural Confucian Temple.

Scale: in the Ming the temple had nearly a thousand bays of halls, the axis running through the Vajra, Heavenly Kings, Mahavira, Vairocana, Dabei and Jinling halls, the Dabei Hall second only to the nine-bay Mahavira Hall; today the temple measures 119.2 m east-west by 71.7 m north-south, covering 8,547 square metres.

name: South Gate of Chongwu Ancient City
sub: Granite gate platform · South gate wall section
era: City built in the 20th year of Hongwu, later repaired
yearNote: 1387 is the founding date of the Chongwu stone city and an approximate timeline placement; the surviving south gate section has undergone later repairs, and the upper gate tower seen in photographs is not labeled as original 1387 fabric.
lede: China's most complete surviving granite coastal fortress town. In 1387 Zhou Dexing, Marquis of Jiangxia, was ordered to build the Chongwu Battalion (qianhusuo) city on the Hui'an headland against pirate raids: a wall of some 2,500 metres, seven metres high, with gates on four sides and barbicans added to the east and west gates. The plate shows a section at the South Gate, a low, massive granite platform with the arched gateway in the middle; the gatehouse above is as it appeared after the comprehensive 1980s restoration 'to the original appearance', and should not be taken as early Ming fabric.
facts: Scale: the walls are built entirely of granite blocks, 2,567 m in circuit, about 500 m north-south and 300 m east-west, 5 m thick at the base and 7 m high; there were originally 26 guard huts, 1,304 crenels and 1,300 arrow slits, with a two- to three-tier rampart walk. The South Gate platform and its arch are one section of this.

History: begun in 1387 and completed in 1394; in 1558 pirates besieged the city for six days and nights and took it; in 1567 Qi Jiguang garrisoned troops here and reorganised the defences. Five major repairs followed between the Yongle and Daoguang reigns, and in 1983-1987 the State Administration of Cultural Heritage funded three phases of restoration, rebuilding 2,517 m of wall to the original appearance.

Comparison: Chongwu was a battalion city in the early Ming coastal garrison (weisuo) system of Fujian, and survives whole because its stone was quarried from local Hui'an granite; within half a square kilometre the town still keeps over twenty temples and nunneries, dozens of ancestral halls and more than two hundred old houses, a live example of the social structure of a southern Fujian military town.

name: Nine-Dragon Screen of Datong
sub: Glazed spirit screen of the Prince of Dai's mansion · Nine-dragon relief
yearNote: The date given by the Palace Museum, the 25th year of Hongwu (1392), is used; the plate depicts only the surviving Nine-Dragon Screen and not the present-day reconstruction of the Prince of Dai's mansion.
place: Shanxi · Datong · Heyang Street, Old city
siteCoordinateSource: 摄影来源页标注40°05′30.47″N、113°17′48.20″E；单体坐标，不改变既有大同城市归并点。
lede: Nine dragons twist among blue-green glazed tiles, with clouds and waves spreading along the long screen. The Nine-Dragon Screen of Datong contains its dense relief between a low coping and a layered Sumeru plinth, leaving behind the screen of an early Ming princely mansion.
facts: The Nine-Dragon Screen was originally the glazed spirit screen in front of the mansion of Zhu Gui, Prince of Dai. The Palace Museum records it as built in the 25th year of Hongwu in the Ming (1392), and it is assigned to the Ming according to the main body of the screen drawn.
The screen is about 45.5 m long and about 8 m high, with nine principal dragons arrayed along its continuous body; the hipped coping and the glazed Sumeru plinth form its upper and lower borders.

A spirit screen serves as a barrier and decoration in front of a building and is not a city wall or fortification. The plate removes the railings, trees and reflecting pool and simplifies the details of the cloud-and-dragon relief, while keeping the multicolored distribution of the actual glazes.

name: Shuanglin Temple, Pingyao
sub: Hall of Heavenly Kings · Painted sculpture
era: Restored in the 2nd year of Wuping, Northern Qi · Rebuilt in the early Ming
lede: It is the first thing you see inside the fortified gate: the five-bay, gable-roofed Hall of the Heavenly Kings, with four guardian Vajra figures three metres tall lined up in its front porch, the opening statement of Shuanglin Temple's more than two thousand Ming painted sculptures. The temple began as Zhongdu Temple; a Northern Song stele in the compound records a rebuilding as early as 571 (2nd year of Wuping, Northern Qi), while today's halls and statues mostly come from a Ming rebuilding, repainted in the Qing. In 1997 it was inscribed as World Heritage with Zhenguo Temple as part of the Ancient City of Pingyao. The plate shows the front of the hall and the porch guardians; the Maitreya, Indra, Brahma and Four Heavenly Kings inside are not in the picture.
facts: Hall of the Heavenly Kings: five bays wide and three deep, single-eave gable (xuanshan) roof; four guardian Vajra figures about 3 m tall stand in the front porch; inside, the crowned Maitreya is 2.2 m high, the attendant Indra and Brahma about 1.75 m, the Four Heavenly Kings face inward from the south wall and the Eight Bodhisattvas line the sides.

Dating: the Gugu Stele of 1011 (4th year of Dazhong Xiangfu, Northern Song) in the temple records that "Zhongdu Temple was rebuilt in the 2nd year of Wuping of Northern Qi (571)"; the Song renamed it after the Buddha's passing between twin sal trees; the existing halls and sculptures come mainly from a Ming rebuilding, repainted in the Qing, and the Ming rammed-earth enclosure with its battlements gives the temple the look of a fort.

Sculpture: ten halls hold 2,052 painted clay figures, 1,566 of them intact, the largest over 3 m and the smallest 30 cm, about three quarters modelled in suspended relief leaning forward 10 to 20 degrees; the clay is local red clay and the eyes are inlaid black glass.

name: Zixiao Palace
era: Built in the Yongle era, Ming
yearNote: The Zixiao Hall is placed by its construction in the Yongle era of the Ming; 1413 is a sorting reference for this phase of the palace's construction and is not presented as the hall's exact completion year. It was later repaired, and the drawing shows the present state seen in research photographs. The Song founding history is kept separate from the Ming hall drawn.
lede: Zixiao Palace’s main hall stands on three stone terraces, with a five-bay timber body and green double-eaved roof. The steps turn mountain slopes into a solemn approach. The palace predates the Ming, while the surviving principal hall belongs to the Yongle emperor’s major building campaign and subsequent repairs. Brackets beneath the eaves and the rising platforms show how Wudang’s Taoist ritual order works with the terrain.
facts: The hall is five bays wide and five deep, with timber framing beneath a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof. Three stone terraces raise it above the approach; stairs lead to the platform, creating an ascending sequence of foundations, columns and eaves.

The palace had a Song-period foundation and underwent major imperially ordered construction during the Ming Yongle reign; the surviving hall belongs to that phase. Later enlargement, beam inscriptions and construction records must be distinguished rather than applying the foundation date to everything visible.

Dedicated to the Supreme Emperor of the Dark Heaven, the hall was important in Wudang’s royal prayer system. Terraces adapted to the slope combine with ordered timberwork to organize worship and display the ritual and building practices of a Taoist palace.

name: Golden Hall of Wudang Mountains
sub: Cast bronze, gilded · Double-eaved hipped roof
yearNote: The drawing shows the surviving Ming Golden Hall on Tianzhu Peak, placed at the 14th year of Yongle (1416); it is not to be confused with the ancient Yuan bronze hall moved into the Zhuanyun Hall. The formal national listing includes both the Yuan and Ming bronze halls; this plate shows only the Ming hall.
lede: The Golden Hall on Wudang’s Tianzhu Peak resembles a small double-eaved timber sanctuary, but columns, beams, brackets, roof tiles, doors and windows are assembled from cast bronze and gilded. Built in 1416, it occupies the ceremonial heart of the summit complex. This surviving Ming hall must be distinguished from the older Yuan bronze hall moved elsewhere. Its metal imitation of timber joins imperial Taoist patronage with casting technology.
facts: The hall is three bays wide and three deep, following a double-eaved, hipped-roof timber form. Cast-bronze columns, beams, brackets, roof surfaces, doors and windows form a complete building while retaining traditional wooden architectural details.

The surviving summit hall was built in Yongle 14, or 1416. Components made in Beijing were transported to Wudang for assembly. The earlier Yuan bronze hall was subsequently moved and is a separate building from the present double-eaved Ming sanctuary.

The summit’s ceremonial centre reflects the scale of Ming imperial support for Taoism. Assembling metal components into a timber-like sanctuary also provides material evidence for historical transport, installation and building techniques.

name: Temple of Heaven, Beijing
sub: Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests
era: Founded in the 18th year of Yongle · Rebuilt in the 22nd year of Guangxu
lede: The Hall of Great Sacrifice was built in the 18th year of Yongle in the Ming (1420); in the Jiajing era it became a round, triple-eaved hall, and under Qianlong it received blue tiles and was renamed the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests. Struck by lightning and burned in the 15th year of Guangxu (1889), it was rebuilt to the original design six years later — what we see today is timber of 1896.
facts: Round, triple-eaved and conical, with blue glazed tiles and a gilded finial; 32.72 m in diameter and 38 m tall overall, it stands on a three-tiered round terrace of white marble.
Twenty-eight columns stand inside: four Dragon Well Columns represent the four seasons, twelve golden columns the twelve months, and twelve eave columns the twelve two-hour periods of the day.
The hall has no great beams; columns, tie-beams and bracket sets support the conical roof layer by layer, the pinnacle of Ming–Qing official-style timber construction.

name: Jimingyi Post Town
sub: East gate platform and flanking old city walls
yearNote: 1420 is the founding year of the Ming post town recognized by the provincial cultural heritage bureau, with further construction in the Ming and Qing; this plate includes a gate tower restored in modern times, and its timber roof is not claimed as Ming original.
siteCoordinateSource: OpenStreetMap node4350819792所标鸡鸣驿古城独立地标，经Mapcarta公开40.45135,115.3088；定位古城，不声称为东门精测点：https://mapcarta.com/N4350819792 。
lede: Jimingyi’s eastern arch compresses the road into a narrow entrance, then its brick platform and flanking walls broaden the view. The Ming and Qing postal and military station accommodated offices, horses and stores alongside residents. The gate gives that transport system a visible boundary. Ming wall history and the restored timber gatehouse belong to different phases, despite their coherent present silhouette.
facts: The nearly square station town has eastern and western gates and walls of rammed earth faced with brick. The eastern platform and adjoining wall sections define the entrance; their mass reveals defensive construction more directly than the timber superstructure.

The provincial authority dates the town’s foundation to 1420, followed by Ming and Qing repairs. The present timber gatehouse includes modern restoration: the founding date describes the station’s history, not the age of every visible timber component.

Offices, horse quarters and stores once stood alongside temples, shops and houses. This mix reflects the station’s role as a transport node; the eastern gate served both defence and the movement of official documents, horses and travellers.

name: Ling'en Hall of Changling, Beijing
sub: Nine-bay nanmu hall · Double-eaved hipped roof
era: Built from Yongle to Xuande · Repaired over the centuries
yearNote: Palace Museum sources record that the sacrificial hall was completed in 1416 and the halls of the mausoleum precinct finished in 1427, while other accounts adopt 1427 as the completion of the hall. 1420 is only an approximate sorting point within the early Ming construction history of the hall drawn; the initial construction of the mausoleum in 1409 is not used as the hall's completion year.
lede: The scale of Changling's Ling'en Hall is easiest to grasp inside: sixty nanmu columns support a hall nine bays wide, with four particularly massive columns at its centre. It housed the spirit tablets of the Yongle Emperor Zhu Di and his empress and formed the ritual heart of the tomb complex. The hall and the whole complex were completed at different times. Palace Museum records date the worship hall to 1416 and completion of the complex's halls to 1427. Its double-eaved hipped roof and stone terrace still express the ceremonial rank of a Ming imperial tomb.
facts: Form: nine bays wide and five deep, the hall has a double-eaved hipped roof carried by sixty columns of solid nanmu timber. The four central columns are about 1.12 metres in diameter; their size and the broad facade convey the scale of the timber structure.

Construction: work on the tomb complex began in 1409. Palace Museum records date completion of the worship hall to 1416 and completion of the complex's halls to 1427. The hall and the larger complex therefore have distinct completion dates.

Ritual: originally called the worship hall, it housed imperial spirit tablets and hosted ceremonies at the tomb. It was renamed Ling'en Hall in 1538: ling evokes blessings received through sacrifice, and en the debt owed to one's parents. The name itself carries ritual meaning.

name: Pagoda of Great Bao'en Temple, Nanjing
era: Begun in the 10th year of Yongle · Completed in the 3rd year of Xuande
lede: Begun in 1412, the tenth year of Yongle of the Ming, and finished in 1428, the third year of Xuande, it had nine storeys and eight sides and rose 78.2 m, its body faced in white porcelain brick, its arched doorways set with lions, elephants and flying rams in five-coloured glazed tile, 152 wind bells hanging from the corner beams and more than a hundred lamps burning through every night; Europeans called it the Porcelain Tower of Nanjing and counted it among the seven wonders of the medieval world. It was blown up in 1856 during the Taiping internal purge at Tianjing, leaving only the finial and stone steles; the ink-numbered glazed components unearthed in 1958 and the Seven-Jewel Ashoka Stupa found in the crypt in 2008 are what remain of it in physical form. The plate is based on a reconstruction model.
facts: Form: the glazed pagoda had nine storeys and eight sides and a total height of 78.2 m, visible from the Yangtze tens of li away; the body was faced in white porcelain, the arched doors framed in glazed tile with lions, white elephants, flying rams and other motifs in five colours; the finial was set with gold, silver and jewels, 152 wind bells hung beneath the corner beams, and the inner walls were lined with Buddha niches.

Dating: in 1412 the Yongle Emperor ordered the Ministry of Works to rebuild Tianxi Temple, and in 1424 he named it the Great Bao'en Temple and composed its stele text himself; the pagoda was begun the same year and completed in 1428, after nineteen years, reportedly under the supervision of Zheng He, then garrison commander of Nanjing. Fire at the end of the Jiajing era left 'only the pagoda, the meditation hall and the kitchen standing'.

Destruction and finds: in 1856, during the Taiping purge at Tianjing, the North King Wei Changhui ordered it blown up to deny the Wing King's troops a platform for cannon, leaving only the finial and steles. In 1958 a large number of glazed components bearing ink-written serial marks were unearthed around Yaogang Village, and tradition says three identical sets were fired; in 2008 an iron casket at the site yielded the Seven-Jewel Ashoka Stupa containing the 'Buddha's parietal bone relic', and the site park opened in 2015.
captions: Nine stories, eight faces · Drawn from the Tushanwan model of the old pagoda
Original pagoda destroyed · Not the modern glass tower

name: Zhihua Temple, Beijing
sub: Tathagata Hall · Ten Thousand Buddha Pavilion
era: Founded in the Zhengtong era · Surviving Ming halls
yearNote: Official descriptions give 1443 and 1444 respectively as the founding year of Zhihua Temple. 1444 is used for approximate sorting; the temple's founding year cannot be taken directly as the precise date of making of every surviving member.
lede: Beneath black glazed tiles, Rulai Hall and Wanfoge form a single two-storey Buddhist hall. The lower storey is five bays wide and the upper narrows to three, making the stepping back of walls and roofs especially clear. Zhihua Temple was commissioned by the Ming eunuch Wang Zhen. Official accounts describe construction beginning in 1443 and completion in 1444. Its densely arranged Buddha niches and surviving Ming timber structure make this temple tucked into a hutong a material record of Ming Buddhist architecture as well as a distinctive black-tiled building.
facts: Storeys: Rulai Hall below and Wanfoge above have separate names but form one building. The lower level is five bays wide and three deep; the upper is three bays square. The narrowing facade and rooflines clearly articulate the two levels.

History: Wang Zhen commissioned Zhihua Temple as his family temple. Beijing government material dates its beginning to 1443, while a municipal heritage research introduction dates completion to 1444. These refer to the building campaign, rather than independently dating every hall.

Details: black glazed tiles and dense rows of Buddha niches are prominent features. The surviving Ming timber halls, decorative painting and bracket sets also provide material evidence for studying the transition from Song and Yuan building traditions to those of the Ming and Qing.

name: Hunyuan Confucian Temple
place: Shanxi · Datong · Old town of Hunyuan · Yong'an West Street
lede: At the prefectural school of Hunyuan below the Northern Sacred Peak, the Dacheng Hall is the one building in the compound with real presence: five bays wide and three deep, roofed in yellow and green glazed tile, its central and second bays fully fitted with six-rail lattice doors while the end bays are solid brick, and the brick rear wall carries the four large characters "loyalty, filial piety, chastity, righteousness". The gazetteer records a large-scale rebuilding in 1472 (8th year of Chenghua, Ming), and the surviving hall is generally taken as a Ming structure; the omission of the front interior columns and the plain four-puzuo bracket sets under the eaves keep an older feel. The plate shows the front of the Dacheng Hall.
facts: Dacheng Hall: five bays and 27.6 m wide, three bays and 14.6 m deep, single-eave hip-and-gable roof in yellow and green glazed tile; four-puzuo bracket sets with two intercolumnar sets each in the central and second bays, the front row of interior columns omitted; the terrace in front is about 13 m long, 6 m wide and 1.5 m high, with a two-dragons-and-pearl imperial ramp in the middle.

Dating: the Qianlong-era Hunyuan Prefecture Gazetteer says the temple predates the Liao and Jin, was enlarged in the early Yuan, rebuilt on a large scale in 1472 (8th year of Chenghua, Ming) and completed in the Wanli reign; the National Cultural Heritage Administration registers it as Ming to Qing, and the hall itself has no firm completion date.

Layout: along the axis only the Ji Gate, Dacheng Hall, Zunjing Pavilion and Chongsheng Shrine survive, the pavilion a brick vault below and a timber loft above; the "loyalty, filial piety, chastity, righteousness" brickwork resembles the carved brick inscriptions of nearby Yong'an Temple, whose glazed roof fittings also match those of this hall.

name: Diamond Throne Pagoda of Zhenjue Temple, Beijing
era: Completed in the 9th year of Chenghua
lede: The five small pagodas do not stand separately on the ground: they share a tall stone-clad platform, the distinctive arrangement of Zhenjue Temple's Vajra Throne. The platform has a brick core faced with pale grey stone, with closely spaced eaves rising on the pagodas above. The group gave the temple its popular name, Five Pagoda Temple. Completed in 1473, the throne draws on Buddhist architecture at Bodh Gaya in India. Buddha images, Sanskrit mantras and Tibetan benedictions carved into its surfaces brought that imported form into the Buddhist art of Ming Beijing.
facts: Form: the tall throne has a brick core clad in pale grey stone and carries five small pagodas with closely spaced eaves. A passage inside reaches the top, making the supporting platform itself a building that could be entered and climbed.

Dating: Zhenjue Temple was founded during the Yongle reign, but the surviving Vajra Throne was completed in 1473, in the Chenghua reign. Restoration during Qianlong's reign brought the name Zhengjue Temple. The temple's names and the throne's construction date are distinct matters.

Exchange: the pagodas draw on architectural forms at Bodh Gaya in India. Buddha images, Sanskrit mantras and Tibetan benedictions carved into the stone combine different languages and imagery in one religious setting, recording exchanges in Chinese and Tibetan Buddhist art during the Ming.
