name: Qingyuan Tower, Xuanhua
sub: Triple-eaved bell tower with cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof, and brick platform
yearNote: Only one Xuanhua city tower is selected as representative; Zhenshuo Tower and the Five-Dragon Screen are not added.
lede: A street passes beneath Qingyuan Tower’s lofty brick platform while the building spreads above it through a cross-shaped roof. Three interlocking eave lines produce a complex but ordered relationship between centre and wings. Founded in the Ming Chenghua era on Xuanhua’s central axis, the tower combines timekeeping, an urban landmark and frontier memory in glazed upper tiles, plain lower roofs and plaques facing four directions.
facts: The tower has three storeys, three eave tiers and a cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof on a brick platform. A gallery surrounds the lower level, with panelled openings above; interlocking roof planes unite four elevations rather than simply stacking roofs.

Founded in 1482, Qingyuan Tower underwent successive repairs. Its present layout and form continue the Ming bell-tower tradition; the founding date should be separated from later replacements and repairs to roofing and timber components.

Glazed tiles cover the upper roof, with plain tiles on the lower tiers; plaques address all four directions. Material hierarchy and directional titles strengthen its street-centre role, organising urban views and preserving Xuanhua’s frontier associations.

name: Jianshui Confucian Temple
sub: Hall of the First Teacher · Dacheng Hall
yearNote: 1495 is only an approximate sorting point within the Hongzhi era (1488–1505); dating follows the Hall of the First Teacher drawn, and the temple's founding date of 1285 is not substituted for it.
place: Yunnan · Jianshui · Old city of Lin'an
lede: Beyond Dacheng Gate, Xianshi Hall occupies a raised platform towards the rear of Jianshui’s Confucian temple axis. A single hip-and-gable roof covers its five-bay front. Stone exterior columns and carved wooden doors reveal local workmanship and cooperation between materials. The temple began in the Yuan period, but this hall is dated to the Ming Hongzhi reign; their histories should be distinguished.
facts: Xianshi Hall, also called Dacheng Hall, has a five-bay front and a single hip-and-gable roof supported by stone columns and timber framing. Its carved exterior columns and lattice doors reward close comparison of materials and details.

The temple was founded in 1285, while the hall is attributed to construction during the Hongzhi reign of 1488–1505. Its precise completion year is not established. The temple’s foundation and the later hall belong to different stages that can be read along the axis.

The principal hall for worshipping Confucius stands high towards the rear to emphasise its ceremonial role. Stone columns, carved timber doors and painted framing show how shared Confucian architectural conventions acquired local workmanship.

name: City God Temple of Yuci
sub: Xuanjian Tower · Music tower and stage
era: Ming · Xuanjian Tower and music tower
yearNote: Xuanjian Tower (1497) and the music tower (1511) are supported by stele records; the date of about 1523 for the stage in front is an inference by the cultural relics survey from a date on the screen wall.
lede: Xuanjian Tower is not one building but a group stacked up by three generations: in 1497 (10th year of Hongzhi, Ming) the five-bay, two-storey, triple-eaved tower, seventeen metres high, went up south of the main hall; later a music hall was fitted against its north eave, less than a metre between the two roofs, and a one-bay, round-ridged, hip-and-gable street stage pushed further north, flanked by Ming glazed-tile splayed screen walls. The peacock-blue glazed roofs rise and fall, and from the courtyard they read as a single whole. The plate shows this northern group; the main hall, Xianyou Hall, and the gate are not in the picture.
facts: Xuanjian Tower: five bays wide and four rafters deep, two storeys under three tiers of hip-and-gable eaves, 17 m high overall, peacock-blue glazed roof, three hollow caisson ceilings inside; to the north adjoins the two-rafter-deep music hall, and beyond it a one-bay street stage with a single round-ridged hip-and-gable roof, flanked by glazed splayed screen walls under hip-and-gable roofs.

Dating: the temple was founded in 1362 (22nd year of Zhizheng, Yuan), moved to the present site in 1431 (6th year of Xuande, Ming) and enlarged in the Chenghua and Hongzhi reigns; the tower was built in 1497 (10th year of Hongzhi), the gate in 1509 (4th year of Zhengde), and the music hall and stage were completed by the early Jiajing reign (around 1523), giving the present scale.

Significance: roofs of three periods interlock, and the screen walls and music hall enclose an acoustic space, a model of the Ming city-god-temple composite of tower, music hall and stage; it became a national key protected site in 1996 and was placed on the World Monuments Fund Watch list in 2000.

name: Zhaoling Palace, Xianyou
era: Ming · Exact date to be determined
place: Fujian · Putian · Dingdonghu Village, Xiyuan Township, Xianyou
lede: Zhaoling Palace’s low hip-and-gable roof shelters a three-bay timber hall on a stone platform. Railings along the front and sides carry rain screens, combining circulation, seating and shelter. A county heritage notice records a mid-Ming foundation and subsequent repairs, with Ming stone column bases still present. Rather than enclosing the hall in high walls, its frame, railings and rain screens create a light appearance, revealing how village timber architecture responds to terrain and weather.
facts: The freestanding timber hall stands on a stone platform. Its main chamber is three bays wide and five purlin lines deep, with a hip-and-gable roof and mixed raised-beam and column-and-tie framing. Rain screens above front and side railings link the roof to the veranda edge.

The county government’s 2024 heritage notice records a mid-Ming foundation and repairs in December 1984. The exact original year remains unknown, and surviving components belong to different phases rather than all being Ming material.

Plain Ming stone column bases shaped like inverted bowls survive alongside timber framing, railings and rain screens. This county-protected building provides material evidence for regional small timber halls and adaptive construction in mountain villages.

name: Yan'an Pagoda (Lingshan Temple Pagoda)
sub: Octagonal nine-story brick pagoda · Surviving Ming form
era: Tang–Song history, restored in the Ming
yearNote: The combined national listing marks it as Song; educational sources describe the surviving pagoda as a Ming building. The plate and timeline list it as Ming according to its surviving restored form; 1500 is only an approximate sorting point, not a confirmed rebuilding year.
lede: Yan’an’s nine-storey octagonal pagoda belongs both to an old temple and to modern collective memory. A tall lower storey supports a narrowing stack, its brick eaves dividing the vertical mass clearly. Lingshan Temple Pagoda has Tang and Song antecedents, while the visible form is treated here as a Ming rebuilding. Later postage stamps record another layer of symbolic meaning.
facts: This nine-storey octagonal brick pagoda has a tall lower storey and progressively narrower upper levels. Projecting cornices alternate with openings and solid walls, creating a compact vertical outline recognisable from a distance.

Tang and Song antecedents are recorded, and the heritage listing says Song, while educational material identifies the standing structure as Ming. Its visible outline is therefore understood as a Ming rebuilding, with an unresolved exact date; earlier foundations do not date its present appearance.

The outline of Pagoda Hill appeared repeatedly on stamps depicting revolutionary sites, giving an old building new symbolic meanings. Its construction history overlaps with modern image circulation, making it both a surviving monument and a city emblem.

name: Dashi Pavilion of Yong'an, Hepu
sub: Low front, high rear · Linked timber pavilions
yearNote: Listed as Ming in the third batch of national protected sites; 1500 is only an approximate sorting point within the Ming, not an established construction year. The plate shows the linked front and rear pavilions; the incense-burner pavilions around them are not part of the subject drawn.
lede: Dashi Pavilion joins two timber pavilions, lower at the front and higher behind. Open ground floors and boarded upper rooms reveal the relationships between columns, beams and projecting eaves. Ridge figures and painted decoration bring mythical subjects and flowers into the timber frame. The building is attributed to Ming and was repaired during the Qing Daoguang reign, without a confirmed construction year. Its name recalls the worship of Avalokiteshvara here.
facts: Two connected pavilions have open lower levels and boarded upper rooms with doors and windows. Columns rest on lotus-carved stone pads; mortise-and-tenon joints connect beams, while projecting beams carry broad eaves.

The pavilion is classified as Ming, with repairs recorded during the Qing Daoguang reign and later conservation reflected today. Its exact construction year requires further study; early carpentry techniques and later repairs should be distinguished.

Column supports, framing and projecting eaves preserve earlier southern carpentry traditions. Ridge figures and painting express local decoration. Worship of Avalokiteshvara gave the pavilion its name, joining religious use with structural continuity.

name: Jiayu Pass
era: Built in the Hongzhi to Zhengde reigns, Ming
yearNote: The drawing shows the Jiayuguan Tower on the west side and its gate platform. The tower was built during the Hongzhi to Zhengde reigns of the Ming and repaired continuously in later periods; 1500 is only an approximate sorting point and does not equal a completion year, nor is the establishment of the pass in 1372 used in place of the tower's date.
lede: A single arch pierces a massive gate platform, with the three-storey Jiayuguan Tower spreading three tiers of eaves above it. It marks the west-facing entrance of the outer enclosure, serving as both a lookout and a threshold within successive defences. The pass and this tower were established more than a century apart, within the gradual strengthening of Ming frontier defence.
facts: The western tower stands on the outer enclosure’s gate platform, above a west-facing arch. Each of its three storeys has eaves. Columns and galleries lighten the upper silhouette, while the substantial platform links entrance and curtain wall.

The fort was established in 1372, while the western gate tower belongs to construction in the Hongzhi–Zhengde period and underwent later repairs. Fort and tower did not originate together; a broad period attribution cannot replace precise construction evidence.

Jiayuguan, Rouyuan and Guanghua towers share an axis but occupy different gateways. Identifying them reveals how the outer enclosure, barbicans and inner city organised both passage and defence in successive layers.

name: Earthen Stupa of the Great Buddha Temple, Zhangye
era: Built in the Ming · Later restored
yearNote: The earthen stupa was built in about the Ming dynasty; 1500 is only an approximate Ming sorting point. An earthquake in 1927 damaged the top, which was restored in 1986. The drawing takes the upper stupa body and finial visible in photographs and does not invent the lower base hidden by the front hall and courtyard walls.
lede: A broad dome supports a niche-bearing section, followed by rings and a finial that stretch the outline upwards. The earthen pagoda at Zhangye’s Great Buddha Temple, also called the Amitabha Thousand-Buddha Pagoda, contrasts with the broad Buddha hall. This view shows the part visible above halls and enclosure walls. It is approximately Ming in date, with a repaired earthquake-damaged summit.
facts: The visible upper section combines a domed body, a Sumeru-base-like niche section, rings and a finial, echoed by small towers. Transitions between rounded mass and rectilinear niches distinguish its silhouette from a storeyed pagoda.

Local historical sources broadly attribute the tower to the Ming period, without a precise construction year. An earthquake damaged its summit in 1927, and restoration followed in 1986; the present finial includes repairs rather than entirely original fabric.

The pagoda and Buddha hall share a temple but use different architectural forms: the dome and rings rise to a point, while a timber hall shelters a reclining Buddha. Even the exposed upper section reveals the pagoda’s separate role.

name: Gongzhu Temple, Fanshi
lede: This small temple in Princess Village, named for a Northern Wei princess, keeps its interest indoors: the Mahavira Hall is only three bays wide under a gable roof, with not even bracket sets under the eaves, yet its four walls are covered with Ming Water-and-Land murals in which Buddhas, bodhisattvas, devas and Daoist gods assemble in tiers, a complete Ming mural cycle of this genre. Tradition credits the founding to Princess Chengxin, fourth daughter of Emperor Wencheng of Northern Wei; the surviving halls are dated by a restoration of 1503 (16th year of Hongzhi, Ming), and the Mahavira Hall and the passage hall before it are the temple's only Ming structures. The plate shows the front of the Mahavira Hall; the murals are inside.
facts: Mahavira Hall: three bays wide and six rafters deep, single-eave gable (xuanshan) roof, no bracket sets under the eaves; the passage hall in front is three bays square under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof with five-puzuo bracket sets, and these two are the only Ming buildings left in the temple.

Dating: tradition attributes the temple to Princess Chengxin, fourth daughter of Emperor Wencheng of Northern Wei; it was restored in 1503 (16th year of Hongzhi, Ming) and is registered by the National Cultural Heritage Administration as Ming to Qing; facing south with three courtyards, it covers 4,347 square metres with 1,116 square metres of buildings.

Murals: the Mahavira Hall preserves Ming Water-and-Land murals with Buddhist and Daoist deities painted in one assembly; the Qielan, Horse King, God of Wealth and Erlang halls on either side were all built in the Qing and belong to a different period from the murals inside.

name: Kaiyuan Temple, Xingtai
sub: Bodhisattva Hall of the old Kaiyuan Temple (third hall / Sakyamuni Hall), full facade and four coiling-dragon stone columns
yearNote: The Vairocana Hall burned in 1988 and was rebuilt in 1997, so it was not chosen. Instead the plate uses the Bodhisattva Hall, restored in the 13th year of Zhengde in the Ming, and its four coiling-dragon stone columns inscribed 1518. It must be distinguished from the new temple of 2013 on the east side.
siteCoordinateSource: Commons实拍 https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:邢台开元寺菩萨殿.jpg 的相机位置37.073486,114.505767、北向1.03°；取菩萨殿近似定位（约十米偏移），非测绘坐标。
lede: The four dragon-carved stone columns beneath Pusa Hall’s eaves invite closer attention than its five-bay roof alone. Dragons project from single stone blocks, surrounded by foliage and clouds, turning load-bearing members into sculpture. This third hall in old Kaiyuan Temple follows a Ming rebuilding phase; dated inscriptions on the columns anchor the visual impression in written evidence, distinct from the temple’s earlier origins.
facts: Pusa Hall, also called Shakyamuni Hall, occupies the third position on the old temple axis. It is five bays wide with a gable roof. Four dragon-carved front columns support the eaves, their varying relief adding depth to the elevation.

The hall is assigned to the rebuilding phase of 1518; the columns carry an inscription for their erection in the seventh month of that year. The earlier temple foundation is distinct, as is the rebuilding of a fire-damaged Pilu Hall.

Dragons, clouds and foliage surround the columns, while donor names and places of origin survive below. Sculpture and building inscriptions share the same stone member, documenting both craftsmanship and local participation in temple construction.

name: Houtu Temple, Jiexiu
sub: Sanqing Tower · Hall and stage combined
yearNote: The construction of the Sanqing Tower and the Offering Tower in about the Zhengde period is used as the sorting point; the dates 1516 and 1519 in stele records and sources each refer to different things, and 1519 is not forced to stand as the completion year of every component drawn.
lede: Jiexiu's Houtu Temple stacks hall, stage and tower into one building: the lower floor of the Sanqing Tower is the Sanqing Hall, the upper floor is wrapped by a gallery on three sides, and the back is a stage facing the Houtu Great Hall, thirteen metres high, the tallest surviving Ming theatre stage; the double-eaved splayed screen walls on either side were forced up to match, with a brick eave below and a timber eave above. The Jiexiu heritage office records its founding in 1519 (14th year of Zhengde, Ming), and every roof in the temple is glazed, five-coloured except for the yellow of the Houtu Hall group; here glazed tile is not trim but the main event. The plate shows the stage on the north face of the Sanqing Tower with its splayed screen walls.
facts: Sanqing Tower: two storeys under three tiers of hip-and-gable eaves, 15.2 m high overall, with a two-storey, triple-eaved cross-ridged porch projecting in front to join the offering hall; the stage at the back is 13 m high, its lower level barely tall enough to stand in; the splayed screen walls on either side have double gable eaves, carved brick below and timber above, their bargeboards decorated with purple-and-white glazed "mice stealing grapes".

Dating: the Jiexiu heritage office dates the founding of the Sanqing Tower to 1519 (14th year of Zhengde, Ming); the restoration of 1516 (11th year of Zhengde) absorbed the Zhenwu Hall and Sanguan Shrine, the Earth God Temple of 1730 (8th year of Yongzheng, Qing) completed the layout of eight linked temples, and repairs followed in 1835 (15th year of Daoguang).

Glazed tile: all 29 buildings are roofed in glazed tile, the Houtu Hall group in yellow and the rest in yellow, green, blue, white and ochre, mostly replaced in Qing repairs, while a few Song tiles survive on the Sanqing Tower; the more than a thousand Ming Daoist painted statues inside are equally rare.

name: Iron Buddha Temple, Gaoping
era: Restored in the 1st year of Jiajing
place: Shanxi · Gaoping · Mishan Town · Mixi Village
lede: In the lanes of Mixi Village, the three-bay main hall of the Iron Buddha Temple is finished with an overhanging gable roof and glazed ridge ornaments. Step inside and the Twenty-Four Devas unfold along the walls — glaring, smiling, eyes lowered — their beards, hair and streamers held out on iron wire, giving the clay figures expressions on the verge of movement.
facts: The main hall is three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved overhanging gable roof. The front-eave bracket sets are five-tiered (wucai) with double cantilevers (ang), and a glazed ornament of a lion bearing a treasure vase stands at the center of the ridge.

The Ming painted clay figures of the Twenty-Four Devas inside the hall are modeled in clay over wooden armatures; their beards, hair, headdresses and streamers are shaped with iron wire, making the details light yet full of tension.

The founding date is unknown. In the 7th year of Dading in the Jin (1167) an iron Buddha was cast and the temple restored; it was repaired again in the 1st year of Jiajing (1522) and the 3rd year of Wanli (1575) in the Ming, and in the Qing. The surviving buildings show a Ming–Qing style.

name: Feihong Pagoda of Guangsheng Temple
era: Begun in the 10th year of Zhengde · Completed in the 6th year of Jiajing
lede: Between 1515 and 1527 (10th year of Zhengde to 6th year of Jiajing, Ming) the monk Dalian raised funds for over a decade and set this brick pagoda, octagonal, thirteen storeys and over forty-seven metres high, at the very front of the axis of the Upper Temple on Mount Huo. Its outer skin, from eaves and bracket sets to Buddhas, guardians and coiling dragons, is entirely fired glaze in red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet, making it the largest and most complete glazed pagoda surviving in China. It stands on the site of a Yuan predecessor and later rode out the great earthquakes of 1556 in Guanzhong and 1695 in Pingyang. The plate shows the whole Feihong Pagoda.
facts: Body: octagonal in plan, thirteen storeys, 47.31 m high overall (47.6 m in another source), tapering sharply into a cone; the core is brick and stone, and on every storey the eaves, bracket sets, niches, figures and coiling dragons are glazed components in red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet.

Dating: rebuilt on the Yuan site from 1515 (10th year of Zhengde, Ming) with funds raised by the eminent monk Dalian and completed in 1527 (6th year of Jiajing); it then survived unharmed the Guanzhong earthquake of 1556 (35th year of Jiajing) and the Pingyang earthquake of 1695 (34th year of Kangxi).

Connections: Guangsheng Temple was listed among the first batch of national key protected sites in 1961; the Yuan murals of the Lower Temple were sold in 1928 and are now divided among three American museums; the "Tang monk sweeps the pagoda" episode of the 1986 television series Journey to the West was filmed here.

name: Ming Xianling Mausoleum
sub: Lingxing Gate · Dragon and Phoenix Gate
yearNote: The surviving Lingxing Gate belongs to the Ming stone remains of the Xianling; 1540 is only a broad sorting point within the Jiajing period, not the exact completion year of this stone archway. Only the stone archway and its linked glazed screen walls are drawn; the stele tower (minglou) restored in 1990 is not drawn, and the founding year of the imperial tomb is not applied to all of its buildings.
lede: Lingxing Gate divides Xianling’s spirit way into three openings between six stone posts. Hou beasts, a flaming jewel and yellow-glazed screen walls mark a ceremonial threshold. Carved beams and panels imitate timber construction in stone. The gate belongs to the mausoleum’s Ming remains, but its precise completion year is unconfirmed. Repairs in 1996 reinstated displaced pieces, leaving the present appearance with a visible history of conservation.
facts: This soaring stone gateway has three openings, six posts and four small roof units. Cloud plaques, lotus bases, hou beasts and a flaming jewel crown the posts; adjoining yellow-glazed screen walls stand on moulded bases.

The stone gate belongs to Ming Xianling, in the historical setting of the Jiajing reign, without a confirmed completion year. Conservation in 1996 reinstated originals, supplied missing pieces and restored connecting walls.

The gateway turns the continuous spirit way into a ranked ceremonial threshold. Timber-like stone carving and yellow glaze express imperial funerary architecture; original pieces and repairs also reveal how its remains have been preserved.

name: Imperial Ancestral Temple, Beijing
lede: Eleven bays across, sixty-eight nanmu columns and a three-tier white marble terrace give the Imperial Ancestral Temple's front worship hall a scale comparable to the palace's great halls. For major ancestral rites, imperial spirit tablets were brought forward from the buildings behind it. The temple was founded in 1420, alongside the Forbidden City, while its principal surviving arrangement follows the reconstruction of 1545. The hall's scale and the division of duties among the buildings express dynastic ritual through architecture, rather than the needs of everyday residence.
facts: Form: the worship hall is eleven bays wide and six deep, with a double-eaved hipped roof of yellow glazed tiles on a three-tier white marble terrace. Sixty-eight solid nanmu columns support its timber frame; the broad facade and high terrace establish the rank of the ritual setting.

History: founded in 1420, the temple was rebuilt in 1545, restoring collective worship with separate chambers in one hall. The principal surviving arrangement follows this rebuilding. The foundation of the temple and the dating adopted for the present worship hall should be described separately.

Ritual: the front worship hall hosted major ancestral ceremonies, while the resting hall and the distant-ancestor hall had different duties in housing spirit tablets. Before a major rite, tablets were moved onto the worship hall's seats. The sequence of halls thus served a specific ritual process.

name: White Pagoda, Fuzhou
lede: The Black Pagoda is stone; the White Pagoda is brick. In 904 Wang Shenzhi built the Bao'en Dingguang Duobao Pagoda at the western foot of Yushan to earn merit for his parents, originally a seven-storey tower with a brick core and timber galleries. Struck by lightning and burnt in 1534, it was rebuilt in 1548, when the brick core was simply made the body of the pagoda itself, coated in white lime, octagonal and seven storeys high with a gourd-shaped finial. The clean, plain silhouette seen today is the Ming rebuilding.
facts: Form: an octagonal seven-storey pavilion-style brick pagoda, 41 m high, with plain white-limed walls and a gourd finial; the brick core contains a hanging-post spiral stair to the top. In 1963, while the surroundings were cleared, fifteen Tang-dynasty carved bluestone panels from a Sumeru-base waist were unearthed, with sea legends, lions and peonies, and are now set up on the spot.

History: the Shiguo Chunqiu records that in 904 Wang Shenzhi built the pagoda for his late parents; the original had a brick core with timber work outside. It was destroyed by lightning fire in 1534 and rebuilt as the present pagoda in 1548; the stair was replaced in a 1958 repair, and in 1991 it was listed as a Fujian provincial protected site.

Counterpart: it faces the Five Dynasties Black Pagoda at the eastern foot of Wushan across the old city; together they are the 'Three Hills and Two Pagodas' that have marked Fuzhou for a millennium, and the pairing of stone with brick, black with white, shows the different materials and methods of Five Dynasties and Ming pagoda building.

name: Twin Pagodas of Haihui Temple, Yangcheng
sub: Hexagonal brick pagoda · Octagonal glazed pagoda
yearNote: 1565 is only a sorting point for the construction period of the large Ming pagoda; sources give either 1561 or 1565–1568. The small pagoda was founded in the Five Dynasties and altered in the Song; the two pagodas were not built in the same year.
place: Shanxi · Yangcheng · Pagoda courtyard of Haihui Temple, Daqiao Village
lede: Two pagodas stand one behind the other, six centuries apart: the small one in front, hexagonal and ten storeys, is the relic pagoda built for the Chan master Shunmin in 922 (2nd year of Longde, Later Liang), studded with little niches and leaning slightly west; the great one behind, octagonal, thirteen storeys and about fifty-seven metres high, was built between 1565 and 1568 (Jiajing to Longqing reigns, Ming) with over two thousand taels of silver donated by the merchant Li Sixiao, its lowest three storeys wrapped in a battlemented wall like a castle while the tenth storey throws out a ring of glazed hanging galleries. Among the storeyed pagodas of north China there is no second example. The plate shows both pagodas together.
facts: Two pagodas: the small pagoda is grey brick, hexagonal, ten storeys with corbelled eaves, about 20 m high, its outer walls covered with Buddha niches; the great pagoda is octagonal, thirteen storeys and about 57 m high, its bottom three storeys enclosed by a battlemented masonry wall, and at the tenth storey a glazed balcony gallery projects, three bays to a side, twenty-four in all, with glazed columns, balustrades and brackets.

Dating: the stele "Later Record of Longquan Chan Cloister" of 956 (3rd year of Xiande, Later Zhou) in the temple dates the small pagoda to 922 (2nd year of Longde, Later Liang); the stele by Wang Guoguang, Ming Minister of Rites, "Record of Rebuilding the Precious Pagoda and Buddha Hall of Longquan Temple", dates the great pagoda to the Jiajing-Longqing years 1565 to 1568, with another view favouring 1561 (40th year of Jiajing).

Assessment: the great pagoda is also called the Glazed Pagoda for its glazed eave edges and galleries, and Zhang Yuhuan ranked it "the crown of the famous pagodas of Shangdang"; the temple housed the Haihui Academy in the Ming and Qing, was among the first provincial protected sites of Shanxi in 1965, and became a national key protected site together with the pagodas in 2006.

name: Zhenwu Pavilion on the Jinglue Terrace
sub: Timber pavilion of Rong County · Triple eaves
yearNote: 1573 is taken as the construction date of the Zhenwu Pavilion; the earlier history of the Jinglue Terrace is listed separately from the surviving pavilion, and later repairs do not amount to rebuilding the whole pavilion.
lede: Zhenwu Pavilion projects three broad tiers of eaves above the older Jinglüe Terrace. Columns and beams meet visibly in the open lower level. Its most unusual detail is on the second level: four internal column feet stop above the floor, with loads transferred through interlocking timbers towards outer supports. The pavilion was built in 1573. Its date should be distinguished from the terrace’s earlier history; tracing the supports reveals more than counting roofs alone.
facts: Mortise-and-tenon joints connect hardwood components and broad eaves. Four internal columns on the second level do not touch its floor. Projecting beams use outer columns as fulcrums to connect the eaves and upper loads.

The surviving pavilion was built in 1573, the first Wanli year of Ming, to honour Zhenwu. The terrace has an earlier history. Later conservation continues the timber structure rather than necessarily creating a wholly new pavilion.

Suspended column feet belong to a structural system, not merely an ornamental curiosity. The framing joins eaves, inner columns and levels, illustrating the balance between projection and load-bearing in southern Ming timber pavilions.

name: Guanyin Hall, Changzhi
lede: A small hall of three bays whose walls, roof frame and the spaces above doors and windows are entirely taken over by sculpture: Guanyin sits in the centre with Manjusri and Samantabhadra at her sides, celestial palaces rise tier upon tier behind her, the Eighteen Arhats, Twenty-four Devas and Twelve Bodhisattvas of Perfect Enlightenment ring the room in layers, and on the top tier the south wall carries Daoist immortals, the north wall Confucian worthies, so that Sakyamuni, Laozi and Confucius share one hall. Over five hundred suspended clay figures of around 1582 (10th year of Wanli, Ming) turn the belief in the unity of the three teachings into a visible world. The plate takes the central Guanyin and part of the celestial palaces and does not stand for the whole hall.
facts: Main hall: three bays wide and four rafters deep, single-eave gable (xuanshan) roof covered in yellow and green glazed tile with coiling-dragon and passion-flower patterns; inside are more than five hundred Ming suspended clay figures, gilded and painted, arranged in tiers on the walls, roof frame and upper parts of doors and windows.

Dating: the Guanyin Hall was built in 1582 (10th year of Wanli, Ming) and repaired in the Qing; the name board was written in 1583 (11th year of Wanli) by Gao Qin, Vice Minister of War; the temple faces west with two courtyards over 7,400 square metres, the main hall Ming and the rest Qing.

Subjects: the altar holds Guanyin, Manjusri and Samantabhadra, the rear wall shows the life of the Buddha, the sides carry the Eighteen Arhats, Twenty-four Devas and Twelve Bodhisattvas of Perfect Enlightenment, and the fourth tier has Daoist figures on the south wall and Confucian ones on the north, with Sakyamuni in the middle and Laozi and Confucius to either side, a physical record of the merging of the three teachings in a village temple.

name: Hanging Temple, Hunyuan
sub: Pavilions on a sheer cliff · Unity of the Three Teachings
place: Shanxi · Hunyuan · Jinlong Gorge, Mount Heng
lede: The whole temple hangs in a recess halfway up Cuiping Mountain, its highest point more than ninety metres above the valley floor. It looks as if dozens of slender timber posts hold it up, but the real load is carried by twenty-seven beams driven into the rock; most of the posts are little more than reassurance. The north and south flying pavilions, three storeys and over ten metres high, float free on three sides and are linked by two plank walks wide enough for one person; the Three Teachings Hall on the top floor of the north pavilion seats Sakyamuni, Confucius and Laozi together. A Northern Wei founding has long been claimed, yet the surviving forty bays of timber work are all products of Ming and Qing rebuilding. The plate shows the two pavilions and the walkways between them.
facts: Structure: 27 timber beams about 50 cm in diameter, soaked in tung oil, are bedded under the temple, one end tenoned into the rock and the other carrying the buildings and projecting about 1 m to support the walkways; the temple has 40 bays and 152.5 square metres of timber building, the two flying pavilions each three storeys with nine-ridged roofs and posts more than ten metres long on the outer side.

History: one account has Emperor Xiaowen of Northern Wei found it in 491 (15th year of Taihe) to relocate the Celestial Masters' Daoist seat, another gives 398 (1st year of Tianxing); it was repaired in the Jin, Ming and the Tongzhi reign of the Qing, and most existing buildings are Ming and Qing rebuildings; the 1978 overhaul that replaced load-bearing beams reconfirmed the cantilevered-beam system.

Three teachings: the upper floor of the main hall holds the Three Buddhas Hall, Taiyi Hall and Guandi Temple; the south pavilion rises through the Chunyang Palace, Sanguan Hall and Leiyin Hall, the north pavilion through the Four Buddhas Hall, Three Sages Hall and Three Teachings Hall, where Sakyamuni, Confucius and Laozi share one shrine; the temple became a national key protected site in 1982.

name: Temple of Bi Gan
sub: Memorial to loyal remonstrance, with temple and tomb joined
yearNote: 1600 is only an approximate sorting point for the Ming–Qing structures. The expansion in the 7th year of Hongzhi in the Ming (1494) belongs to the history of the temple complex and is not taken directly as the construction year of every component of the front of the Sacrificial Hall drawn here.
lede: Bigan Temple’s sacrificial hall opens a five-bay façade among old cypresses, while the tomb behind extends the memorial into the rear of the precinct. The commemorated figure belongs to the Shang, but the surviving buildings largely reflect Ming and Qing rebuilding and repairs. Gate, inscription corridor and hall form a route from worship to the tomb, and successive inscriptions reveal changing interpretations of loyal remonstrance.
facts: The hall is five bays wide and three deep, with doors, windows and columns forming a broad front. Gate, inscription corridor, hall and rear tomb align to establish the sequence of ritual movement.

The temple’s history reaches back to the Northern Wei; it was enlarged in 1494. Surviving buildings mostly reflect Ming–Qing rebuilding and repairs. Around 1600 is an approximate timeline position, not the date of every hall component.

Cypresses, inscriptions and the temple-before-tomb layout preserve successive forms of commemoration. Traditions of loyal remonstrance and surname ancestry are later cultural memories rather than direct evidence for Shang events.

name: Wahuang Palace and Stone Carvings
sub: Front of the cliff-hugging Wahuang Pavilion
yearNote: The Hebei Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau lists the Wahuang Pavilion and other buildings on the mountain as Ming–Qing remains; Handan cultural tourism sources record that a three-story timber pavilion was added on the stone vault in the Ming. 1600 is used only as an approximate sorting value for the Ming–Qing pavilion, and the pavilion is not dated by the year of the Northern Qi carved sutras.
siteCoordinateSource: Commons Category:Nüwa Imperial Palace 公布36°38′36″N,113°37′02″E，山上主体附近定位：https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Nüwa_Imperial_Palace 。
lede: Wahuang Pavilion is defined by a rock chamber, stone vault and timber storeys stacked against the cliff. Three upper wooden levels draw a tall silhouette unlike halls on level ground. The surviving pavilion belongs to Ming and Qing building and repair phases, while adjacent carved scriptures reach back to the Northern Qi. Their proximity records accumulated history, not a single construction date.
facts: A stone vault fronts the natural lower chamber, supporting three timber storeys above to form a four-level structure. Eaves, columns and galleries face outward from the cliff; rock, stone and wood together determine the pavilion’s form.

The provincial authority assigns the upper buildings, including Wahuang Pavilion, to the Ming and Qing periods. The exact date of this building remains unconfirmed. Northern Qi scriptures nearby are earlier and cannot date the surviving timber pavilion.

Mountain paths link lower precincts with the upper pavilions. Nüwa worship and Buddhist cliff scriptures survive in the same landscape; viewing architecture and inscriptions together reveals layers crossing periods and religious traditions.

name: Da Zhao Temple, Hohhot
era: Founded in the Ming · Altered in the Qing
yearNote: 1600 is only an approximate sorting point for the Ming–Qing main structure and does not claim an exact completion year for the Mahavira Hall; the temple was completed in 1580, and the Qing expansion and the relaying of yellow glazed tiles are recorded separately.
lede: Dazhao’s main hall stands on the temple axis, its broad roof, layered eaves and substantial body forming a solemn frontage. Also called Wuliang Temple, Dazhao was founded in the Ming period and enlarged and altered under the Qing. The hall combines Han Chinese and Tibetan architectural forms and participates in a sequence of worship spaces with the entrance and Heavenly Kings Hall. The temple’s foundation date does not date every surviving component.
facts: The main hall anchors an axis approached through the entrance, Heavenly Kings Hall and Bodhi passage hall. Its broad body and roof combine Han Chinese and Tibetan architectural forms.

Dazhao was founded in 1579 and renamed Wuliang Temple after repairs in 1640. Surviving halls reflect Ming and Qing construction and alteration; the approximate seventeenth-century placement is not a precise completion date for this hall.

Looking back from the hall reveals the progression from entrance to the core worship space. The building provides material evidence of Hohhot’s temple culture and exchanges between Han Chinese and Tibetan architecture.

name: Triple Gate of the Foshan Ancestral Temple
yearNote: 1600 is only an approximate sorting point for the surviving Ming–Qing main structure, not the exact completion year of the Triple Gate. The founding of the Ancestral Temple in the Northern Song, its rebuilding in the Hongwu reign of the Ming and the date of the Triple Gate's present form must not be conflated.
lede: The Three Gates of Foshan’s Ancestral Temple welcome worshippers through three arched openings. A continuous ceramic ridge turns stories and figures into a lively roof-top panorama. Its horizontal scale and dense ornament make the entrance both a ceremonial boundary and a display of craft. The temple developed from a Northern Song foundation through Ming and Qing work; modern repairs add further layers to the visible gate.
facts: Three arched openings pierce the central gate wall. A long ceramic ridge spans the roof, with gilded woodcarving beneath the eaves. Substantial masonry and densely modelled figures combine in a layered horizontal elevation.

The temple was founded under the Northern Song and rebuilt under the Ming. Its gate reflects Ming and Qing building work and later repairs, including the 2007–2010 conservation campaign. Neither the temple’s foundation date nor a single year describes its entire present form.

Ceramic and wooden narrative ornament links Foshan craftsmanship with worship of the Northern Emperor. The entrance is a threshold to the shrine and a visible meeting place of artisans’ work, stories and community ceremony.

name: Chongwen Pagoda, Jingyang
yearNote: According to the Record of the Permanent Fields Endowed for the Community of the Iron Buddha Chongwen Pagoda Temple, as cited in published reports, construction began in 1591 and was completed in 1608; other accounts give different dates. This drawing follows present-day photographs and does not add the earlier finial.
lede: Chongwen Pagoda stretches upward through thirteen brick storeys, with doors and niches staggered around its eight sides. Built during the Ming Wanli period, its recorded purpose encouraged learning, while Buddhist niches retained a religious setting. The Jingyang tower brings educational aspirations into a pagoda form. Its truncated summit and repairs also distinguish today’s fabric from its earlier appearance.
facts: The hollow octagonal brick tower has thirteen storeys and an internal brick stair. Except at the summit level, doors and Buddhist niches occupy its eight faces in staggered arrangements. Receding storeys and cornices create a slender rhythm.

A published report cites a temple land inscription recording construction from 1591 to 1608, the nineteenth to thirty-sixth Wanli years. Other dates circulate; the inscription provides construction evidence, while today’s fabric also incorporates later repairs.

The inscription links construction with encouraging local children to study, while stone Buddhist images occupy the niches. Educational ambition and Buddhist architectural form meet here. This dual context offers more than judging Chongwen Pagoda by height alone.

name: Twin Pagodas of Yongzuo Temple, Taiyuan
yearNote: 1612 is only an approximate sorting point for the period in which the twin pagodas took shape; the two were built one after the other, and this year is not given as the founding year of both.
lede: On the high ground southeast of Taiyuan two thirteen-storey brick pagodas stand shoulder to shoulder, forty-six metres apart and both around fifty-four metres tall, the tallest pair of twin pagodas surviving in China. The east pagoda, Wenfeng Pagoda, came first, built in 1599 (27th year of Wanli, Ming) under Fu Lin and his son Fu Zhimo as a geomantic tower to mend the city's literary fortunes; the west pagoda, Xuanwen Pagoda, followed more than a decade later, completed in 1612 (40th year of Wanli) for the Prince of Jin by the eminent Wutai monk Miaofeng, its eaves edged entirely in peacock-blue glaze and named for the honorific title of the Wanli emperor's mother. The plate shows both pagodas, each with its own finial and taper.
facts: Twin pagodas: both are octagonal thirteen-storey brick pagodas of storeyed type, hollow double-shell structures with spiral stairs inside; the west Xuanwen Pagoda is 54.78 m high and the east Wenfeng Pagoda 53.3 m, 46 m apart, and all thirteen eaves of the Xuanwen Pagoda are edged with peacock-blue glazed tile.

Dating: Yongming Temple was founded in 1597 (25th year of Wanli, Ming) and the east pagoda finished in 1599; in 1608 (36th year of Wanli) Zhu Minchun, Prince of Jin, invited the Chan master Miaofeng to enlarge it, and in 1612 (40th year) the west pagoda and the beamless brick hall were completed and the temple renamed Yongzuo; additions in the Shunzhi and Kangxi reigns of the Qing gave it its present form.

Conservation: the east pagoda once leaned 2.87 m and was righted and strengthened in 1995 to 1996, the west pagoda was strengthened in 1981 to 1984, and only the west pagoda is now open to climb; the pair has been the emblem of Taiyuan since 1985, and the temple also keeps a Ming beamless brick hall and more than 260 stone steles.

name: Tomb of Prince Jian of Lu
short: Tomb of the Prince of Lu
yearNote: 1615 is only an approximate sorting point for the tomb's construction phase in the late Wanli reign; the conversion error found online, “the 40th year of Wanli (1615),” is not carried over as the exact construction year of the stone archway.
place: Henan · Xinxiang · Southern foot of Mount Fenghuang, Fengquan District
lede: The Lufan Jiacheng stone gateway marks the beginning of the Prince Jian of Lu’s funerary avenue. Its central opening rises above the side openings, and independent ceremonial pillars stand beyond the four main posts. Cloud-and-dragon carving gives the heavy stonework an upward movement. It belongs to the late Wanli-period tomb complex, serving as both passage and ritual marker leading toward stone figures, gates and the burial precinct.
facts: This outer gateway has three openings and four soaring posts, with the Lufan Jiacheng inscription above the higher central opening. Separate pillars flank it; cloud-and-dragon carvings cover posts and beams, while drum-shaped supports brace the posts.

The precinct is the Ming tomb of Prince Jian of Lu, Zhu Yiliu. The gateway is assigned approximately to the late Wanli period; around 1615 is a timeline position, not a verified completion year for this structure.

The avenue passes through the central opening toward rows of stone figures and the tomb gates. Comparing this roofless gateway with roofed examples inside the precinct reveals varied entrance forms within one mausoleum.

name: Rulong Bridge
yearNote: According to the county gazetteer it was built in 1625; later repairs do not mean that every component of the bridge is original Ming fabric.
lede: A long gallery spans the stream, a tall tower lifts its ridge at the bridgehead, and the timber arch traces a broad angular line beneath the board siding. Rulong Bridge joins the road across the stream with a gallery where people can linger; it is the Ming timber-arch covered bridge of Yueshan Village.
facts: Built in the Tianqi reign: the county gazetteer records that Rulong Bridge was built in the 5th year of Tianqi in the Ming (1625); it is one of the surviving Ming timber-arch covered bridges in Qingyuan.

Timber arch structure: the bridge spans the stream on a timber arch frame, its ends resting on masonry abutments; protective boards shield the arch frame, and the gallery shelters travelers from wind and rain.

Staggered heights: the bell tower at the north end, with a triple-eaved hip-and-gable roof, rises high and, together with the central roof and the south entrance, forms a layered outline along the long bridge.

name: Dazheng Hall, Shenyang Imperial Palace
sub: Octagonal hall with double-eaved pyramidal roof
yearNote: 1625 is an approximate sorting point for the early Qing construction; the construction span of the whole palace complex is not taken as the exact completion year of this single hall.
lede: The octagonal Dazheng Hall rises to the point of a double-eaved pyramidal roof, while dragon-wrapped columns draw attention back beneath the eaves. Doors surround its timber frame on eight sides above a pedestal. Begun when the Later Jin court moved to Shenyang in 1625, it is an early focus of the palace’s eastern precinct; its relationship with the Ten Princes’ Pavilions brings banner politics and varied decorative traditions into the court.
facts: Two tiers of eaves rise above an octagonal plan and converge into a central roof point. Doors enclose each side. Dragon columns, brackets and column-head ornaments meet beneath the eaves, while the pedestal provides a solemn base for the timber structure.

The hall was begun in 1625 following Nurhaci’s move to Shenyang. It belongs to the palace’s early construction, but the complex continued to expand; its complete Qing-period layout was not all finished in that year.

The arrangement of the hall and Ten Princes’ Pavilions reflects the Eight Banners, while the decoration draws on several traditions. Recent conservation used historical evidence to restore flaming-jewel patterns between brackets, making small details clues to the early Qing court.

name: Kaiyuan Temple, Quanzhou
sub: Mahavira Hall · Hall of a Hundred Columns
era: Ming · Restored in the 10th year of Chongzhen
lede: Nine bays across the front under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof: the highest grade of Buddhist hall in China. The hall should hold a hundred stone columns, but to make room for the huge Five Buddhas and the worship space two rows of fourteen were omitted, leaving eighty-six, and the name 'Hall of a Hundred Columns' stuck anyway. More remarkable still are the twenty-four bracket sets carved as celestial musicians, kalavinka with human bodies, feathered wings and bird legs, holding instruments or scholars' implements: structural members that carry the beams and at the same time a scene of music before the Buddha. The present form dates from the rebuilding of 1637 by the general Zheng Zhilong and others.
facts: Form: nine bays wide and six deep, about 1,388 square metres in area, with a double-eave hip-and-gable roof about 20 m high; a palatial-type frame with two rows of 14 columns omitted in the middle, leaving 86 stone columns and 76 bracket sets; where the two central rows of stone columns meet the beams, the brackets are carved as 24 flying musicians.

History: founded in 686 (second year of Chuigong, Tang); the present plan and frame proportions largely follow the rebuilding of 1155 in the Southern Song, the outer eaves were extended in 1389, and the hall was rebuilt to its present state in 1637 by the general Zheng Zhilong and others. The Sumeru base of the terrace in front carries 73 panels of lions and sphinx-like figures, moved here during the Ming rebuilding from a Hindu temple abandoned at the end of the Yuan.

Plurality: the hall enshrines the Five Buddhas of esoteric Buddhism, each 6 m high; two Hindu stone columns under the rear gallery eaves were also reused in the 1637 rebuilding, nine of their 24 medallions showing Vishnu, Krishna and other myths. That a Buddhist hall was rebuilt with Hindu members is the most tangible evidence of the port's mixed cultures.

name: Xiaoxitian, Xi County
sub: Hall filled with suspended sculpture · Thousand Buddha Hermitage
lede: The Mahavira Hall is under one hundred and seventy square metres, yet nearly two thousand painted figures are packed into it: celestial palaces rise tier upon tier above the main Buddha, twelve musician bodhisattvas dance on the balustraded platform in front, human-faced apsaras and divine birds perch on clouds, the largest over three metres, the smallest no bigger than a thumb. All are clay, gilded and painted, suspended between roof frame and walls, begun in the Chongzhen reign at the end of the Ming and finished under Shunzhi in the early Qing. Qianfo Nunnery itself covers barely eleven hundred square metres, two thirds of its halls built in two storeys with cave-like openings for doors. The plate takes the central shrine and part of the celestial palaces and does not stand for the whole hall.
facts: Mahavira Hall: five bays wide and six rafters deep, single-eave gable (xuanshan) roof, interior under 170 square metres; nearly two thousand suspended figures are arranged in tiers on the roof frame, walls and shrines, the largest over 3 m high and the smallest able to sit in a palm.

Dating: Qianfo Nunnery was founded at the end of the Ming by the Chan master Dongming; the suspended sculpture of the Mahavira Hall was begun in the Chongzhen reign and completed in the Shunzhi reign of the Qing, about thirty years in all; the temple faces east on the hillside in an upper and a lower court, and became a national key protected site in 1996.

Layout: the whole temple has little over 1,100 square metres of building, two thirds of its halls in two storeys, with cave-like doorways dividing the upper, middle and front courts; the upper court holds the Mahavira, Manjusri and Samantabhadra halls, the lower court the Wuliang Hall, Weituo Hall, Moyun Pavilion and the bell and drum towers.

name: Confucian Temple, Tianjin
sub: Dacheng Hall of the prefectural temple · Central facade and ceremonial stair
era: Founded in the 1st year of Zhengtong · Present form from Ming–Qing repairs
yearNote: 1436 is the year the Confucian Temple was founded and is not used directly as the date of manufacture of all the surviving components of the Dacheng Hall drawn here. 1650 is only an approximate sorting point for the present form shaped by Ming–Qing repairs, not the exact completion year of the Dacheng Hall.
place: Tianjin · Nankai · Inside the East Gate of the Old City
lede: The central entrance of the prefectural temple’s Dacheng Hall is framed by yellow-glazed roofing, painted beams and dark red doors. A stone ceremonial ramp leads towards the ritual space. Tianjin’s Confucian temple and school developed together, later forming adjacent prefectural and county temples under Qing administration. The date 1436 concerns the foundation of the garrison school. The present hall reflects successive Ming and Qing repairs; its entrance offers a starting point for understanding temple and education together.
facts: Glazed eaves, painted beams and doors frame the central facade, with a stone ceremonial ramp in front. Entrance and terrace organize ritual movement. This central section does not establish the bay count of the complete hall.

Tianjin’s garrison school was founded in 1436, followed by hall construction and Ming–Qing additions and repairs. The school’s foundation and the hall’s development are separate phases; the initial date cannot date every surviving beam or column.

Dacheng Hall centres worship of Confucius. Adjacent prefectural and county temples and Minglun Hall express local administration and the link between temple and school. Steps and doors connect education and ceremonial movement in visible architectural space.

name: Xianshen Tower, Jiexiu
sub: Street-spanning tower and music tower · Composite pavilion
era: Qing · Late Shunzhi to early Kangxi
lede: One building does three jobs: the street runs beneath it, making it the over-street tower of Shuncheng Gate Street; one floor up it is the gate of the Temple of the Three Sworn Brothers; above that a five-bay theatre stage faces back to the north, the whole stacking into a four-storey silhouette. It is also the only surviving building in China linked to Zoroastrianism, the carved bull-headed and camel-headed beasts under its eaves read by Jiang Boqin as incarnations of Zoroastrian deities. Tradition credits the temple to Wen Yanbo of the Northern Song; it burned in the early Qing, and the present tower is a rebuilding of 1660 to 1668 (late Shunzhi to early Kangxi), with an inscription of 1667 (6th year of Kangxi) under the finial of the music hall ridge. The plate shows the over-street tower and the music hall.
facts: Form: the plan is T-shaped, about 20 m deep in all; the over-street tower at the front and the porch before the stage are each three bays square, the stage block behind is five bays wide and four deep with a surrounding gallery; the lower floor is the gate, the upper floor the stage, and with the music hall and double eaves it rises four storeys.

Dating: the Temple of the Three Sworn Brothers burned in the early Qing and was rebuilt from 1660 (17th year of Shunzhi) to 1668 (7th year of Kangxi), with an inscription of 1667 (6th year of Kangxi) under the vase finial of the music hall ridge and an offering pavilion added in 1786 (51st year of Qianlong); in 1985 the over-street tower was jacked up 1.5 m as a whole and the restoration was completed in 1987.

Zoroastrian link: the stele record says Duke Wen Lu (Wen Yanbo) of the Song built the temple for the Xian god, and a Jiajing-era magistrate of the Ming turned it into the Temple of the Three Sworn Brothers; Jiang Boqin judged from the bull- and camel-headed carvings under the eaves that it is the remnant of a Zoroastrian shrine, and Chen Mingda's 1951 survey already called its artistry outstanding and warned against dismissing it for its late date.

name: Wenchang Pavilion, Guiyang
sub: East of the old city · Three stories, three eaves
era: Rebuilt in the 8th year of Kangxi
yearNote: First built in 1609; the entry is placed according to the surviving pavilion formed by the 1669 rebuilding and later repairs, as given in official Guiyang municipal sources, and the founding year is not substituted for the surviving main structure.
lede: Nine-cornered roofs spread across three eave tiers at Guiyang’s Wenchang Pavilion, distinguishing it from ordinary rectangular towers and neighbouring defences. First built in 1609 for Wenchang worship, it was rebuilt in 1669 and repeatedly repaired later. Its three-storey form preserves both the eastern old-city landscape and a tradition associated with learning.
facts: The pavilion has three storeys, three eave tiers and nine-cornered roofs. Repeated corners and stacked levels create its distinctive profile; the nearby city gate tower is a separate building.

Guiyang’s official account records construction in 1609 and rebuilding in 1669, followed by repairs and enlargement under later Qing reigns. The rebuilding dates the main surviving form, not every individual component.

Originally dedicated to Wenchang, it represents civic beliefs associated with examinations and learning. Its unusual roofs, old walls and gate setting make it a surviving reference for Guiyang’s historic urban layout.

name: Golden Hall, Kunming
era: Recast in the 10th year of Kangxi
yearNote: The surviving bronze hall drawn here was rebuilt by Wu Sangui in 1671; the bronze hall first built in 1602 and its relocation are recorded separately, and the Golden Hall of the Wudang Mountains is not mistakenly used as a reference.
lede: Roof, columns and doors resemble a timber hall, but close inspection reveals cast copper. Taihe Palace’s Golden Hall on Kunming’s Mingfeng Mountain reproduces traditional building details in metal. A stone platform supports its darkened surfaces and double eaves. The surviving hall was rebuilt by Wu Sangui in 1671; the earlier Ming copper hall had a separate history of relocation.
facts: Cast columns, beams, brackets, lattice doors and roof tiles assemble into a timber-like hall with double eaves on a stone platform. Metal replaces wood, but the relationships between components retain timber architectural forms rather than making a simple copper shell.

The existing hall follows Wu Sangui’s rebuilding in 1671, the tenth Kangxi year, confirmed by an inscription cast on a beam. The copper hall first founded in 1602 was later removed, so its date does not describe the surviving building.

Part of the Daoist Taihe Palace, it preserves an example of casting joined with traditional hall design. It historically followed Wudang’s Golden Hall, but the surviving forms, treatment of materials and histories at the two sites must be understood separately.

name: Eastern Qing Tombs
sub: Stone memorial archway on the Xiaoling spirit way
yearNote: The date 1672 is adopted for the stone archway drawn here: Wang Qiheng, on the basis of the Xiaoling drawings and the archives on the transport of stone, established that the components were transported at the end of 1671 and the archway completed in early 1672. The early main works of the Xiaoling in 1663–1664 and the traditionally recorded ancillary works of 1668 are not used as the date of this stone archway.
siteCoordinateSource: Commons实拍 https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:清东陵石牌坊_-_panoramio.jpg 公布相机点40.145608,117.681508；取其北方石牌坊附近40.146,117.6815作约百米精度图鉴定位，非测绘坐标。
lede: The stone archway at the southern end of Xiaoling’s spirit road establishes the scale of the Eastern Qing Tombs through five openings and a sequence of stone roofs. Eaves, beams and columns resemble timber but are carved in stone; eleven roofed elements rise around a clear centre. This was not among Xiaoling’s earliest completed structures: archival research places completion in 1672. The ceremonial approach unfolds northward from here.
facts: The timber-inspired stone archway has five bays, six columns and eleven roofed elements. Its central passage and side bays rise in a hierarchy; continuous columns, beams and roofs emphasise a broad ceremonial frontage rather than a single narrow gateway.

Wang Qiheng’s study of Xiaoling drawings and transport records finds the stone components arriving in 1671 and the archway completed early in 1672. This date is distinguished from earlier completion and burial phases of the mausoleum.

At the southern end of Xiaoling’s ceremonial axis, the archway precedes gates, stele towers and ritual buildings. Stone versions of timber roofs give lasting material form to imperial hierarchy and order the visitor’s movement from the entrance onward.

name: Yasheng Hall of the Mencius Temple, Zoucheng
sub: Seven bays, double-eaved hip-and-gable roof · Green glazed tiles
era: Rebuilt in the 12th year of Kangxi, later repaired
yearNote: The surviving hall is placed at 1673, when it was rebuilt five years after the earthquake damage of 1668; the comprehensive repair of 1736 and modern renovations are described separately. It is not the original fabric of the hall first built in the Northern Song.
lede: Yasheng Hall’s seven-bay body is enclosed by two tiers of green glazed eaves, marking the principal hall for worship of Mencius. It retains the ritual position within his temple but is not the original Northern Song hall. Rebuilding followed the earthquake of 1668, with further Qing and modern repairs. Its scale and roof rank correspond to Mencius’s status as the Second Sage, making Confucian ritual visible in architecture.
facts: Form: the hall is seven bays wide beneath a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof with green glazed tiles. Columns enclose its broad body. Its scale and roof distinguish the ritual centre from the single-eaved subsidiary halls.

Dating: the earthquake of 1668 damaged the hall, which was rebuilt five years later; 1673 anchors the surviving building. A comprehensive temple repair followed in 1736, with later work continuing. This is not the Northern Song foundation hall.

Significance: roof form, tile colour and bay dimensions translate the honours accorded to Mencius into architectural hierarchy. The relationship between this hall and lesser buildings illustrates Confucian worship and ranked construction.

name: Tiankuang Hall of the Dai Temple
lede: Tiankuang Hall’s nine-bay front and double-eaved hipped roof give worship of the Mount Tai deity a palatial scale. Its ritual position follows a Song foundation, while the surviving timber dimensions and methods reflect Qing repair. A Kangxi rebuilding inscription describes retained columns and beams alongside replaced timbers and newly fired tiles. Murals repainted in the early Qing show the deity’s procession and return, adding another historical layer.
facts: Form: the hall is nine bays wide and five deep beneath a double-eaved hipped roof with yellow glazed tiles. Its broad body and eaves establish the high rank of this mountain cult building, with columns and three walls enclosing the deity’s hall.

Dating: the Kangxi repair inscription records completion in 1677, retaining usable beams and columns while replacing decayed purlins, rafters, boards and tiles. Surviving work reflects Qing methods, with later repairs; the completion date does not date every component.

Significance: the procession and return murals were repainted in the early Qing on the basis of Song subjects, combining ritual, landscapes and buildings. Separate phases of timberwork and painting provide tangible evidence for the continuity of mountain worship.

name: Forbidden City, Beijing
lede: The Hall of Supreme Harmony owes its imposing presence to an eleven-bay facade, a double-eaved hipped roof and a three-tier white marble terrace. Ten ridge beasts at the roof corners also proclaim its architectural rank. The hall seen today was rebuilt after a fire during the Kangxi reign and completed in 1697; it is not the original Yongle-period hall. Imperial enthronements, weddings and major seasonal ceremonies took place here. At the centre of the Forbidden City's Outer Court, it served grand state ritual rather than the routine conduct of government.
facts: Form: eleven bays wide and five deep, the hall has a double-eaved hipped roof covered with yellow glazed tiles and stands on a three-tier white marble terrace. Its broad facade, raised platform and layered eaves create the most conspicuous outline in the Forbidden City's Outer Court.

Rebuilding: its predecessor was founded in 1420 and destroyed by a lightning fire in 1679. Reconstruction began in 1695 and was completed in 1697. The surviving hall belongs to this Qing building campaign rather than the date of the original Ming foundation.

Rank: ten ridge beasts line the roof corners, expressing the decorative hierarchy of a high-ranking hall. Imperial enthronements, weddings, New Year and winter-solstice ceremonies were held here. Its scale served ceremonial occasions rather than daily office work.

name: Mimi Temple, Fanshi
place: Shanxi · Fanshi · Yantou Township · Mimo Cliff
lede: Thirty-eight kilometres southwest of Taihuai on Mount Wutai, this temple below Mimo Cliff on Mount Weiping was once the place of the saying that to visit Wutai without the Dragon Cave was to see only half the mountain. Tradition takes it back to the Northern Qi; the Tang monk Mucha retreated and built here, and it flourished in the Tang and Song, leaving outside the walls the Tang-founded, Ming-repaired pagoda of Patriarch Mucha and the pagoda of Master Xuanjue of 963 (7th year of Tianhui, Northern Han). The halls themselves are Qing rebuildings, the main halls of the front and middle courts both five bays wide. The plate shows the front of the Manjusri Hall: five bays with a front porch, a central stair climbing to the raised platform, and Qing paintings surviving on the porch panels and inside.
facts: Manjusri Hall: as drawn, five bays wide with a front porch under a flush-gable (yingshan) roof, standing on a raised platform reached by a central stone stair; in the temple the main halls of the front and middle courts are both five bays, the north and south sutra lofts five bays each, and only a five-bay north pavilion survives in the rear court.

Dating: the Qingliang Shan Gazetteer records that the Tang monk Mucha founded the temple while in retreat at Mimi Cliff, and another account has a Northern Qi nun's hermitage before it; of thirty-two hermitages once here the front, middle and rear courts and the West and Middle hermitages remain; the National Cultural Heritage Administration registers it as Qing, and it became a national key protected site in 2006.

Stonework: before the temple stand a Jin-dynasty stone pillar and two brick pagodas, the pagoda of Patriarch Mucha, Tang-founded and Ming-repaired, hexagonal, four storeys and about 10 m high, and the pagoda of Master Xuanjue of 963 (7th year of Tianhui, Northern Han), hexagonal and two storeys; the Golden Buddha Loft in the Middle Hermitage holds a stone Amitabha about 7 m high carved in 1535 (14th year of Jiajing, Ming).

name: Kang Baiwan Manor
era: Late Ming–early Qing · Extended over generations
yearNote: The Zhengzhou Municipal Bureau of Cultural Heritage dates the manor as a whole to the late Ming–early Qing, with continued construction in later periods. 1700 is only an approximate sorting point for the manor's Ming–Qing structures; the storied cave dwelling shown in the photographs has as yet no exact construction date of its own, and neither the Kang family's move here nor any individual's life dates are used as the date of the building.
lede: Kang Baiwan Manor combines cliff-side cave rooms with multistorey houses. Superimposed arched openings and inward-facing side buildings enclose a long courtyard. The estate accumulated through generations of the Kang family rather than a single building campaign, joining living and working spaces. Wood, brick and stone carving reveal household customs, while the architecture shows how builders in the Heluo region adapted housing to the terrain.
facts: Cave rooms were cut against the cliff and buildings erected along the streets, with residences arranged around quadrangular courtyards. Arched cave openings and inward-facing side houses connect underground spaces, upper floors and courtyard life.

Zhengzhou’s heritage bureau dates the estate broadly to the late Ming and early Qing, with later additions. Around 1700 is an approximate timeline position; the individual cave building has no verified construction year.

The estate includes residences, workshops and storage. Its wood, brick and stone carving also conveys ornament and family teachings, preserving evidence of family enterprise alongside regional domestic architecture.

name: Dacheng Hall of the Gongcheng Confucian Temple
sub: Double-eaved hip-and-gable roof · Main hall of the Confucian temple
era: Built in the Ming–Qing · Later repaired and maintained
yearNote: The sixth-batch list of national protected sites gives the Gongcheng historic building complex as Ming to Qing. 1700 is only an approximate sorting point for the surviving Ming–Qing main structure; the founding, successive restorations and the dates of the present hall's components are not merged into a single precise year.
lede: Gongcheng’s Dacheng Hall stands on the ascending ceremonial axis of the Confucian temple. Its double-eaved hip-and-gable roof and lifted corners spread above a high terrace. Ridge figures, painting and carved doors make a ritual building a repository of local craftsmanship. The temple originated in Ming, but the surviving halls reflect Qing rebuilding and later repairs. The foundation of the temple does not date every beam and column visible today.
facts: The raised hall has a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof, carved doors and eaves, and painted ridge figures. Steps connect it with the ceremonial platform; elevation, roofing and ornament emphasize the hall on the axis.

The temple originated in 1410 and was rebuilt during the Qing Daoguang reign, followed by further repairs. The protected complex is dated Ming through Qing. Foundation and rebuilding must be distinguished; later repairs also leave surviving components of different ages.

The hall worships Confucius, translating ceremonial order into an axis and terraces. Ridge figures and carved and painted decoration place local craftsmanship within ritual forms, preserving Guangxi’s interpretation of Confucian temple architecture.

name: Historic Buildings of Zhangguying Village
sub: Ming–Qing dwellings · Linked roofs and skywells
era: Built over generations in the Ming–Qing
yearNote: The surviving dwellings form a complex built in multiple phases during the Ming and Qing; 1700 is only a broad sorting point and does not refer to the exact construction year of any single house. The drawing shows part of the roofscape visible in photographs; it does not claim to reconstruct the whole village, nor does it equate the date of the Zhang family's settlement with the date of the surviving houses.
lede: One grey-tiled roof meets another at Zhang Guying Village, with courtyards and gable walls tucked between continuous ridges. This is only a portion of the residential complex, yet its connected halls, side rooms and covered passages make the larger organisation legible. Courtyards admit light and help drain water. Built and extended through the Ming and Qing periods, the intricate roofscape records the expansion of family life.
facts: Courtyards, halls and paired side rooms form basic units linked by covered passages and lanes. In this roofscape, flush gable walls, tile ridges and courtyard openings express the organisation of the living spaces below.

Construction began in the Ming period and continued through Qing extensions; the surviving complex includes several phases. The ancestors’ settlement history differs from the dates of individual houses and cannot assign every residence one foundation year.

Connected passages maintain links between households, while courtyards admit light and assist drainage. The clustered houses reveal a pattern of extended-family residence in which everyday movement and social contact are closely tied to the architecture.

name: Jingzhen Octagonal Pavilion
sub: Dai Theravada Buddhist temple · Ordination hall
yearNote: 1701 is the year the Octagonal Pavilion was founded; later repairs, such as those of 1978 and 1993, are recorded separately, and the other, now destroyed buildings of Jingzhen Temple are not invented in the drawing.
lede: Roof layers spread in eight directions and gather towards a pointed summit. Jingzhen’s Octagonal Pavilion combines a brick body with timber roofs into a light silhouette. Despite its name, it is a Theravada Buddhist ordination hall for monastic ceremonies. Founded in 1701 and repaired in modern times, it includes surviving and renewed details rather than an entirely untouched original.
facts: Timber roof tiers rise above a brick body in eight directions, converging at the summit. Decorations on walls and eaves are organised around the centre, giving a small building a richly layered appearance.

The pavilion was founded in 1701, the fortieth Kangxi year, and repaired repeatedly thereafter. Foundation and restoration are separate events; renewal of components does not mean that the whole building originated in modern times.

Within a Dai Theravada monastery, it serves ordination and uposatha ceremonies rather than primarily providing a scenic resting place. Reading its religious use together with the eight-direction roof explains its distinctive local form.

name: Chengqi Lou, Yongding
sub: Gaobei tulou cluster · Circular rammed-earth dwelling
era: Completed in the 48th year of Kangxi
yearNote: The completion year of Chengqi Lou, 1709, is adopted; the start of construction in the Ming and the completion in the Qing are described separately. The plate shows the surviving exterior and does not reconstruct the interior from postage stamps.
lede: 'Four storeys high, four rings round, four hundred rooms up and down; circle within circle, ring within ring, three hundred years of weathering.' The local rhyme describes Chengqi Lou: inside a round building 73 metres across sit three concentric ring-houses and an ancestral hall, the outer ring four storeys with seventy-two rooms to a floor, the second ring two storeys, the third one, each stepping lower towards the centre. The Jiang clan is said to have broken ground in the Chongzhen era and finished only in 1709, the 48th year of Kangxi; at its peak more than six hundred people lived here. The plate shows only the complete exterior, with no section cut.
facts: Form: a four-ring concentric earthen building, 73 m in diameter on a site of 5,376.17 square metres; the outer ring is four storeys and 16.4 m high with 72 rooms per floor, the second ring two storeys with 40 rooms per floor, the third ring a single storey of 32 rooms, and an ancestral hall at the centre, over four hundred rooms in all, with 3 main gates and 2 wells. The rammed-earth outer wall is 1.5 m thick at the base and 1 m at the top, and the eaves project nearly 4 m.

Dating: ground is said to have been broken in the Chongzhen era of the Ming and the building completed in 1709, spanning three generations and about half a century. More than six hundred people lived here at its height and some three hundred of the Jiang clan still do; the Fujian dwelling in the 1986 Chinese folk-dwelling stamp series is this building.

Comparison: Chengqi Lou is the core of the Gaobei tulou cluster, home of the Yongding Jiang clan, together with Wuyun Lou, Shize Lou and Qiaofu Lou; by size and number of rings it ranks among the foremost surviving round tulou and is called the 'king of tulou'. In 2008 the Gaobei cluster was inscribed on the World Heritage List as part of 'Fujian Tulou', six clusters and four single buildings.

name: Wuhou Shrine, Nanyang
sub: Honoring a worthy beneath the eaves
era: Qing structure · Repaired over the centuries
yearNote: 1711 — the comprehensive restoration of the whole shrine in the 50th year of Kangxi in the Qing, as officially recorded — is taken as an approximate sorting point, without asserting on this basis that the surviving Great Worship Hall was built entirely in that year. The construction of the main hall in the 11th year of Hongzhi in the Ming and the later Qing and modern repairs are recorded separately; the dates of the specific components beneath the eaves drawn here still need to be distinguished through measured documentation.
lede: Beneath the eaves of Nanyang’s Wuhou Shrine, columns, beams, doors and layers of inscribed plaques frame a place of worship for Zhuge Liang. The Great Worship Hall occupies the front precinct, contrasting with the commemorative cottage and pavilions behind. Ming, Qing and modern repairs shaped its present appearance, while plaques and inscriptions preserve later writers’ assessments. The historical figure’s lifetime and the shrine’s building dates must be distinguished.
facts: The Great Worship Hall is the principal ritual building in the front precinct. Plaques hang beneath the beams and inscriptions line the walls; images of Zhuge Liang, Zhuge Zhan and Zhuge Shang are enshrined inside.

Local records describe construction of a main hall in 1498 and a shrine-wide restoration in 1711, followed by later repairs. The 1711 campaign cannot date every surviving component beneath these eaves.

Front ritual halls and rear commemorative pavilions combine temple and memorial-garden functions. Plaques and inscriptions document continuing veneration, expressing later cultural memories of Zhuge Liang.
