name: Guandi Temple, Xiezhou
sub: Chongning Hall · Ancestral temple of Guandi
yearLabel: Qing · Rebuilt after the Kangxi-era fire
yearNote: 1725 is only an approximate sorting point for the rebuilding phase in the early 18th century, not the exact completion year of the Chongning Hall; 1702 is the year of the temple fire.
lede: The ancestral temple of all Guandi temples, its main hall, Chongning Hall, is named for the title "Perfected Lord Chongning" conferred on Guan Yu by Emperor Huizong of Song in 1104 (3rd year of Chongning). The seven-bay hall under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof closes the axis of the front court, a ring of coiling-dragon stone columns in the gallery around it, and under its eaves hang imperial boards of four reigns: Kangxi's "righteousness lights heaven and earth", Qianlong's "divine valour", Xianfeng's "the pole of humanity for all ages" and Cixi's "awesome power shakes all". The temple was founded in 589 (9th year of Kaihuang, Sui); the existing buildings follow the rebuilding after the fire of 1702 (41st year of Kangxi, Qing). The plate takes the Chongning Hall alone; the Spring and Autumn Tower behind it is not in the picture.
facts: Chongning Hall: seven bays wide and six deep, double-eave hip-and-gable roof, with a surrounding gallery carried on coiling-dragon stone columns; a bell pavilion and a stele pavilion, added in the Qing, flank the front; inside and out hang the boards of Kangxi, Qianlong, Xianfeng and Cixi and dozens of late-Qing and Republican boards.

Dating: founded in 589 (9th year of Kaihuang, Sui) and rebuilt in 1014 (7th year of Dazhong Xiangfu, Song), the temple was destroyed and rebuilt repeatedly; the rebuilding after the fire of 1702 (41st year of Kangxi, Qing) produced today's front-court-and-rear-palace layout, and it became a national key protected site in 1988.

Layout: the temple covers 220,000 square metres; to the south lies the Garden of the Sworn Oath of 1620 (48th year of Wanli, Ming), to the north the main temple, whose front axis runs through screen wall, Duan Gate, Zhi Gate, Meridian Gate, Imperial Calligraphy Tower and Chongning Hall, while the rear palace centres on the Spring and Autumn Tower flanked by the Sabre and Seal towers; with over a hundred bays of halls it is called the crown of martial temples.

name: Temple of Confucius, Qufu
lede: Dacheng Hall locates the centre of Confucian worship in a nine-bay front, yellow glazed tiles and carved dragon columns. The colonnade beneath its double-eaved hip-and-gable roof joins the forecourt terrace to organize movement and ceremony. The surviving hall follows a rebuilding after the Yongzheng-era fire, continuing a much older ritual tradition without sharing the temple’s foundation date. Deep stone carving beside layered timberwork gives architectural expression to ritual rank.
facts: Form: the hall is nine bays wide and five deep, with a surrounding colonnade beneath a yellow-glazed double-eaved hip-and-gable roof. Ten front stone columns bear deeply carved dragons; the terrace and stairs extend its ceremonial space.

Dating: rebuilding followed the fire of 1724 and finished in 1730, the eighth Yongzheng year. These dates concern the surviving main hall rather than the temple’s foundation. Later repairs form additional phases.

Significance: dragon columns, yellow tiles and the nine-by-five plan express the honours accorded to Confucius through architectural rank. The hall and terrace place offerings, ritual and spectators within an ordered setting, illustrating Qing official construction.

name: Five Pagoda Temple, Hohhot
yearNote: The completion phase of the pagoda's construction, 1732, is adopted; 1727 is the year construction began, and the restored temple halls are not entered as original Qing fabric.
lede: Five small towers rise from one broad vajra platform at Hohhot’s Five Pagoda Temple. Their close grouping matters more than individual height. Built from 1727 to 1732, the brick-and-stone reliquary tower bears Buddhist images and texts. A Mongolian astronomical chart behind it brings knowledge of the sky into a Buddhist setting.
facts: A base, vajra platform and five small towers form the monument, with the centre higher than the corners. Its arch inscription uses Mongolian, Tibetan and Chinese; images, texts and ritual objects cover the outer masonry.
The reliquary tower was built from 1727 to 1732. These dates concern the historic tower, not later reconstructed temple halls, which are not treated as original Qing buildings of the same campaign.

The shared-platform form draws on Bodh Gaya in India while using local masonry carving. Charts of the sky, Mount Sumeru and rebirth on the rear screen wall place learned knowledge alongside Buddhist belief.

name: Guandi Temple, Zhoukou
sub: Merchant guild hall of a trading port
yearNote: The construction year of the gate drawn here, 1735, is adopted; it is not replaced by the dates for the guild hall as a whole, whether its founding in 1693 or its full completion in 1852.
lede: Zhoukou’s Guandi Temple gate presents five bays, with three entrances and round windows at either side. Brackets, plaques and red doors articulate the space beneath its hip-and-gable roof. Behind lies a guild complex enlarged by Shanxi and Shaanxi merchants over successive reigns. The gate’s own Yongzheng date is distinct from that longer history; ritual halls and theatre spaces further inside recall the prosperity of the trading town.
facts: Five bays wide and three deep, the gate has a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof with glazed ridge pieces. Three entrances and side round windows organize the front, beneath brackets, a gilded plaque and red-painted doors.
The gate was built in 1735, the thirteenth year of the Qing Yongzheng era. The complex began in 1693 and reached completion in 1852; those dates describe the whole ensemble rather than this gate.

Shanxi and Shaanxi merchants working in Zhoukou financed the complex as both Guandi temple and fellow-provincials’ guild hall. Axial halls and a theatre link commercial association, religious performance and urban life.

name: Western Qing Tombs
sub: Front elevation of the Long'en Hall of the Tailing
yearNote: The whole tomb complex forms one entry, represented by the Long'en Hall of the Tailing; the Palace Museum gives 1736 as the completion date, which is recorded separately from the burial in 1737.
siteCoordinateSource: Wikimedia Commons Category:Tailing Tomb 公布39°22′09.3942″N,115°20′42.2039″E，作泰陵核心区近似定位：https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Tailing_Tomb 。
lede: Long’en Hall at Tailing marks the ritual centre of the earliest imperial tomb in the Western Qing group through double eaves, yellow glazed tiles and a broad terrace. A five-bay hall and side buildings form the court; worship space precedes the burial zone along the axis. Begun under Yongzheng and completed early in Qianlong’s reign, the mausoleum separates construction, ritual use and interment as distinct events.
facts: Long’en Hall is five bays wide and three deep, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof in yellow glazed tiles. A terrace fronts the hall and subsidiary halls stand to either side, making the hierarchy of the ritual court visible.

The Palace Museum dates Tailing’s construction from 1730 to 1736. Subsequent interment is a different event; building history and burial ceremonies are recorded separately rather than used interchangeably to date the halls.

Behind Long’en Hall, gates and a sacrificial platform lead towards the square enclosure, spirit tower, burial enclosure and underground chamber. This sequence shows how imperial tombs link worship and burial while keeping their spaces distinct.

name: Dongyue Temple, Wanrong
era: Restored in the 11th year of Qianlong
lede: This three-storey timber tower in the county town of Wanrong stands 23.19 m high. Four through-columns run from the ground floor straight to the top, and 345 bracket sets and 32 upturned eave corners project tier upon tier, so that from a distance clouds seem to gather about the tower, hence the name Feiyun, Flying Clouds. The timber is left unpainted. It stands at the very front of the axis of the Dongyue Temple; its founding date is unknown, a repair stele of 1617 (45th year of Wanli, Ming) already exists, and the present state is that of the repair of 1746 (11th year of Qianlong, Qing). The plate shows the front of Feiyun Lou.
facts: Form: square in plan, five bays wide and deep, three visible storeys with five inside, three tiers and four eaves, crowned by a cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof; on the second and third storeys a hip-and-gable baosha projects on each of the four sides above a balcony. The whole tower is jointed without iron nails; the four cypress through-columns are 0.7 m in diameter and over 15 m tall.

Dating: the Qianlong-era Record of Repairing Feiyun Lou says the Dongyue Temple already existed in the 1st year of Zhenguan (627); the tower's own founding date is unknown, steles record repairs in 1617 (45th year of Wanli, Ming) and 1746 (11th year of Qianlong, Qing), and the present fabric follows the latter. Listed as a national key protected site in 1988.

Assessment: Chai Zejun wrote that it 'holds an important place among surviving ancient storeyed buildings in China', and with the Yingxian pagoda it is called Shanxi's 'southern tower and northern pagoda'; behind it the Wumen gate and offering hall are Yuan structures, and the stone columns of the main Dongyue hall bear Ming inscriptions of the Zhengtong and Zhengde reigns, none of which is in the plate.

name: Tianhou Temple, Zhijiang
sub: Gate of the Tianhou Temple · Bluestone relief
yearNote: Placed by the construction date, 1748, of the surviving bluestone gate archway; the history of the Fujian Guild Hall from 1684 is listed separately. The drawing shows the stone archway and the steps immediately adjoining it, not the whole compound of the Tianhou Temple.
place: Hunan · Zhijiang · West bank of the Wushui River
lede: Figures, animals and plants unfold across stone-carved eaves and brackets at Zhijiang’s Tianhou Temple gateway, as if a journey had been inscribed into the building. A raised centre and lower side roofs organise its elevation, while carved bridges and towns recall the routes of Fujian merchants. The surviving gateway belongs to the 1748 construction campaign, serving both Mazu worship and the meeting of coastal culture with western Hunan.
facts: The blue-stone gateway imitates timber architecture with double-eaved hip-and-gable roofs and carved brackets. Its central doorway, plaque and dense reliefs are held within a clear framework of stepped rooflines.

The temple has a Kangxi-period history as a Fujian merchants’ guildhall. Merchants rebuilt on the site in 1748, the phase to which the stone gateway belongs. That earlier history and the present gateway must be distinguished, without treating the whole compound as original to one year.

Reliefs of Luoyang Bridge and the three towns of Wuhan recall merchants’ home region and travels. Popular stories appear alongside dragons, phoenixes and plants. Small carvings thus preserve memories of commerce and migration and show Mazu worship crossing regional boundaries.

name: Zhongyue Temple, Mount Song
sub: Central facade of the Junji Hall (detail)
yearNote: 1750 is an approximate sorting point for the Qing appearance, not the exact rebuilding year of the Junji Hall; the hall underwent a major repair in 1986.
lede: Junji Hall stands on a raised terrace within Zhongyue Temple. Central doors and stone steps emerge between old trees, while its double-eaved hipped roof extends to either side. The complete nine-bay hall is the ritual focus for worship of Mount Song’s deity; the visible centre is only part of its broad façade. Qing rebuilding and later repairs give architectural form to a much older mountain cult and culminate the sequence of axial courtyards.
facts: The complete hall is nine bays wide and five deep, with a double-eaved hipped roof of yellow glazed tiles and a raised front terrace. Its central five bays and steps reveal the main axis through the trees.

Many surviving buildings were rebuilt under the Qing and subsequently repaired. Around 1750 is an approximate position for the present appearance, not a verified rebuilding date; the earlier Taishi Shrine history does not date this hall.

The temple rises northward with the terrain. Gates, gateways, pavilions and halls create successive courtyards culminating at Junji Hall, joining the approach route to the ritual order of mountain worship.

name: City God Temple, Jiexiu
yearNote: 1750 is only an approximate timeline position for the Qing building, not the exact completion year of the stage; the founding of the temple and the surviving Ming main hall have their own dates.
lede: The stage of the Jiexiu City God Temple is built 'reversed' beside the gate: toward the courtyard it throws out a hip-and-gable baosha as the stage front, with a round-ridged flush-gable backstage behind. The roof is covered in blue-green glazed tile, and along the main ridge pavilions, vases and ridge beasts stand in a row; beneath the platform a passage is left, so one enters the temple under the stage. The Jiexiu cultural heritage bureau records that the founding date is unknown and that steles note four repairs from 1495 (8th year of Hongzhi, Ming) onward; the roof glaze is among the few Ming remains left in Jiexiu. The plate shows the courtyard face of the stage and its glazed ridge.
facts: Stage: the main body has a round-ridged flush-gable roof, with a three-bay hip-and-gable baosha projecting both toward the courtyard and outward, the inner one serving as the stage; the platform is raised with a stone balustrade in front and a passage below; bell and drum towers flank it, and as drawn the sparrow braces under the eaves are carved all over with flowers.

Dating: steles record repairs in 1495 (8th year of Hongzhi), 1572 (6th year of Longqing), 1724 (2nd year of Yongzheng, Qing) and 1814 (19th year of Jiaqing); Wikipedia additionally gives a founding in 1370 (3rd year of Hongwu, Ming). Listed in 2013 in the seventh batch of national key protected sites.

Glaze: the glazed ridge tiles, owl-tail finials, immortals and beasts, pavilions and vases on the roof are Ming remains, complete in colour and form; the main hall, seven bays wide under a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof, has slender columns and brackets of marked Ming character, and is not in the plate.

name: Chengde Mountain Resort
sub: Front elevation of the Danbo Jingcheng Hall
yearNote: The whole resort forms one entry; the founding of the hall in 1711 and the rebuilding of the present main structure in 1754 are kept separate.
siteCoordinateSource: 携程澹泊敬诚殿独立POI https://hk.trip.com/travel-guide/attraction/chengde/danbo-jingcheng-76717/ 的结构化数据坐标GCJ-02 40.983264,117.941597；按GCJ-02反算为WGS84约40.98170,117.93531，仅作图鉴近似定位。
lede: Danbo Jingcheng Hall balances palatial scale with restrained materials. Beneath its broad rounded hip-and-gable roof, nanmu columns, doors and ceiling retain their natural colour, giving dignity without dense painted ornament. Founded under Kangxi and rebuilt in nanmu under Qianlong, this principal palace hall hosted audiences and ceremonies, bringing the Mountain Resort’s landscape sensibility into imperial ritual.
facts: The principal hall is seven bays wide, with a single-eaved rounded hip-and-gable roof. Nanmu columns, panelled doors and ceiling largely retain their natural colour; the rounded roof without a sharp main ridge softens the broad elevation.

Resort records give a foundation in 1711 and rebuilding in nanmu in 1754. The surviving principal structure is dated to the rebuilding phase; the initial foundation year does not date every part of today’s nanmu hall.

Major ceremonies, official audiences and receptions for ethnic leaders and foreign envoys took place here. Restrained timber colour carried formal court functions, giving the resort palace a different material character from Beijing’s imperial courts.

name: Wudang Monastery
yearNote: The Suguqin Hall is a building of the Qianlong period of the Qing; sources differ between 1755 and 1757, and 1755 serves only as an approximate sorting point. The 1749 expansion of the monastery is not used to fix the completion of the hall drawn here.
lede: In a valley of the Yin Mountains, Wudang Monastery spreads its white-walled, flat-roofed Tibetan-style halls tier by tier along the slope. The Suguqin Hall at the front of the monastery is the space where the whole community gathers to chant sutras; its broad, steady mass contrasts sharply with the curved roofs of the timber halls of the Central Plains.
facts: Subject drawn: the Suguqin Hall, also called the Suguqin Dugong; it is not merged with the whole monastery or with the Nuni Hall rebuilt in 2005 into a single building.
Date: the monastery was expanded in the 14th year of Qianlong (1749); the Suguqin Hall is placed approximately in the Qianlong period, as sources differ on the hall's own construction year.
Form: a Tibetan-style flat roof, white walls, stepped terraces and a dark eave band; Wudang Monastery was listed as a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level in 1996.

name: Puning Temple
sub: Complete elevation of the Mahayana Pavilion
yearNote: The Chinese-Tibetan building complex forms a single entry, without a separate entry for the great Buddha statue; the Mahayana Pavilion is the representative.
lede: The six eave lines on Dacheng Pavilion’s south front are not six usable storeys. The tall building follows the terrain and houses a monumental wooden Thousand-Armed, Thousand-Eyed Guanyin; its sides and back show different tier counts. Built under Qianlong, Puning Temple combines a Chinese-style front axis with a rear layout drawing on Tibetan Buddhism. The pavilion brings sculpture, hillside space and timber architecture together.
facts: The south elevation has six eave tiers, the east and west five, and the north four, while the interior has three storeys. Eave counts respond to terrain and appearance rather than a uniform floor count; the large Guanyin stands at the centre.

Puning Temple was built from 1755 to 1758, with its rear layout drawing on Samye Monastery in Tibet. This is the history of a Qing temple, not the earlier date of the monastery that inspired its design.

Chinese-style timber construction and surrounding Tibetan-style halls and platforms form the worship space. The wooden Guanyin requires continuous internal height; differing eave and floor counts show coordination between sculpture, symbolic layout and building technique.

name: Dingcun Folk Houses
sub: Ding Kun Compound · Southern Shanxi courtyard house
era: Qianlong period, Qing · Ding Kun Compound
yearNote: 1760 is only for approximate sorting within the Qianlong period. The Ding Kun family built over three generations across about 50 years, and no precise completion year is invented for the hall drawn here.
lede: Dingcun lies on the east bank of the Fen River and keeps more than twenty Ming and Qing residences: the northern group are single-court siheyuan from the Wanli reign of the Ming onward, the central and southern groups two-court compounds of the Yongzheng to Xianfeng reigns of the Qing. The Ding Kun compound, now Courtyard No. 1 and the Dingcun Folk Museum, was founded in 1745 (10th year of Qianlong, Qing); its owners Ding Kun and his son Ding Jialun both purchased the status of imperial student, and the grandson Ding Xilian purchased a sub-prefectural post in 1795 (60th year of Qianlong), whereupon the 'Xuandelang' archway was raised before the gate. The plate shows the three-bay hall inside the courtyard and the wing rooms on either side.
facts: Courtyard: as drawn, a three-bay hall with a front porch, with wing rooms on both sides enclosing a long narrow court; Dingcun houses are northern siheyuan of brick, stone and timber, richly carved on eave boards, sparrow braces, column bases and gate stones, and in one Qianlong-era house the railing panels of the central hall carry 'hundred plays' carvings such as 'Ningwu Pass' and 'Yue Fei's mother tattooing'.

Dating: the earliest house of the northern group dates to 1593 (21st year of Wanli, Ming), the central and southern groups to the Yongzheng-Xianfeng reigns of the Qing; Courtyard No. 1 was founded in 1745 (10th year of Qianlong), and the 'Xuandelang' archway was erected after Ding Xilian's purchase of office in 1795 (60th year of Qianlong). The Dingcun residences were listed as a national key protected site in 1988.

Value: Dingcun is a group of residences built continuously by one family in one village for over two hundred years; the Dingcun Folk Museum, opened in 1985, was China's first folk museum of the Han people. The Dingcun site on the Fen River terrace beside the village is a Palaeolithic site, protected separately from the houses.

name: Quanzhou Prefectural Confucian Temple
sub: Dacheng Hall · Qing structure in Song style
lede: A Hall of Great Achievement for a prefectural school, yet roofed with a double-eave hip roof, yellow glazed tiles and stone columns carved with coiling dragons: extraordinarily rare among Confucian temples anywhere in China. The temple moved to its present site in the early Taiping Xingguo era of the Northern Song and took its 'school on the left, temple on the right' layout after a rebuilding in 1137; the hall was rebuilt in the Xianchun era and the present hall was thoroughly repaired in 1761, yet its column grid, beam frame and true cantilever brackets keep twelfth-century practice. The six relief dragon columns along the front eaves are known locally as 'six dragons bearing up the sage'.
facts: Form: seven bays wide and five deep, about 801 square metres in area, with a double-eave hip roof of yellow glazed tiles; the hall body is carried on 48 round white stone columns in a two-ring 'double-trough' grid, with six relief dragon columns at the front eaves and two more dragon columns inside; the bracket sets use true ang inside and out, the beams are fully painted, and the ridges carry cut-porcelain ornament.

Dating: moved to the present site early in the Taiping Xingguo era of the Northern Song and rebuilt in 1137; the hall was rebuilt in the Xianchun era (1265-1274), and the present hall is the product of a major repair in 1761 that kept its Song structural character. A 2014-2015 restoration to the original form and materials was named one of the outstanding heritage conservation projects of 2020 nationwide.

Significance: the Quanzhou Confucian Temple and its school symbolised the officials and scholars of Song-Yuan Quanzhou, and its building scale is the largest among Confucian temples in China's seven southeastern provinces; the waist of the Sumeru base of the terrace in front still carries Song bluestone reliefs of scrolling foliage. In 2021 it was inscribed as a component of the World Heritage property 'Quanzhou: Emporium of the World in Song-Yuan China'.

name: Putuo Zongcheng Temple
sub: Complete front of the Great Red Terrace and its surviving upper roofs
yearNote: An independent temple complex forming one entry; it is not combined with the Xumi Fushou Temple into one entry, nor split into separate courtyards to pad the count.
lede: The immense red terrace conceals halls behind its walls, while roof edges emerge above. White terraces climb the slope towards the central mass. Built under Qianlong with the Potala Palace as an important model, Putuo Zongcheng combines Chinese roofs and Tibetan-style terrace forms; its most revealing relationship is between the massive shell and the enclosed worship courts.
facts: The Great Red Terrace is the core, raised above stepped white terraces. Windows and central decoration divide the broad wall; roofs appear above, but the halls mostly lie within. This exterior is not an ordinary hall frontage.
The temple was built from 1767 to 1771, drawing on the Potala Palace. It is a newly built Qing temple: the antiquity of its model does not change the date of the surviving structure.

Wanfaguiyi Hall stands within the red terrace. Its Chinese-style double eaves and the Tibetan-style mass organise worship together; reading the rising exterior alongside enclosed courts explains the synthesis.

name: Shanxi-Shaanxi-Gansu Guild Hall, Kaifeng
sub: Front of the timber memorial archway
yearNote: The subject drawn is dated to the Qing; the numerical year is only for approximate sorting.
lede: The timber gateway of Kaifeng’s Shanxi–Shaanxi–Gansu Guild Hall welcomes visitors beneath five roofs of varying height. A broad central passage lies between two clusters of posts spreading forward and backward from carved stone bases. The gateway belonged to both the guild precinct and Guandi worship. Merchants of the three provinces used the hall for fellowship and assistance, while its carved stories and auspicious motifs expressed prosperity, moral aspirations and memories of home.
facts: The gateway has three openings, six posts and five roofs. The posts form two groups of three, spreading in a “chicken-foot” plan. The central roof rises above the flanking roofs, with drum-shaped braces and tall stone bases framing the passage.
Merchants from Shanxi, Shaanxi and Gansu founded the guild hall in 1776. The gateway is a Qing structure; its timeline position around 1780 is approximate rather than a verified completion date.

The guild combined Guandi worship, fellow-provincials’ association and relief. Carved historical stories and auspicious imagery at the gateway show how merchant architecture also expressed ethical ideals and regional identity.

name: Longxing Temple, Xinjiang County
era: Qing · Qianlong restoration with added stories
yearNote: This year is the date of the Qing restoration that added stories, producing the surviving thirteen-story exterior; neither the temple's Tang history nor early remains inside the pagoda are equated directly with the date of the exterior.
lede: The Longxing Pagoda on the high ground north of the old Jiangzhou city is octagonal and thirteen storeys, over 42 m high, the highest point in the town. The pagoda originally had eight storeys; it collapsed in 1777 (42nd year of Qianlong, Qing) and was rebuilt in 1784 (49th year of Qianlong), cased in grey brick and raised to thirteen storeys, and the flat corbelled brick eaves and taper seen today were fixed then. The temple was founded in the early Tang as the Biluo Daoist abbey and renamed Longxing Temple in 670 (1st year of Xianheng); early remains inside the pagoda do not date its exterior. The plate shows the whole pagoda.
facts: Form: an octagonal brick pagoda of pavilion type, built of grey brick, thirteen storeys tapering upward, each storey divided by corbelled brick eaves, with brick-carved bracket sets under the first-storey eaves; its height is given as 42.4 m by one source and 43.7 m by another, and each storey carries a plaque, from 'one column holding up heaven' to 'ten continents and three isles'.

Dating: originally eight storeys, the pagoda fell in 1777 (42nd year of Qianlong, Qing) and was rebuilt in 1784 (49th year of Qianlong) at thirteen storeys; another account has it cased and heightened during the 1777 repair. Repaired in 1941, with a Record of Repairing the Longxing Temple of Xinjiang. The whole temple became a national key protected site in 2006.

Curiosity: the county gazetteer and steles record 'smoke rising' from the top of the pagoda on several occasions, in 1875 (1st year of Guangxu), 1937, 1971, 1976 and 1993, the 1971 episode lasting over ten days, its cause unexplained; the temple also holds a Yuan main hall and the Tang Biluo Stele, not in the plate.

name: Guanlin, Luoyang
yearNote: The plate takes the Qianqiujian Stage Tower and is dated by its construction in 1791; the history of the Guanlin hall complex from the Wanli reign of the Ming is not used for the coloring of this stage tower.
lede: Qianqiu Jian Theatre stands on a raised stage before Guanlin’s main gate, opening toward the square and temple. A hip-and-gable roof over the front stage joins a flush-gabled roof behind; together they resemble a double-eaved pavilion, although the two functional parts remain distinct. Built later than the Ming development of the main halls, the theatre shows how ritual precincts acquired new facilities as performance and Guandi worship became part of public life.
facts: The theatre has a projecting-front plan, joining a hip-and-gable stage roof to a flush-gabled backstage roof. Its raised platform faces Guanlin’s gate across a square used for performance and viewing.

Qianqiu Jian Theatre was built in 1791, the fifty-sixth year of the Qing Qianlong era. Guanlin’s hall complex has a separate Ming Wanli-period expansion history, which should not be used to date this theatre.

At the front of Guanlin’s axis, the theatre begins a sequence of gates, halls and a rear tomb with different functions. Performances offered to the deity extended temple worship into public gatherings and cultural activity.

name: Shanxi-Shaanxi Guild Hall, Shedian
yearNote: 1800 is an approximate sorting point for the Qing construction phase to which the Xuanjian Tower belongs. Officially reproduced material contains the conversion error “1st year of Jiaqing = 1786,” so that figure is not adopted as a precise completion year; 1756–1892 is the construction span of the whole guild hall complex.
place: Henan · Nanyang · Shedian Town, Sheqi County
lede: Xuanjian Theatre at Shedian’s Shanxi–Shaanxi Guild Hall rises beneath a central triple-eaved roof flanked by smaller towers. Wood and stone carving surround the stage. In a town where waterborne and overland trade met, merchants required Guandi worship, fellowship and ritual theatre. Built during an early phase of the repeatedly enlarged complex, the theatre turned merchant wealth into a shared cultural space, preserving the scale of Qing guild life.
facts: The theatre’s triple-eaved hip-and-gable roof joins symmetrical side towers. A raised stage and open performance area are enriched by carved beams and stone balustrades whose subjects relate to theatre.

The guild complex was built in phases between 1756 and 1892, with Xuanjian Theatre belonging to an early phase. Around 1800 is only a timeline position; available sources do not establish a separate completion year reliably.

Shanxi and Shaanxi merchants financed a complex combining a Guandi shrine with commercial fellowship. Historical and theatrical carving brought worship, entertainment and Confucian aspirations into their meeting place.

name: Jingjue Temple
sub: Xiangfu Palace and its projecting round-ridge front annex
yearNote: The provincial cultural heritage bureau identifies the surviving temple buildings as Qing; 1800 is only an approximate Qing sorting value. No precise construction year has been found for the Xiangfu Palace itself, and the tradition of a Tang founding is not used to date the present structure.
siteCoordinateSource: 维基百科《净觉寺（玉田）》39°48′40.356″N,117°55′12.576″E，作为寺院独立地点近似定位：https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/净觉寺_(玉田) 。
lede: Xiangfu Hall’s projecting rounded-roof porch extends a lower roof into the courtyard. Stone columns and timber framing join unequal roof heights, creating depth. Jingjue Temple’s surviving buildings chiefly belong to Qing repairs; the principal hall uses a suspended-beam and hanging-post arrangement. It differs from the double-eaved Mahavira Hall behind, rewarding close attention to roof connections rather than founding legends.
facts: Xiangfu Hall has a timber hip-and-gable roof and projecting rounded-roof porch. Columns connect porch and hall; the lower front roof creates depth and must not be confused with the rear double-eaved Mahavira Hall.

The provincial authority assigns the surviving temple to the Qing and records repeated repairs. No exact construction year for Xiangfu Hall is established; the temple’s early history is distinguished from the present frame.

Suspended beams and hanging posts organise the hall’s support, while brick, stone and wood carving display different crafts. The porch-to-hall junction offers a concrete way to study local adjustments of space and structure.

name: Fuxi Temple, Tianshui
era: Enlarged in the 10th year of Jiaqing, Qing
yearNote: The Ceremonial Gate was first built in 1523 and changed from three bays to five during the 1805 restoration; the drawing shows the surviving five-bay gate, dated by its 1805 form, and does not take the founding of the whole temple in 1483–1484 as the date of this gate. Repairs to the roofs and eaves, including those of the Ceremonial Gate, were completed in early 2026.
lede: Red columns carry a five-bay ritual gate, whose central passage links the forecourt with the main ceremonial courtyard. At Tianshui’s Fuxi Temple, successive gates and halls unfold along an axis, giving worship a measured pace. Originally a three-bay Ming gate, it was widened to five bays in the Qing period; its present breadth preserves that change.
facts: The ritual gate stands beyond the main gate and before Xiantian Hall, with a central passage in its five-bay front. A single roof and red columns extend sideways. This second courtyard gateway is smaller in scale than the principal ritual halls.

The gate was founded in 1523 and widened from three bays to five during repairs begun in 1805. Its broad present form reflects that later change, and the temple’s earlier Chenghua-period foundation does not directly date this gate.

Successive gates and courtyards organise Fuxi worship as a gradual progression, and this gate marks a significant transition. Its enlargement shows how ritual architecture could adapt to use over time.

name: Dingzhou Examination Hall
sub: Complete front elevation of the Kui Pavilion and examination cells
yearNote: The intention is to use the Qing enlarged form shown by the surviving Kui Pavilion and examination cells; the precise founding year of the individual building needs further verification at the photograph stage.
lede: The Kuige and examination cells form a stepped mountain-like frontage, highest at the centre. They are not seven separate towers: a front pavilion and the gable ends of the examination building combine, with long windows lighting the interior. Founded under Qianlong and expanded under Daoguang, Dingzhou’s examination compound preserves rooms for candidates, officials and ritual as well as the history of the examination system.
facts: Kuige adjoins the south side of the examination building, following its gable profile through seven roof groups descending from the centre. Long lattice windows admit light; the silhouette is not a row of seven independent towers.

The compound was founded in 1738 and repaired and enlarged in 1834. Its present scale chiefly reflects the later expansion; these complex-wide dates do not establish the same building year for every individual structure.

Kuige honoured Kuixing, the cells accommodated examinations, the northern hall handled submitted and sealed scripts, and the rear building served examiners. Distinct functions translate scholarly ambition, ritual and administration into connected rooms and courts.

name: Jiwang Temple, Jishan
sub: Offering Hall · Bell and drum towers
yearNote: The Offering Hall, bell and drum towers and Houji Tower drawn here are Qing rebuildings; the Yuan-dynasty Jiangyuan Hall in the temple is not drawn.
place: Shanxi · Jishan · West Street of the county town
lede: The sparrow braces under the front eaves of the offering hall of the Jiwang Temple carry no dragons or phoenixes; they show Hou Ji teaching the people to farm, spring sowing and the grain harvest. On either wing of this small three-bay hall stands a bell or drum tower, four metres square under a double-eaved cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof, and behind rises the thirty-metre Hou Ji Tower, three glazed roofs crowded together. The temple was founded in 1345 (5th year of Zhizheng, Yuan), burned in the Daoguang reign of the Qing, and was rebuilt in 1843 (23rd year of Daoguang) by subscription led by the magistrate Li Jingchun; all three buildings drawn belong to that rebuilding. The plate shows the offering hall and the bell and drum towers, with only the upper eaves of the Hou Ji Tower visible.
facts: Offering hall: three bays and 14 m wide, 10 m deep, roofed in coloured glazed tile, the roof described as overhanging-gable by one source and flush-gable by another; the sparrow braces under front and rear eaves are wood reliefs of farming, Hou Ji teaching agriculture in the central bay, spring ploughing in the east bay and harvest in the west bay. The bell and drum towers are 4 m square under double-eaved cross-shaped hip-and-gable roofs.

Dating: founded in 1345 (5th year of Zhizheng, Yuan), the temple burned down in the 10th year of Daoguang (some say the 16th) and was rebuilt in 1843 (23rd year of Daoguang) by subscription led by magistrate Li Jingchun; his seven-character poem on its completion is carved in the west gable wall, and the eight views of Jishan in the east. Listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Comparison: the temple is known for the 'three marvels' of glaze, wood carving and stone carving; the gallery of the Hou Ji Tower has twenty carved stone eave columns and fifty-two carved stone balustrade panels. The Jiangyuan Hall inside is a Yuan structure and the National Cultural Heritage Administration registers the temple as 'Yuan to Qing', but everything drawn is Qing.

name: Ancient Opera Stages of Ninghai
sub: Hu Clan Ancestral Hall, Aohu · Chongxing Temple · City God Temple
era: Qing to Republic · Aohu stage, 4th year of Xianfeng
lede: Ninghai County has 125 surviving old opera stages, ten of them listed as national protected sites, all built inside ancestral halls and temples between the Qing and the Republic. A stage one bay square is raised half a person's height into the air, the upturned corners of its hip-and-gable roof curling like ox horns, and inside a caisson ceiling spirals upward.
facts: Most stages are one bay wide, with the stage floor raised off the ground and a carved balustrade around the stage front; the column heads support the eaves with carved brackets (niutui, “ox legs”) rather than bracket sets.

Caisson ceilings are the specialty of Ninghai's stages: the stage of the Hu Clan Ancestral Hall in Aohu and its linking corridor have three caisson ceilings in a row, one of only three surviving “three linked caisson ceilings” in Zhejiang.

The Hu Clan Ancestral Hall in Aohu was built in the 4th year of Xianfeng in the Qing (1854); the stage connects with viewing galleries on either side, from whose upper floors the audience watched performances.

name: Houtu Shrine, Wanrong
era: Qing · Rebuilt in the 9th year of Tongzhi
place: Shanxi · Wanrong · Ronghe Town · Miaoqian Village
lede: Emperor Wu of Han sacrificed to Houtu at Fenyin and, boating on the Fen, wrote the Song of the Autumn Wind; two thousand years later this tower still bears its name. It stands at the northern end of the Houtu Shrine on a brick-and-stone platform sixteen metres square, three storeys and over thirty-two metres high, galleried on all four sides under a cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof; the platform is pierced east-west like a street gate, with 'Gazing at Lu' over the east arch and 'Looking to Qin' over the west. As the Yellow River repeatedly shifted, the shrine was moved east again and again; the present site was rebuilt in 1870 (9th year of Tongzhi, Qing) by magistrate Dai Ruzhen, and the tower was then moved to the rear of the temple. The plate shows the front of Qiufeng Lou.
facts: Form: platform 16 m square, tower of three storeys, 32.6 m high (33 m by another account), five bays wide and deep, cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof, galleries on each storey, a warrior figure on each upturned corner; inside the south gate of the platform a small niche is inscribed 'Sweeping-the-ground Altar', and the storeys hold, from bottom to top, modern, Qing and Yuan carvings of the Song of the Autumn Wind.

History: in the Yuan an Autumn Wind Pavilion behind the temple held the stele of the song carved in 1271 (8th year of Zhiyuan); in the Longqing reign of the Ming the pavilion was lost to the Fen and a tower built before the temple; in 1662 (1st year of Kangxi, Qing) the river breached and the tower was lost, and it was rebuilt elsewhere the next year; destroyed again in 1862 (1st year of Tongzhi) and moved to the present site in 1870 (9th year of Tongzhi). After the Guangxu-era Ronghe County Gazetteer.

Background: the Houtu Shrine at Fenyin was the imperial temple for sacrifice to the earth established by Emperor Wu of Han, and emperors of Han, Tang and Song sacrificed here in person; a temple-plan stele of 1137 (15th year of Tianhui, Jin) depicts the layout after the Northern Song enlargement. Apart from the Yuan gate, most of today's shrine is late Qing; listed as a national key protected site in 1996.

name: Shi Family Compound, Yangliuqing, Tianjin
era: Large-scale construction in the early Guangxu reign · Later repairs
yearNote: 1875 is the starting point of the large-scale construction of the Shi family residence; the date of manufacture of the inner-courtyard gate drawn here as a separate element is unconfirmed, and this sorting point is not called the gate's exact completion year.
lede: Gray-brick gateways recede one behind another along the axis of the nested courtyards, with dark red timber frames and pale drum-shaped stones finishing the entrance. The inner-courtyard gate and the receding gateway courtyards are chosen here; the stone lions and eave ornaments of another, outer gateway are not pieced into the same plate.
facts: The surviving Shi Family Compound is the Zunmei Tang residence; its large-scale construction began early in the Guangxu reign of the Qing (1875), and later conservation repairs have their own dates.

The plate is based on photographs of the inner-courtyard gate, keeping the low tiled roof, gray-brick gate piers, short walls on either side, drum-shaped stones and the gates of the nested courtyards behind.

Gray brick and gray tile, near-black reddish-brown door frames, dark red inset panels and a few ocher-gold edge lines are distinguished as they appear today; no bird's-eye view of the whole residence is drawn, and the outer gateway is not spliced in.

name: Yueyang Tower
era: Rebuilt in the 6th year of Guangxu, Qing
yearNote: Dated by the surviving tower form produced by the rebuilding of the 6th year of Guangxu in the Qing (1880); the 1984 dismantling and major repair continued the old form, and neither the Three Kingdoms legend of a troop-review tower nor the year of the Northern Song restoration is used as the date of this drawing.
place: Hunan · Yueyang · Shore of Dongting Lake
lede: Three storeys send their eaves outward, while the helmet-shaped upper roof curves inward, giving Yueyang Tower an outline both lively and steady. On Dongting Lake, timber columns and jointed beams carry the roofs, and galleries open the climbing experience toward the water. Its present form arose from the 1880 reconstruction and was retained in modern conservation; literary fame and the surviving building’s date need separate readings.
facts: The three-storey timber structure joins projecting eaves to a helmet-shaped roof. Beams and columns form a mortise-and-tenon framework. Open galleries, railings and raised corners maintain accessible, airy spaces beneath the substantial roofs.

The current form derives from the 1880 reconstruction. Later conservation included complete dismantling and reassembly, finished in 1984 with the earlier design retained. Older tower history and literary memories do not date every surviving timber component.

Views over the lake and the reading of Fan Zhongyan’s Account of Yueyang Tower bring landscape and literature together. The Qing design preserves that experience of ascent, but the essay’s Northern Song date cannot date the present structure.

name: Nanyue Grand Temple
era: Rebuilt in the Guangxu reign, Qing
yearNote: 1882 is taken as the rebuilding date of the surviving main structures of the Nanyue Grand Temple; the Shengdi Hall later underwent changes such as repairs and column replacement. The drawing shows the present state as photographed and does not take the Tang founding of the whole temple as the date of this hall.
lede: Seven bays extend beneath the double-eaved hip-and-gable roof of Nanyue Temple’s Shengdi Hall, where a stone-columned gallery opens the deep shade beneath the eaves. The palatial axis reaches a principal ritual space here, with timber, stone and carving shaping an orderly front. Its present principal fabric is dated to the Guangxu reconstruction, with later repairs altering details; the long history of mountain worship does not date every component.
facts: The hall is seven bays wide, with a stone-columned outer gallery beneath a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof. Roof, brackets and lower eaves extend in successive lines, while columns divide the broad front into clear bays and carving enriches the details.

The temple’s surviving principal buildings took shape after reconstruction in 1882, and the hall underwent subsequent repairs. Earlier temple history, Qing reconstruction and later conservation are distinct phases; today’s appearance cannot be described as an original Tang building.

This principal ritual hall gathers worship at the foot of the mountain before ascent. The axial palatial buildings stand beside the temple’s Buddhist and Daoist precincts, showing a setting where state mountain rites and local religious practice have long intersected.

name: Chen Clan Academy, Guangzhou
sub: Front gate · Lingnan ceramic sculpture and stone carving
yearNote: 1893 is the completion year of the Chen Clan Academy; the plate takes the present state of the central front gate, and components repaired later are not all regarded as original work of that year.
lede: The central entrance of the Chen Clan Ancestral Hall brings grey brick, stone columns and ceramic ridge figures into a richly layered facade beneath gabled roofs. Chen’s Academy was funded by Chen lineage groups across Guangdong, serving clan affairs and accommodating members visiting Guangzhou for examinations and other business. Completed in the late nineteenth century and repeatedly maintained, its entrance introduces both Lingnan craft and lineage organization.
facts: The central entrance has roofs ending at the gable walls, with stone columns and beams meeting grey brickwork. Ceramic ridge figures, brick reliefs and woodcarving concentrate different materials at the doorway in layers that invite close viewing.

Planning began in 1888. An inscribed couplet records completion of the principal complex in 1893, while some ridge inscriptions document work in the following year. The entrance and its ornament have since been repaired and are not all unchanged originals from one year.

Chen lineage groups jointly built the academy to accommodate members visiting the provincial capital for examinations, appointments and business. Its entrance concentrates regional carving and modelling while expressing a network of support across local clan communities.

name: Guangdong Guild Hall, Tianjin
sub: Stage · Detail of the chicken-cage caisson ceiling
era: Completed in the 33rd year of Guangxu
lede: The Guangdong Guildhall’s stage projects towards its audience. Above it, a chicken-coop-shaped coffered ceiling spirals from a square frame towards a circular centre, combining carving and bracket work overhead. Two tiers of seating allow performances to be watched from three sides. Completed in 1907, the hall served Guangdong residents in Tianjin for gatherings and theatre, later becoming a theatre museum. Its stage connects migrant community life with the city’s theatrical memory.
facts: The projecting stage faces the audience on three sides without freestanding columns obstructing the front. Its square-framed, circular coffered ceiling uses spiralling interlocked brackets; two seating tiers surround the performance space.

The guildhall was completed in 1907, the thirty-third Guangxu year of Qing. After restoration it became a theatre museum in 1986. Initial construction, conservation and museum use represent separate phases.

The narrowing ceiling joins ornamental carpentry with sound projection, while the projecting stage brings performers close to spectators. This Guangdong community hall preserves the meeting of travelling merchants, theatre and Tianjin’s urban culture.

name: Dacheng Hall of the Jilin Confucian Temple
era: Main buildings completed in the 1st year of Xuantong
yearNote: 1909 is the completion year of the surviving main buildings; 1736 is the founding of the Confucian temple, and the repairs of the 1920s and modern times are recorded separately, not merged into one year.
lede: Eleven bays spread beneath yellow glazed tiles and double eaves, placing Dacheng Hall at the centre of Jilin’s Confucian ceremonial axis. It belongs to the main buildings completed at the relocated temple in 1909, not the original foundation of 1736. Republican and modern repairs add further layers to this late Qing educational landmark.
facts: The hall is eleven bays wide excluding the side corridors, with twelve front columns and a double-eaved yellow-tiled roof. A balustraded terrace with a central cloud-and-dragon carving emphasises the ceremonial axis.

The temple was founded in 1736, relocated for building in 1907 and completed its main halls in 1909. Repairs followed from 1920; foundation, surviving principal construction and later repairs are distinct stages.

The hall occupies the centre of a three-courtyard complex and serves Confucius worship. Its continuous columns and raised terrace direct visitors inward, expressing ritual hierarchy and local educational history.

name: Jiaxiu Tower, Guiyang
sub: Nanming River · Three stories, three eaves
era: Rebuilt in the 1st year of Xuantong · Later repairs
yearNote: The present appearance follows the 1909 restoration design and later repairs such as those of 1981; the Ming founding date does not replace the date of the surviving tower's form.
lede: Jiaxiu Pavilion stands on a rocky base in the Nanming River, its three storeys and three tiers of eaves rising to a pyramidal roof with four corners. Fuyu Bridge connects it to the banks, bringing pavilion, bridge and water into one urban landscape. Founded in the Ming period, it suffered repeated destruction and rebuilding. Its present form follows the 1909 reconstruction and a further twentieth-century restoration, preserving an older arrangement while recording Guiyang’s efforts to sustain its landmark.
facts: The three-storey pavilion has three tiers of eaves and a four-cornered pyramidal roof. Red lattice windows, stone eaves-supporting columns and balustrades stand above Aoji Rock; Fuyu Bridge connects the pavilion to pedestrian space on both banks.

Founded in the Ming Wanli period, Jiaxiu Pavilion was repeatedly damaged and repaired. Its present appearance follows the 1909 rebuilding and a further restoration in 1981, so all its materials should not be treated as Ming originals.

The name Jiaxiu expresses hopes for distinction in examinations and the emergence of talent. Long celebrated in verse, its combination of pavilion, river and bridge gives Guiyang’s educational ideals a tangible place in the city.

name: Chengyang Yongji Bridge
sub: Dong wind-and-rain bridge · Timber gallery with five pavilions
yearNote: Following volume 7 of Sanjiang Historical and Literary Materials, completion is taken as 1924; the proposal to build it in 1911 or the start of work in 1912 does not equal the completion year. The bridge has been repaired in later times, and the plate draws the complete bridge with all five pavilions as photographed today.
lede: Chengyang Yongji Bridge links five pavilions with a continuous timber corridor above stone piers and abutments. Tiered pavilion roofs turn the river crossing into an undulating line of buildings. Railings and benches provide places to pause, joining transport with shelter and social use. Local historical records give completion in 1924, separately from earlier proposals and construction. Later repairs continue a carpentry tradition rooted in the shared life of Dong villages.
facts: Stone supports carry a timber deck and five pavilions connected by a tiled corridor. Railings and benches run along both sides. Tiered roofs rise above the passage, with piers, framing and roofing forming the complete river crossing.

Sanjiang Historical Materials, volume seven, records a proposal in 1911 and completion in 1924; another account gives construction from 1912. Proposal, building and completion are separate stages, followed by later repairs.

The corridor shelters travellers and benches turn a route into a place for rest and interaction. Timber joints connect deck and pavilions, expressing Dong traditions that join daily travel, community life and architectural form.

name: Ruishi Lou, Kaiping
sub: Diaolou of Jinjiangli · Blend of Chinese and Western styles
yearNote: 1925 is taken as the completion year of Ruishi Lou, not the date of all the Kaiping diaolou; the national protected site listing falls under “Kaiping Diaolou,” and World Heritage inscription belongs to a separate system.
lede: Ruishi Lou rises above Jinjiangli village as a rectangular reinforced-concrete tower, topped by colonnades, rounded lookout turrets and ornamental pediments. Built between 1923 and 1925, it combined residence and defence while bringing materials supplied through Hong Kong and Western architectural tastes into the village. Traditional auspicious motifs in its plaster decoration reveal how emigrant-linked communities accommodated several architectural languages.
facts: The nine-level reinforced-concrete diaolou has colonnades and lookout turrets above a regular body, with Western-style window mouldings and pediments. Its simple lower volume and complex crown provide both domestic space and positions for observation and defence.

Local government sources describe construction in 1923–1925, commissioned by Huang Bixiu after prospering in Hong Kong and carried out by nearby craftsmen. Completion and commencement must be distinguished; these dates do not apply to other diaolou.

Building materials came through Hong Kong, while plaster decoration included traditional motifs of blessing, rank, joy and longevity. The tower brings together defence, overseas commerce and local craft, offering a concrete way to understand Kaiping’s emigrant-linked society.

name: Saint Sophia Cathedral, Harbin
yearNote: The surviving brick church was begun in 1923 and completed in 1932; the early wooden church of 1907 is not used as the date of the plate's subject.
lede: A Latin-cross church of red brick: at the crossing four brick piers carry a drum 10 m across and a huge onion dome, above the main door rises a tent-roofed bell tower, and the whole stands 53.35 m to the top of the cross, the largest Orthodox church in the Far East. A wooden garrison church was first built here in 1907 and cased in brick in 1912; the brick building seen today was begun in September 1923 to the design of the Russian architect Oskolkov, modelled on the Epiphany Church in St Petersburg, and completed in November 1932. The plate shows the 1932 building and omits the modern ticket annex.
facts: Form: fair-faced red brick with a sheet-iron roof painted green; the plan is a Latin cross about 28 m north to south and 42 m east to west, with a floor area of 721 square metres holding 1,500 people. At the crossing four brick piers carry a drum 10 m in outer diameter and the onion dome; tent-roofed spires stand over the main door, the two transepts and the rear door, the central dome highest and the bell tower next.

Dating: built in March 1907 as a timber garrison church for the Russian 4th East Siberian Infantry Division and enlarged in August that year at the expense of the tea merchant Chistyakov; cased in brick in 1912 to become a brick-and-timber building; the cornerstone of the rebuilding was laid on 27 September 1923, the architect Oskolkov taking Kosyakov's Epiphany Church in St Petersburg as his model, and the work was completed on 25 November 1932.

Significance: it unites the centralised dome of Byzantine building with the onion domes and tent roofs of Russian vernacular timber architecture, and the Japanese architectural historian Nishizawa Yasuhiko judged it comparable in scale and conception to St Basil's in Moscow. It was listed as a Major National Historical and Cultural Site in 1996 and became the Harbin Museum of Architecture and Art in 1997.

name: Stork Tower, Yongji
sub: On the bank of the Yellow River · Contemporary reconstruction
place: Shanxi · Yongji · West of the old city of Puzhou
lede: The famous tower of Wang Zhihuan's poem stands again today on the bank of the Yellow River west of the old city of Puzhou. The present tower was rebuilt and completed in 2002: a high platform raises four tiers of eaves, and tier upon tier of colonnades bring the poetry of climbing high to gaze afar back into reality.
facts: Surviving tower: reconstruction began in December 1997, and the tower was completed and opened on September 26, 2002; this drawing and the timeline both register it under 2002.
Tang-style tower: externally it has four tiers of eaves and three stories, is 73.9 m tall overall and faces north, with Tang-style painted decoration and spreading eaves.

History of the old tower: the original tower was first built in the Northern Zhou, survived through the Tang and Song, and was destroyed by war in the early Yuan; its founding date and the surviving reconstruction are recorded separately.

name: Hōryū-ji
era: Asuka period · Second half of the 7th century
lede: Two tiled roofs rise above a lower board-roofed mokoshi at Horyuji’s Main Hall, whose deep eaves convey the timber architecture of the Asuka period. Slightly swelling columns support cloud-shaped brackets, and geometric upper railings add delicate detail between substantial roofs. The surviving hall belongs to the late seventh-century rebuilding of the Western Precinct, distinct from the temple’s foundation; its pairing with the pagoda preserves clues to early Buddhist planning.
facts: The main structure is five bays wide and four deep, with two tiled hip-and-gable roofs and a surrounding board-roofed mokoshi. Curving cloud brackets, swelling round columns and the upper railings establish a detailed rhythm beneath the deep eaves.

The temple’s early foundation is placed around the beginning of the seventh century. Records describe a fire in 670, followed by rebuilding of the Western Precinct. The hall is attributed to the late seventh century; the 607 foundation date does not date its completion.

In the Western Precinct, the hall stands to the east and the five-storey pagoda to the west within enclosing corridors. Their arrangement and cloud-shaped members preserve evidence of early East Asian Buddhist architecture and its wider cultural exchanges.

name: Tōshōdai-ji
era: Nara period · Second half of the 8th century
lede: Eight round columns carry the broad single-eaved roof of the Kondō of Tōshōdai-ji, and the open portico in front adds a quiet layer of transition between the courtyard and the inner chamber where the Buddha images stand. After Jianzhen (Ganjin) founded the temple, his disciples completed this Kondō in the second half of the 8th century.
facts: Jianzhen (Ganjin) founded Tōshōdai-ji in 759, while the surviving Kondō was built in the second half of the 8th century; the temple's official account links its construction to his disciple Nyohō.
The Kondō is seven bays across the front and four bays deep, with a yosemune (hipped) roof covered in hongawara tiles; the front bay is left open to form a colonnade.

Three-stepped bracket sets (mitesaki kumimono) beneath the eaves carry the deep overhang, and the shibi ridge-end ornaments at both ends of the ridge and the broad single eave together define its exterior.

name: Byōdō-in
lede: Across the Aji Pond, the central hall and its two wing corridors spread like a bird with outstretched wings, and twin phoenixes face each other on the ridge. The Amida Hall built by Fujiwara no Yorimichi in 1053 sets the Heian-period vision of the Pure Land above the waters of Uji.
facts: Heian structure: the Phoenix Hall was built in 1053 by Fujiwara no Yorimichi; the surviving central hall and wing corridors reflect the layout of an Amida hall of the late Heian period.

Twin phoenixes and two wings: the left and right wing corridors enclose the central hall, and a pair of phoenixes stands on the ridge; the name Phoenix Hall gradually came into use in the Edo period, and the phoenixes now on the roof are replacements installed in 1968.

Worship across the pond: the building sits in the west facing east, and worshippers on the east bank of the Aji Pond face west to venerate the Buddha; garden and hall together express the image of the Western Pure Land.

name: Tōdai-ji
lede: With round columns rising straight to the heights and tier upon tier of tie beams passing through them, the Nandaimon shows the structural power of the Daibutsuyō style. Three passages run beneath the broad double eaves, and Niō guardian statues on either side protect the entrance to Tōdai-ji.
facts: The surviving Nandaimon was rebuilt under the direction of Chōgen; its ridgepole was raised in 1199, and it was completed in 1203 together with the Kongō Rikishi statues within the gate.
The gate has an irimoya (hip-and-gable) roof, five bays across the front with three central doorways and double eaves; it is an important surviving example of Daibutsuyō architecture.
The gate has 18 great round columns in all, with six columns across the front dividing it into five bays; according to the temple, the gate is 25.46 m tall above the platform.

name: Kiyomizu-dera
lede: Look beneath the stage first: zelkova pillars some 12 m long, interlocked with horizontal ties and not a single nail, carry a nine-by-seven-bay hall out over the cliff of Mt Otowa. This is the Main Hall rebuilt in 1633 at the expense of Tokugawa Iemitsu after the fire of 1629; its hipped, cypress-bark roof sends out hip-and-gable wing corridors at both ends, with the stage spread in front. The Agency for Cultural Affairs calls it a masterpiece of early-Edo revivalist wayō architecture; it was designated a National Treasure in 1952 and inscribed with the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto in 1994.
facts: Form: a kakezukuri (stilted) hall nine bays by seven, single-storey under a hipped (yosemune) roof of cypress bark, with lean-to mokoshi on the east, west and north sides, a hip-and-gable wing corridor at each front corner and a stage of about 200 sq m between them. Including mokoshi and wings the plan measures roughly 36 m by 31 m.

History: tradition dates the founding to 778 and the precinct burned repeatedly. The present hall was rebuilt in 1633 (Kan'ei 10) at the expense of Tokugawa Iemitsu after the fire of 1629; it was listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1897 and designated a National Treasure in 1952. A twelve-year restoration begun in 2008 replaced all the cypress floorboards of the stage.

Value: judged by the Agency for Cultural Affairs a masterpiece of early-Edo revivalist wayō architecture, with gently curved roof planes and details that keep a Momoyama flavour. The stage rests on long zelkova pillars joined by through-ties without nails, the front row about 12 m long; the main halls of Hase-dera and Ishiyama-dera, also Kannon pilgrimage temples, use the same kakezukuri construction.

name: Tō-ji
lede: At 54.8 m this is the tallest surviving wooden pagoda in Japan. Since Kūkai vowed to build it in 826 the Tō-ji pagoda has burned four times from lightning or fire; the present one is the fifth, raised after the 1641 fire at the expense of Tokugawa Iemitsu under the master carpenter Nakai Masazumi and completed in the seventh month of 1644. All five storeys are three bays square under hongawara tiles, without railings; the bracket sets are three-stepped and there is not one decorative nosing — the Agency for Cultural Affairs calls it a masterpiece of early-Edo revivalist wayō in Kyoto, designated a National Treasure in 1952.
facts: Form: a five-storey pagoda three bays square, tiled with hongawara, 54.8 m tall on a cut-stone podium. Every storey is three bays to a side with no verandah or railing; the brackets are three-stepped with intermediate strut blocks, the central pillar runs down to the first storey, and the details omit nosings and other ornament — robust, pure wayō.

History: the pagoda is said to date from the Tenchō era (824–834) but was actually finished around the end of the ninth century, and was then destroyed four times by lightning or fire. The present tower was rebuilt after the fire of 1641, begun that twelfth month and completed in the seventh month of 1644; listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1897 and designated a National Treasure in 1952.

Esoteric space: on the first storey the central pillar stands for Dainichi Nyorai, with the four Buddhas of the Diamond Realm and eight bodhisattvas placed around it and the Mandalas of the Two Realms and the Eight Shingon Patriarchs painted on walls and pillars; the images date from 1643–44. Tō-ji (Kyōō-gokoku-ji), to which the pagoda belongs, was inscribed among the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto in 1994.

name: Guangyue Tower
era: Completed in the 7th year of Hongwu, Ming
yearNote: The date corresponds to the surviving Guangyue Tower; repairs over the centuries and its completion in the 7th year of Hongwu in the Ming (1374) are described separately.
place: Shandong · Liaocheng · Old city of Dongchang Prefecture
lede: Guangyue Tower combines a substantial terrace with a timber tower at the old city’s centre. Arched passages connect the streets below, four levels of eaves change as they rise, and a cross-ridged roof crowns the top. Completed in 1374, it has undergone repeated repairs while preserving features of the transition from Song and Yuan towers to Ming construction. The relationship between the heavy base and open galleries links urban movement with ascent.
facts: Form: four timber storeys with surrounding galleries and projecting eaves stand on a square masonry terrace beneath a cross-ridged roof. Semicircular arched openings connect streets through the base, with separate stairs organizing ascent.

Dating: the tower was completed in 1374, the seventh Hongwu year, and repaired repeatedly. The city gazetteer records surviving early principal components, but the present fabric also includes repairs; not every timber is an original Ming piece.

Significance: the terrace, galleries, eaves and internal structure carry Song and Yuan traditions into Ming building practice. At the meeting point of the city’s streets, its form accommodates the functions of drum signalling, lookout and ascent.

name: Fujian Guild Hall, Yantai
era: Begun in the 10th year of Guangxu · Completed in the 32nd year
yearNote: Begun in 1884 and completed in 1906; the drawing shows the street-front exterior in 2023 photographs, which predate the 2025 repairs.
lede: The street front of the Fujian Guild Hall brings a southern architectural outline to Yantai: red walls, firebreak gables and swallowtail ridges join around carved entrances. Fujian shipping merchants funded this Tianhou sanctuary, using materials selected and worked around Quanzhou before shipment north. It was completed in 1906. The frontage reveals only one edge of the compound, yet connects Mazu worship, maritime trade and the movement of craftsmanship between regions.
facts: Form: walls, gates and roofs form a continuous street front, with firebreak gables, swallowtail ridges and layered stone and timber decoration. A stage and main hall lie within; the frontage does not reveal the entire courtyard plan.

Dating: Fujian shipping merchants financed construction from 1884 to completion in 1906, with later maintenance and repair. Completion dates the original building campaign, rather than proving every component and surface of the frontage has remained unchanged.

Significance: the guild hall worships Mazu. Much of its brick, tile, timber and stone was selected and worked near Quanzhou before shipment, bringing southern craft north. Its entrance decoration and roofs record merchant organization, belief and interregional construction.

name: Nine-Top Pagoda
yearNote: 750 is used only to place it approximately in the Tang on the timeline, not as an exact construction year; the surviving pagoda includes later repairs, and the date of the folk-culture park is not counted as the date of the ancient pagoda.
lede: Jiuding Pagoda takes its outline from nine towers above one chamber: eight small square towers ring an octagonal platform, with a taller one at the centre. Corbelled brick courses project outwards and then recede to form their support. Construction style and associated finds generally place the main tower in the Tang period, without a secure year. Its complete outline also reflects later repairs rather than an untouched Tang appearance.
facts: Form: the main body is a single-storey octagonal brick pagoda. Corbelled eaves project and recede into an octagonal platform, carrying eight three-tiered square towers around a taller central tower: the nine tops named by the pagoda.

Dating: architectural form, sculptural style and associated finds support a Tang attribution, but the exact construction year is unproven. Later repairs are part of the surviving fabric; an approximate timeline date cannot substitute for an inscription.

Significance: one body supports nine towers, dividing the usual central summit into a surrounding ring and a raised centre. Small towers combined with a single chamber demonstrate variation in Buddhist pagoda form and brick construction.

name: Hongjialou Catholic Church
sub: Cathedral of the Sacred Heart of Jesus · Front elevation
era: Completed in the 31st year of Guangxu, Qing
yearNote: The date corresponds to the surviving church completed in 1905, distinguishing it from the earlier old church at Hongjialou and from later repairs.
lede: The front of Hongjialou Cathedral repeatedly draws the eye upwards. Twin spires frame a central rose window; pointed entrances and tall windows echo one another, while masonry buttresses anchor the outline. The present Cathedral of the Sacred Heart was completed in 1905, distinct from an earlier destroyed church and later repairs. European church forms and decoration became part of Jinan’s architectural landscape through this building.
facts: Form: twin spires frame a symmetrical front with a central rose window and three pointed entrances. Masonry walls and buttresses create vertical lines that reinforce the upward rhythm of its Gothic architecture.

Dating: the earlier church at Hongjialou was damaged in 1900; the rebuilt cathedral was completed in 1905. That date concerns the surviving cathedral, not its predecessor or subsequent repair campaigns.

Significance: twin towers, pointed arches and a rose window combine European ecclesiastical forms within Jinan. The facade serves both as an entrance and a religious landmark, recording encounters between local construction and architectural cultures from elsewhere.

name: Qingdao Catholic Church
yearNote: Begun in 1932 and completed in 1934; the date corresponds to the surviving St. Michael's Church and does not borrow the Qing-era dates of nearby German buildings.
lede: St Michael’s western front is organized by two bell towers and a central rose window. Pale yellow walls and red-tiled spires frame layered openings and crosses. Construction began in 1932 and finished in 1934, placing it in a later phase of Qingdao’s religious architecture rather than the dates of nearby German colonial buildings. Its symmetrical twin towers also differ clearly from the hall and single bell tower of the Jiangsu Road Protestant church.
facts: Form: the church has a cross-shaped plan, with symmetrical bell towers and crosses above their spires on the western facade. A circular rose window stands above the entrances; red tiles and pale walls distinguish roof, tower and openings.

Dating: construction ran from 1932 to completion in 1934, during the Republican period. Its location beside a former German colonial quarter does not place this church in the same period as nearby late-Qing buildings.

Significance: twin towers and a central window-and-door axis turn the entrance into an urban landmark. European church forms create a distinctive port-city streetscape; comparison with Jiangsu Road shows different periods and compositions of modern churches.

name: Qingdao Protestant Church
sub: Jiangsu Road · Main hall and bell tower
yearNote: The date refers to the main hall and bell tower built in 1908–1910; the church is kept separate from the Qingdao Catholic Church, completed in 1934.
lede: The Jiangsu Road church combines its main hall and bell tower asymmetrically. A clock face and green spire mark the higher tower, while a red-tiled roof slopes towards the lower hall. Rough granite frames windows and corners, giving the masonry a castle-like weight. Built from 1908 to 1910 during German occupation, this individual building is distinct in both date and composition from the twin-towered Catholic church on Zhejiang Road.
facts: Form: the hall stands beside one bell tower, whose facade uses rough granite and semicircular window frames beneath a large clock. Steep red-tiled roofs and a green spire belong to separate volumes, creating an uneven outline.

Dating: construction began in 1908 and finished in 1910. Subsequent repairs include restoration and reopening near the end of the twentieth century. The dates concern the hall and tower, separately from the other church completed in 1934.

Significance: rough stone, red-tiled slopes and a clock tower introduce German architectural forms into Qingdao. The asymmetrical relationship joins a place of worship with a visible urban timekeeping landmark.

name: Yan Temple of Qufu
era: Fusheng Hall rebuilt in the 2nd year of Zhengde, Ming
yearNote: The plate corresponds to the seven-bay Fusheng Hall as rebuilt in 1507, which continued to be repaired in the Ming and Qing and in 1934, 1978 and 2006; neither the date of the Yan Temple's relocation in the Yuan nor the 1509 construction date of the stele pavilion is used to date this hall.
lede: Fusheng Hall’s seven-bay front and two tiers of green-tiled eaves express Yan Hui’s place in Confucian worship. Four deeply carved dragon columns contrast with the other octagonal stone columns, while a terrace and colonnade extend the ceremonial space. The present scale follows the rebuilding of 1507, with Ming, Qing and modern repairs. Expansion from the earlier five-bay hall shows how changing honours entered architectural dimensions and decoration.
facts: Form: the seven-bay hall has a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof with green tiles, surrounding colonnades and a front terrace. Four columns bear deeply carved dragons; eighteen other octagonal columns have shallow dragon, phoenix and floral carvings.

Dating: rebuilding in 1507 enlarged the earlier five-bay hall to seven bays, followed by repeated Ming and Qing repairs. Campaigns in 1934, 1978 and from 2006 replaced some timbers. Its present fabric is not an untouched Ming original.

Significance: dedicated to Yan Hui, the hall’s name and rank express the honours accorded to him. Expansion and carved dragon columns provide evidence for the development of sage worship and temple organization, distinct from Confucius’s Dacheng Hall.

name: Iron Pagoda of Chongjue Temple
era: Seven stories built in the 4th year of Chongning, Song · Two stories added in the 9th year of Wanli, Ming
yearNote: 1105 refers to the seven-story cast-iron main body of the Song; two stories and the finial were added in 1581, so the nine stories standing today cannot all be labeled as Song construction. The plate shows only the pagoda body and the upper platform visible in the photograph.
lede: Chongjue Temple’s iron pagoda imitates timber architecture in its cast exterior: brackets, eaves and railings taper upwards, with Buddhist images and blind doors on the octagonal walls. A brick core lies inside; the pavilion-like tower has no access for ascent. Seven lower storeys originated in 1105, with two storeys and a finial added in 1581. Its nine-storey outline thus joins different materials and two periods.
facts: Form: the octagonal nine-storey pagoda has an iron shell around a brick core. Cast brackets, eaves and railings imitate timberwork; blind doors alternate with Buddhist images. There are no internal stairs despite the pavilion-like exterior.

Dating: casting began with seven storeys in 1105, the fourth Chongning year. Two storeys and a finial were added in 1581. Cast inscriptions and dated finds from the added levels support these separate phases; not all nine storeys are Song work.

Significance: cast components turn timber eaves, galleries and brackets into metal surfaces carrying Buddhist imagery. Song and Ming phases show a votive project completed across centuries, with components and inscriptions preserving its building history after repairs.

name: Stone Shrine of the Guo Family Tomb on Mount Xiaotang
sub: Eastern Han stone chamber · Modern shelter excluded
yearNote: The plate shows the Eastern Han stone shrine itself inside its shelter; “about the 1st century” is an archaeological dating, not an exact construction year.
lede: Xiaotangshan’s stone shrine translates a Han house into stone. Large slabs form walls and a pitched roof; a central column divides the open front into two bays, with roof surfaces imitating tile courses. Images and later inscriptions remain on the building, preserving both construction and the people who visited it. It is generally attributed to the early Eastern Han, around the first century rather than a precise year. Its traditional association with Guo Ju is not a proven identification.
facts: Form: the shrine is two bays wide and one deep, with an open front and a central column and stone beam supporting the roof. Large slabs form walls and projecting gables; carved tile courses reproduce the outline of a Han house in stone.

Dating: architecture, imagery and inscriptions generally place it in the early Eastern Han, approximately the first century. A visitor’s inscription of 129 proves it existed by then. Later supporting columns record additional repair phases.

Significance: interior images depict processions, daily life and mythology, while later inscriptions document viewing and maintenance. The traditional Guo Ju story must be distinguished from material dating; the shrine’s name does not establish its owner.
