name: Ginkaku-ji
yearNote: Temple records state that the ridgepole of the Kannon-den was raised in 1489 and that it was still unfinished when Ashikaga Yoshimasa died in 1490; the timeline marks the documented year of the ridgepole raising and does not presume a completion year.
lede: There is not a flake of silver on it. The Kannon Hall of Jishō-ji is one of only two buildings surviving from Ashikaga Yoshimasa's Higashiyama villa; its pillars were raised and ridge set in the third month of 1489, and it was still unfinished when Yoshimasa died the following year. Two storeys under a pyramidal shingle roof: the lower Shinkūden is a residential, shoin-like room, the upper Chōonkaku has bell-shaped windows and panelled doors like a small Zen Buddha hall. About 8 m on a side, it is smaller and quieter than his grandfather Yoshimitsu's Kinkaku, yet it is the only original pavilion-in-a-garden of the Muromachi period.
facts: Form: a two-storey pavilion facing east over Kinkyō-chi pond, 8.2 m on the east and west sides, 7.0 m on the north and 5.9 m on the south, with a pyramidal shingled roof topped by a bronze phoenix (a jewel finial until the late 18th century). The lower Shinkūden uses waist-high paper doors; the upper Chōonkaku is three bays square with panelled doors to north and south, bell-shaped windows east and west, a railed verandah all round and a seated Kannon inside.

History: Yoshimasa began the Higashiyama villa in 1482 and the Kannon Hall was framed in the third month of 1489 (Chōkyō 3). In the fighting of 1550 only it and the Tōgu-dō survived among the villa's buildings. Listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1900 and designated a National Treasure in 1951; excavation in 2009 found a Muromachi levelling layer beneath it, supporting its being an original on its original site.

Comparison: the Agency for Cultural Affairs records it as modelled on the Ruri-den of Saihō-ji, and the temple adds that it follows the reliquary hall of Rokuon-ji. The upper floor treats its four sides differently and has no door on the east front, suggesting worship originally from the south across a pond; when built it was black-lacquered inside and out with painted details. 'Silver Pavilion' is an Edo-period name coined by analogy with the Golden Pavilion, not a reference to silver leaf.

name: Sensō-ji
yearNote: The timeline marks the 1958 completion of the reinforced-concrete main hall seen today, rather than the temple's founding legend or the old Edo-period main hall.
lede: Senso-ji’s main hall preserves the impression of its Edo-period Kannon Hall, but its supporting structure is postwar reinforced concrete. The former hall burned in the Tokyo air raid; the present building was completed in 1958 and later received lighter titanium roof tiles. Its deep eaves show how traditional form and religious use continue in new materials, separately from the temple’s much earlier foundation legend.
facts: The reinforced-concrete hall has a tall hip-and-gable roof and a central worship porch above the steps. Inside, inner and outer precincts distinguish the sanctuary from the worshippers’ space; the building is more than an old-style shell.

The Edo-period hall burned in the Tokyo air raid of 1945; its replacement was completed in 1958. Titanium tiles were installed in 2010 for safety and maintenance. Traditional outlines do not make the present hall original Edo fabric.

Rebuilding based on the old hall’s appearance gave Kannon worship a familiar centre. The building shows both formal continuity and changing materials. The nearby Asakusa Shrine’s surviving Edo timber architecture offers a different path of continuity.

name: Himeji Castle
lede: White plaster and overlapping gables lift Himeji’s main keep above its massive stone base. Completed in 1609, it has five exterior roof tiers and an additional basement within. A defensive structure and demonstration of large timber construction, it now also records major Showa and Heisei conservation campaigns.
facts: The main keep has five exterior tiers but six above-ground floors and one basement. White plaster alternates with tiled roofs above a high stone base; roof tiers and internal floors must be counted separately.

Ikeda Terumasa began major reconstruction in 1601, completing the interconnected keep group in 1609. Later dismantling and conservation campaigns explain renewed roofs and plaster, rather than wholly original surfaces.
The main keep belongs to a defensive core of smaller keeps and connecting turrets. The main keep stands on a substantial stone base whose defences support the seemingly light gables and white walls.

name: Itsukushima Shrine
sub: Seaside main shrine buildings and corridors
era: Built in the 12th century · Main surviving buildings rebuilt in 1241
yearNote: The UNESCO evaluation records that the main surviving shrine buildings were rebuilt in 1241; the main shrine complex has undergone repeated repairs and additions, and the timeline point indicates only the rebuilding phase of the main surviving structures.
lede: Itsukushima Shrine’s main complex stretches along the shore, its vermilion corridors joining worship halls, waterfront platforms and stages. The tide changes the scene around the supporting posts, while island mountains and sea form its setting. Twelfth-century construction established the layout; the principal surviving halls were rebuilt after thirteenth-century fires and later repaired. Worship, circulation and seascape together shape the experience.
facts: The purification, worship, offering and main halls follow the ritual approach. East and west corridors connect the halls and waterfront platforms. Raised timber floors, vermilion posts and continuous eaves keep the walking route closely tied to the sea.

The principal layout was established in 1168, followed by two fires and rebuilding campaigns. The World Heritage evaluation identifies 1241 as the reconstruction phase of the principal surviving buildings, with later repairs and additions to individual parts.

The halls and corridors reflect the shinden-style residences of Heian aristocrats, adapted to worship between the mountainous island and sea. The changing tide brings nature worship, ritual activity and architectural experience together.

name: Nikkō Tōshō-gū
lede: Yomeimon at Nikko Toshogu forms an ornate entrance with a two-tier gate, curved karahafu gables and dense carving. White columns contrast with polychrome surfaces and metal ornament. Built in 1636 during Tokugawa Iemitsu’s major rebuilding of the shrine, it brings together early Edo carpentry, sculpture and decoration. Its human, animal and plant motifs reward close attention.
facts: The two-tier gate is three bays wide with one passage, a hip-and-gable roof, karahafu gables on all four sides and flanking walls. Layers of decoration between columns, brackets and roof make the composition unfold upward.

The Agency for Cultural Affairs dates Yomeimon to Kan’ei 13, or 1636, in the early Edo period. The age of the structure and that of subsequently repaired decorative surfaces must be distinguished; the present appearance is not wholly unchanged from construction.

More than 500 carvings include narrative figures, children at play and sages, combined with lacquer, painting and metalwork. The gate expresses Toshogu’s political role in commemorating Tokugawa Ieyasu while concentrating early Edo craftsmanship.

name: Five-Story Pagoda of Daigo-ji
lede: The oldest wooden building in Kyoto Prefecture. The pagoda of Daigo-ji was built for the repose of Emperor Daigo: begun under Emperor Suzaku and planned in the Jōhei era (931–938), it dragged on for twenty years and was completed only in 951 under Emperor Murakami (the Agency for Cultural Affairs lists completion as 952). When the Ōnin War burned lower Daigo to the ground, this tower alone was left standing. Its timbers are thick, its bracket sets have not yet matured into the standard three-step form, and the murals on the first storey are regarded as the fountainhead of Japanese esoteric Buddhist painting.
facts: Form: a five-storey pagoda three bays square with hongawara tiles; the members are heavy in section and the carpentry bold. The dismantling repair of fiscal 1954–59 restored the parts and confirmed that the brackets remain an unsettled, not yet fully developed three-step type — physical evidence of mid-Heian pagoda practice.

History: built for the repose of Emperor Daigo and planned in the Jōhei era together with the (lost) Golden Hall, it was completed in 951 (Tenryaku 5); the temple and the Agency for Cultural Affairs give 951 and 952 respectively. Lower Daigo was almost wholly destroyed in the Ōnin War and only this pagoda survived. Listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1897, National Treasure in 1951.

Murals: the Mandalas of the Two Realms and the Eight Shingon Patriarchs painted inside the first storey are a separate National Treasure, called the source of Japanese esoteric painting; the Kūkai among them is the oldest surviving portrait of him. The 1995 Kobe earthquake shook plaster off the tower. Daigo-ji was inscribed as a World Heritage property in 1994.

Heian period · 951

name: Sanjūsangen-dō
lede: A single run of eaves 118 m long. The main hall of Rengeō-in was built in 1164 by Taira no Kiyomori for the retired emperor Go-Shirakawa, burned in 1249, and was rebuilt in 1266 under the retired emperor Go-Saga; it is one of only two Kamakura-period buildings left in the old city centre. Thirty-five bays outside, thirty-three in the inner core — hence Sanjūsangen-dō — and inside, 1,001 Thousand-armed Kannon stand on ten-stepped tiers. In the Edo period archers of the domains shot the 'tōshiya' along the west verandah; what they were measuring was these 120 metres.
facts: Form: thirty-five bays long by five deep, single-storey, hip-and-gable (the Agency database field reads 'gabled') with hongawara tiles; actual length 118.2 m by 16.4 m. The thirty-three-bay core is ringed by a one-bay aisle on all sides and an outer verandah; the front is entirely panelled doors, the sides and rear latticed windows. The seven-bay front porch was remodelled in the great repair of 1649–51.

History: founded in 1164 (Chōkan 2), destroyed in the great fire of 1249, rebuilt and dedicated in 1266 (Bun'ei 3). Repairs in 1930 uncovered polychrome patterns under the tie-beams, proving the hall was originally painted inside and out. Listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1897, National Treasure in 1952.

Value: the Agency for Cultural Affairs calls it the representative Kamakura-period wayō building in Kyoto, its elongated plan made for housing a thousand images and extremely rare among surviving Japanese buildings. A 2016 survey by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute found the ground beneath it built up in alternating layers of sand and clay, working much like modern base isolation. The tōshiya record is 8,133 arrows shot through by Wasa Daihachirō in 1686.
captions: Sanjūsangen-dō · Main hall
Kamakura period · Rebuilt 1266

name: Ninomaru Palace, Nijō Castle
sub: Kurumayose carriage porch and Tozamurai, exterior
yearNote: The timeline is placed by the major renovation of the surviving palace complex around 1626; the plate takes the exterior of the Kurumayose and Tozamurai and does not mean that the whole castle was completed in the same year.
lede: Behind the carriage porch with its curved Chinese gable stands the first of six palace buildings set out in echelon — the Tōzamurai, the largest of them, where visitors waited in the 'Tiger Rooms'. Nijō Castle was completed by Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1603; for the visit of Emperor Go-Mizunoo in 1626 the palace was so thoroughly remodelled in 1624–26 as to be almost new, and what stands today is that Kan'ei-era fabric. With the palaces of Edo, Osaka and Nagoya castles all gone, this is the only palace complex surviving in any Japanese castle, and all six buildings are National Treasures.
facts: Form: the carriage porch (kurumayose) is the entrance; the Tōzamurai, where callers waited and imperial envoys were received, is the largest of the six buildings and contains the Tiger Rooms. Behind it the Shikidai, Ōhiroma, Sotetsu-no-ma, Kuroshoin and Shiroshoin step back in echelon from south-east to north-west, linked by inner corridors and verandahs.

History: Ieyasu built the castle in 1603. For Emperor Go-Mizunoo's visit in the ninth month of 1626 (Kan'ei 3) the palace was remodelled from 1624; surveys by Kawakami Mitsugu and others show the work amounted almost to new construction, and the Kanō-school wall paintings inside are also Kan'ei work. The roofs, originally shingled, had been tiled by 1686; the Imperial Household Ministry transferred the castle to Kyoto City in 1939.

Value: the Tōzamurai and carriage porch count as one building and, with the other five, are National Treasures, representative of early-Edo shoin architecture. With the palaces of Edo, Osaka and Nagoya castles lost, Nijō is the only surviving palace complex in a Japanese castle. Its 954 wall paintings are a separate Important Cultural Property, 273 of them in the Tōzamurai. Inscribed as World Heritage in 1994.
captions: Nijō Castle · Carriage porch of the Ninomaru Palace
Edo period · Around 1626

name: Main Hall of Yasaka Shrine
lede: Sanctuary and worship hall (raidō) sit under one great cypress-bark roof — the 'Gion-zukuri' found only at Yasaka Shrine. The hall repaired in 1646 burned that same winter and was rebuilt in 1654 at the expense of the fourth shogun, Tokugawa Ietsuna, the last time the shogunate built a shrine or temple directly. Seven bays by six, with lean-to extensions on three further sides, it carries the largest roof of any shrine building; the Agency for Cultural Affairs judges this way of enlarging a hall by adding aisles to be a Heian-period method, the form fixed by the Kamakura period, and promoted it to National Treasure in 2020.
facts: Form: seven bays by six, hip-and-gable roof of cypress bark, a three-bay porch at the front, lean-to aisles on both sides and the rear, the rear one projecting three bays. The core is divided into an innermost and an inner sanctum, each with a three-bay-long altar shelf; an outer sanctum runs right round the core and a worship hall adjoins the front, all contained beneath the single roof, while the side aisles are partitioned into small rooms.

History: from the damage report of the 1220 fire preserved in Kujō Michiie's diary, the shrine infers that the hall rebuilt in 1148 was already close to the present form. Repaired by the shogunate in 1646 it burned that November, and was rebuilt in 1654 (Jōō 3) by Tokugawa Ietsuna. Listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1911, designated a National Treasure in December 2020.

Value: extending a building outward with successive aisles is a Heian-period technique; this hall's form was established by the Kamakura period and was rebuilt to the old pattern in the early Edo period, preserving Heian spatial organisation and its relation to medieval ritual. The Agency also notes that it has been maintained to this day by the townspeople who run the Gion Festival, and it has the largest floor area of any shrine building.
captions: Yasaka Shrine · Main hall
Edo period · 1654

name: East Pagoda of Yakushi-ji
sub: East Pagoda · Three stories, six roofs
yearNote: The temple gives the 2nd year of Tenpyō (730) as the completion date of the East Pagoda; the timeline point is an approximate completion date for the surviving structure.
lede: Yakushiji’s East Pagoda seems to have six tiers of eaves but is actually three storeys: each principal roof has a smaller mokoshi beneath it. Alternating roofs give the tapering timber tower its distinctive rhythm, and celestial figures decorate the openwork finial. Temple records place its construction around 730. This Nara-period survival has also undergone repeated repairs, so its present appearance carries both ancient architecture and modern conservation.
facts: Each of the three storeys has a surrounding mokoshi, producing six alternating rooflines. The smaller roofs do not mark extra storeys; they are subsidiary roofs around the main levels. Their proportions give the tower its distinctive appearance.

Temple records assign its establishment to Tenpyo 2, around 730. Repeated partial repairs were followed by recent complete dismantling and conservation. The Nara-period structure and modern repairs should be read as connected historical layers.

The openwork finial depicts heavenly beings making music and holding flowers in Buddhist praise, echoing the rhythm of the timber structure below. The East Pagoda preserves ancient form, while the West Pagoda has a separate reconstruction history; their dates are not interchangeable.
captions: Yakushi-ji · East Pagoda
Nara period · About 730

name: Main Hall of Gangō-ji Gokurakubō
yearNote: The surviving main hall was converted from an old monks' dormitory; its date is placed approximately according to the cultural heritage database's record of the mid-Kamakura period.
lede: A low, broad tiled roof and continuous columns preserve the scale of a former monks’ residence at Gangoji’s Gokurakubo Main Hall. Its history lies in reused materials and altered space: devotion to the Chiko Mandala turned part of the residence into a worship hall, reshaped during the Kamakura period. The neighbouring Zen Room has its own heritage identity; the Main Hall brings ancient domestic architecture into contact with medieval devotion.
facts: The single-storey hall has a tiled hip roof and a continuous one-bay porch at the front. Columns carry the broad eaves. Roof proportions and bay organisation retain connections with the former residence, within which a worship space was created.

The surviving hall is thought to have been remodelled around Kangen 2, approximately 1244. Earlier residential materials remain around the inner sanctuary and in the roof frame. Kamakura form and Nara-period reused fabric coexist, so not every component has the same age.

Devotion to the Chiko Mandala transformed part of the residence into a worship hall; the remaining portion became the separate Zen Room. Their distinct identities show how a temple sustained religious practice and reorganised space through periods of change.
captions: Gangō-ji · Gokurakubō main hall
Kamakura period · About mid-13th century

name: Hokuen-dō of Kōfuku-ji
lede: Kofukuji’s North Octagonal Hall encloses its Buddhist images within a compact eight-sided plan and roof. Brackets beneath the deep eaves give the small hall a dignified, forceful presence. Originally built to commemorate Fujiwara no Fuhito, the surviving hall was reconstructed around 1210 after a twelfth-century fire. Maitreya, Asanga and Vasubandhu bring memorial practice, architecture and Kamakura sculpture into one space.
facts: The octagonal plan supports a roof extending evenly on every side. Three-step brackets carry the deep eaves. The inner ceiling and painted decoration frame the Buddhist images, adding successive structural details within a compact building.

The hall was founded in 721 for the first anniversary of Fujiwara no Fuhito’s death. After damage in 1180, it was rebuilt around 1210. The surviving timber building belongs to the Kamakura period, rather than being the original Nara-period hall.

Maitreya is the central image, accompanied by Asanga, Vasubandhu and other figures. The octagonal sanctuary continues the commemoration of Kofukuji’s founder while preserving a setting where Kamakura sculpture and architecture work together.
captions: Kōfuku-ji · Hokuen-dō
Kamakura period · About 1210

name: Four Main Sanctuaries of Kasuga Taisha
sub: Four main sanctuaries in Kasuga-zukuri style
lede: Kasuga Taisha’s four main sanctuaries stand together in the compact kasuga style. Vermilion columns, white walls and cypress-bark roofs create a repeated rhythm within the sacred precinct. Each hall enshrines a different deity while sharing an old architectural tradition. The present buildings were renewed in 1863, with subsequent maintenance continuing their inherited forms. Shrine history and the age of the visible buildings must be distinguished.
facts: All four are one-bay kasuga-style sanctuaries with cypress-bark roofs and connecting walls between and beside them. Repeated small volumes, vermilion timber and white walls create an ordered sacred inner court.

Heritage records date the present sanctuaries to renewal in Bunkyu 3, or 1863. The shrine’s foundation tradition reaches back to 768. Periodic maintenance and renewal preserve older forms without implying that every original component survives unchanged.

The halls respectively enshrine Takemikazuchi, Futsunushi, Ame no Koyane and Himegami. The kasuga style became widely adopted in shrine architecture. Repeated buildings and separate enshrinement together express the organization of Kasuga worship.
captions: Kasuga Taisha · Four main sanctuaries, illustration

name: Four Main Sanctuaries of Sumiyoshi Taisha
sub: Four main sanctuaries in Sumiyoshi-zukuri style
lede: Four equally sized sanctuaries face west in an unusual arrangement: three stand in succession, with the fourth south of the third. These surviving halls were rebuilt in 1810. Straight gables, low floors and paired inner rooms retain the austere form known as Sumiyoshi-zukuri.
facts: All four have cypress-bark gabled roofs with entrances in the gable ends and two rooms arranged front to back. Sanctuaries one to three form a line; the fourth stands south of the third. All face west.

The cultural property database dates the surviving halls to the 1810 rebuilding. Periodic renewal resumed in the early seventeenth century after interruption by warfare; an ancient form does not imply unchanged timber.

Straight bargeboards, low floors and the absence of surrounding verandas distinguish Sumiyoshi-zukuri. Plank walls enclose the paired rooms, and round columns stand on foundation stones, producing a restrained outline.

name: Sengan Turret of Osaka Castle
lede: A two-storey turret rises above the stone corner beside the Ote entrance, overlooking the moat and gate. Smaller than a keep, Sengan-yagura served the practical defence of the entrance. Built during the Tokugawa reconstruction in 1620, it retains a foundation-timber inscription recording its column-raising date.
facts: The tile-roofed corner turret has two roof tiers and two floors. It stands on the Ote entrance stonework facing the gate and moat; each floor contains four rooms surrounded by a corridor.

Built in 1620 under Kobori Masakazu, it was dismantled for repair from 1960. An inscription on foundation timber records column raising on the thirteenth day of the ninth month of Genna 6, providing physical dating evidence.

Its name is traditionally linked to a hard-to-capture turret during the siege of Ishiyama Honganji. That story does not make this building a Honganji survivor; it and Inui-yagura preserve early Tokugawa castle defences.

name: Tahōtō of Jigen-in
lede: At Jigenin, a round upper body rests above a square lower storey beneath two spreading cypress-bark roofs. This compact tahoto is dated to 1271, a date supported by its architectural style. Layered brackets, carved struts and the original-period altar preserve varied details of Kamakura timber architecture.
facts: The lower storey has a square three-bay plan, while the upper body is circular. Both roofs use cypress bark; four-step upper and two-step lower brackets create elaborate eave supports within a compact building.

The database records 1271 and considers the style consistent with that date. The tower was moved during a Meiji-period repair and given a new platform, so its present base is not simply the Kamakura arrangement.

The interior lacks the customary four central columns, leaving a single room with an altar contemporary with the tower. Fin-like patterns in carved struts illustrate the growing elaboration of Kamakura ornament.

name: Kondō of Kanshin-ji
yearNote: Cultural property records date the Kondō to between 1346 and 1369; 1355 is only an approximate position on the timeline, not an exact completion year.
lede: A seven-bay hall with a single hip-and-gable roof projects a three-bay worship porch towards visitors. Kanshinji Kondo combines native wayo timber forms with Daibutsuyo and Zen elements. The database dates the surviving building to 1346–1369; its present appearance also includes successive repairs.
facts: The hall is seven bays wide and deep, with a three-bay porch beneath its single hip-and-gable roof. Diamond lattice transoms and sliding lattice doors strictly divide inner and outer sanctuaries, organising esoteric Buddhist worship.

The database assigns construction to 1346–1369, and its commentary places rebuilding before the late fourteenth century. Numerous later repairs are recorded; no unconfirmed single completion year is asserted.

Wayo forms provide the basis, with paired Daibutsuyo brackets and Zen construction details. Differences in column bases, the porch and interior framing reveal the exchange of techniques more clearly than one style label.

name: Sanmon of Tōfuku-ji
lede: The oldest surviving Zen temple gate — yet not in the Zen style: the Agency for Cultural Affairs points out that structurally it is closer to the Daibutsu style, with heavy timbers and something of the grandeur of Tōdai-ji's Great South Gate. Tōfuku-ji was founded by Kujō Michiie in 1236; after fires in 1319, 1334 and 1336 the gate was rebuilt, by temple tradition begun in 1384 and finished in 1425. Ink inscriptions found in the 1969–77 dismantling repair show the tiling and upper-storey work going on around 1405–13, so the Agency registers it as 1405. The 'Myōunkaku' tablet brushed by Ashikaga Yoshimochi still hangs on the upper storey.
facts: Form: a two-storey, double-roofed gate five bays wide with three doorways, hip-and-gable roof of hongawara tiles, facing south, with a gabled, tiled stair-wing on either side. 'Five bays, three doors' means a five-bay front with the central three bays open as passages; 'double-roofed' means both storeys carry eaves. The upper storey enshrines Shaka and the Sixteen Arhats, and its ceiling and pillars are painted in brilliant colours by Minchō and his pupils.

History: the temple was founded in 1236 (Katei 2); the gate was rebuilt after fires in 1319, 1334 and 1336, by tradition begun in 1384 and completed in 1425 (Ōei 32). Ink inscriptions discovered in the 1969–77 dismantling repair show tiling and upper-storey work continuing to about 1405–13. Tilted by the earthquake of 1585 it was righted under Hideyoshi, and repaired again in 1792. Listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1897, National Treasure in 1952.

Value: the oldest extant Zen sanmon, yet structurally not pure Zen style but close to the Daibutsu style, massive in its members and bold in effect — a gate the Agency calls singular in Japanese architecture. The upper-storey tablet 'Myōunkaku' is in the hand of Ashikaga Yoshimochi. The Edo-period gates of Chion-in and Nanzen-ji belong to the same lineage of five-bay, three-door, double-roofed gates.

Muromachi period · 1425

name: Main Hall of Fushimi Inari Taisha
lede: Look at the roof first: a great sweep of cypress-bark shingles runs from the ridge straight down over the front eaves, covering the five-bay core and the porch in a single slope — this is the nagare-zukuri form. The subject is the honden of Fushimi Inari Taisha. The shrine buildings were burned in the Ōnin War; after it the hall was rebuilt through fund-raising by shrine monks, dated by the Agency for Cultural Affairs to 1494 (Meiō 3), with the dedication rite held in 1499 (Meiō 8). This is the main sanctuary of the head shrine of some 30,000 Inari shrines nationwide; beyond the thousand torii, this vermilion timber hall is the real architectural protagonist.
facts: Form: a five-bay nagare-zukuri hall roofed in cypress bark, five bays across the front, the forward slope of the roof extending to shelter the space before the steps. Inside, five deities share one chamber: Ukanomitama (lower shrine), Satahiko (middle) and Ōmiyanome (upper), joined in 1499 by Tanaka-no-Ōkami and Shi-no-Ōkami.

History: the Inari deity is said to have descended on Mt Inari in 711 (Wadō 4). The old buildings were lost in the Ōnin War (1467–77); rebuilt through fund-raising, the present honden was completed in 1494, with the dedication in 1499. Designated an Important Cultural Property in 1909; in 2014 seven further buildings, including the gonden and the gate, were added to the designation.

Value: nagare-zukuri is the most widespread honden form in Japan, and a five-bay example counts as large. Behind the honden stand the gonden (1635), the gate built by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in 1589 and the north and south corridors, which together form the shrine's front. The thousand torii are offerings by worshippers; architecturally the core remains this late-Muromachi honden.

name: Main Hall of Kitano Tenman-gū
sub: Main hall, ishi-no-ma and worship hall
lede: Between sanctuary and worship hall lies a sunken 'stone room' (ishi-no-ma) that binds them into one building; music rooms attach to either end of the worship hall, so the cypress-bark ridges, dormer gables and curved eave gables pile up and interlock — hence the name 'eight-ridge style'. The complex was built in 1607 by Toyotomi Hideyori with Katagiri Katsumoto as commissioner, and the 'gongen-zukuri' later seen at Nikkō Tōshōgū has its origin here. Above the stone room great tie-beams and bottle-shaped struts carry an exposed ridge — the part the Agency for Cultural Affairs singles out — and it was designated a National Treasure in 1959.
facts: Form: the sanctuary (honden) is five bays by four, hip-and-gable, with a three-bay lean-to on its right side; the stone room is three bays by one with a two-slope roof; the worship hall (haiden) is seven bays by three, hip-and-gable, with a dormer gable on the front and a seven-bay porch under a curved eave gable; a music room adjoins each end of the haiden. All roofs are cypress bark, and the whole counts as a single building.

History: tradition puts the foundation in 947 (Tenryaku 1), with an enlargement by Fujiwara no Morosuke in 959, followed by repeated fires. The present buildings were erected in 1607 (Keichō 12) by Toyotomi Hideyori, with Katagiri Katsumoto as commissioner of works. Listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1897, designated a National Treasure in 1959.

Value: the gongen-zukuri scheme of joining sanctuary and worship hall by a stone room took shape here; the framing above the stone room — great tie-beams, bottle struts and frog-leg struts supporting an exposed ridge — are the heart of the building. The Agency credits it with both an old plan inherited from Heian times and representative status among early-modern shrine architecture; Wikipedia calls it the only Momoyama shrine preserved at its original scale.
captions: Kitano Tenman-gū · Main hall complex
Early Edo period · 1607

name: Kondō of Ninna-ji
sub: Former Shishinden of the Imperial Palace, relocated
era: Original structure 1613 · Relocated in the early Edo period
yearNote: The timeline uses 1613, the date of the original structure listed in the cultural heritage database; temple records state that it was relocated as the Kondō between 1624 and 1643, and the present roof has also been altered.
lede: A palace turned into a Buddha hall. The Golden Hall of Ninna-ji was originally the Shishinden, the ceremonial hall of the Kyoto Imperial Palace, completed in 1613 (Keichō 18). In 1634 the abbot-prince Kakushin asked Tokugawa Iemitsu to revive the temple, derelict since the Ōnin War; the palace was being rebuilt at the time, so the old Shishinden was granted to the temple and re-erected here, its ridge raised in 1643. The cypress-bark roof became tile and the west aisle was removed, but the latticed shutters and gilt fittings remain — the only building anywhere that was once a Shishinden, designated a National Treasure in 1953.
facts: Form: seven bays by five, single-storey hip-and-gable with a one-bay porch, roofed in hongawara tiles. The core shows an open roof structure on tie-beams and frog-leg struts, the porch is carved, and the front keeps its latticed shutters (shitomi) and palace-style gilt fittings. In the move the west aisle was taken off, the cypress-bark roofing changed to tile and fittings and partitions slightly altered, but the structure was not fundamentally changed.

History: Ninna-ji was begun in 886 and completed in 888, and burned entirely in the Ōnin War. In 1634 (Kan'ei 11) Prince-Abbot Kakushin asked Tokugawa Iemitsu for its revival; as the palace was then being rebuilt, the Shishinden completed in 1613 (Keichō 18) was granted and moved along with the Seiryōden and other halls. The Golden Hall's ridge was raised in 1643 (Kan'ei 20) and the precinct was finished in 1646. Listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1900, National Treasure in 1953.

Value: the only surviving building moved from a Shishinden and the oldest Shishinden in existence, a key specimen of early-modern shinden-style architecture; the Shishinden of today's Kyoto Imperial Palace is an 1855 rebuilding, more than two centuries younger. The Agency's summary gives the original hall's construction as 1611 (Keichō 16) while its detailed note gives completion in 1613; the timeline follows the latter.

Momoyama original structure · Relocated in the early Edo period

name: Hiunkaku of Nishi Hongan-ji
sub: Three-story pavilion in the Tekisui-en garden
yearNote: 1600 is only an approximate timeline placement, not an exact construction year; the tradition that it was relocated from the Jurakudai has been handed down but is unproven. The cultural heritage database assigns it to the Momoyama period.
lede: Three storeys that shrink as they rise, each shifting its centre eastward, each roofed differently: a hip-and-gable ground floor with a curved Chinese gable and a dormer gable, a hipped second floor with small curved gables on three sides, a plain hipped third. Slender posts and many paper screens make it seem to float like a cloud over the Sōrō pond of the Tekisui-en garden — hence 'Flying Cloud Pavilion'. Temple tradition calls it a relic of Toyotomi Hideyoshi's Jurakudai palace moved here in the Kan'ei era, but the Agency for Cultural Affairs notes that 'details are unclear' and most architectural historians are sceptical; a Momoyama-period date is as far as the evidence goes.
facts: Form: a three-storey pavilion under shingle roofs, 25.8 m on the north and south, 11.8 m on the east and 12.5 m on the west, facing north onto the Sōrō pond. The ground floor holds the Shōkenden, the Eight Views Room, the Boat Entry Room and the later tea room Ikujaku; the second-floor Poets' Room is painted with the Thirty-six Immortal Poets; the third-floor Tekiseirō opens bell-shaped windows on all sides. Boats could enter the Boat Entry Room directly from the pond — its only formal entrance.

Date: the Agency assigns it to the Momoyama period (1573–1614). The temple's Shiundenn yuenki, compiled in 1638, calls it a relic of Hideyoshi, whence the tradition of removal from Jurakudai (built 1589–90, demolished 1595), but there is no proof and the style looks later; rival theories hold that Hongan-ji built it in the Kan'ei era or that it came from Hideyoshi's Kyoto Shinjō. Listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1897, National Treasure in 1951.

Value: the Agency praises its slender members and light, unconventional form as a model of garden architecture; with the Golden and Silver Pavilions it is counted among Kyoto's three famous pavilions. The Ikujaku tea room, added in 1795 (Kansei 7) by Yabunouchi Chikuin and others, is securely dated; a roofed passage links the pavilion westward to the Kōkakudai bathhouse, designed with it as one ensemble in the Tekisui-en garden.
captions: Nishi Hongan-ji · Hiunkaku
Momoyama period · Date unknown

name: Daiyūhōden of Manpuku-ji
sub: Mahavira Hall of the Ōbaku school
lede: Look up as you enter: under the eaves of the front bay the rafters are bent into a half-round vault the temple calls the 'Ōbaku ceiling'; the doors carry carved peach-shaped charms, and round windows open on either side — late-Ming practices seen at no other temple in Japan. The subject is the Daiō-hōden (Buddha hall) of Manpuku-ji. Yinyuan Longqi (Ingen) founded the temple at Uji in 1661; the hall was completed in 1668 (Kanbun 8), three bays by three with a mokoshi skirt roof, hip-and-gable and tiled, with a 'moon terrace' in front. It is the only historic building in Japan built of teak, and in December 2024 it was raised to National Treasure together with the Dharma hall and the Tennōden.
facts: Form: three bays by three, a single storey with a mokoshi skirt roof that makes it read as two storeys; hip-and-gable roof of hongawara tiles, a moon terrace attached at the front. The upper tablet 'Daiō-hōden' is in Ingen's hand, the lower 'Bantokuson' in Mokuan's. The timber is Siamese teak, donated by the lay devotee Shō Shōin and the shogunate.

History: Ingen crossed to Japan at the invitation in 1654 and received the site in 1661; construction of the compound ran from 1661 to a broadly complete state in 1679. The Buddha hall was built in 1668, and its Śākyamuni image was carved in 1669 by the Kyoto sculptor Hyōbu. Designated an Important Cultural Property in 1913 and a National Treasure on 9 December 2024.

Value: the Agency for Cultural Affairs notes that the layout and style reflect late-Ming and early-Qing Buddhist architecture. Following Ming temple custom the hall houses eighteen arhats (by Fan Daosheng, 1663) rather than the sixteen usual in Japan. The Ōbaku ceiling, swastika-pattern balustrades, peach charms and round windows form a complete Chinese design vocabulary.

name: Main Shrine of Iwashimizu Hachimangū
sub: Front of the tower gate and corridors, detail
lede: What faces you is the vermilion-lacquered rōmon: a one-bay, one-door two-storey gate under a hip-and-gable roof, with a two-bay worship porch projecting in front beneath a curved karahafu gable, its cypress-bark roof packed with polychrome carved friezes; to either side the corridors, tiled and thirteen bays long, ring the main sanctuary. The subject is the front of the gate and corridors of the main shrine of Iwashimizu Hachimangū. Founded in 860 (Jōgan 2), the present group of buildings was rebuilt in 1634 (Kan'ei 11) under Tokugawa Iemitsu. Hidden behind the corridors is the oldest and largest surviving honden of the Hachiman type; in 2016 the ten buildings of the main shrine were designated National Treasures together.
facts: Form: the rōmon is a one-bay, one-door gate with a hip-and-gable roof; its front worship porch is two bays by one under a curved karahafu, all cypress-bark roofed. The corridors on either side are thirteen bays by two, with a one-bay lean-to along the outside, hip-and-gable roofs of hongawara tiles; with the east and west gates and the rear corridor they enclose the honden.

History: founded in 860 and repeatedly destroyed and restored; Oda Nobunaga repaired the buildings in 1580, Toyotomi Hideyori began a rebuilding of the precinct in 1598, and the shogunate rebuilt the present group in 1634. Listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1897; on 9 February 2016 the ten buildings of the main shrine, with three ridge tablets, were designated National Treasures.

Value: inside the enclosure the honden is of the Hachiman type, an inner and an outer hall of eleven bays each set one behind the other — the oldest and largest surviving example of the form. The Agency for Cultural Affairs describes the ensemble as 'preserving a solemn shrine form established in antiquity while carrying early-modern ornament'. With Ise it is one of the two ancestral shrines of the imperial house.
captions: Iwashimizu Hachimangū · Front of the main shrine, detail
Edo period · 1634

name: Tahōtō of Ishiyama-dera
lede: Two cypress-bark roofs frame the transition from a square lower storey to a round upper body. Ishiyamadera Tahoto balances weight and curvature. An inscription on an altar component records 1194, providing direct dating evidence. The Dainichi image and paintings on four inner columns link architecture with Buddhist art; the roof has undergone later repair.
facts: A square lower storey supports a circular upper body beneath two spreading cypress-bark roofs. Kongokai Dainichi Nyorai occupies the centre, surrounded by four columns; the square-and-round plan is characteristic of a tahoto.

An inscription behind the upper frame of the lower-storey altar records 1194. This is an early tahoto with documented dating; later reroofing means its surface materials are not all original to that year.

The principal image is attributed to Kaikei. Paintings of Kongokai deities and the Five Great Wisdom Kings cover the four columns, connecting the building with contemporary art and the visual order of worship.

Kamakura period · 1194

name: Main Hall of Ishiyama-dera
era: Inner hall rebuilt 1096 · Worship hall added 1602
yearNote: The timeline uses 1096, the year the surviving inner hall was rebuilt; the worship hall in front was added in 1602, and the roof and exterior seen in the plate belong to both periods.
lede: A projecting worship hall joins the older sanctuary at Ishiyamadera, bringing two periods beneath connected roofs. The sanctuary was rebuilt in 1096 after a fire; the worship hall was added in 1602, joined by an intermediate space. The roofline crosses the rocky slope, showing how one ancient hall can incorporate several ages.
facts: The main hall comprises the rear sanctuary, front worship hall and connecting ai-no-ma. Timber supports project the worship hall beyond the rocky slope, while cypress-bark roofs connect inner worship and outer assembly spaces.

Fire destroyed the earlier hall in 1078. The surviving sanctuary was rebuilt in 1096, and Yodo-dono sponsored the worship hall in 1602. These phases explain the current building; it was not completed in a single year.

The projecting construction adapts worship space to the rocky terrain. Changes in the connected roofs reveal older and added sections, making the meeting of late Heian and early modern construction visible.

name: Sanmon of Chion-in
lede: At 24 m this is the largest surviving two-storey, double-roofed gate in Japan, bigger even than the Great South Gate of Tōdai-ji. Tokugawa Hidetada ordered it in 1619 and it was essentially complete by the autumn of 1621, built by master carpenters of the Nakai house in shogunal service; during the Heisei repair finished in 1992 an ink inscription dated Genna 7 (1621) was found on a shingle board of the upper roof, fixing the date. The great fire of 1633 destroyed almost all of Chion-in, but the gate, the sutra repository and the Seishi-dō escaped, so it is older than nearly everything else in the precinct. It was designated a National Treasure in 2002 together with the Mieidō.
facts: Form: a two-storey, double-roofed gate five bays wide with three doorways, hip-and-gable roof of hongawara tiles, facing west, 24 m high; the stair-wings on either side are three bays by two, gabled and tiled. The details are Zen-style: closely packed bracket sets, round posts with tapered tops on plinths, fan rafters on the upper storey. Inside the upper storey are Shaka and the Sixteen Arhats beneath a ceiling painted with a dragon, all in brilliant colour.

History: in 1619 (Genna 5) Tokugawa Hidetada ordered the gate and sutra repository built; they were largely finished in the autumn of 1621 (Genna 7) under carpenters of the Nakai house. The Heisei repair completed in 1992 found an ink inscription of Genna 7 on a shingle board of the upper roof. The gate survived the great fire of 1633 (Kan'ei 10) with the sutra repository and Seishi-dō; listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1902, National Treasure in 2002.

Value: the Agency for Cultural Affairs ranks it a monument in which early-Edo building technique reached its height, of exceptional finish — the largest extant two-storey double-roofed gate, its ornament of the utmost solemnity, and the symbol of the Jōdo sect's head temple. 'Sanmon' means the gate of the three liberations. Before building Nanzen-ji's gate (1628) its planners surveyed this one; both are giant gates of the Tokugawa age in Higashiyama.
captions: Chion-in · Sanmon
Edo period · 1621

name: Sanmon of Nanzen-ji
lede: In the kabuki theatre Ishikawa Goemon cries 'What a view!' from atop this gate — though in fact it was built more than thirty years after his death. The gate of Nanzen-ji was first raised in 1295 and burned in 1447; the present one was donated in 1628 by Tōdō Takatora, lord of Tsu, for his retainers killed in the summer campaign at Osaka, and is nicknamed the 'Dragon Gate under Heaven'. Before building it, Ishin Sūden had the gates of Shōkoku-ji and Chion-in surveyed for reference, so it belongs with Chion-in's to the same family of five-bay, three-door double-roofed gates, about 22 m high; the phoenixes and celestials on the ceiling of the upper 'Gohōrō' storey are attributed to Kanō Tan'yū and others.
facts: Form: a two-storey, double-roofed gate five bays wide with three doorways, hip-and-gable roof of hongawara tiles, facing west, about 22 m high; the stair-wings on either side are three bays by two, gabled and tiled. The upper storey, the Gohōrō, holds a crowned Shaka, the Sixteen Arhats and statues of Tokugawa Ieyasu, Tōdō Takatora and others; the phoenix and celestial paintings on its ceiling are attributed to Kanō Tan'yū and Tosa Tokuetsu.

History: the first gate was donated in 1295 (Einin 3) by Saionji Sanekane, rebuilt in the Ōan era and destroyed in the great fire of 1447 (Bun'an 4). In 1628 (Kan'ei 5) Tōdō Takatora rebuilt it for the repose of retainers killed in the Osaka summer campaign, with Yoshida Sadaemon as commissioner and Ishin Sūden directing that the gates of Shōkoku-ji and Chion-in be used as models. Designated an Important Cultural Property in 1899.

Value: counted with the Chion-in gate and the Mieidō gate of Higashi Hongan-ji among Kyoto's three great gates, notable for the massive Zen-style volume and ranks of great pillars; the stone lantern before it, over 6 m tall, was offered by Sakuma Katsuyuki in 1628. Goemon's 'What a view!' comes from the kabuki play Sanmon Gosan no Kiri and has no basis in history, yet it made this gate famous.
captions: Nanzen-ji · Sanmon
Edo period · 1628

name: Main Hall of Ujigami Shrine
sub: Outer sheltering hall of the main sanctuary
yearNote: 1100 serves only as an approximate timeline placement; the main hall is generally dated to the late 11th century, and its outer sheltering hall contains three inner sanctuaries.
lede: From outside it reads as a long nagare-style building five bays by three; in fact it is a cover (ōiya) over three one-bay nagare-style inner shrines — side walls and rear roof slope shared with the left and right shrines, the slightly smaller central one tucked wholly inside. The Agency for Cultural Affairs dates it by its details to the early 12th century; tree-ring dating by the Nara National Research Institute for Cultural Properties in 2004 pushed the timber to around 1060, the generation of the Phoenix Hall of Byōdō-in (1053) across the river: the oldest shrine building in existence. The timeline keeps only the approximate 'late 11th century'.
facts: Form: the cover building is five bays by three, single-storey nagare style with a cypress-bark roof, housing three one-bay nagare inner shrines. Its side and rear walls, posts and rear roof slope are shared with the left and right shrines, showing that inner shrines and cover were conceived together; the central shrine is smaller, with boat-shaped bracket arms and no frog-leg struts, while the left shrine (on the viewer's right) has the most archaic struts, made of two boards.

Date: the Agency infers the early 12th century from the details and classes it as late Heian; tree-ring dating in February 2004 by the Nara institute and Uji City gave about 1060 and noted a close link with Byōdō-in, founded in 1052. Listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1902, National Treasure in 1952; the painted boys and attendants inside the doors of the left and right shrines are a separate Important Cultural Property.

Value: recognised as the oldest surviving shrine architecture, its inner shrines are early textbook examples of the nagare style found throughout Japan. The three shrines enshrine Uji no Wakiiratsuko, Emperor Ōjin and Emperor Nintoku, the left shrine being the earliest. Inscribed with Byōdō-in among the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto in 1994; the surrounding hills were designated the Place of Scenic Beauty 'Ujiyama' in 2018.

name: Worship Hall of Ujigami Shrine
yearNote: 1210 serves only as an approximate timeline placement, not an exact completion year; the worship hall is generally dated to the early Kamakura period.
lede: A house rather than a temple. The gabled main block of the worship hall has a one-bay aisle at each end whose roof is dropped down with a 'sugaru' gable, so that from a distance it looks hip-and-gable; a railed verandah runs all round, a one-bay porch with steps marks the centre of the front, and the walls are almost all latticed shutters — the Agency for Cultural Affairs says it is 'in every respect close to residential architecture', and it is often called a relic of the shinden style. Built in the early Kamakura period, it preserves old struts and panelled doors from the first half of the 14th century, when it may have been rebuilt or heavily remodelled. It is Ujigami Shrine's second National Treasure after the main sanctuary.
facts: Form: six bays by three, single-storey gabled roof of cypress bark, a one-bay aisle under each gable end, one-bay porch. The core is really five bays with a short extra bay on the left absorbed into the aisle. A railed verandah surrounds it; the core has round posts, the aisles and porch chamfered square ones, all with boat-shaped bracket arms. Panelled doors stand at the centre of front and rear, latticed shutters elsewhere; the core has double eaves with widely spaced rafters, the porch close-set rafters. Inside are three rooms.

Date: the Agency assigns it to the early Kamakura period (1185–1274); listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1902, National Treasure in November 1952. A set of old struts and panelled doors kept inside dates to about the first half of the 14th century, suggesting a rebuilding or near-total remodelling then; the tale that it was moved from an Uji imperial villa is, in the Agency's view, a modern invention.

Value: the aisle roofs joined to the gabled core by 'sugaru' gables, producing a hip-and-gable look, are its most distinctive feature; board floors, ceilings and many shutters bring it close to a medieval dwelling and make it an important reference for shinden-style studies. It belongs to a different age from the late-Heian main sanctuary and must not be dated with it; both are components of the World Heritage inscription of 1994.
captions: Ujigami Shrine · Worship hall
Early Kamakura · About early 13th century

name: Sekisui-in of Kōzan-ji
sub: Interior of the open veranda of Sekisui-in
era: Early Kamakura original · Relocated in the Meiji period
yearNote: 1230 serves only as an approximate timeline placement; Sekisui-in is an early Kamakura building, and its present site is the location to which it was moved in 1889.
lede: An open one-bay gallery faces the valley, with nothing beyond its wooden rail but the forest of Toganoo — that is the stretch drawn here. The Sekisui-in was originally the eastern sutra repository built when the monk Myōe revived Kōzan-ji in 1206; after a flood swept away the first Sekisui-in in 1228 this building took over the name, also enshrining the Kasuga and Sumiyoshi deities, and only in 1889 was it moved from east of the Golden Hall to its present site. Much altered, it is nonetheless the only building left from Myōe's time; the tablet inside, 'The rising sun first lights the temple on the high mountain', is attributed to the retired emperor Go-Toba.
facts: Form: three bays across the front and four across the back, three bays deep, with a further one-bay open gallery along the front; single-storey hip-and-gable roof entered at the gable end, the gallery roof sweeping down from the main roof, a one-bay porch, shingle roofing. A plan of 1637 (Kan'ei 14) shows the present eastern room as the exoteric sutra store, a long narrow western room housing the Kasuga and Sumiyoshi deities, and a one-bay room to the north as the esoteric store — traces on the posts still confirm it.

History: Kōzan-ji is said to have been founded by the Tendai monk Son'i; in 1206 (Ken'ei 1) Myōe received the site from Go-Toba and revived it. The original Sekisui-in was lost in the flood of 1228 (Antei 2), after which this eastern repository took the name and came to be regarded as Myōe's lodging; in 1889 (Meiji 22) it was moved here from east of the Golden Hall. Listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1898, National Treasure in 1953.

Value: the Agency for Cultural Affairs dates it to the early Kamakura period and notes that, heavily altered as it is, it is the sole surviving building of Myōe's revival; residential in look yet a sutra store by origin, it illustrates the drift of early-Kamakura temple buildings toward domestic form. The temple's National Treasures such as the Chōjū jinbutsu giga scrolls are mostly deposited in the Tokyo and Kyoto National Museums; Kōzan-ji was inscribed as World Heritage in 1994.
captions: Kōzan-ji · Open veranda of Sekisui-in
Early Kamakura · Relocated in the Meiji period

name: Honden and Gonden of Kamigamo Shrine
sub: Front of the honden and gonden
lede: Two identical three-bay nagare-zukuri halls stand side by side on a raised platform: the east (right) is the honden, the west (left) the gonden, which serves as the temporary sanctuary during the periodic rebuilding rite — the 'one in use, one in reserve' arrangement is itself the thing to see. The subject is the front of the honden and gonden of Kamigamo Shrine (Kamo Wakeikazuchi-jinja). The present pair was rebuilt in 1863 (Bunkyū 3); the Agency for Cultural Affairs holds that they differ little from the rebuilding of around 1303 and regards them as the classic nagare-zukuri, designated National Treasures in 1953. Under the eaves of each hall is a pair of 'shadow lion-dogs' painted by the Kanō school.
facts: Form: honden and gonden are both three-bay nagare-zukuri halls roofed in cypress bark: a core three bays by two with a three-bay porch in front, the roof flowing in one gentle slope from the rear down over the front eaves — the source of the name 'flowing style'. On the front of each hall is a painted pair of lion-dogs, the 'kage-koma', by Edo-period Kanō painters.

History: the shrine's record of rebuilding goes back to the reign of Tenmu (673–686); from the late Heian to the mid-Muromachi period the halls were rebuilt roughly every twenty-odd years, a custom revived in the Edo period; the present pair dates from the 1863 rebuilding. Listed as Specially Protected Buildings in 1901, designated National Treasures on 31 March 1953, and inscribed as World Heritage in 1994.

Value: nagare-zukuri is the most widespread honden form in Japan — the shrine says about sixty per cent of all shrines use it — and the Agency states that this honden 'differs little' from the one rebuilt around 1303 and 'transmits the old form well'. Kamigamo holds two National Treasure and forty-one Important Cultural Property buildings, and with Shimogamo it guarded the Heian capital.
captions: Kamigamo Shrine · Honden and gonden
Edo period · 1863

name: East and West Main Sanctuaries of Shimogamo Shrine
sub: Front of the east and west main sanctuaries, illustration
lede: Deep in the precinct two honden stand side by side: the west hall enshrines Kamo Taketsunumi, the east his daughter Tamayorihime — mother and grandfather of the Kamigamo deity, each with a hall of their own, which is why the shrine is called 'Mioya', the ancestors. The subject is the front of the east and west honden of Shimogamo Shrine (Kamo Mioya-jinja). Both are three-bay nagare-zukuri halls roofed in cypress bark, rebuilt in 1863 (Bunkyū 3), identical in form to the Kamigamo honden, and designated National Treasures in 1953. The twenty-one-year rebuilding cycle fixed in 1036 (Chōgen 9) still continues, though rebuilding has become repair.
facts: Form: the east and west honden are both three-bay nagare-zukuri halls under cypress-bark roofs, a core three bays by two with a one-bay porch in front and the forward roof slope running long and low. The two stand side by side on a platform, with steps and a front porch; most of their exterior is screened by corridors, so worshippers see only the front members.

History: a rebuilding is recorded in 677 (Hakuhō 6); in 1036 (Chōgen 9) a rebuilding every twenty-one years was fixed, lapsing in the Muromachi period and revived after the Kan'ei era; the present pair dates from the 1863 rebuilding. Listed as Specially Protected Buildings in 1901, designated National Treasures in 1953 and inscribed as World Heritage in 1994.

Value: the Agency for Cultural Affairs calls them 'exactly the same form as Kamigamo, and classic nagare-zukuri'. Because the two honden are National Treasures and fifty-three other buildings are Important Cultural Properties, the 34th periodic rebuilding (2015) took the form of repair rather than replacement — a compromise between ancient rite and heritage protection.

name: Enryaku-ji Konponchūdō
lede: An eleven-bay facade shelters spaces set at different levels in Enryakuji Konponchudo. The surviving main hall was rebuilt in 1640, long after Saicho founded the temple. Wooden floors in the outer and middle sections contrast with the stone-floored inner sanctuary, where three shrine-like enclosures organise worship.
facts: The hall is eleven bays wide and six deep, divided into outer, middle and inner sanctuaries. The first two have wooden floors; the rear inner area has a stone-paved earth floor and three shrine-like enclosures.

Enryakuji grew from Saicho’s late-eighth-century Hieizanji and endured fires and warfare. The surviving Konponchudo dates to rebuilding in 1640, so the temple’s foundation and this hall’s age are distinct.
Wooden floors and the lower stone sanctuary create different spaces beneath one large roof. Their relationship expresses Tendai ritual organisation more clearly than the exterior scale alone.

Edo period · Rebuilt 1640

name: Old Shoin of Katsura Imperial Villa
yearNote: 1615 is only an approximate timeline placement; the Imperial Household Agency assigns the Old Shoin to about the early 17th century, and the shoin complex as a whole is not regarded as built all at once in the same year.
lede: Look first at the strip of bamboo decking that reaches toward the pond — the moon-viewing platform. From the broad veranda of the Old Shoin a terrace projects further out, facing the Shōkintei teahouse across the water; it was here that Bruno Taut wept over Katsura in 1933. The subject is the Old Shoin (Ko-shoin) of the Katsura Imperial Villa, the earliest building of Prince Toshihito's Hachijō-no-miya retreat. The survey made during the great Shōwa repair (1976–82) dates it to around 1615 (Genna 1) and shows it first stood alone; the Middle Shoin (c. 1641) and the New Palace (c. 1662) were attached later, the three stepping back in echelon. The Imperial Household Agency assigns it only to the early seventeenth century, without a precise year.
facts: Form: an east–west hip-and-gable building roofed in wooden shingles (kokera-buki), seven and a half by five and a half ken in plan, measuring 15.8 by 10.9 metres, its gable end turned to the pond and finished with a lattice gable screen; square pine posts, no nageshi tie-rails, white plaster walls. Inside are eight rooms large and small, the principal room of ten mats; a one-bay veranda runs along the east, with the moon-viewing platform beyond.

History: Shimo-Katsura village was Hachijō-no-miya land, and a visit by an imperial consort to Katsura is recorded in 1616; the Old Shoin is thought to have been completed around 1615. Prince Toshitada added the Middle Shoin (c. 1641) and the New Palace (c. 1662); in 1883 the estate passed to the Imperial Household Ministry and took the name Katsura Rikyū; the shoin group was repaired in 1976–82.

Value: shoin-style in its bones and sukiya in its skin, never burned since its founding, it is the most completely preserved early-Edo ensemble of garden and buildings. Traces of alteration at the joint between Old and Middle Shoin prove the three-phase construction. Taut and Gropius alike held it up as the model of beauty through plainness.

name: Main Hall of Jōruri-ji
yearNote: 1150 serves only as an approximate timeline placement; the main hall is a late Heian survival.
lede: Eleven bays long and only four deep, with nine Amida seated side by side behind a row of latticed doors — the sole survivor of the 'nine-Amida halls' that Heian aristocrats vied to build. By temple record the temple was revived in 1047, a new hall and its images made in 1107 and dedicated the next year; in 1157 (Hōgen 2) the hall was taken down and moved to the west bank of the pond, its present site, which is why the Agency for Cultural Affairs dates it to around 1157. A low-pitched hipped roof of hongawara tiles, bracket arms only at the four corners, the ceiling raised one step over the central image: plain almost to austerity, yet the most complete spatial specimen of Pure Land devotion.
facts: Form: eleven bays by four, single-storey hipped roof of hongawara tiles; the one-bay porch is an Edo-period addition. Boat-shaped bracket arms appear only at the corners. The inner sanctum, nine bays by two, holds an altar running the full nine bays on which nine seated Amida (National Treasures) sit in a row; both sanctum and outer hall have open roof structures, the ceiling raised a step above the central image.

History: founded by Gyōki according to tradition and revived in 1047 (Eishō 2) by the monk Gimyō; in 1107 (Kashō 2) the old hall was dismantled and a new hall and images made, dedicated in 1108 (Tennin 1); in 1157 (Hōgen 2) the hall was moved to the west bank of the pond, its present site; repaired in 1328 (Karyaku 3), porch added in the Edo period. Listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1897, National Treasure in 1952; the garden was designated a Special Place of Scenic Beauty and Historic Site in 1965.

Value: nine-Amida halls were built in numbers in the late Heian period, and this is the only one left; the Agency notes that its elongated plan exists solely to seat the row of nine Buddhas, and that its style and workmanship fit the late Heian date. Hall and pagoda face each other east and west across the pond in the classic layout of a Pure Land garden; the hall also houses standing Four Guardian Kings (National Treasure) and a standing Kichijōten (Important Cultural Property).
captions: Jōruri-ji · Main hall
Late Heian · About 12th century

name: Three-Story Pagoda of Jōruri-ji
yearNote: 1150 serves only as an approximate timeline placement, not the exact date of the original structure; 1178 is the year it was moved to its present site, not the year it was built.
lede: On the east bank of the pond stands a small three-storey pagoda: slender timbers, triple-stepped bracket sets carrying deep eaves on every storey, a cypress-bark roof of very shallow pitch, the eave lines straight rather than curved — the manner of a Heian-period pagoda. The subject is the three-storey pagoda of Jōruri-ji. Temple records say it was moved here in 1178 (Jishō 2) from Ichijō-Ōmiya in Kyoto, so it must have been built before that; the Agency for Cultural Affairs dates it 'before 1178', and it was designated a National Treasure in 1952. It faces the nine-Amida hall on the west bank: Yakushi to the east, Amida to the west, the pond itself the line between this shore and the far one.
facts: Form: a three-bay, three-storey pagoda roofed in cypress bark, each storey carried on triple-stepped bracket sets under deep eaves, with gently pitched rafters. The ground storey has no interior columns; the central pillar rises only from above its ceiling. On an altar in the ground storey sits a seated Yakushi (Important Cultural Property, 85.7 cm, a hidden image), and the walls are painted with the sixteen arhats.

History: moved from Ichijō-Ōmiya in Kyoto in 1178; its original temple is unknown. An inscription on the roof finial records repairs in 1292 (Shōō 5), and details show Kamakura-period mending. Listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1897 and designated a National Treasure on 29 March 1952; the garden was designated a historic site and place of scenic beauty in 1965 and raised to Special Place of Scenic Beauty in 1985.

Value: the Agency notes that the brackets, rafters and eave structure 'show the Fujiwara-period style', and that the polychromy inside the ground storey is important evidence for Heian decorative painting. Pagoda to the east, hall to the west, facing across the pond — the classic layout of a late-Heian Pure Land garden.

name: Rock Garden of Ryōan-ji
sub: Dry landscape rock garden of the hōjō
era: Garden made in the Muromachi period · Date unknown
yearNote: 1500 serves only as an approximate timeline placement; the garden's creator and exact date of creation are still disputed, and this sorting point is not treated as an exact date.
lede: In a rectangle of white gravel about 25 metres wide and 10 deep there are only fifteen stones, grouped from the east in fives, twos, threes, twos and threes, and not a single tree. The subject is the dry-landscape rock garden before the abbot's hall of Ryōan-ji. Hosokawa Katsumoto founded the temple in 1450 (Hōtoku 2); temple tradition places the garden around the raising of the hall in 1499 (Meiō 8), but maker, date and meaning are all unsettled — the long stone by the wall is cut with the names 'Kotarō · □jirō', who can only be guessed to have taken part. The garden survived the fire that took the temple in 1797, was designated a historic site and place of scenic beauty in 1924, and later raised to Special Place of Scenic Beauty.
facts: Form: the south garden of the abbot's hall, about 25 metres east–west by 10 north–south, some 75 tsubo; the white gravel is raked into wave patterns, the fifteen stones set from the east in groups of five, two, three, two and three, with an oil-earth wall on three sides and trees beyond it as backdrop. The stones are of three kinds: chert from the hill behind the temple, mountain stone from the Tanba region, and green schist.

History: Katsumoto acquired the Tokudaiji villa and founded the temple in 1450; it burned in the Ōnin War in 1468, was rebuilt by his son Masamoto from 1488, and the abbot's hall was raised in 1499. The fire of 1797 destroyed the hall and other main buildings while the garden survived; the present hall is the Seigen-in hall of 1606, moved here. Designated a historic site and place of scenic beauty on 9 December 1924.

Value: the Agency for Cultural Affairs calls it 'the archetype of the abbot's-hall garden'; it is also known as 'the tiger cubs crossing'. After a cloudburst in 1951 the hill behind collapsed and mud briefly covered the garden; a visit by Queen Elizabeth II in 1975 greatly raised its international fame. The temple itself lists four riddles — the carved names, the making, the perspective and the wall.
captions: Ryōan-ji · Rock garden, detail
Muromachi period · Date unknown

name: Sōgen Pond Garden of Tenryū-ji
era: Garden made in the mid-14th century
yearNote: 1340 is only an approximate timeline placement; the garden was reworked by Musō Soseki around the founding of the temple in 1339, and the present scene shows changes from later maintenance.
lede: Look out from the west veranda of the abbot's hall: on the far shore of the Sōgen Pond two great upright rocks form the Dragon Gate cascade, and a 'carp stone' lies not below the fall but beside it — a carp halfway to becoming a dragon; beyond rise Mt Kameyama and, across the Ōi River, Arashiyama, all borrowed into the garden. The subject is the Sōgenchi garden of Tenryū-ji. Ashikaga Takauji founded the temple in 1339 (Ryakuō 2) for the repose of Emperor Go-Daigo, and the founding abbot Musō Soseki laid out the garden. The temple burned eight times and most of its halls date from an 1899 rebuilding; only this pond and its rockwork keep the look of the founding years. In 1923 it was among the first sites in Japan designated a historic site and Special Place of Scenic Beauty.
facts: Form: a stroll garden around the Sōgen Pond, borrowing Arashiyama and Kameyama as backdrop. On the west bank the Dragon Gate cascade is built of two great standing rocks with the carp stone set beside it; rock groups line the shore and the head of the fall, with a stone bridge and a triad of stones. The Agency for Cultural Affairs notes that 'the rockwork at the head of the fall is especially fine and best conveys the scenery of the time'.

History: in 1339 Takauji petitioned the retired emperor Kōgon to convert the Kameyama palace into a Zen temple, with Musō Soseki as founder and garden-maker; in 1346 (Jōwa 2) he named the 'Ten Views of Tenryū-ji', the Sōgen Pond among them. The temple burned eight times; after the Kinmon incident of 1864 most of it was lost, and the Dharma hall and great abbot's hall were rebuilt in 1899. Designated a historic site and place of scenic beauty on 7 March 1923.

Value: few Zen temples preserve both their front court and inner garden intact, which is why the Agency rates it so highly. The pond's name comes from a stone tablet inscribed 'a single drop of Sōgen', said to have been unearthed when Soseki dredged it. Inscribed as World Heritage with the monuments of ancient Kyoto in 1994.
captions: Tenryū-ji · Sōgen Pond Garden
Early Muromachi · About mid-14th century
searchAliases: 日本 · 京都府 · 京都

name: Garden of Saihō-ji
yearNote: 1340 serves only as an approximate timeline placement; Musō Soseki reworked the garden in the mid-14th century, and the moss that now spreads so widely is a landscape that formed gradually later.
lede: In the lower garden the shoreline of the Golden Pond twists and turns around three islands — Morning Sun, Evening Sun and Long Island — and more than 120 kinds of moss carpet the ground about it. The subject is a corner of the Golden Pond in the garden of Saihō-ji. Tradition names Gyōki as founder; in 1339 (Ryakuō 2) Musō Soseki revived the temple, converted it to Rinzai Zen and made the garden, whose upper rock composition is regarded as Japan's earliest dry landscape. But the moss that fills the eye today is not the fourteenth-century scene: floods in the Kan'ei and Genroku eras left the garden derelict, and the moss garden took shape only at the end of the Edo period. Designated a historic site and place of scenic beauty in 1923, now a Special Place of Scenic Beauty.
facts: Form: two levels. The lower is a stroll garden around the Golden Pond (also called the heart-shaped pond), its three islands spread with white sand and planted with pines, with the Shōnantei teahouse (Important Cultural Property) and others on the shore; the upper, at the foot of Mt Kōin, is a dry landscape with a three-tiered cascade of rocks beside the Shitō-an. The Agency for Cultural Affairs records that the two are linked by the small Kōjōkan gate.

History: tradition places the founding by Gyōki in 731 (Tenpyō 3); in 1339 Musō Soseki became abbot, rebuilt the halls and laid out the grounds, naming 'ten views of the Golden Pond' and 'ten views of Mt Kōin'. Burned in the Ōnin War in 1469, then ruined again by floods in the Kan'ei and Genroku eras; designated a historic site and place of scenic beauty on 7 March 1923; visits by reservation since 1977.

Value: Ashikaga Yoshimitsu and later Yoshimasa sat in meditation here, and the gardens of Rokuon-ji and Jishō-ji were modelled on it — the Agency says the Jishō-ji garden 'took its conception from Saihō-ji'. A two-storey reliquary hall, the Ruriden, once stood by the pond: the very prototype of the Silver Pavilion. The moss is a latecomer; the skeleton is fourteenth-century.
captions: Saihō-ji · Golden Pond and moss garden
Early Muromachi · Moss formed later

name: Yasaka Pagoda of Hōkan-ji
lede: The pagoda stands about 46 metres high, its five tiled roofs shrinking tier by tier, and only the topmost storey carries a balcony and railing — a rarity among five-storey pagodas. The subject is the five-storey pagoda of Hōkan-ji, popularly the Yasaka Pagoda. The present tower was rebuilt in 1440 (Eikyō 12) with the support of Ashikaga Yoshinori, after the third burning since 1179 (Jishō 3), and was designated an Important Cultural Property in 1897. Tradition credits Prince Shōtoku with the founding; excavations in 2009 produced seventh-century clay Buddha tiles and roof tiles, confirming that the temple does go back to the Asuka period. The foundation stone beneath the central pillar is still the ancient sunken type, so every successive pagoda has been rebuilt on the same base.
facts: Form: a three-bay, five-storey pagoda roofed in hongawara tiles, in pure Japanese style, about 46 metres high — after Tō-ji and Kōfuku-ji the tallest of its kind. The ground storey houses the Five Wisdom Buddhas centred on Dainichi; the central pillar stands on the original sunken foundation stone. Balcony and railing appear only on the fifth storey, and visitors may climb inside as far as the second.

History: burned in 1179 amid fighting between Kiyomizu-dera and the Gion shrine, and rebuilt in 1191 with Minamoto no Yoritomo's help; struck by lightning in 1291 and rebuilt in 1309 with the support of Emperor Go-Uda; destroyed again in the great Higashiyama fire of 1436 and rebuilt in 1440 by Yoshinori — the present tower. Designated an Important Cultural Property on 28 December 1897.

Value: one of the oldest surviving temples in Kyoto, its precinct a city-designated historic site. Rising from the terrace at the western foot of Higashiyama, the pagoda is the landmark on the kilometre or so between Yasaka Shrine and Kiyomizu-dera, and the only Important Cultural Property five-storey pagoda in Japan whose interior can be entered.
captions: Hōkan-ji · Yasaka Pagoda
Muromachi period · Rebuilt 1440

name: Shishinden of the Kyoto Imperial Palace
lede: Nine bays across, unpainted timber, a cypress-bark roof; a ring of lean-to aisles around the core, and outside that a railed plank veranda; from the front, eighteen steps — the 'south stair' — drop to the white-gravelled south court, with the cherry of the Left Guards and the orange of the Right Guards planted to either side. The subject is the Shishinden of the Kyoto Imperial Palace, the hall of enthronements and the great rites. The present building was rebuilt in 1855 (Ansei 2), on the scale of the Kansei rebuilding, after the palace burned in 1854 (Ansei 1); and that Kansei work of 1790 had already restored the Heian form on the basis of Uramatsu Kozen's Daidairi-zu kōshō. So it is a nineteenth-century building that deliberately grew up to look like the Heian period.
facts: Form: a single-storey timber hall roofed in cypress bark; the core, nine bays by three, is surrounded by lean-to aisles, with a plank veranda and railing outside. The outer fittings are hinged lattice shutters and panelled doors; inside, an open roof structure and polished board floors. The imperial throne (takamikura) stands at the centre of the core, which is divided from the north aisle by the Kenjō-no-shōji screens; the south aisle has a stair of eighteen steps at its centre.

History: the Tsuchimikado-Higashinotōin palace became the settled imperial residence from the Northern and Southern Courts period. After the great fire of 1788 (Tenmei 8), Matsudaira Sadanobu rebuilt the Jōmeimon gate, Shishinden and Seiryōden in 1790 in archaising form following Uramatsu Kozen's research; destroyed again in 1854 and rebuilt to the same scale in 1855 — the present hall, which the Imperial Household Agency assigns to the 'Ansei-period palace'.

Value: once the Daigokuden had fallen into disuse, enthronements moved here, becoming the rule from Emperor Go-Kashiwabara in 1521 (Daiei 1) and continuing, even after the court moved to Tokyo, down to Emperor Shōwa. The Agency says it 'transmits the architectural style of the Heian period'; it is the only surviving example of the form of a palace main hall.

name: Karamon of Daitoku-ji
sub: Karamon gate of the main temple
yearNote: 1590 serves only as an approximate timeline placement, not a construction date; the account that it was moved here from the Jurakudai remains legend.
lede: Look at the carving first: beneath the curved karahafu gables front and back, dragons, fish and flowers fill every member, and in places carving simply takes the place of the bracket sets — the Agency for Cultural Affairs calls it 'exceedingly rich, yet without formal exaggeration, free and unconstrained'. The subject is the karamon of the main compound of Daitoku-ji: a four-legged gate under a gabled cypress-bark roof, stylistically assigned to the Momoyama period. Temple tradition says it was a gate of Toyotomi Hideyoshi's Jurakudai palace, given through Murakami, lord of Suō; the Agency notes that 'no reliable evidence' exists. In a dismantling repair of 2003 the character 'Tenshō' was found cut into a metal fitting, which made the tradition a little more credible, though still not settled. Designated a National Treasure in 1952.
facts: Form: a four-legged gate with a gabled roof, a curved karahafu eave on both front and back, roofed in cypress bark; high-relief carving covers the whole, dragons and carp everywhere, and on some members carving replaces the bracketing. Because one could look at it all day it is nicknamed the 'Sunset Gate', and with the karamon of Nishi Hongwan-ji and Toyokuni Shrine it is counted among the three Momoyama karamon.

History: a plan of 1891 (Meiji 24) shows it standing west of the imperial messenger's gate, facing east; after the Akechi gate was sold to Konchi-in in 1886 it was moved to that site to face south as the front gate of the abbot's hall. The 2003 repair found fittings inscribed 'Tenshō' and a ridge tablet of 1603 (Keichō 8) recording the donation by Murakami Yorikatsu, lord of Suō. Listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1897.

Value: the Agency ranks it 'an architecture representative of the Momoyama period'. If the Jurakudai tradition holds, it is one of the very few surviving fragments of Hideyoshi's long-demolished palace. The south garden of the abbot's hall takes this gate as its southern boundary, forming one composition with the standing rocks and white gravel.
