name: Hōjō of Daitoku-ji
yearNote: The cultural heritage database listing gives 1635, while its building description gives 1636; the timeline uses the latter for approximate placement.
lede: An abbot's hall usually has six rooms; this one has eight. It is 29.8 metres long and 17 deep, a row of latticed doors spread beneath a grey tiled roof, and the front and back rooms of the second bay from the right form the Unmon-an, the memorial chapel of the founder Shūhō Myōchō, which even juts north beyond the veranda. The subject is the abbot's hall (hōjō) of the main compound of Daitoku-ji. In 1636 (Kan'ei 13), the old hall having become cramped, the merchant Gotō Masukatsu paid for a new one, completed together with the six-bay entrance hall projecting from its south-west corner; the Unmon-an's wall paintings carry an inscription of 1641, slightly later than the hall. Hall and entrance were designated National Treasures as two buildings in 1957.
facts: Form: 29.8 by 17.0 metres, single-storey hip-and-gable roof of pan tiles (originally cypress bark), with the Unmon-an attached at the rear; the plan is two rows deep and four bays wide, eight rooms in all, unlike the usual six. The entrance hall is six bays by one under a karahafu roof, a long projecting earthen-floored corridor. The eighty-four wall paintings are by Kanō Tan'yū.

History: the hall burned repeatedly and was rebuilt by Taisō in 1478 (Bunmei 10); in 1636 Gotō Masukatsu built the present hall to mark the founder's 300th memorial. Listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1909 and designated a National Treasure on 18 June 1957. The south garden was designated a historic site and place of scenic beauty in 1924, later a Special Place of Scenic Beauty; it is attributed to the monk Ten'yū.

Value: the Agency judges that 'the style and workmanship of every part keep faithfully to the norms of hōjō architecture, plain and lucid — a fine example of a large early-modern Zen abbot's hall'. In the south garden standing rocks on white gravel form a dry cascade, with Mt Hiei borrowed in the distance: likewise the archetype of the abbot's-hall garden.

Early Edo period · About 1635–1636

name: Tōgu-dō of Jishō-ji
yearNote: The cultural heritage database listing gives 1485, while its description gives 1486; the timeline takes the latter for approximate placement.
lede: The four-and-a-half-mat 'Dōjinsai' in the north-east corner is the real point: on its north wall a half-bay staggered shelf and a one-bay built-in desk alcove form the oldest surviving set of such room fittings — the shoin style starts here. When the hall was dismantled for repair, the words 'hearth room' were found inked on its timbers, showing that a hearth was once cut into the floor and that Yoshimasa made tea here. The subject is the Tōgudō of Jishō-ji, Ashikaga Yoshimasa's private Buddha hall, built in 1486 (Bunmei 18) on the north side of the pond in imitation of the Sairaidō at Saihō-ji. It measures 6.9 metres on each side, a single storey under a hip-and-gable roof of cypress bark, with slender timbers, chamfered square posts, boat-shaped bracket arms and widely spaced rafters — altogether clean and plain. Designated a National Treasure in 1951.
facts: Form: three and a half bays square, 6.9 metres on every side, a single storey with a hip-and-gable cypress-bark roof, facing south. Four rooms inside: the eight-mat Buddha room at the south-west, board-floored with a coved and latticed ceiling and panelled doors on the front, housing a standing Amida and a statue of Yoshimasa; a four-mat room at the south-east, a six-mat room at the north-west, and the four-and-a-half-mat Dōjinsai at the north-east. On the west exterior a section of wall is recessed to form a bench.

History: Yoshimasa began his Higashiyama villa in 1482 and built the Tōgudō as his private chapel in 1486. In the battle of Nakao Castle in 1550 the whole temple burned, leaving only the Silver Pavilion and the Tōgudō. Repairs in 1742 and in the Bunsei era altered the altar and the north room; a dismantling repair of 1964–65 restored everything to the original state. Listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1903 and designated a National Treasure in 1951.

Value: the staggered shelf and desk alcove of the Dōjinsai are the oldest surviving fittings of their kind, regarded as the source of the shoin style before it crystallised, and tea history has long held the room to be the beginning of the four-and-a-half-mat tearoom. The tablet 'Tōgudō' is in Yoshimasa's own hand, and the name comes from the Platform Sutra: 'the people of the East pray to be reborn in the West'.

Muromachi period · About 1485–1486

name: Kondō of Tō-ji
lede: The easiest thing to spot is the raised section in the middle of the lower roof: the central bay of the skirt roof is lifted a step and fitted with a pair of doors, opened during services so that flower petals could be scattered outward — a device also seen at the Great Buddha Hall of Tōdai-ji and the Phoenix Hall of Byōdō-in. The subject is the Kondō of Tō-ji, the main hall whose construction began first when the temple was founded in 796. It burned in a peasant uprising in 1486 and lay unrestored for nearly a century, until Toyotomi Hideyori paid for its rebuilding in 1603 (Keichō 8), as a ridge tablet records. Five bays by three with a mokoshi skirt roof, hip-and-gable and tiled, it combines the Japanese, Zen and Great Buddha styles; designated a National Treasure in 1953.
facts: Form: a core of five bays by three with a single mokoshi skirt roof, so that it reads as two storeys; hip-and-gable roof of hongawara tiles. The skirt roof uses triple-stepped brackets of the Great Buddha style and its central bay is raised; inside, through-ties and inserted bracket arms carry a lofty space with Zen-style details. The Yakushi triad, nearly 2.9 metres tall, was carved by Kōshō in 1603.

History: begun with the temple's founding in 796 and complete before the temple was granted to Kūkai in 823; burned in 1486; rebuilt in 1603 (ridge tablet). Listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1897 and designated a National Treasure on 31 March 1953. A dismantling repair in 1940 uncovered the original foundation stones and part of the altar platform beneath the floor, proving that position and scale are essentially those of the Heian period.

Value: the Agency for Cultural Affairs calls it 'a fine work of Momoyama temple architecture that blends three styles with splendid unity'. Temple tradition says it was modelled on Hideyoshi's Great Buddha Hall at Hōkō-ji, and the Miyako meisho zue likewise calls it 'a model of the Great Buddha Hall in eastern Kyoto'; the ridge tablet's phrase 'peace for the state, joy for the people' echoes the wording of the Hōkō-ji bell inscription that triggered the siege of Ōsaka.
captions: Tō-ji · Kondō
Momoyama period · Rebuilt 1603

name: Omote Shoin of Sanbō-in, Daigo-ji
lede: The long shoin opens entirely toward the garden: a broad veranda runs the length of the front, at its left end a gabled 'spring pavilion' juts toward the pond, and on the west an entrance porch with a curved karahafu gable is attached — devices the Agency for Cultural Affairs calls standard for the shoin style and a tradition inherited from the shinden palaces. The subject is the Omote Shoin of Sanbō-in at Daigo-ji. In 1598 (Keichō 3) Toyotomi Hideyoshi, planning his 'Daigo blossom-viewing', personally directed the revival of Sanbō-in, and the Omote Shoin dates from that work — plain in technique, grand in scale. Designated a National Treasure in 1954; the garden before it is a Special Place of Scenic Beauty and Special Historic Site.
facts: Form: a single storey under a hip-and-gable roof of pan tiles, the spring pavilion gabled, the west porch with a karahafu gable roofed in cypress bark. Inside are three rooms: the raised room of fifteen mats (with a two-bay alcove and one-bay staggered shelves), eighteen mats and twenty-seven mats, with an inner corridor on all four sides. By temple tradition the lowest room becomes a Noh stage when its mats are lifted, hence its name 'the stage-raising room'.

History: Sanbō-in had gone unrebuilt since 1470 (Bunmei 2); in 1598 Hideyoshi came to view the blossoms and personally directed its revival, and most of the surviving buildings date from then. Listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1897, designated a National Treasure on 20 March 1954. The garden was designated a place of scenic beauty in 1927: Hideyoshi laid out its plan himself, three garden commissioners built it, and Gien later had it repaired.

Value: the Agency calls it 'the relic that best expresses the character of Momoyama shoin architecture, of the highest value for the history of the house'. The wall paintings are by the school of Hasegawa Tōhaku and by Ishida Yūtei. The famous Fujito stone in the garden was brought from the Jurakudai palace; the pond has three islands and nine bridges — Hideyoshi's taste and Hideyoshi's power made visible in one place.
captions: Daigo-ji · Omote Shoin of Sanbō-in
Momoyama period · 1598

name: Goei-dō of Nishi Hongan-ji
lede: Look at the columns first: in the 441-mat outer hall stout posts stand in ranks with rainbow beams laid across them, all so that thousands of followers could hear the teaching at once. The subject is the Goeidō (Founder's Hall) of Nishi Hongwan-ji — 62.1 metres long, 48.3 deep and 29 high, among the largest surviving buildings of the Edo period, and bigger than the Amida hall to its north: at a Shin head temple the founder's hall comes first and the Buddha hall second. After a fire in 1617 (Genna 3) the hall was rebuilt, the ridge raised in 1636 (Kan'ei 13), with the wooden image of Shinran at its centre. A ten-year dismantling repair ran from 1999 to 2009, and in September 2014 it was designated a National Treasure.
facts: Form: 62.1 by 48.3 metres, a single storey under a hip-and-gable roof of hongawara tiles with a three-bay porch, facing east and linked to the Amida hall on the north by a covered passage. The outer hall holds 441 mats; the inner sanctuary is dressed with gold leaf, carved friezes and wall paintings. The Agency for Cultural Affairs singles out the raised posts, eave props and varied rainbow beams as advanced early-Edo structural work.

History: Hongwan-ji moved to Horikawa-Rokujō in 1591; the Goeidō and other halls burned in 1617 and were rebuilt in 1636. Two dismantling repairs followed, in 1800–1810 (Kansei 12 to Bunka 7) and in 1999–2009. Listed as an Important Cultural Property in 1913, designated a National Treasure on 18 September 2014, and inscribed as World Heritage with the precinct in 1994.

Value: the Agency places it at 'the summit of the Shin main hall, which set out from a small meeting-house and arrived at a vast Buddha hall'. The two rain-water tubs at the front have been held up since 1636 by eight 'amanojaku' imps about 38 cm tall; the patches in the veranda and corridor boards are carved as fish, aubergines and sake flasks — the humour of the repairing carpenters.
captions: Nishi Hongan-ji · Goei-dō
Edo period · Rebuilt 1636

name: Miei-dō of Chion-in
lede: Eleven bays long, nine deep, a five-bay porch across the front, hip-and-gable roof of hongawara tiles — a hall 44.8 metres wide sits heavily on the middle terrace of the compound, and the five-bay eave in front takes worshippers wholly under its cover. The subject is the Mieidō of Chion-in, named for the image of the founder Hōnen enshrined within. After the great fire of 1633 (Kan'ei 10) Tokugawa Iemitsu rebuilt it in 1639 (Kan'ei 16); the Agency for Cultural Affairs says it 'gathers the exterior in the Japanese style while deploying Zen-style technique inside, with columns standing like a forest', and ranks it the representative work of the Tokugawa family's great building campaign of the early Edo period. It was designated a National Treasure in 2002 together with the Sanmon gate.
facts: Form: eleven bays by nine, a single storey under a hip-and-gable roof with a five-bay porch at the front and a three-bay porch at the rear, tiled in hongawara; 44.8 metres wide and 34.5 deep. The front three bays form a mat-floored outer hall, the inner sanctuary is five bays square, and at the very back four pillars mark the innermost sanctuary, where a palace-shaped shrine holds the wooden image of Hōnen.

History: Ieyasu made Chion-in his family's perpetual memorial temple in 1603; Hidetada built the Sanmon and sutra repository in 1621. In the fire of 1633 only the Sanmon, sutra repository and Seishidō survived; Iemitsu directed the rebuilding, and the Mieidō was completed in 1639. Listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1910, designated a National Treasure on 23 May 2002; a major repair ran from 2011 to 2019, with the dedication ceremony on 13 April 2020.

Value: the Agency rates it 'extremely fine in design and technique, highly finished, of the greatest value in architectural history' — the summit of the main hall of the Jōdo sect's head temple. The precinct is laid out on three terraces; the Mieidō occupies the middle one, while the upper terrace is the true site of Hōnen's hermitage. As at Nishi Hongwan-ji, the founder's hall outranks the Amida hall, and the sect's priorities can be read at a glance.
captions: Chion-in · Miei-dō
Edo period · Rebuilt 1639

name: Tianyi Pavilion
era: Pavilion built in the 45th year of Jiajing, Ming
yearNote: 1566 is the year the pavilion was built; not every element seen today is regarded as original Ming material.
lede: Tianyige’s book repository nestles among Ningbo gardens, with white walls, dark tiles and regular windows. This modest two-storey building housed Fan Qin’s collection. Its open upper room, divided ground floor and pool express the desire to protect books from fire. Ming Jiajing construction established its identity; subsequent repairs sustained building and collection together. Its significance includes both architecture and the transformation of private collecting into a lasting cultural undertaking.
facts: Form: the two-storey repository has one open upper room and six rooms below, with windows front and rear. Tianyi Pool accompanies the building; its layout and name invoke water as protection against fire.

Dating: Fan Qin built the repository in the Jiajing era. Official descriptions give 1561–1566 as the construction period. Later garden additions and building repairs are separate phases, and not all present components are original.

Significance: building, books and the Fan family’s preservation practices form a shared history. The repository influenced later library architecture and retains a physical setting for collecting and transmitting local documents and examination records.

name: Qing'an Guild Hall
era: Built in the 3rd year of Xianfeng, Qing
lede: Qing’an Guild Hall’s front stage uses timber columns, brackets and adjoining galleries to create a layered performance space. Its domed caisson rises inwards, while red-and-gold carvings give beams and fittings narrative detail. Ningbo shipping merchants financed the hall for worship of Mazu as well as meetings. The stage linked theatre with rituals for safe voyages and everyday port life, leaving a distinctive record of Qing timber craftsmanship in eastern Zhejiang.
facts: Form: a timber frame supports the stage roof and a domed caisson assembled from interlocking carved boards. Columns, beams and brackets join adjacent galleries; red-and-gold carving often depicts stories and theatrical figures.

Dating: the guild hall was begun in 1850 and completed in 1853, during the Qing. Later conservation repairs form part of its history, and the front stage belongs within the compound’s construction and maintenance sequence.

Significance: Mazu worship and shipping merchants’ professional gatherings shared the hall, with theatre integrated into that social network. Carving and caisson construction preserve local crafts supported by port commerce.

name: Pagoda of Yong'an Temple, Anji
sub: Surviving body of the Lingzhi Pagoda
era: Survival from the Five Dynasties to the Southern Song
yearNote: 1100 is only an approximate timeline placement; the building is dated to a range from the Five Dynasties to the Southern Song.
lede: Anji’s Yong’an Temple Pagoda, also called Lingzhi Pagoda, rises in closely spaced brick eaves near the Xitiaoxi River. Temple and pagoda names changed over time, while finial inscriptions and excavated offerings preserve evidence of Northern and Southern Song repairs. Its broad Five Dynasties-to-Southern Song dating reflects an accumulated history, including modern restoration. The tower can be read both as a silhouette and through the memories retained within its components.
facts: Form: closely spaced projecting eaves taper up the brick body, ending at a finial. An upper chamber once held devotional offerings, adding internal evidence of relic worship to the tower’s exterior structure.

Dating: the national listing gives the Five Dynasties through Southern Song, not one certain construction year. Inscriptions on finial sleeves and offerings record repairs in 1047 and 1260; modern repairs also shaped the surviving tower.

Significance: inscriptions and excavated objects link its building history to donors and religious practice rather than appearance alone. Despite changes to the monastery, the pagoda documents a continuing local Buddhist setting.

name: Pagoda of Da'an Temple, Yiwu
yearNote: 1110 is an approximate placement point within the Northern Song, not a confirmed construction date.
lede: Da’an Temple Pagoda stands beside Xiuhu Lake in Yiwu, its hexagonal, five-storey body tapering through brick walls and projecting eaves. Although its former monastery has changed, columns, beams and brackets imitated in brick preserve the language of timber pavilions. The surviving monument is listed as Northern Song, with Ming and modern repairs. Its eaves and summit cannot all be treated as the work of one campaign. It records the linked growth of temple and townscape.
facts: Form: this hexagonal, five-storey pavilion pagoda combines brick and timber. Attached corner columns and brick representations of beams and brackets divide its faces, with doorways, niches, eaves and platforms marking the storeys.

Dating: the national listing assigns it to the Northern Song; local records place construction in the Daguan era and note Ming Yongle repairs. The body, restored eaves and summit belong to different phases, not one universal building date.

Significance: masonry imitating timber details provides evidence for Song pavilion forms. The pagoda’s historic location survives changes to monastery and lake surroundings, helping explain Yiwu’s old religious and public landscape.

name: Pagoda of Dashan Temple, Shaoxing
yearNote: 1250 serves only as an approximate timeline placement for the Southern Song stage.
lede: Shaoxing’s Dashan Temple Pagoda stands as a hexagonal, seven-storey brick tower in the old city. With former timber eaves and internal stairs lost, walls, openings and projecting storey divisions reveal its construction. The surviving core belongs to a Southern Song rebuilding, followed by Ming, Qing and modern repairs. The Southern Dynasties foundation of the monastery does not date today’s tower. This surviving pagoda continues to mark changes in the city’s religious landscape.
facts: Form: seven storeys rise on a hexagonal brick body, with doorways, niches and projecting elements expressing a pavilion tower. Lost wooden eaves and stairs leave traces of its former mixed brick-and-timber construction.

Dating: an internal brick inscription records rebuilding in the Southern Song Shaoding wuzi year, 1228. Fire preceded that campaign and later repairs followed. The tower’s Southern Song core is distinct from the monastery’s earlier foundation.

Significance: openings, brick imitations of timber and rebuilding inscriptions remain evidence for Song pavilion pagodas despite loss. The tower’s location and silhouette also preserve urban memory through a changing monastery landscape.

name: Chaoyin Bridge, Huzhou
lede: Chaoyin Bridge crosses the Zha Stream in Huzhou’s old city with three stone arches, a raised deck and stepped approaches to riverside streets. A former ferry was replaced by a Ming bridge and later rebuilding. A smaller crossing beneath the western opening allowed passage along the bank, giving rise to the local phrase “bridge beneath a bridge”. Subsequent repairs shaped the monument, whose outline still reveals the meeting of water routes and streets in a Jiangnan city.
facts: Form: three stone arches support a raised deck reached by steps from the banks. Piers and arches define its side profile, while crossing the river and moving along the bank intersect in one arrangement.

Dating: a stone bridge replaced the ferry in the Ming Jiajing era and was rebuilt in the Wanli era. The surviving structure includes later repairs; ferry, bridge and subsequent additions are separate phases.

Significance: the “bridge beneath a bridge” describes overlapping transport routes rather than unusual appearance alone. The link with waterside streets preserves experience of coordinating crossings, bank access and river traffic.

name: Tongji Bridge, Yuyao
yearNote: 1731 is an approximate timeline placement for the rebuilding in the Yongzheng reign.
lede: Yuyao’s Tongji Bridge crosses the Yao River with a high central arch and smaller side openings, linking the north and south parts of the city. Steps climb over the bridge while the main opening leaves clearance for boats. Its site reaches back to the Northern Song, but the surviving stone bridge largely results from Qing Yongzheng rebuilding. Together with Shunjiang Tower on the north bank it marks the old city; the bridge alone reveals Yuyao’s river-based layout.
facts: Form: this steeply arched stone bridge has three openings and two piers. A high main arch meets smaller side arches; stepped pedestrian access, the waterway and bank streets converge at the crossing.

Dating: a Northern Song timber bridge preceded a Yuan three-arch stone structure. The surviving bridge was rebuilt in the Qing Yongzheng era. Foundation, change of material and rebuilding are separate events.

Significance: the crossing has long connected the two city halves and records the transition from timber to stone arches. Its pairing with Shunjiang Tower makes it a transport structure and an anchor of urban memory.

name: Guyue Bridge
era: Built in the 6th year of Jiading (Southern Song)
lede: Guyue Bridge crosses Longxi beside Yazhijie village in Yiwu. From a distance it resembles a high arch, but its underside is a five-segment outline formed by joined long stones rather than a continuous curve. Six parallel ribs support the deck, demonstrating a method distinct from ordinary wedge-stone arches. A side inscription dates construction to 1213, the sixth Jiading year of the Southern Song. Subsequent conservation preserves a structure that can itself be read as historical evidence.
facts: Form: six parallel polygonal stone ribs support a single opening. Each has five long-stone segments joined with transverse locking stones. Deck and sidewalls lie above; the segmented underside explains the construction better than its distant silhouette.

Dating: an inscription records construction in the Southern Song Jiading guiyou year, 1213. It provides a verifiable building date distinct from later conservation, reinforcement and replacement of damaged stone.
Significance: long-stone ribs and locking members make the load-bearing arrangement visible. The dated inscription allows the structure to be compared with written records and other Song bridges.

name: Former Site of the Zhejiang Library
sub: Red Building of the Gushan premises
era: Library premises, late Qing to Republican era
yearNote: 1909 is only an approximate placement for the library-premises phase; the national protected site comprises several buildings.
lede: The Red Building at Gushan presents red brick and an arcaded veranda towards West Lake. Its two-storey Western form became part of Hangzhou’s library history. Built as a late-Qing guest accommodation, it later stored books from Wenlange. This change of identity shows that the former library is a collection of buildings with separate histories: the Red Building, nearby White Building and other premises have different dates, united by the preservation of books.
facts: Form: this two-storey Western building has a rhythmic brick-and-column façade with arched decoration between columns. The veranda and main body form one building; the White Building and hilltop premises are separate structures.

Dating: built in 1906 as guest accommodation, it moved into book storage in the Republican period and formally passed to the library in 1916. The White Building, completed in 1912, has a different construction date.

Significance: the shift from guest accommodation to ancient-book preservation illustrates the growth of public cultural space. Storage and cataloguing of Wenlange books link the building to West Lake’s collecting tradition.

name: Shinantang Xu Clan Ancestral Hall
yearNote: 1700 is used only to place the Ming–Qing phase approximately on the timeline.
lede: The entrance pavilion and white walls of Shinantang’s Xu Ancestral Hall define a shared ritual place beside the Wuyi River in Jinhua. The wider ancestral complex links several Xu settlements; its courtyards, halls and structure record collective funding and repairs. Founded in the Ming, it was modified in the Qing and modern periods, so its present appearance is not identical to the Wanli foundation. Beyond dark tiles and white walls, it preserves memories of communities organising relationships through ancestral ritual.
facts: Form: the entrance pavilion and continuous walls define the front boundary. Halls and courtyards follow a central axis within; the relatively simple exterior contrasts with the more complex structure inside.

Dating: field research places the foundation in 1599, the twenty-seventh Wanli year. Repeated repairs included Qing replacement of some structural members and modern conservation. The Ming–Qing listing does not make the whole building original Ming fabric.

Significance: several Xu villages in the Wuyi River region worshipped common ancestors here, with a location intended to ease their journeys. Funding, repairs and seasonal rites made the hall a network connecting villages.

name: Square Fort and Ming Tower, Ming Xiaoling Mausoleum
yearNote: 1398 places the early Ming mausoleum phase; it does not represent the construction date of every surviving component of the Ming Tower.
lede: A square fortress with a tower on top: the combination began here, and every imperial tomb afterward, at the Ming Tombs outside Beijing and the Qing Eastern and Western Tombs, copied it. The Square City of the Ming Xiaoling is built of huge stone blocks, and the Soul Tower above it is brick, 39.25 m from east to west and 18.4 m deep, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof in yellow glazed tile; the central arched passage leads to the burial mound behind, inside which Zhu Yuanzhang and Empress Ma lie. The tower's roof burnt in 1853 and for more than a hundred and fifty years only the four walls stood; the present roof was added in 2009, so the plate shows what is seen today, not an early Ming original.
facts: Form: the Soul Tower is brick, 39.25 m wide east to west and 18.4 m deep north to south, under a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof of yellow glazed tile, its outer walls washed red and inner walls yellow; three arched openings face south and one each faces east, west and north. The Square City below is built of huge stone blocks, its central arched passage leading to an inner court before the mound, from which stepped ramps climb to the tower.

Dating: work on the Xiaoling began in 1381, the fourteenth year of Hongwu, the sacrificial hall and other main structures were finished in 1383, and the whole was completed in 1405, the third year of Yongle; in 1853, in the fighting between Qing and Taiping forces, the timber parts, including the hall and the tower's roof, all burnt. In 2007 the Zhongshan Cemetery Administration decided to rebuild the tower's roof, the State Administration of Cultural Heritage approved it in 2008, and it was completed in July 2009.

Value: the pairing of Square City and Soul Tower with the walled mound took its fixed form at the Xiaoling, and the imperial tombs of the Ming and Qing followed it for more than five hundred years; the mound covers an underground palace cut into the body of Wanzhu Peak, heaped with cobbles and loess into a rounded hill about 400 m across, and magnetic survey in 1998 traced the entrance tunnel east of the tower, about 120 m long. The Ming Xiaoling was inscribed as World Heritage in 2003.

name: Sacrificial Hall, Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum
sub: Sacrificial Hall and main stone stairway
lede: From the Bo'ai Gateway to the Sacrificial Hall is seven hundred metres and a climb of seventy-three, and the plan of the whole mausoleum is a bell. Lü Yanzhi won first prize in the design competition of 1925 with this scheme; work began in 1926, the hall was finished in the spring of 1929, and on 1 June that year Sun Yat-sen's coffin was interred. The hall is a stone palace imitating timber: 28 m long, 22.5 m wide and 26 m high, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof in blue glazed tile, three arched doors on the front inscribed 'Nationalism, Democracy, People's Livelihood', and fortress-like square turrets at the four corners, a Chinese great roof and a Western tripartite composition laid over one another in a single building.
facts: Form: the hall faces south, a stone palace imitating timber construction, 28 m long, 22.5 m wide and 26 m high; the double-eaved hip-and-gable roof is covered in blue glazed tile with two tiers of stone bracket sets beneath the eaves; the three arched doors on the front carry bronze doors with pierced plum-blossom lattice, the lintels bear Zhang Jingjiang's seal-script 'Minzu', 'Minquan' and 'Minsheng', the band between the eaves holds Sun Yat-sen's inscription 'Righteous Spirit of Heaven and Earth', and each corner has a fortress-like square turret.

Dating: in 1925 the funeral preparatory committee held a prize competition for designs and Lü Yanzhi's scheme took first place; the first phase, covering the hall, the tomb chamber, the terrace and the steps, began on 15 January 1926 and was finished in the spring of 1929, Lü Yanzhi dying of illness that March; the state funeral was held on 1 June, and the whole project was completed by the end of 1931.

Interior and value: inside stand twelve stone columns with reinforced-concrete cores clad in black Qingdao granite; slightly north of centre sits the marble statue of Sun Yat-sen by Paul Landowski, 4.6 m high; the tomb chamber behind is a hemisphere 18 m across and 11 m high. The whole mausoleum is bell-shaped in plan, 700 m horizontally and 73 m in height from gateway to hall, and it is regarded as a representative work of modern China's fusion of Chinese and Western architecture.

name: Zhonghua Gate, Nanjing City Wall
yearNote: 1393 is an approximate placement for the construction period of Nanjing's Ming city wall.
lede: Pass the first gate and three more lie ahead: the Zhonghua Gate fortress measures 128 m north to south and 118.5 m east to west, three barbican courts and four arched gateways nested one inside the next, with 27 soldier-hiding chambers hollowed into the walls to hold three thousand men. Enlarged on the site of the south gate of the Southern Tang capital, it was the grandest of the thirteen gates of the Ming capital built in the Hongwu era; first called Jubao Gate, it took its present name in 1931 and is regarded as the largest surviving barbican gate. The plate shows only the central gateway of Zhonghua Gate with the adjoining wall, not the whole Nanjing city wall as a single object.
facts: Form: the fortress is laid out like the character 'mu', 118.5 m wide east to west and 128 m long north to south, covering 15,168 square metres; one main gate and three barbican courts are linked by four arched gateways, the first gate 21.45 m high; each gateway once had a lowering portcullis and double timber doors, of which the slots and door positions survive, and ramps on either side allowed horses to ride up onto the wall.

Dating: Zhu Yuanzhang began building the Nanjing city wall in 1366, and Jubao Gate was enlarged in the Hongwu era on the site of the south gate of Southern Tang Jiangning and Southern Song Jiankang, with a legend that the treasure bowl of the magnate Shen Wansan is buried beneath it; in 1931 it was renamed Zhonghua Gate, the name board written by Chiang Kai-shek just before that year's National Day.

Soldier chambers: there are 13 chambers above and below in the barbican and 14 beneath the ramps on either side, 27 in all, for storing supplies and hiding troops in wartime, estimated to hold three thousand men; it is regarded as the largest and most complex fortress-style barbican surviving in China, and the scheme of three courts and four gateways is unique among Ming city gates.

name: Dacheng Hall of Chaotian Palace
yearNote: 1870 is an approximate placement for the rebuilding in the Tongzhi reign.
lede: After the Taiping war, Nanjing moved its prefectural school and Confucian temple into a ruined Daoist monastery: the surviving Dacheng Hall of Chaotian Palace was rebuilt in 1866, the fifth year of Tongzhi, its double-eaved roof standing on a tall platform with a central stone stair rising straight to the hall. Before that the site was a Daoist palace built by imperial order in 1384, the seventeenth year of Hongwu, which also administered Daoism for the whole empire and where civil and military officials rehearsed the rites of audience with the emperor, hence the name 'Facing Heaven'. The hall is now an exhibition hall of the Nanjing Municipal Museum. The plate shows only the Dacheng Hall and its stairs, and the earlier history of the palace is not taken as the hall's date.
facts: Form: the Dacheng Hall is the main building on the axis of Chaotian Palace, with a double-eaved roof of glazed tile on a tall platform and a stone stair at the centre; for the Tongzhi rebuilding the timber was brought from overseas and the glazed tiles came from Jingdezhen in Jiangxi. The plate shows the hall itself and its stairs.

Dating: rebuilt in 1384 and named Chaotian Palace, with the Daoist Registry housed inside, it was completed in 1395 as the court's place for rehearsing ceremonies; the buildings were destroyed in the Taiping period. In 1865 the Jiangning prefectural school and Confucian temple moved in, the Dacheng Hall, Lingxing Gate, Ji Gate and side halls were rebuilt by the ninth month of 1866, and from 1867 to 1869 the Chongsheng Hall, Zunjing Pavilion and Minglun Hall were added under Zeng Guofan.

Value: Chaotian Palace is described as the largest and best-preserved group of official-style Ming-Qing buildings in the Jiangnan region, and its change from Daoist palace to prefectural school and temple records the rebuilding of late-Qing Nanjing; in 1936 the Palace Museum built its Nanjing branch and storehouse on the school site to house the collections moved south, and it is now the Nanjing Municipal Museum.

name: Guanyun Peak, Lingering Garden
yearNote: 1873 is an approximate placement for the garden phase, not the exact year Guanyun Peak was formed or set in place.
lede: A single stone as the protagonist of a whole courtyard: Cloud-Capped Peak stands about 6.5 m high, the largest Lake Tai rock in the Jiangnan region, slender, perforated, wrinkled and hollowed all at once, and said to be a leftover from the Northern Song 'flower and rock' tribute. It rises in the north court of the Hall of Woodland Sages in the east of the Lingering Garden, with the Washing Clouds Pool in front, the Cloud-Capped Tower behind and the Ruiyun and Xiuyun peaks flanking it; the whole court was built for looking at the stone. The garden began as the East Garden of 1593, the twenty-first year of Wanli, but today's layout comes from the rebuilding after Sheng Kang bought it in 1873, completed in 1876, when 'Liu Garden' became the homophonous 'Lingering Garden'.
facts: Form: Cloud-Capped Peak is a Lake Tai limestone about 6.5 m high, standing alone, combining the qualities of hollowness, slenderness, perforation, wrinkling and grace, the largest such rock in Jiangnan; with Ruiyun and Xiuyun it forms the Three Peaks of the garden, standing at the centre, with the Washing Clouds Pool before it and the Cloud-Capped Tower behind, from which the whole garden can be surveyed. The plate shows the rock with part of the neighbouring pavilions.

Dating: the garden was begun in 1593 as the East Garden of Xu Taishi, a vice minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud; in 1798, the third year of Jiaqing, Liu Shu rebuilt it as the Hanbi Villa, popularly called Liu's Garden; in 1873 Sheng Kang, lieutenant governor of Hubei, bought it and spent three years on large-scale rebuilding and additions, completed in 1876, when it was renamed the Lingering Garden. The year 1873 serves only to place the garden's Qing phase on the timeline.

Value: the garden is divided into central, east, west and north sections, famed for the variety of its buildings and the number of its rocks, with a winding gallery more than 700 m long whose walls hold over three hundred stone inscriptions of successive dynasties; its three principal owners, Xu Taishi, Liu Shu and Sheng Kang, were all lovers of stone. It was listed among the first national key protected sites in 1961 and inscribed as World Heritage in 1997.

name: Baodai Bridge
yearNote: 1872 is an approximate placement for the restoration phase, not the original construction date of the whole bridge.
lede: Fifty-three arches, 318 m: one bridge draws the wide mouth of Dantai Lake into a low, flat ribbon of stone, and Baodai Bridge has more arches than any other surviving multi-arch stone bridge in China. It was part of the towpath of the Grand Canal, which is why its parapet has no solid panels: haulers could walk the whole length pulling their boats. Begun in 816-819, the eleventh to fourteenth years of Yuanhe of the Tang, it is said that the Suzhou prefect Wang Zhongshu gave his jewelled belt to fund it, and the bridge looks like a belt as well; rebuilt four or five times since, the present structure is Qing, repaired again in modern times, so the timeline takes only the repair phase and the bridge is not called a Tang original.
facts: Form: a stone bridge of 53 linked arches, 318 m long and 4.1 m wide, spanning the Daidai River at the mouth of Dantai Lake; as a towpath bridge its parapet has no solid panels; a pair of stone lions stands at each end, those at the north surviving, while those at the south were blown up by Japanese troops and restored in the winter of 1956.

Dating: begun in 816-819 in the Yuanhe era of the Tang, when the Suzhou prefect Wang Zhongshu is said to have donated his jewelled belt, baodai, toward the cost, the bridge's shape also resembling a belt; rebuilt four or five times since, the present structure dates from the Qing and has been repaired again in modern times.

Value: the longest surviving multi-arch old stone bridge in Jiangsu and the one with the most arches in China, standing beside the Grand Canal and used as a towpath through the centuries, a physical survival of canal navigation; it is often named with the Anji Bridge at Zhaozhou, the Zhupu Bridge at Dujiangyan and the Chengyang Bridge at Sanjiang as one of China's four great ancient bridges.

name: Zhaoguan Stone Pagoda
yearNote: 1311 is an approximate Yuan placement, not a confirmed construction year.
lede: To pass beneath the pagoda is to pay homage to the Buddha; that is why the Yuan built street-spanning stupas. The Zhaoguan Stone Pagoda stands at the highest point of the old street of Xijin Ferry in Zhenjiang, four stone columns carrying a square bluestone slab on which sits a Tibetan-style stupa: a double Sumeru base, a flattened drum-shaped body, the thirteen 'heavens' and the crown, the whole 3.8 m long from east to west, with the passage below exactly straddling the narrow street. Begun by Liu Gao in the Zhiyuan era of the Yuan and completed in 1311, the fourth year of Zhida, it was repaired in 1582, the tenth year of Wanli of the Ming, when the two characters 'Zhaoguan' were cut over the opening; during repairs in 2000 two mandalas were found in the chamber at its core.
facts: Form: a street-spanning stupa of bluestone in Tibetan style, 3.80 m long east to west and 3.20 m wide north to south; four stone columns carry a square bluestone slab, with eight pairs of stone brackets between columns and slab shortening the span, open for passage east and west and closed with brick north and south. The stupa has five parts, base, body, neck, thirteen heavens and crown; the body is a flattened drum 4.69 m high carved with thirteen bands of relief.

Dating: begun by Liu Gao in the Zhiyuan era of the Yuan and completed in 1311; repaired in 1582 by the Zhenjiang prefect Wang Shisheng and others, when the characters 'Zhaoguan' were carved on the lintel stone over the opening, with the names of the repairing officials and the fund-raising monks dated 'repaired in the tenth month of the renwu year, tenth of Wanli' cut at the sides. Repaired again in 1980 and 2000, it received a UNESCO Asia-Pacific Heritage Award in 2001.

Value: the inner faces of the columns are carved 'Homage to the Great Vaipulya Buddha Avatamsaka Sutra' and the stupa bears the six-syllable mantra in Sanskrit script; in 2000 two mandalas were found in the core chamber, each with nine figures of the Yellow Jambhala and nine of Guanyin, now graded as national first-class relics. It is one of only three Tibetan-style stupas left in Jiangsu and is held to be the best-preserved street-spanning stone stupa in China.

name: Rockeries of Ge Garden
lede: Four seasons walked through in one garden: the spring mountain is stone shoots planted among bamboo, the summer mountain is grey-blue Lake Tai rock piled into rolling clouds and mist, the autumn mountain is rugged yellow stone with a square pavilion on its summit, and the winter mountain is snow-white Xuan stone heaped against a wall pierced with rows of round holes that sound when the north wind blows. Ge Garden was rebuilt in 1818, the twenty-third year of Jiaqing, by the Lianghuai salt merchant Huang Zhiyun on the site of the Ming Shouzhi Garden; the character 'ge' is half of the character for bamboo. The seven-bay Baoshan Lou, the 'mountain-embracing tower', spreads its two arms to gather the summer and autumn mountains in. The plate takes one rockery with a neighbouring pavilion and does not stand for the whole garden.
facts: Four-season rockeries: the spring mountain sets stone shoots among bamboo as 'bamboo shoots after rain'; the summer mountain is piled from grey-blue Lake Tai rock like rolling clouds, with a thin stream beneath; the autumn mountain is yellow stone, the tallest and largest, with caves and stone chambers inside and a square pavilion on top; the winter mountain heaps white, rounded Xuan stone against a wall, with four rows of round holes in the south wall as wind-sounding openings.

Dating: in 1818 Huang Zhiyun, head of the Lianghuai salt merchants, enlarged the site of the Ming Shouzhi Garden into a private garden, taking its name from the line 'moonlight on bamboo makes a thousand ge characters'; in the early Tongzhi years (1862) it was sold to the Zhenjiang salt merchant Li Wen'an, whose family kept it for about sixty years and built much of the rockery from the ballast stones of their boats; after 1949 it passed to the state.

Value: Baoshan Lou is a seven-bay tower whose galleries extend east and west to embrace the autumn and summer mountains; the device of building four seasonal rockeries from four kinds of stone was called 'a unique case in the country' by Chen Congzhou. The garden was listed as a national key protected site in 1988 and is described as a component of the Grand Canal World Heritage site in its Yangzhou section.

name: Boat Hall of He Garden
yearNote: 1883 is an approximate placement for the garden's construction phase, not a confirmed separate construction date for the Boat Hall.
lede: There is no water, yet it is a boat: the Boat Hall is ringed by a gallery and shaped like a cabin, and the ground around it is paved with pebbles and tile fragments in a band of water ripples, so that standing under the eaves feels like standing at a gunwale. It is the most refined building in the east garden of He Garden, 15.65 m wide and 9.5 m deep under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, with a couplet on the columns reading 'the moon is host and the plum is guest; flowers are my four walls and a boat my home'. He Garden, originally Jixiao Villa, was begun by He Zhidao in 1862, the first year of Tongzhi, completed in 1875, the first year of Guangxu, and absorbed the Pianshi Shanfang rockery in 1883; a 1,500 m two-storey gallery ties house and garden into one. The plate shows only the Boat Hall and part of the adjoining gallery.
facts: Form: the Boat Hall is 15.65 m wide and 9.50 m deep under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof with a gallery on all four sides, the whole resembling a boat's cabin; the ground around it is paved with pebbles and tile fragments in a water-ripple pattern, the lattice windows are glazed with clear glass, and the columns carry the couplet 'the moon is host and the plum is guest; flowers are my four walls and a boat my home'. The plate shows the hall with part of the adjoining gallery.

Dating: He Garden was begun in 1862 and completed in 1875 after thirteen years, as the private garden of He Zhidao, intendant of the Han-Huang-De circuit in Hubei, who named it Jixiao Villa after Tao Yuanming's lines about leaning on the south window and whistling from the eastern knoll; in 1883, the ninth year of Guangxu, the Wu family's Pianshi Shanfang rockery was added to the garden.

Value: a 1,500 m two-storey gallery links the residence, rear garden, Pianshi Shanfang and family shrine, earning the name 'first gallery under heaven', the only case of its kind among Chinese gardens; the Pianshi Shanfang rockery is attributed to the painter-monk Shitao. Tong Jun, Liu Dunzhen, Chen Congzhou and others praised its design, and Luo Zhewen inscribed it 'the first garden of the late Qing'.

name: Southern Dynasties Tomb Stone Carvings · East Bixie of the Tomb of Xiao Jing
era: Stone carving of the Liang (Southern Dynasties)
yearNote: 523 is used only to place the Liang phase of the Southern Dynasties approximately on the timeline; it is not a confirmed carving date for this stone beast.
lede: Nanjing's civic emblem was traced from this stone beast. The east bixie at the tomb of Xiao Jing lifts its head, thrusts out its chest, opens its mouth with tongue extended, carries wings on its shoulders and strides forward, the whole block carved into a single forward surge. It once had a partner: the west bixie was too shattered to repair and was buried back into the ground in 1956 and again in 2009, leaving this one alone above the surface. Xiao Jing was a cousin of Emperor Wu of Liang and died in 523, the fourth year of Putong; a stone column still stands on the spirit road, its twenty-three-character title cut in the rare mirror-reversed script, naming the tomb's owner and fixing its date.
facts: Form: the east bixie is a winged beast carved from a single stone, head raised and chest thrust out, mouth open with tongue extended, wings carved on the shoulders and the four legs staggered in a walking pose; it was one of a pair flanking the spirit road, but the west bixie, broken beyond repair, was buried in its original soil in 1956 and again in 2009, so only the east one remains above ground. The plate shows the east bixie itself, not any other Southern Dynasties beast.

Dating: Xiao Jing (477-523) was the son of Xiao Chongzhi, uncle of Emperor Wu of Liang, enfeoffed as Loyal Marquis of Wuping, and died in 523, the fourth year of Putong; the spirit-road column bears on its tablet the twenty-three characters 'Spirit road of Lord Xiao, late Palace Attendant, General Pacifying the Centre, Commander Unequalled in Honour, Loyal Marquis of Wuping of Liang' in incised mirror-reversed script, the direct evidence for the owner and date, and the carvings were presumably finished soon after his death.

Value: 33 groups of Southern Dynasties tomb sculpture survive around Nanjing, Danyang and Jurong, 13 of them from the Liang, the largest share; the bixie of Xiao Jing's tomb is regarded as the symbol of Nanjing and is the original model from which the city's official emblem was drawn. Only after the carvings at the tombs of Xiao Jing and Xiao Dan were illegally rubbed in 2014 did Nanjing begin to fit its open-air sculptures with surveillance, shelters and other protection.

name: Luoyang Bridge
sub: Stone beam bridge · Run of piers (detail)
era: Completed in the 4th year of Jiayou
yearNote: Begun in 1053 and completed in 1059; the plate takes only one section and does not use this detail to represent the whole bridge.
lede: At the mouth of the Luoyang River the Song builders did three things that later generations never tired of praising: they dumped rock along the bridge line to form a low submerged dyke as a 'raft foundation', they farmed oysters on the footing stones so that the shellfish cemented the blocks together, and they used the rise and fall of the tide to float stone beams of more than ten tonnes on rafts and set them onto the piers. Begun in 1053 by Wang Shi and others, the bridge was completed in 1059 under the prefect Cai Xiang, and is the earliest surviving sea-crossing stone bridge in China. The plate takes a stretch of several consecutive boat-shaped piers and their beams.
facts: Form: a stone beam bridge running northeast-southwest, now about 731 m long and 4.5 m wide, with 47 spans and 45 stone piers in the main section, built in two parts around the mid-river islet of Zhongzhou; every pier has a boat-shaped cutwater on the upstream side; the deck beams are single slabs of stone up to 11 m long, 0.98 m wide and 0.8 m thick, weighing over ten tonnes.

Dating: in 1053 Wang Shi, Lu Xi and thirteen others jointly began a stone bridge and failed to finish it in three years; between 1056 and 1059 Cai Xiang, twice prefect of Quanzhou, directed its completion and wrote the 153-character Record of Wan'an Bridge, carved on a stele. The bridge was repaired 27 times down to 1993 and came through the great Quanzhou earthquake of 1604 unharmed.

Significance: the earliest surviving sea-crossing stone bridge in China, it opened three centuries of bridge building in Song-Yuan Quanzhou; its raft foundations, oyster-cemented footings and tidal floating of beams were inherited by Anping Bridge and others. Seven stone pagodas from the Song onward and four guardian stone generals survive on the bridge and the islet, and in 2021 it was inscribed on the World Heritage List.

name: Tianhou Temple, Quanzhou
sub: Main hall · Southern Fujian upswept ridges
era: Founded in the 2nd year of Qingyuan
yearNote: 1196 is the founding year of the Tianhou Temple; the main hall has been repaired in successive periods, and the plate shows its present state.
lede: Leaving Quanzhou by the south gate, Deji Gate, one came first to the Tianhou Temple and then went down to the Jin River to put to sea: this was the first stop for sailors paying their respects to Mazu in the Song and Yuan. The temple was built in 1196 as the Shunji Palace; in 1232 the prefect Zhen Dexiu came in person to sacrifice, bringing Mazu into the official cult, and in 1278 the court titled her 'Celestial Consort'. The main hall in the plate is five bays wide under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof with steeply upturned ridges; its surviving main structure took shape in the 19th century, and it sits on a granite platform a metre high.
facts: Form: the main hall is five bays (24.6 m) wide and five bays (23 m) deep under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof with the high upswept ridges of southern Fujian; it stands on a granite platform 1 m above the ground whose four faces carry reliefs of carp turning into dragons, galloping steeds and cranes among clouds. The surviving main structure took shape in the 19th century.

History: founded in 1196 as the Shunji Palace; brought into official ritual after Zhen Dexiu's sacrifice in 1232; Mazu was titled Tianfei in 1278 and the investiture was conducted in 1281 by Pu Shiwen, superintendent of the Maritime Trade Office; Zheng He petitioned for repairs in 1407 and Shi Lang for the title 'Tianhou' in 1684; the hall was repaired to its original regulations in 1815 and 1821.

Layout: set at the southern end of the old city, linking the town within to the port without, the temple keeps a front-hall-and-rear-chamber layout formed before the 16th century, with gate, stage, worship court, main hall, rear chamber and dressing tower along the axis on a site of about 6,800 square metres; the rear chamber holds a reused pair of Yuan-dynasty sixteen-sided Hindu diabase columns. Inscribed as World Heritage in 2021.

name: Zhangzhou Stone Memorial Archways · Sanshi Zai'er Archway
yearNote: Sources differ on the exact construction year of the Sanshi Zai'er Archway, so it is placed approximately in the Wanli reign; the plate shows only this archway and does not represent the whole group of four.
place: Fujian · Zhangzhou · Hong Kong Road, Xiangcheng
lede: On Hong Kong Road in the old town of Zhangzhou, two Ming stone archways face each other 28.5 m apart along a north-south line; this is the northern one. In 1619 the court raised it to honour Jiang Mengyu, Right Vice Minister of Personnel at Nanjing, together with his father and grandfather, three generations in all; the two faces of the tablet read 'Three Generations of Vice Ministers' and 'Served with Distinction in Both Capitals'. It is 8.09 m wide and 11 m high, three bays, five roofs and twelve columns, built of alternating grey-green and white stone, a representative use of southern Fujian stone carving in a commemorative gateway.
facts: Form: a stone archway of three bays, five roofs and twelve columns, 8.09 m wide and 11 m high, oriented north-south; built of alternating bluestone and white stone, with fish-shaped ridge ornaments on the roofs, upturned eave corners, and beams and lintels dividing the tiers below the main tablet; brackets, sparrow braces, panels and hanging posts are all carved in stone.

Date: according to the Fujian Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau the archway was erected in 1619, the 47th year of Wanli, to honour Jiang Mengyu, Right Vice Minister of Personnel at Nanjing, and his father and grandfather; the main tablet is inscribed in regular script 'Sanshi Zai'er' on one face and 'Liangjing Yangli' on the other. The 'Minister and Third-Place Graduate' archway just to the south, for Lin Shizhang, is fourteen years older.

A set of four: the national heritage listing 'Zhangzhou Stone Archways' comprises the two Ming archways on Hong Kong Road and two Kangxi-era archways for military commanders on Yuekou Street; the panels of the latter even carry carved foreigners with curly hair and hats, a reflection of overseas trade in the Yuegang era. The plate shows only the Sanshi Zai'er archway.

name: Jiangdong Bridge
yearNote: Built 1237–1241; the bridge was repeatedly repaired in later periods, and the plate shows a surviving section of stone beams and piers.
place: Fujian · Zhangzhou · North Stream of the Jiulong River
lede: Each stone beam is twenty-two or twenty-three metres long and weighs close to two hundred tonnes; how craftsmen eight centuries ago set them onto piers in a racing current was something the bridge engineer Mao Yisheng, writing in 1962, still called 'not fully understood'. Jiangdong Bridge, formerly Hudu Bridge, was rebuilt in stone after the timber bridge burnt in 1237, at the urging of the Zhangzhou prefect Li Shao, and took a little over three years. Today only five intact piers on the west bank, two spans of deck and nine ruined pier bases remain, with a 1970 road bridge carried above them. The plate takes a surviving stretch of beams and piers.
facts: Form: a multi-span stone beam bridge. Surviving are 5 intact piers, two spans of original deck, 9 ruined pier bases and the east and west abutment walls, a remnant 100.35 m long; the piers are built of interlocking stone blocks 0.35 x 0.4 x 5.2 m into a ship's-prow shape, 11.4 m long and 5.3 m wide; each span carries 3 to 5 stone beams 22-23 m long, 1.15-1.5 m wide and 1.3-1.6 m thick, weighing nearly 200 tonnes.

Dating: a pontoon bridge was laid here in 1190 and the prefect Zhuang Xia replaced it in the Jiading era with a timber bridge on stone piers; after the timber bridge burnt in 1237 the prefect Li Shao urged a stone rebuilding, completed in a little over three years. The Longxi County Gazetteer records it as 'twenty chi wide and two thousand chi long' with fifteen openings. In 1970 a reinforced-concrete road bridge was raised on top of the old bridge.

Significance: counted with the Luoyang, Anping and Longjiang bridges as the four great stone bridges of Fujian, its beams are of a size rare in the history of bridge building anywhere, and Joseph Needham's Science and Civilisation in China calls it 'an interesting historical problem'; Zheng Chenggong defeated Qing forces here in 1652, and Japanese bombing in the war of resistance left only the five piers on the west bank.

name: Guandi Temple, Dongshan
sub: Gate tower · Southern Fujian cut-porcelain ridge decoration
era: Founded in the 20th year of Hongwu
yearNote: 1387 is the temple's founding year; the plate takes the surviving gate tower and entrance, and the ridge decoration and buildings have been repaired.
lede: The temple gate is not a wall but a pavilion carried on six stone columns, known locally as the Taizi Ting. The three columns on either side lean slightly inward to form a triangular brace; above them close-set bracket clusters carry a palace-style pavilion roof whose ridges are covered in jianci diao, cut-porcelain mosaic: shards of coloured ware pieced into the Eight Immortals crossing the sea, auspicious beasts and figures from Tang and Song tales, their colours unfading. The temple was founded in 1387, the twentieth year of Hongwu, and was enlarged and rebuilt in the Zhengde and Kangxi reigns; it is the ancestral temple from which many Guandi temples in Taiwan drew their incense. The plate shows this gate pavilion and the stone steps before it.
facts: Form: the gate is of the pailou type, six round stone columns carrying tiers of brackets and a palace-style pavilion roof, the three columns on each side leaning inward for triangular stability; the roof and ridges are covered with cut-porcelain mosaic, the Eight Immortals and beasts such as qilin, elephant and lion on the front, Tang and Song story figures on the back. The whole temple is three bays wide and six deep, on a site of more than 680 square metres.

Dating: founded in 1387 (Hongwu 20), enlarged from 1508 (Zhengde 3) and completed in 1512 (Zhengde 7), rebuilt in 1680 (Kangxi 19); repeatedly added to since, so that the timberwork is partly Ming and partly Qing and modern. The halls still keep a carved wooden couplet composed by Huang Daozhou and a board inscribed by the Xianfeng emperor reading 'Wanshi renji'.

Significance: together with the Guandi temples at Yuncheng in Shanxi, Luoyang in Henan and Dangyang in Hubei it is counted among the four great Guandi temples of China, and it is the ancestral temple of nearly a thousand Guandi temples in Taiwan. The Taizi Ting, with its leaning columns and bracket sets, has stood through centuries of island typhoons and earthquakes, a representative work in which Minnan builders fused structural mechanics with cut-porcelain ornament.

name: Eryi Building, Hua'an
era: Built in the 5th year of Qianlong
lede: A huge ring 73.4 m across, four storeys and 16 m high, its outer wall 2.53 m thick at the base, yet not the gallery-type round house of the Hakka but a Minnan unit house: sixteen units, each with its own stair running from ground to top, divided from one another by walls and linked only by a concealed corridor along the outer wall. Jiang Shixiong of the fourteenth generation of the Jiang clan began it in 1740, the fifth year of Qianlong, and the work took thirty years. More than two hundred murals and as many painted panels survive inside. The plate shows the rammed-earth face of the outer ring.
facts: Form: a double-ring round tulou; the outer ring is four storeys, 16 m high and 73.4 m in outer diameter, with a wall up to 2.53 m thick. It is divided into 16 units with 213 rooms in all, each unit with its own stair; there is no continuous front gallery, but a concealed corridor runs along the inner face of the outer wall. The single-storey inner ring is joined to each unit by a passage.

Dating: begun in 1740 (Qianlong 5) by Jiang Shixiong, fourteenth generation of the Jiang clan and holder of the honorific 'xiangyin dabin', and completed around 1770 (Qianlong 34), after thirty years. Inside survive 226 murals, 228 painted panels, 349 wood carvings and 163 couplets, direct evidence for the mid-Qing date of its fittings.

Comparison: Eryi Lou combines features of the Hakka inner-gallery type and the Minnan unit type; in 1996 it became the first tulou listed as a Major National Historical and Cultural Site, and in 2008 it was inscribed as World Heritage together with the tulou of Yongding and Nanjing as 'Fujian Tulou', of which it is the largest single building by area.

name: Hegui Building, Nanjing County
yearNote: Placed approximately in the Yongzheng reign of the Qing; the traditionally reported year is not treated as a verified construction date for each story.
place: Fujian · Zhangzhou · Pushan Village, Nanjing County
lede: A five-storey square building 21.5 m high, the tallest of all the Fujian tulou, yet built on a swamp. When the Jian clan of Changjiao raised it in 1732 they first drove more than two hundred pine piles into the soft ground, laid timber over them and built a cobblestone footing before ramming up the earth walls; after more than two centuries the building still stands level. Each floor has 28 rooms, 140 in all, with a single door in the middle of the front. The plate takes the five-storey earthen front and the low wall before it, without showing the inner court.
facts: Form: a square tulou of the inner-corridor type, five storeys and 21.5 m high, on a site of 1,547 square metres with a floor area of 3,574 square metres; 28 rooms per floor and 140 in all, one central door and a stair at each of the four corners; the massive rammed-earth outer wall is pierced by close rows of small windows, a defensive form different from the round tulou.

Dating: built in 1732, the tenth year of Yongzheng, by Jian Ciping of the thirteenth generation of the Changjiao Jian clan at a cost of fifteen thousand taels of silver; first raised to four storeys and given a fifth when rebuilt. It stands on marshland, on a foundation of more than two hundred pine piles and timber bedding with a cobblestone wall footing, which is why it has stayed sound for over two hundred years.

Comparison: Hegui Lou is known as the 'tallest' of the Fujian tulou, also called Shanjiao Lou, and is one of the few single tulou listed individually as World Heritage; in 2008 it was inscribed together with Huaiyuan Lou and the Tianluokeng and Hekeng clusters as the Nanjing portion of 'Fujian Tulou'.

name: Hulishan Fort
yearNote: The plate shows part of the surviving Krupp gun emplacement; 1894 is an approximate placement for the fort's late Qing construction phase and does not mean all installations were mounted in the same year.
lede: A Krupp breech-loading coastal gun of 280 mm calibre, thirteen metres long and fifty tonnes in weight, still mounted on the emplacement it occupied more than a century ago: the largest surviving nineteenth-century coastal gun in the world. Hulishan Fort was built on the memorial of Peng Chuhan, commander of the Fujian naval forces, and Bian Baodi, governor-general of Fujian and Zhejiang; work began in the third month of 1894 and finished in the tenth month of 1896, a half-bunker, half-rampart fort commanding the entrance to Xiamen harbour. The plate takes only the Krupp gun and its emplacement on the east battery, not the whole fort.
facts: Form: a fort of half-bunker, half-rampart type with east and west batteries for the main and supporting guns, over 70,000 square metres in all, of which the citadel is over 13,000; the gun platforms are rammed from a mortar of camphor-tree sap, glutinous rice, lime, paper fibre and sand. The surviving east gun has a calibre of 280 mm, a length of 13.13 m and a weight of 50 tonnes, turns through 360 degrees and has a range of 16,000 m.

Dating: begun on the eighth day of the third month of 1894 and completed on the eighth day of the tenth month of 1896, a construction period of two years and eight months; the east gun is marked '28 cm K.L/40 C/87', made by Krupp in Germany in 1887; the west gun was scrapped in the Great Steel Drive of 1958, and the two 150 mm secondary guns were carried off by the Japanese occupying Xiamen in 1938.

Significance: in the late Qing four 280 mm coastal guns were bought from Krupp to strengthen the southeastern coast; the two at Dianguangshan at the mouth of the Min River are gone and this is the only one left at Hulishan, certified in 2000 as the largest surviving 19th-century coastal gun in the world. Its crossfire with the Yuziwei fort on the opposite shore closed the channel, a surviving piece of the Self-Strengthening Movement's coastal defences.

name: Laojun Rock Statue, Mount Qingyuan
sub: Seated Lord Lao · Song stone carving
yearNote: 1150 is only an approximate placement on the Song timeline, not a confirmed carving date for Laojun Rock; the subject is registered under the third-batch listing of the Laojun Rock Statue.
lede: A single natural granite boulder, lightly carved to follow the shape of the rock, became a seated Laozi leaning on an armrest with his beard falling to his chest. The Quanzhou Prefectural Gazetteer puts it plainly: 'the stone image was formed by heaven; enthusiasts merely added a little carving.' At 5.63 m high it is the largest surviving Song-dynasty Daoist stone statue in China. A group of Daoist halls, the Zhenjun and Beidou halls, once stood below Qingyuan Mountain; the buildings are all gone, and only this Laojun remains seated at the foot of the hill, looking south over Quanzhou and the Jin River.
facts: Form: carved from one free-standing natural granite boulder, 5.63 m high, 8.01 m wide and 6.85 m deep; the Old Lord has a bald, high forehead, ears reaching his shoulders and a flowing beard, wears a Daoist robe with overlapping lapels and sits on the ground, right hand on an armrest, left hand on his knee, legs folded, the robe folds rendered in a few clear lines. The stone armrest shows Yuan-dynasty furniture features and is probably a later addition.

Dating: He Qiaoyuan's Minshu records that Zhu Xi visited this 'Yuxian Rock', so the statue existed by the 12th century; stone building members excavated around it, including cap-blocks with wedge tenons and arch keystones, match the work of the Southern Song twin pagodas of Kaiyuan Temple and the Liusheng Pagoda, the archaeological basis for dating it to the Song.

Significance: the largest surviving Song Daoist stone sculpture in China, which together with the Confucian Temple represents the native mainstream culture behind the Song-Yuan port of Quanzhou; it is the largest of the seven groups and nine Song-Yuan stone statues on Qingyuan Mountain, and in 2021 was inscribed as one of the 22 component sites of the World Heritage property 'Quanzhou: Emporium of the World in Song-Yuan China'.

name: Fuzhou Confucian Temple
era: Present structure from the Xianfeng reign
yearNote: The Confucian Temple has earlier origins; the Dacheng Hall is placed approximately by its 1851–1854 construction phase, and the plate shows its present state after the 2026 restoration.
lede: In the eighth month of 1851 a fire destroyed the Fuzhou Confucian Temple; rebuilding began that twelfth month and was finished in the sixth month of 1854, and what stands today is that layout. The Hall of Great Achievement is seven bays wide and four deep under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof, on a stone platform a metre and a half high; a ring of twenty-two stone eave columns runs under the lower eaves, the eight stone interior columns weigh about nine tonnes each, and timber columns are jointed onto the stone column heads, a Fujian practice of mixing stone and timber. At the end of 2025 it completed its first major repair in the more than 170 years since the rebuilding.
facts: Form: seven bays wide and four deep, with a double-eave hip-and-gable roof, 19.6 m high, standing on a stone platform 1.46 m above the forecourt; the lower part of the column-and-tie timber frame is stone, 22 stone eave columns and 8 stone interior columns, with 18 full-height timber columns jointed above their heads; between the upper and lower eaves are 42 bracket sets of five tiers and eight layers, and the ceiling well is painted with a star chart.

Dating: in 773 the commissioner Li Yi moved the prefectural school here, a temple to Confucius was first made in the Taiping Xingguo era of the Song, and the Hall of Great Achievement was built in 1374; fire struck on the third day of the eighth month of 1851, and the surviving temple was built between the twelfth month of 1851 and the sixth month of 1854. The year-long major repair of 2024-2025 was the first in more than 170 years since the rebuilding.

Layout: the surviving temple covers 7,552 square metres with about 4,000 square metres of buildings; along the axis from south to north are the outer forecourt, Lingxing Gate, the half-moon pool, Dacheng Gate, the moon terrace and the Hall of Great Achievement, flanked by galleries, official halls and shrines to local worthies; the hall's floor area ranks among the largest of its kind in China, and inside stand bluestone seated figures of Confucius and his four attendants with the seventy-two disciples.

name: Dacheng Hall, Tainan Confucian Temple
yearNote: 1665 marks the founding of the temple and school, and the Dacheng Hall was enlarged in 1712; the surviving hall was dismantled, restored and rebuilt in 1917, and the timeline is placed by the most recent large-scale restoration of the present main structure.
lede: Dacheng Hall at Tainan’s Confucius Temple presents a solemn frontage with a broad roof and double eaves. The terrace, low enclosure walls and axial steps organize the ceremonial space before it. Founded in the Ming-Zheng period, the temple gained important forms through Qing reconstruction, while major repairs under Japanese rule shaped its current appearance. Education and ritual meet here: rooftop Tongtian vessels and continuing ceremonies keep cultural traditions visible in architecture and practice.
facts: The roof accounts for roughly half the hall’s total height. Double eaves and a rounded ridge emphasize its central status; an axial stair and terrace organize ceremony, with Tongtian vessels decorating the ridge.

The temple dates to 1665, while reconstruction of Dacheng Hall in 1712 established its double-eaved roof. Major repairs followed under Japanese rule, so the Ming-Zheng foundation date cannot date all present building materials.

The hall is used for rites honouring Confucius. The terrace axis and side passages express ritual hierarchy; the temple’s union of schooling and worship, and continuing ceremonies, sustain links with local educational life.

name: Five-Door Hall, Lukang Longshan Temple
yearNote: The temple moved to its present site in 1786, and the 1831 renovation established its scale; the plate shows the present state of the Five-Door Hall after component replacements in the 1960s and later restoration, and does not date every column and beam to the Qing.
lede: The Five-Gate Hall at Lukang Longshan Temple faces an inner court, its entrances, dragon columns and layered eaves forming the temple’s inward threshold. Connected to a theatre, it serves circulation, worship and performances offered to the gods. The temple moved here under Qianlong, and Daoguang-period rebuilding established its present arrangement. Earthquake repairs and replaced components followed. Stone carvings and timber work show how Quanzhou immigrant beliefs became part of Lukang’s architectural traditions.
facts: The hall and theatre stand between the entrance gate and main hall. An extra front eave added to the double-eaved hip-and-gable roof creates three tiers; openings, dragon columns and side carvings organize the frontage.

The temple moved to this site in 1786, and rebuilding in 1831 established its main arrangement. Twentieth-century painting and replacement of columns and beams in the Five-Gate Hall mean its materials have not remained entirely unchanged since the Qing.

Paired dragon columns and dragon-and-tiger stone reliefs display refined carving. Quanzhou immigrants and Lukang merchants supported the temple; the shared passage and ritual theatre connect religious life, commercial communities and craftsmanship.

name: North Gate of Taipei Prefectural City
era: Completed in the 10th year of Guangxu (1884)
lede: Taipei’s North Gate, also called Cheng’en Gate, has thick brick walls above a stone base. A single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and swallowtail ridge add lighter lines to its fortified body. Part of Taipei’s late-Qing city defences, it once connected the enclosed city with Dadaocheng. The walls and outer enclosure were later removed, leaving the gate among modern streets. Its closed form and former traffic role reveal both late-Qing defence and urban transformation.
facts: The enclosed gate combines stone blocks and brick, with two layers of walls inside and a traditional timber roof frame above. A single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and upturned swallowtail ridge contrast with the massive walls and stone arch.
Construction of Taipei’s city defences began in 1882 and finished in 1884. The North Gate’s inscription dates to 1882: gates preceded the walls, and 1884 marks completion of the city-defence project.

The gate once carried traffic toward Dadaocheng, while its enclosed structure answered the demands of firearm defence. Retaining its earlier outward form after the walls disappeared, it offers material evidence of Taipei’s growth.

name: Leshan Giant Buddha
yearNote: The timeline is placed by 803, the year the Buddha statue was completed. The plate covers the surviving head down to the chest and abdomen and does not represent the complete 71-meter seated figure.
lede: The head is 14.7 m high, the ears 7 m long, and 1,021 spiral curls are set in 18 rows, with a transverse drainage channel hidden in the 4th, 9th and 18th rows and a pair of connected tunnels cut behind the ears: the Tang builders put the drainage inside the Buddha's head, and so this 71 m seated Maitreya has held to its cliff for twelve centuries. The monk Haitong vowed to carve it in 713 (Kaiyuan 1); the work passed through Zhangqiu Jianqiong and was completed under Wei Gao in 803 (Zhenyuan 19), about ninety years in all. The plate takes the surviving head and torso down to the belly and does not draw the legs or the base.
facts: Form: a Maitreya seated with feet down, hands on knees, cut into the cliff of Lingyun Hill in an open-topped niche, 71 m high in all; the head is 10 m wide and 14.7 m high, the ears 7 m long, the nose 5.6 m, eyes and mouth 3.3 m each, the shoulders 24 m across; the 1,021 spiral curls on the head form 18 rows. The right ear and the nose are later repairs in timber coated with plaster, not original stone.

Dating: Haitong began carving in 713 (Kaiyuan 1) and work stopped at his death; in 739 (Kaiyuan 27) Zhangqiu Jianqiong, military governor of Jiannan, gave his salary to resume it, and it halted again in 746 at the knees; in 785 (Zhenyuan 1) Wei Gao gave his salary for a third campaign, finished in 803 (Zhenyuan 19), and Wei Gao's 'Record of the Great Maitreya Stone Image of Lingyun Temple, Jiazhou' was cut on the cliff to the right of the niche.

Significance: when finished the figure was painted and gilded and sheltered by a timber pavilion, already ruined by the early Northern Song; the pavilion was rebuilt under Renzong and later lost for good. In 1925 a red-sandstone mask was put over the face and removed in the 1930s. Around the Buddha some 206 niches with about 452 figures survive. Listed as a Major National Historical and Cultural Site in 1982 and, with Mount Emei, as a mixed cultural and natural World Heritage site in 1996.

Begun 713 · Completed 803

name: Bao'en Temple, Pingwu
yearNote: Work on the temple began in 1439, its main buildings had taken shape by 1446, and the whole was completed in 1460. The Mahavira Hall is placed at about 1450 within this construction period; no unconfirmed completion date is given for the single hall.
lede: Deep in the mountains of north-west Sichuan, a monastery built by the local chieftain Wang Xi and his son uses glazed-tile roofs, nanmu timber throughout and more than two thousand bracket sets, official northern practice at every turn, which has earned it the name 'Forbidden City of the deep hills'. The Mahavira Hall is the main hall of the monastery, roofed in green glazed tile, with three gilded seated Buddhas inside and Ming murals on all four walls. Work began in 1440 (Zhengtong 5), the main halls were finished by 1446 (Zhengtong 11), and the sculpture and murals were completed in 1460 (Tianshun 4). The plate shows the front of the Mahavira Hall only, without the gate or side halls.
facts: Form: the Mahavira Hall is the principal hall, roofed in green glazed tile, its ceiling painted, with three gilded seated Buddhas at the front and Ming murals on the walls; every timber member in the monastery is nanmu, and the buildings use more than two thousand bracket sets of some forty types (counts range from 36 to 48), hence the name 'museum of dougong'.

Dating: begun in 1440 (Zhengtong 5) by Wang Xi, native chieftain of Pingwu, and his son; the main halls were finished by 1446 (Zhengtong 11) and the sculpture, murals and other ornament by 1460 (Tianshun 4); the great bell in the hall was also cast in 1446. The monastery faces east, 278 m from east to west and 100 m from north to south, with a built area of 3,518 square metres.

Significance: glazed roofs and dragon ornament throughout the halls belong to the official architecture of Ming north China and are rare in the hills of north-west Sichuan; the name 'Bao'en', repaying a debt of gratitude, was chosen to thank the court for permitting the building. The monastery also holds a nanmu Thousand-armed Guanyin and a revolving sutra cabinet, neither shown in the plate. Listed as a Major National Historical and Cultural Site in 1996.
