name: Wuliang Pagoda
yearNote: The State Council's sixth-batch list dates it to the Song. The timeline position of about 1000 is for placement within the dynasty and is not a confirmed completion year; the traditional attribution to the Jianlong reign is not presented as a proven exact date.
lede: A plaque set into the tenth storey on the east face reads 'Pagoda of Ten Thousand Years of Jianlong', and for a long time the tower was taken to be a work of the Jianlong era of the Northern Song (960–963); yet its square plan and massive brackets look like a Tang pagoda, and recently some have pushed it, on the evidence of its imitation timber details, to the Jiading era of the Southern Song. Whichever view holds, it is one of the earliest Song pagodas in Sichuan. A square thirteen-storey brick pagoda of pavilion type, 39.56 m high, its walls carry columns, beams and bracket sets built in brick, and the first storey even has a flat plate-beam with camel-hump blocks. The plate follows the White Pagoda as it stands.
facts: Form: a square thirteen-storey brick pagoda imitating a timber pavilion, 39.56 m high, on a dressed-stone platform that was originally a Sumeru pedestal carved with dragon scales; each face is built with four columns and three bays, and the whole has 93 small niches, 10 doors and 9 windows. The brackets are four-step sets with a single arm or a single ang; the architraves of the lower three storeys are shaped like round timbers, only the first storey has a plate-beam with camel-hump blocks, and the finial is a cast-iron millstone shape.

Dating: the pagoda bears no construction date. A plaque on the east face of the tenth storey reads 'Pagoda of Ten Thousand Years of Jianlong', on which the New Gazetteer of Nanchong County dated it to the Jianlong era of the Northern Song; other views place it in the late Tang or Five Dynasties, or around the Southern Song Jiading era, and when listed as a Major National Historical and Cultural Site in 2006 it was dated Song. The base was repaired in 1641 (Chongzhen 14), and the platform and cracks in the body were repaired in 1981 and 1995.

Significance: the lower four storeys have a solid central pillar with brick stairs winding up around it, and from the fifth storey up the levels are joined by corbelling; it is a case study in the transition from Tang to Song pagodas and has been called 'the first Song pagoda of Sichuan'. The body is plastered greyish-white throughout, hence the name White Pagoda, while the imitation timber members are painted ochre; the plate follows the present colouring and does not reconstruct historical colours.

name: Zhang Huanhou Shrine
yearNote: Diwan Tower belongs to the surviving Ming–Qing shrine complex; about 1600 is only a timeline placement, does not assert that all components were built in the same year, and is certainly not based on the year of Zhang Fei's death.
lede: The most striking thing in the shrine is not the main hall but the Diwan Lou behind the gate, a tower more than ten metres high: double eaves on a hip-and-gable roof, and beneath them every bracket set thrusts out a slanting ang at forty-five degrees, like a rack of halberds. The name takes up Zhang Fei's fame as 'a match for ten thousand', and the board reads 'Not ten thousand men could withstand him'. Zhang Fei died at Langzhong in 221 (Zhangwu 1) and was buried here, and the townspeople raised a temple before the tomb; the present buildings are the result of repeated loss and rebuilding in the Ming and Qing, and the Diwan Lou dates from the Ming. The plate takes the Diwan Lou and its attached front eaves only, without the main hall, tomb pavilion or tomb.
facts: Form: the Diwan Lou is over ten metres high with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof, a pavilion storey above and a broad front eave below, and every bracket set under the eaves projects a slanting ang at 45 degrees. It is the second building on the shrine's axis, with the gate before it and the paired gateways and main hall behind; the red columns and the doors and windows between them in the plate are its lower front eave.

Dating: the shrine takes its name from Zhang Fei's posthumous title Marquis Huan; he was killed by his own officers in 221 (Zhangwu 1) and buried at Langzhong, and a temple has stood over the tomb for more than seventeen hundred years. The present complex of several courtyards is Ming and Qing rebuilding, with the Diwan Lou a surviving Ming structure. Listed as a Sichuan provincial protected site in 1991 and a Major National Historical and Cultural Site in 1996.

Significance: the shrine covers more than 6,600 square metres with over 2,400 square metres of buildings; along the axis stand the gate, the Diwan Lou, the gateways, the main hall, the rear hall, the tomb pavilion and Zhang Fei's tomb, whose mound is 8 m high, 25 m east to west and 42 m north to south. Langzhong is counted among the four great ancient cities of China, and this shrine is an important Three Kingdoms site within its walls.

name: Luodai Guild Halls
era: First built in the Qing · Rebuilt 1913
yearNote: Yuwang Palace was first built in the Qianlong period of the Qing and rebuilt in 1913 after a fire in 1912. The timeline uses the rebuilding year of the surviving main structure and does not follow the parent unit's "Qing" label to mark the present gate tower as original Qianlong work.
lede: Three arched doorways side by side, the middle one tallest, and above them the rolling, upturned outline of fire-walls topped with moulded clouds and dragons: this is the gate of the Huguang Guild Hall at Luodai. The hall is dedicated to Yu the Great and so is also called the Yuwang Gong, the place where Qing-era migrants of the 'Huguang fills Sichuan' movement met, worshipped and watched opera in the eastern hills of Chengdu. Built in 1746 (Qianlong 11), rebuilt in 1860 (Xianfeng 10), burnt in 1912 and rebuilt the next year, so that the gate seen today dates from 1913. With the neighbouring Guangdong, Jiangxi and Chuanbei halls it forms the group known as the Luodai Guild Halls. The plate shows the gate only.
facts: Form: a gate of pailou type with three arched openings, the central bay higher than the flanking ones, finished above with undulating fire-walls crested with moulded clouds and dragons. Inside lie the stage, courtyard and main hall, the central court framed in nanmu timber; the courtyard has no drains yet is said never to flood, which local tradition credits to the protection of King Yu.

Dating: the Huguang Guild Hall was built by subscription among migrants from Huguang in 1746 (Qianlong 11) and rebuilt in 1860 (Xianfeng 10); it burned in 1912 and was rebuilt in 1913, and the present gate belongs to that rebuilding. Listed as a Sichuan provincial protected site in 2002 and in 2006, together with the Guangdong, Jiangxi and Chuanbei halls under the name 'Luodai Guild Halls', as a Major National Historical and Cultural Site.

Significance: more than eighty per cent of Luodai's people are of Hakka descent, and four guild halls, Guangdong, Jiangxi, Huguang and Chuanbei, stand in one town, which has been called 'the home of guild halls', a material record of Qing migrant society in Sichuan. The Chuanbei hall originally stood at Wolong Bridge in Chengdu and was moved here in 1998. The plate omits the street shops and modern signs.

name: Que of Lord Shen
era: Eastern Han stone que · Approximate date
yearNote: The que is an Eastern Han relic; about 150 is a placement within the dynasty on the timeline, not a precise construction date from an inscription. The plate shows only one surviving main que and does not add the lost subsidiary que.
lede: Of the seven Han que in Quxian only the Shen Fujun que survives as a pair, facing each other east and west some twenty-one metres apart, each 4.84 m high. Down the middle of each shaft runs a single line of clerical script: on the eastern que 'Spirit road of Lord Shen, Internuncio, Commandant of the Northern Camp, Marquis of the Left', on the western 'Spirit road of Lord Shen, Magistrate of Xinfeng, Commandant of Jiaozhi', in a free, flowing hand that keeps to no ruled line, a style of its own among Han clerical inscriptions. A red bird is carved in relief at the top of the shaft and a taotie mask below; on the inner faces the eastern que bears a green dragon and the western a white tiger. It dates from about the Yanguang era of the Eastern Han (122–125). The plate shows one of the two main pillars only; the attached child-pillars are lost.
facts: Form: a mother-and-child que in sandstone imitating timber construction; the two main pillars are each 4.84 m high, the shaft 1.10 m wide and 0.76 m thick, built up in four parts, base, shaft, storey and cap, with the shaft battered inward. Among the brackets of the storey appears a huagong, the only one on any Sichuan que. The outer faces of both pillars are rough and undecorated, proof that child-pillars once stood against them; they no longer survive.

Dating: the shafts carry no date. In form they resemble the Feng Huan que built around 121 (Jianguang 1) but are slightly later, and are generally placed in the Yanguang era of Emperor An of the Eastern Han (122–125); nothing is known of the Shen family who owned them. In 1849 (Daoguang 29) the magistrate Wang Chunyuan set up a 'Record of the Stele Pavilion of Lord Shen's Spirit Road' behind the western que. Listed in 1961 among the first Major National Historical and Cultural Sites.

Significance: the shafts are carved in relief with a red bird, taotie, green dragon, white tiger, door-ring masks and strongmen, and with stories such as riding a deer, playing with a tiger, Dong Yong serving his father and Yang Youji shooting the ape; the jade disc and white tiger on the inner faces are especially fine. The six sites and seven pillars of Quxian make up nearly a quarter of all surviving Han que in China, and since 2019 each has stood under a steel-and-glass shelter, which the plate omits.

name: Shibaozhai
era: Founded in the Ming · Enlarged in the Qing
yearNote: Founded in the Wanli reign of the Ming and enlarged several times from the Kangxi to the Tongzhi reigns of the Qing; about 1800 places the surviving tower within the dynasty. Sources differ on when the top three stories took shape, and the whole present tower is not dated to 1956.
lede: Red timber storeys climb the steep Yuyin cliff, narrowing beneath successive eaves and joining a three-storey Kuixing Pavilion to form Shibaozhai’s twelve-level silhouette. The building relies on the mountain, while stairs connect foot and summit. Ming and Qing projects shaped it over time; early photographs already show the upper pavilion, so its full height cannot be assigned a casual modern enlargement date.
facts: The lower nine storeys recede against the cliff and meet the upper three-storey Kuixing Pavilion. Mortise-and-tenon timber framing includes posts inserted into rock. Round and rectangular windows alternate, while building and mountain cooperate structurally.

Shibaozhai originated in the Ming Wanli period and was expanded repeatedly from Kangxi to Tongzhi; different phases shaped its present form. Accounts differ over the upper three storeys, but a 1909 archival photograph already shows them. The entire building cannot be dated to 1956.

The tower also serves as a route uphill, approaching the summit along the sheer cliff. Its adaptation of timber construction to terrain distinguishes it from a freestanding pagoda: the mountain is essential to its stability and spaces.

name: Huguang Guild Hall, Chongqing
era: Qing guild hall · Enlarged in the Daoguang reign
yearNote: The guild hall complex took shape in the Qing and was enlarged in the Daoguang reign; about 1846 places the surviving Qing structure, and the plate shows the opera stage as repaired in 2003–2005, without asserting that every beam and column is original 1846 work.
lede: Carved balustrades front a raised stage, while columns and beams frame its open performance area and bring narrative carvings into spectators’ view. The theatre at Chongqing’s Huguang Guildhall belongs to a migrant communal setting where worship, deliberation and entertainment shared courtyard spaces. Qing expansions and modern conservation shaped the buildings; this single theatre front does not date every associated guildhall together.
facts: A raised stage, columns and carved rails organise the façade, with timber carvings beneath the eaves. Facing a courtyard and related to viewing halls and galleries, it forms one theatre within the guildhall complex.

The complex developed throughout the Qing period, with substantial Daoguang-period work; individual associations have different histories. Modern conservation also shaped its present condition. A building’s formation period does not date every surviving beam or column.

Migrant associations established shared places for worship, discussion and social contact away from home. The theatre added public performance to these activities, while carved stories and viewing spaces preserve aspects of migrant life in Chongqing.

name: Diaoyu Fortress Site
era: Fortifications expanded 1243 · Gate tower built later
yearNote: 1243 is a key milestone in the building of the Southern Song defensive system at Diaoyu Fortress, and the timeline is placed by the site. The upper timber gate tower of Huguo Gate was built later, and not all the structure in the photographs is taken as original Song work.
lede: A stone arch pierces a heavy wall, reached by stairs turning beside the cliff. Huguo Gate shows how Diaoyucheng’s defence used terrain directly. A later timber gatehouse stands above it, so the present structure is not entirely original Song work. An important construction phase took place in 1243, while the gateway reveals how wall, cliff and access route cooperate.
facts: The masonry arch forms part of the wall, with stairs climbing beside the cliff and terrain constraining the entrance. A later timber gatehouse adds a different historical layer above the heavy stone structure.

1243 marks a major phase in Southern Song defensive construction, followed by further extensions and repairs. It dates the site’s history, not every surviving component of this gate, especially its later timber gatehouse.

The fortress joins natural mountain obstacles to walls, organising limited access routes for defence. Huguo Gate makes that visible. Residential and administrative remains also show that resistance depended on sustained habitation and supplies.

name: Cliff Carvings of the Great Buddha Temple, Tongnan
era: Head carved in the Tang · Whole statue completed 1151
yearNote: The Buddha's head was carved in the Tang and the body continued in the Northern Song, with the whole statue completed in 1151; the surviving gold leaf includes the results of conservation and restoration in the 2010s, and the timeline is not placed by the temple's founding year.
lede: Dark curls frame a golden face, with robe folds spreading over the broad body. Tongnan’s giant Buddha combines rock carving with gilded surfaces. Its head was carved first and its body later, across Tang and Song; the gold also includes later renewals and modern conservation. Reading face, gestures and drapery requires distinguishing the image from its changing surface decoration.
facts: The image uses the cliff as its core, with curls and a high cranial protuberance framing the face and robes covering the body. Its right palm faces upwards before the abdomen and its left hand rests on the knee. Gold contrasts with dark hair; the sculpted mass remains connected to the cliff behind.

The head was begun in the Tang period and the body continued in Northern Song, with the whole image completed in 1151 and subsequently gilded. Completion of the image and the temple’s foundation have distinct dates. Its hair and gold include later conservation.

Restoration research distinguishes rock, modelled hair repairs, lacquer and gold leaf as separate materials requiring care. Their layers form the present image, documenting both Tang–Song sculptural continuity and the evolving gilding tradition.

name: Zishou Temple, Lingshi
sub: Front of the Hall of Heavenly Kings
yearNote: 1500 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted front of the Hall of Heavenly Kings on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
lede: The front of the Heavenly Kings Hall of Zishou Temple is not a row of lattice doors but a solid wall of grey brick with a single doorway in the middle, over which hangs the plaque 'Secluded Delight of Hills and Woods'; the grey-tiled roof is edged in blue-green glaze and the main ridge is crowded with glazed pavilions and beasts. The temple is at Suxi village in Jingsheng town, Lingshi; steles record its founding in 870 (11th year of Xiantong, Tang), destruction by fire at the end of the Jin, rebuilding in 1467 (3rd year of Chenghua, Ming), large-scale repair in 1521 (16th year of Zhengde) and its present extent by 1622 (2nd year of Tianqi), the surviving halls all being Ming. The plate shows the front of the Heavenly Kings Hall.
facts: Heavenly Kings Hall: as drawn, a single-eaved hall whose front is a brick wall without lattice doors, with one central door, a pair of stone lions before it, bracket sets under the eaves, a grey-tile roof with glazed edging and a glazed main ridge; bell and drum towers stand to either side, and inside, along both sides, four Heavenly Kings about 3 m tall.

Dating: founded in 870 (11th year of Xiantong, Tang), burned at the end of the Jin, repaired in the Yuan, rebuilt in 1467 (3rd year of Chenghua, Ming), repaired in 1521 (16th year of Zhengde) and brought to its present form in 1622 (2nd year of Tianqi); about 17,000 square metres in two courts, front and rear. Listed as a national key protected site in 2001.

Loss: the temple is known for its Ming painted sculpture and murals, with 248.34 square metres of murals and over a hundred statues; in 1993 the heads of its eighteen arhats were cut off, stolen and sold abroad, later bought back and returned by the Taiwanese businessman Chen Yongtai, one of the cases of lost Shanxi relics coming home.

name: Ruicheng City God Temple
sub: Gable side of the main hall
era: Original Song structure · Repaired over the centuries
yearLabel: Original Song structure · Repaired over the centuries
yearNote: 1100 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted gable side of the main hall on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
lede: The earliest surviving City God temple in Shanxi. Its main hall is a Song structure under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, with five-puzuo bracket sets and two downward cantilevers of split-bamboo profile on the front column heads; seen from the gable end, a Ming glazed panel of 'two dragons playing with a pearl' is set in the gable, the owl-tail finials and ridge ornaments are glazed too, while below is plain red wall. Known locally as the 'South Temple', it was founded according to the Republican-era Ruicheng County Gazetteer in the Dazhong Xiangfu reign of the Northern Song (1008-1016) and repaired under the Yuan, Ming and Qing; on the axis the offering pavilion is Yuan and the offering hall and rear hall Qing, so four dynasties of carpentry stand in one court. The plate shows the gable end of the main hall.
facts: Main hall: five bays wide and three deep under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the front column-head bracket sets are five-puzuo with two downward cantilevers of split-bamboo profile and grasshopper-head beam ends; the gable carries a Ming glazed panel of two dragons playing with a pearl, the glazed owl-tails and ridge ornaments are bright in colour, and the red wall sits on a grey-brick dado.

Dating: according to the Republican-era Ruicheng County Gazetteer the temple was founded in the Dazhong Xiangfu reign of the Northern Song (1008-1016) and repaired in the Yuan, Ming and Qing; the main hall is original Song work, the offering pavilion Yuan, the offering hall and rear hall Qing, and the gate, stage and bell and drum towers recent rebuildings. Listed as a national key protected site in 2001.

Steles: the stele gallery displays 98 steles and image steles from the Northern Wei to the Ming and Qing, among them the Preface to the Jingyuan Daoist Hall of Mount Zhongtiao of 798 (14th year of Zhenyuan, Tang), composed by Wang Yan, prefect of Guozhou, and written by Yuan Zi; the offering pavilion, a four-rafter hall with two columns spanning the full depth, has massive architraves and leaning corner columns, typical of Yuan work, and is not in the plate.

name: Qiao Family Compound
sub: Inner tower and flanking side rooms of the Zaizhong Hall courtyard
yearNote: 1800 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted inner tower and flanking side rooms of the Zaizhong Hall courtyard on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
lede: The proper name of the Qiao Family Compound is Zaizhongtang, the residence of the Shanxi merchant Qiao Zhiyong. An eighty-metre stone walk divides six large courts into a northern and a southern row, and seen from above the whole house forms the character for double happiness; each court is a long narrow one like this, wing rooms on both sides closing in the yard and a two-storey main house at the far end. Building began in 1755 (20th year of Qianlong, Qing), with enlargements in the Tongzhi and Guangxu reigns, and the present extent was reached only in the early Republic, so any single court can be dated only approximately. The plate shows the end house and the flanking wing rooms of one court of Zaizhongtang.
facts: Courts: Zaizhongtang covers 10,642 square metres with six large courts, twenty small ones and 313 rooms; the main gate faces east, an arched gateway with a tower above. As drawn, the two sides are single-storey wing rooms and the end house is two storeys with an upper gallery, grey brick walls, lattice doors and brick carving and painting under the eaves stacked tier on tier.

Dating: begun in 1755 (20th year of Qianlong, Qing), enlarged in the Tongzhi and Guangxu reigns and completed in the early Republic; the courts were built in stages and no single court has a firm completion date. Listed as a national key protected site in 2001; made the Qixian Folk Museum in 1985 and opened the next year.

Family: the Qiaos rose from Qiao Guifa, who 'went west beyond the pass' to Baotou in the early Qianlong years and founded the Fushenggong firm, giving rise to the saying 'first Fushenggong, then Baotou city'; under Qiao Zhiyong the firm's branches spread far and wide. The Dexingtang, Ningshoutang, Baoyuantang and garden are recent reconstructions on their old sites and are not in the plate.

name: Wang Family Compound
sub: Courtyard walls and roofs of Hongmen Fort (detail)
yearNote: 1750 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted courtyard walls and roofs of Hongmen Fort on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
lede: The Hongmen Fort of the Wang Family Compound is a fort in earnest: a wall eight metres high and two thick encloses a circuit of over six hundred metres, inside which eighty-eight courtyards climb the slope in four tiers with a single main street running up the middle, so that the plan resembles the character wang. Seen from above, grey-tiled roofs, brick courtyard walls, openwork screen walls and one small gatehouse after another pile up in layers, and that is the corner the plate takes. Hongmen Fort, also called Hengzhen Fort, was built in the Qianlong reign of the Qing and housed eight generations of the Jingsheng Wangs, from the fourteenth to the twenty-first; the compound as a whole went up over nearly ninety years from the Kangxi to the Jiaqing reigns.
facts: Fort: Hongmen Fort, or Hengzhen Fort, is the west compound of the Wang Family Compound, laid out on the hillside in four tiers of courtyards from low to high, symmetrical left and right, with 88 courtyards and 776 rooms in all; the wall is 8 m high, 2 m wide and over 600 m round, and the south gate bears the stone plaque 'Hengzhen'. The plate shows the layering of roofs, screen walls and courtyard gates inside the fort.

Dating: Hongmen Fort was built in the Qianlong reign of the Qing, and Gaojiaya to its east in the Jiaqing reign by the brothers Wang Rucong and Wang Rucheng of the seventeenth generation; the compound was built mainly over nearly 90 years from Kangxi to Jiaqing, with 123 courtyards and 1,118 rooms. Listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Family: the Jingsheng Wangs moved here as farmers in 1313 (2nd year of Huangqing, Yuan), took to trade in the Ming, grew rich on salt and tea in the Qing, and declined after the fall of Yangzhou in 1853 (3rd year of Xianfeng). The total area is given as 150,000 or 250,000 square metres, making it one of the largest Qing residential complexes in Shanxi.

name: Dai County Confucian Temple
sub: Front and platform of the Dacheng Hall
era: Ming–Qing buildings · Repaired over the centuries
yearLabel: Ming–Qing buildings · Repaired over the centuries
yearNote: 1500 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted front and platform of the Dacheng Hall on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
lede: The largest surviving prefectural Confucian temple in north China. The Dacheng Hall is seven bays wide and ten rafters deep under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof entirely covered in peacock-blue glazed tile, with nine-step bracket sets of one upward and three downward cantilevers under the eaves and a row of front lattice doors in twelve different patterns; it stands on a white-marble platform with stone balustrades on three sides and a carved dragon ramp in the centre. The temple is said to have been founded in the Tang; it was rebuilt from 1367 (27th year of Zhizheng, Yuan) and completed in 1369 (2nd year of Hongwu, Ming), enlarged in the Chenghua and Jiajing reigns and repeatedly repaired in the Qing, the surviving fabric being mainly Ming. The plate shows the front of the Dacheng Hall and its terrace, with the steles in the foreground omitted.
facts: Dacheng Hall: seven bays wide (five according to the Daixian county government page), ten rafters deep, single-eaved hip-and-gable roof in peacock-blue glazed tile; nine-step bracket sets with one upward and three downward cantilevers under the eaves; front lattice doors in twelve patterns; inside, a caisson ceiling converging on an eight-trigram apex, square, octagonal and round tiers carried on four layers of brackets.

Dating: traditionally founded in the Tang, destroyed by war at the end of the Yuan, rebuilt from 1367 (27th year of Zhizheng) and completed in 1369 (2nd year of Hongwu, Ming), enlarged in the Chenghua and Jiajing reigns and repeatedly repaired in the Qing; it survived after 1949 by serving as a granary. The National Cultural Heritage Administration registers it as Ming to Qing; listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Layout: about 14,400 square metres in four courts, the axis running Wanren archway, Lingxing gate, Pan pool, Ji gate, Dacheng Hall and Jingyi pavilion, with the shrines of worthy officials and local worthies east and west of the pool; the Lingxing gate has six columns and five roofs, its side roofs set with glazed coiled-dragon roundels. The plate takes only the Dacheng Hall.

name: Ciyun Temple, Tianzhen
yearNote: 1450 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted front of the Mahavira Hall on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
lede: The Mahavira Hall of Ciyun Temple is only three bays square under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, its bracket sets stepping out tier on tier beneath the eaves, and inside it keeps over fifty square metres of Ming murals: the twelve bodhisattvas of complete enlightenment on the main wall, the twenty-four devas and the eight classes of beings on the sides. The temple stands on West Street in the county town of Tianzhen; originally Fahua Temple, it was founded in the Tang according to the Guangxu-era Tianzhen County Gazetteer, repaired in 1019 (8th year of Kaitai, Liao) and again from 1428 to 1430 (3rd to 5th years of Xuande, Ming), when the chiliarch Xiong Liang petitioned for the name Ciyun Temple, 'the great monastery north of the pass'; today's layout is that left by the Xuande repair. The plate shows the front of the Mahavira Hall and the steps before it.
facts: Mahavira Hall: also called the Sakyamuni Hall, three bays wide and deep under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, standing on a high platform reached by a central stone stair, with dense bracket sets under the eaves as drawn; inside are over 50 square metres of Ming murals and a seated Sakyamuni flanked by the Medicine Buddha and Amitabha.

Dating: the Guangxu-era Tianzhen County Gazetteer records that the temple was 'built in the Tang, originally named Fahua', repaired in 1019 (8th year of Kaitai, Liao), rebuilt from 1428 to 1430 (3rd to 5th years of Xuande, Ming) and granted the name Ciyun Temple, with further repairs in 1539 (18th year of Jiajing, Ming) and 1761 (26th year of Qianlong, Qing). Listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Bell and drum towers: the bell and drum towers before the Heavenly Kings Hall are octagonal in plan with round domed roofs, a brick chamber ringed by eight columns below and an open railed storey above, a form found nowhere else among Yuan and Ming bell and drum towers in Shanxi; the bell tower hangs an iron bell of 1432 (7th year of Xuande, Ming). The temple has 31 surviving buildings on about 1.6 hectares.

name: Wuyue Temple, Jiexiu
yearNote: 1750 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted front of the opera stage on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
lede: The Wuyue Temple of Jiexiu merges gate, stage and bell and drum towers into one building, known locally as the Haishen Lou, the 'mirage tower'. On the courtyard side the upper storey is five bays wide, the central bay pushed forward as the stage front under a small hip-and-gable roof, with the gables of the two wings turned to face front; below are five brick arches, the middle one the passage into the temple. The roofs are of peacock-blue glaze; Jiexiu calls itself the home of glazed tile, and the colour here is among the purest. The temple was founded in 1456 (7th year of Jingtai, Ming), destroyed in 1750 (15th year of Qianlong, Qing) and rebuilt in 1763 (28th year of Qianlong), so the surviving buildings are Qing. The plate shows the courtyard front of the stage.
facts: Stage: built on a high platform, five bays wide, the central bay projecting one bay northward, with elaborate bracket sets under the eaves; the upper stage front has a wooden railing and the gables of both wings face forward, while below a central passage is flanked by four arched openings; gate, stage and bell and drum towers form one body, called the Haishen Lou.

Dating: according to temple steles, founded in 1456 (7th year of Jingtai, Ming), destroyed in 1750 (15th year of Qianlong, Qing), rebuilt in 1763 (28th year of Qianlong) and repaired in 2001; the National Cultural Heritage Administration registers it as Qing, and it was listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Glaze: the peacock-blue glazed roof ornaments are pure in colour and fine in form, and the Jiexiu cultural heritage bureau calls them another treasure of the 'home of glazed tile'; the temple faces south in two courts on 4,149 square metres, with 13 surviving buildings including screen wall, offering pavilion, main hall and rear hall, the main hall five bays under a flush-gable roof.

name: Pingyao City God Temple
sub: South face of the Zhaoge Lou stage tower
yearNote: 1750 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted front of the front hall on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
lede: To enter the Pingyao City God Temple one first passes through a low gateway beneath a tower; over the passage hang the two characters 'Dare you enter', the 'enter' written like a knife. The tower is the stage, the Zhaoge Lou, double-eaved hip-and-gable and three bays wide; on its south face a hip-and-gable baosha projects above the passage, thick with bracket sets, and the bell and drum towers join it on either side. The temple's founding date is unknown; it was repaired after a fire in 1554 (33rd year of Jiajing, Ming), another fire in 1859 (9th year of Xianfeng, Qing) left only the rear hall, and most of the surviving buildings date from the rebuilding of 1864-1869 (3rd to 8th years of Tongzhi). The plate shows the south face of this tower and the passage.
facts: Stage: two storeys under a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof, three bays wide, glazed tile; the south plaque reads 'Dare you enter' and the north 'Zhaoge Lou', and the passage beneath leads into the front court; ten earthenware jars are buried under the stage floor to resonate with the ceiling. The bell and drum towers join it east and west; the plate shows the south face and the baosha.

Dating: founding date unknown; repaired after the fire of 1554 (33rd year of Jiajing, Ming), reduced to the rear hall by the fire of 1859 (9th year of Xianfeng, Qing), rebuilt from 1864 to 1869 (3rd to 8th years of Tongzhi), the Procession of the City God painted in the main hall in 1868 (7th year of Tongzhi). Listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Layout: the temple and the Pingyao county yamen stand on opposite sides of South Street in east-west symmetry; three courts on 7,302 square metres, the axis running archway, gate, stage, offering hall, main hall and rear hall, with the Six Bureaus and the Earth God shrine on the sides and the Kitchen God and God of Wealth temples east and west of the rear court, 'all the gods dwelling in one temple'.

name: Former Site of Rishengchang
era: Former Qing draft bank · Surviving street frontage
yearLabel: Former Qing draft bank · Surviving street frontage
yearNote: 1823 is the commonly cited year the draft bank opened; the construction year of the surviving frontage itself is undetermined, and the timeline places it approximately by that period.
lede: This row of shopfronts on the south side of West Street in Pingyao was the head office of China's first draft bank. The front is a run of dark wooden plank doors with a line of small painted panels above the lintels and a grey-tiled pitched roof above that, as unassuming as any shop; behind it two parallel courts face north, with a floor area of over 1,700 square metres. Rishengchang was reorganised from the Xiyucheng dye shop; the customary date is 1823 (3rd year of Daoguang, Qing), though the steles allow the reorganisation to be placed only between 1819 and 1838, and no record gives the construction date of the shopfront itself. The plate shows the street front.
facts: Shopfront: the head office stands on the south side of West Street, facing north, with two courts side by side, on 2,324 square metres of land and over 1,700 square metres of floor area; as drawn the front is single-storey, a continuous row of plank doors with a line of small painted windows above and the plaque 'Rishengchang Ji' under the eaves.

Dating: Rishengchang was reorganised from the Xiyucheng dye shop of the Li family of Dapu, with the owner Li Daquan contributing 300,000 taels and Lei Lütai 20,000; a stele of 1819 (24th year of Jiaqing) still lists Xiyucheng and one of 1838 (18th year of Daoguang) no longer does, so the change fell between, conventionally in 1823 (3rd year of Daoguang). Listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Influence: Rishengchang pioneered remittance between cities, with branches in Hankou, Tianjin, Shanghai, Guangzhou and elsewhere, and by 1891 (17th year of Guangxu) remitted thirty million taels a year; it was sealed in 1914 over a guarantee case and closed in 1932. Pingyao thereby became the financial centre of all China in the nineteenth century, and was inscribed as a World Heritage site in 1997.

name: Pujiu Temple Pagoda
era: Rebuilt in the Jiajing reign (Ming) · Thirteen-story brick pagoda
yearLabel: Rebuilt in the Jiajing reign (Ming) · Thirteen-story brick pagoda
yearNote: The surviving pagoda was rebuilt after an earthquake in the Jiajing reign of the Ming; sources differ on the exact year of rebuilding, and the timeline uses an approximate value of around 1560.
lede: In the Romance of the Western Chamber the student Zhang 'climbed the pagoda and walked the whole cloister'; this is that pagoda. A square brick pagoda of thirteen storeys with close-set eaves, 39.5 m high and 8.3 m on a side, its eaves corbelled and its taper slight, it is close in form to the Great Wild Goose Pagoda of Xi'an. In 1555 (34th year of Jiajing, Ming) a great earthquake at Puzhou destroyed temple and pagoda alike; in 1564 (43rd year of Jiajing) the prefect Zhang Jiayin gave his salary to lead the rebuilding, and the pagoda rose six storeys higher than its Tang predecessor to thirteen, the present Yingying Pagoda. The other halls were later lost to fire and rebuilt from 1986 to 1990; the pagoda is the only Ming survivor. The plate shows the whole pagoda.
facts: Form: square in plan, a thirteen-storey brick pagoda with close-set eaves, 39.5 m high and 8.3 m on a side, with a door on the south; the first storey has no windows and a Buddha niche on the north wall, from the second to the ninth storey brick stairs spiral up inside the walls and each storey has window openings; the square cloister round it, eleven bays to a side, was rebuilt after 1986.

Dating: a Ming stele in the temple says Pujiu Temple was 'founded in the Sui and Tang', and an excavated sutra pillar is dated 872 (13th year of Xiantong, Tang); the pagoda fell in the earthquake of 1555 (34th year of Jiajing, Ming) and was rebuilt in 1564 (43rd year of Jiajing) by Zhang Jiayin, whose poem stele stands before it. The pagoda was listed as a provincial protected site in 1965 and a national key protected site in 2019.

Echo: strike a stone on the ground before the pagoda and it answers from within like a croaking frog, for which it is counted among China's four great echoing buildings; Ding Shizhang and others of Shanxi University found the cause in the eaves of each storey, unequal in length and concave, and the smooth surface of the body, which send sound waves back and forth around the pagoda into resonance.

name: Bailin Temple Pagoda
yearNote: 1330 corresponds to the construction of the surviving Yuan pagoda of Bailin Temple; the timeline is not placed by the temple's traditional founding date.
lede: Bailin Temple Pagoda rises from layered lotus petals into seven tapering eave tiers. Brick balustrades, platforms and brackets evoke timber, while an iron finial contrasts with stone and brick below. Built in the Yuan, the tower should not take its date from earlier temple traditions. Close study of the base and eave details reveals how a substantial mass gains a finely articulated scale.
facts: The octagonal seven-tier brick pagoda stands on stone steps, a brick Sumeru base, timber-like platform and layered lotus petals. Close upper eaves lead to an iron finial with bowl, lotus, rings and jewel forms.
The provincial authority records construction in September 1330. The Yuan tower and earlier temple traditions have distinct chronologies, which later repairs do not erase.

Timber-like platforms, brackets and rafters become masonry details, with lotus ornament placed beneath the tower. Their material and component junctions offer a close view of Yuan pagoda construction.

name: Zhengding Prefectural Confucian Temple
yearNote: The surviving Halberd Gate is a Yuan structure whose exact construction year is unknown; 1300 is only an approximate timeline placement. The Prefectural Confucian Temple was founded in the 3rd year of Xining in the Northern Song (1070), and the two are recorded separately.
lede: The five-bay Jimen Gate at Zhengding’s prefectural Confucian temple holds a ritual entrance beneath a low gable roof. Two bays of depth give it the scale of both gateway and hall. The temple originated in the Northern Song, but this timber building is Yuan. Its columns and eaves, rather than elaborate ornament, reveal the organisation of northern Yuan construction.
facts: The gate is five bays wide and two deep, with a single-eaved projecting gable roof in plain tiles. Internal central columns support the six-rafter arrangement; a broad front and shallow depth shape this gateway hall.
The temple was founded in 1070 and repaired and expanded under later dynasties. Jimen is separately identified as Yuan, with no exact building year; the Song foundation cannot date this frame.

Unlike a principal worship hall, the gate defines entry and movement between courts. Its Yuan column arrangement and frame show that ritual gateways are also valuable evidence for architectural history.

name: Lingyan Temple, Yuzhou
era: Rebuilt in the 6th year of Zhengtong (Ming)
yearNote: 1441, the 6th year of Zhengtong in the Ming, is the date of the temple's rebuilding, and the hall depicted is the surviving Ming main structure; the record of a Liao founding is not used as the date of the surviving hall.
lede: Lingyan Temple’s Mahavira Hall spreads through a gentle roof slope and deep eaves. A hipped roof unites four planes, while bracket groups connect timber columns to the roof. Rebuilt in the Ming Zhengtong era, it also preserves painted ceilings and a refined coffer. Structure and decoration together show how a local Ming temple developed while retaining earlier techniques.
facts: The hall is five bays wide and four deep, with a single-eaved hipped roof and double-arm brackets. A gentle slope and deep eaves explain its substantial but unsteep appearance.

The provincial authority records destruction at the end of the Yuan and rebuilding in 1441. The surviving hall is Ming; an unknown earlier foundation cannot date it, and subsequent repairs remain distinct.

Coffers and Ming painted ceilings preserve interior craftsmanship, while the neighbouring Heavenly Kings Hall retains earlier methods. Together they show continuity in local building practice rather than an abrupt stylistic replacement.

name: Zhenwu Temple, Yuzhou
era: Ming–Qing buildings · Exact date of the gate unknown
yearNote: The national protected site is dated to the Ming, and the temple was repaired in 1720; the exact construction year of the depicted gate is unknown, 1700 is only an approximate placement for the Ming–Qing buildings, and 1720 is not taken as the exact construction year of the gate.
lede: The gate and stone steps at Zhenwu Temple make entry part of the religious setting: visitors climb before passing into the court, separating worship space from the street. The gate’s exact date is unconfirmed within a Ming–Qing temple context. Ming heritage attribution and Kangxi-era repairs indicate several phases, while the changing level and enclosed court establish a clear boundary between everyday streets and ritual space.
facts: The entrance consists of a gate, stone steps and a passage into the court. The climb and narrowed opening change the pace of movement, separating the worship precinct from the surrounding streets.

The temple is registered as Ming and a repair is recorded in 1720. The individual gate’s date remains unknown; neither the complex attribution nor a temple-wide repair establishes its precise foundation year.
Halls and subsidiary rooms form an enclosed court. The gate and steps regulate movement from street to worship, showing how a local temple establishes a ritual boundary within limited space.

name: Dingzhou Confucian Temple
yearNote: The surviving main structure is registered under the national protected site's Qing dating, and 1750 is only an approximate Qing placement; neither the Tang founding nor the Song rebuilding date of the Confucian Temple is taken as the exact construction date of the hall in the photographs.
lede: Dacheng Hall at Dingzhou Confucian Temple organises the central worship court through a five-bay front and terrace, enclosed with side buildings. Although temple history reaches back to the Tang, the principal surviving fabric is Qing. The age of the ritual tradition is not the age of every column. The hall’s position explains how worship and education occupied connected but differentiated precincts.
facts: Dacheng Hall is five bays wide and three deep. Its front terrace connects to the courtyard route, while side buildings enclose the central court. The hall’s bays, terrace and flanking buildings establish a clear focus for Confucian worship.

The site became a Confucian temple in the Tang, expanded in the Song, burned in the late Ming and was rebuilt in the Qing. The hall’s precise year is unknown; early temple dates do not replace its Qing attribution.

The central route serves worship, the western route includes teaching spaces such as Minglun Hall, and eastern courts contain ancestral and Kuixing shrines. Reverence, education and scholarly aspiration share the complex.

name: Xumi Fushou Temple
sub: Golden roof of the Miaogao Zhuangyan Hall and upper Great Red Platform
yearNote: 1780 is the construction date of Xumi Fushou Temple and its main group of buildings; this plate shows only the golden roof of the Miaogao Zhuangyan Hall and the upper part of the Great Red Platform, not the lower base or the complete temple.
lede: Miaogao Zhuangyan Hall’s gilded roof emerges above the Great Red Terrace, contrasting Tibetan-style mass with Chinese eaves. Gilded copper tiles and dragons make it a visible worship centre. Built to receive the Sixth Panchen Lama using his Tibetan residence as a model, Xumi Fushou Temple joins court ceremony and Tibetan Buddhism. This view concerns only the roof and upper terrace, not the entire temple.
facts: Miaogao Zhuangyan Hall sits within the Great Red Terrace. Its pointed gilded-copper roof and ridge dragons rise above the terrace; thick enclosing walls and exposed eaves reveal the layered space containing the hall.
The temple was built in 1780 to receive the Sixth Panchen Lama for Qianlong’s birthday, drawing on Tashilhunpo in Shigatse. The Qing date is not replaced by the earlier history of its Tibetan model.

Enclosed halls and the visible golden roof combine internal worship space with an exterior landmark, while the front precinct follows a Chinese axis. Materials and forms meet in the roof, though the full temple layout remains a separate subject.

name: Yuzhou Ever-Normal Granary
sub: Granary God Temple and connected opera stage
era: Ming granary system · Exact date of surviving temple and stage unknown
yearNote: The Ever-Normal Granary is registered as a Ming national protected site; the exact construction years of the Granary God Temple and the opera stage are unknown, 1650 is only an approximate Ming–Qing placement, and the date of the granary administration system is not taken as the exact construction date of the two buildings.
lede: The granary deity shrine and linked theatre at Changping Granary add worship and performance to a storage complex. Set between northern storehouses, the shrine faces a stage towards the court. Some granary frames retain Ming fabric, but the shrine and theatre have no confirmed individual date. This pairing shows that historical grain storage included protective ritual as well as practical management.
facts: The shrine stands between two northern storehouses with a linked theatre in front. Shrine and stage organise the court for worship and performance, functions distinct from ordinary grain storage.

The complex is registered as Ming, with original Ming timber in some stores, but no exact foundation year. The shrine and theatre are individually undated; the history of the storage system cannot date either building.
The paired ritual spaces show that grain storage accommodated beliefs concerning protection and safety. Their position among stores links everyday use, local ceremony and architectural organisation.

name: Daci Pavilion
yearNote: The surviving pavilion was rebuilt in the Qianlong reign of the Qing, and 1760 is only an approximate placement within the 1736–1795 range; the 1227–1232 founding of the temple pavilion is not taken as the date of the pavilion in the photographs.
lede: Daci Pavilion rises from a high stone platform through three eave tiers, with steps making entry an ascent. A five-bay lower level supports the hip-and-gable roof; images and scripture storage give the storeys religious functions. The pavilion’s origins predate today’s Qing Qianlong rebuilding. Stone platform, timber body and worship space preserve a maintained monument rather than an unchanged early building.
facts: The pavilion has three eave tiers and a five-bay-wide, three-bay-deep lower level on a high balustraded stone platform. Steps and roofs organise movement from court to elevated hall.

Its foundation history reaches the thirteenth century, but the surviving pavilion was rebuilt during Qianlong’s reign. No single completion year is established; an approximate Qing date cannot be replaced by its early origins.
Guanyin occupies the lower level, with Buddhist images and scripture storage above. The high platform and roofs create an urban landmark while stacking different religious spaces within one building.

name: Puren Temple
sub: Gable and side eaves of the main hall (detail)
era: Founded in the 52nd year of Kangxi (Qing)
yearNote: Puren Temple was founded in 1713; the plate shows the gable pediment and part of the under-eave area of the surviving Qing main hall. This date corresponds to the building of the temple, and the plate does not show the complete hall.
lede: The gable panel and side eaves of Puren Temple’s principal hall bring monumental architecture into close detail. The triangular upper gable, supports and yellow glazed tiles reveal more than a distant roofline. Founded under Kangxi, the hall occupies a Chinese-style temple axis. This fragment shows how an early Chengde imperial Buddhist temple used traditional timber craft to create worship space.
facts: Ciwang Puyin Hall is seven bays wide and five deep, with a single-eaved yellow-glazed hip-and-gable roof. Its upper side gable and timber-supported eaves reveal how the triangular panel and sloping roof shape the side elevation.
Puren Temple was founded in 1713. The surviving Qing hall includes later repairs; the foundation dates a building phase, not every material visible in this close view.
An axial sequence of gate, Heavenly Kings Hall and principal halls follows Chinese temple planning. The gable and eaves reveal connections between glazed roofing, timber framing and worship space.

name: Xingwen Pagoda, Laiyuan
sub: Body and finial of the five-story octagonal brick pagoda
yearNote: The surviving pagoda is attributed to the Liao by its form, and 1050 is only an approximate placement; sources record a first construction in the 3rd year of Tianbao in the Tang (744), a Ming restoration in 1539 and modern repairs, and the founding date is not taken as the exact date of the surviving pagoda's form.
lede: Xingwen Pagoda’s five separated eave tiers express a pavilion rhythm more clearly than close-eaved towers. Octagonal walls and brackets imitate timber, but the solid interior is not climbable. It shares a high platform with neighbouring Taishan Palace, bringing Buddhist and Daoist buildings together. Tang founding records, Ming repairs and a Liao-form attribution are distinct evidence, not one precise construction date.
facts: The solid octagonal five-tier brick pagoda comprises a Sumeru base, body and finial. Timber-like brackets articulate each level; five exterior tiers are not five usable interior floors.

An embedded inscription records a Tang foundation in 744 and repair in 1539, while the provincial authority attributes its form to the Liao. These are distinct kinds of evidence; the surviving tower’s exact year is unsettled.

The tower and Ming-Qing Taishan Palace share a raised platform, with records of Buddhist and Daoist participation in repairs. Their setting reveals coexisting local religious spaces rather than an isolated monument.

name: Yanqing Daoist Temple
era: Surviving Yuan Jade Emperor Pavilion; approximate timeline placement
yearNote: Surviving Yuan Jade Emperor Pavilion; approximate timeline placement.
lede: Yuhuang Pavilion at Yanqing Guan rises from a square brick body to an octagonal upper level. Glazed details and layered eaves imitate a timber pavilion, but its structure relies on masonry. The surviving Yuan building also records the challenges posed by groundwater and foundation movement in Kaifeng. A conservation project raised the entire pavilion while preserving Yuan ground layers, allowing ancient construction and modern protection to be read together.
facts: Built entirely of grey brick without load-bearing timber beams, the pavilion appears three-storeyed, square below and octagonal above. Glazed ornament and masonry eaves reproduce the visual layers of timber architecture.

The surviving pavilion is assigned to the Yuan. Around 1280 is an approximate timeline position, not a verified completion year; changes in the monastery’s name and later repairs are separate from the building date.

An integral lifting project addressing cracking and foundation problems raised the pavilion by 3.1 metres while retaining Yuan ground layers. It illustrates conservation that protects both the monument and archaeological information beneath it.

name: Yue Fei Temple, Tangyin
era: Ming–Qing buildings and later repairs; exact construction year of the Second Hall unknown
yearNote: Ming–Qing buildings and later repairs; the exact construction year of the Second Hall is unknown.
lede: The second hall of Tangyin’s Yue Fei Temple presents five bays of red doors and windows beneath a grey roof. In Yue Fei’s home region, the temple sustains commemoration through buildings shaped by Ming–Qing construction and later repair; these are not a residence from the general’s Southern Song lifetime. Successive courtyards, inscriptions and commemorative writing reveal how later generations expressed the heroic image while giving the memorial architecture a history of its own.
facts: The hall’s five-bay front places doors and windows between columns beneath a single eave. Red-painted timber contrasts with grey brick and tiles, while the hall links preceding and following buildings within successive ritual courtyards.

The county government describes the surviving precinct as a Ming–Qing architectural group and records rebuilding in 1450. The second hall’s exact year remains unverified; around 1650 is only an approximate timeline position.

The temple is a public memorial to Yue Fei in his home region. Halls, inscriptions and writings preserve later expressions of remembrance. The buildings postdate his life by centuries, giving the memorial both personal and architectural histories.

name: Songyang Academy
sub: Front of the Qing main gate
era: Surviving gate is Qing, with later repairs; approximately placed in the Kangxi period
yearNote: The surviving gate is Qing and has been repaired; it is placed approximately in the Kangxi period.
lede: Songyang Academy’s gate covers three openings with a low curved-ridge roof, modest stone columns and grey brickwork. Beyond it, the Hall of Former Sages, lecture hall, lineage shrine and library unfold along an axis, organizing reverence, teaching and books in successive courtyards. The academy is famed for Song scholarship, but its present gate and layout largely reflect Qing work. The unassuming entrance offers a human-scaled approach to these layers of educational history.
facts: The three-bay gate has a curved-ridge roof without a prominent ridge crest, framed by stone columns and grey brick walls. The axis beyond links the Hall of Former Sages, lecture hall, lineage shrine and library through successive courtyards.

Earlier religious institutions occupied the site, and the Song emperor bestowed the academy’s name in 1035. The surviving buildings and layout are largely Qing; around 1680 is approximate and is not replaced by the earlier foundation or naming dates.

The courtyards connect veneration of sages, teaching and book storage, preserving spatial evidence of traditional education. Proceeding inward from the modest gate, functional sequence conveys the academy’s character more clearly than lavish ornament.

name: Daxiangguo Temple
era: Qianlong rebuilding phase (Qing), not the Northern Qi founding year
yearNote: The Qianlong rebuilding phase of the Qing, not the Northern Qi founding year of the temple.
lede: In 1642 a breach of the Yellow River buried Kaifeng, and Daxiangguo Temple with it, under silt; the halls seen today follow the layout fixed by a rebuilding in 1661 (Shunzhi 18) and a renovation in 1766 (Qianlong 31). The Daxiong Baodian (Mahavira Hall) shown here stands at the centre of the second courtyard: seven bays wide, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof, set on a Sumeru-base terrace ringed by stone balustrades whose posts are carved with small lions. The Northern Song complex of sixty-four cloisters is long gone, but the scale of a Qing state-sponsored monastery remains.
facts: Form: the Daxiong Baodian is seven bays wide and five deep, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof of yellow and green glazed tile and a total height of about 13 m. In front lies a Sumeru-base terrace; white stone balustrades surround hall and terrace, their post-heads carved with more than fifty small lions, no two alike.

History: in 712 (Yanhe 1) Emperor Ruizong of Tang bestowed the name Xiangguo Si. After the flood of 1642, the gate, Hall of Heavenly Kings and Daxiong Baodian were rebuilt in 1661 (Shunzhi 18) and renovated again in 1766 (Qianlong 31); the existing halls took their present form then, and Qianlong wrote the plaque 'Imperially Built Xiangguo Si'.

Fortunes: in 1927 troops of Feng Yuxiang destroyed every Buddhist image in the temple except the Thousand-Armed Guanyin and turned the temple into the Zhongshan Market; the main hall long stood empty and was used for exhibitions. In Northern Song the temple governed sixty-four cloisters on 540 mu of land; what stands today is only a corner of that core.

name: Zhengzhou City God Temple
era: Surviving Ming–Qing historic buildings; exact construction year of the individual building unknown
yearNote: Surviving Ming–Qing historic buildings; the exact construction year of the individual building is unknown.
lede: The best-preserved group of Ming-Qing buildings in old Zhengzhou is not a government office but this City God Temple. The Republican-era Zhengxian Gazetteer records renovations led by seven prefectural magistrates between 1501 (Hongzhi 14) and 1890 (Guangxu 16), and the gate, passage hall, stage, main hall and rear chambers still line up on one axis. The three-bay front shown here, with its green glazed-tile overhanging-gable roof, four small-octagonal stone columns in the central bay and three pairs of red plank doors, corresponds in the gazetteer's description to the temple's front gate hall; the main hall proper, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, stands north of the stage.
facts: Form: the front shown is three bays wide and two deep, with a green glazed-tile overhanging-gable roof and seven-tier bracket sets with three ang under the eaves, the ang-tips shaped as triple clouds and the beam-ends as elephant trunks. Four small-octagonal stone columns stand front and back in the central bay; three pairs of solid plank doors hang on the through-columns, with a fan-shaped flight of six steps and a pair of stone lions before them.

History: originally named the Temple of the City God, Marquis Lingyou, it enshrines Ji Xin, a general of Liu Bang of Han, and was founded in the early Ming. According to the Republican-era Zhengxian Gazetteer it was repeatedly renovated by magistrates: Shi Chuncui in 1501 (Hongzhi 14), Liu Ru in Jiajing 6, Li Shixuan in Longqing 4, and others in the Kangxi, Qianlong and Guangxu reigns. A stele with the cursive 'Eulogy of Fortune' by the early-Ming deputy magistrate Zhang Dayou survives in the temple.

Comparison: on the axis, the stage is a two-storey hip-and-gable pavilion whose nineteen roof ridges cross and overlap; the main hall is three bays square under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof with gilt-style bracket sets in the central bay; the five-bay rear chamber has an overhanging-gable roof fronted by a rolled-ridge worship porch. With gate, tower, hall and chamber roof types all present, it is one of the larger and more complete surviving City God temples in Henan.

name: Jia County Confucian Temple
era: Surviving Dacheng Hall with Ming–Qing repairs; Five Dynasties founding year not used
yearNote: Surviving Dacheng Hall with Ming–Qing repairs; the Five Dynasties founding year of the temple is not used.
lede: The four front-eave columns of the Dacheng Hall are carved through their whole length with coiling dragons, their capitals cut as tiger heads, and the dragon columns are of wood: Qing wooden dragon columns of this kind survive nowhere else in Henan. The hall is five bays wide under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof of green glazed tile, and the dragon slab before its terrace shows two dragons playing with a 'spider' rather than a flaming pearl. The temple began as a Kong family shrine completed in 954 (Xiande 1 of Later Zhou) and became the official Confucian temple in 1206 (Taihe 6 of Jin); the Dacheng Hall shown here is the Qing timber structure left by repeated Ming and Qing renovations.
facts: Form: the Dacheng Hall is five bays wide and three deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof of green glazed tile, 15.5 m high and 19.7 m across the front. The four wooden eave columns are carved through with coiling dragons, their capitals cut as fanged tiger faces looking down on the dragons; the column bases are covered with auspicious scenes, and the architraves, bracket sets and sparrow braces are also pierced with figures, carts, birds, flowers and clouds.

History: descendants of Confucius built a family shrine here in 954 (Xiande 1 of Later Zhou); in 1206 (Taihe 6 of Jin) the magistrate Zhang Zhixing enlarged it on the same site into the official Confucian temple. The Dacheng Hall was restored and its dragon slab carved under the Yingzong emperor of Ming (1459); the temple was rebuilt eleven times, and the surviving Dacheng Hall, Ji Gate and side halls are all Qing timber structures.

Comparison: the wooden dragon columns are later than the Song dragon columns of the Sage Mother Hall at Jinci, yet they are the only surviving example in Henan. The outer bracket sets and purlins keep original painted decoration that is neither the Beijing 'palace style' nor the Suzhou-Hangzhou 'Su style' but a Central Plains local manner. The temple retains 22 buildings with 71 bays, laid out with the school on the left and the shrine on the right, serving as both Kong family shrine and county school.

name: Shanxi-Shaanxi Guild Hall, Jia County
sub: Gate tower with bell and drum towers
era: Qing buildings; exact dates of the individual buildings in the surviving group unknown
yearNote: Qing buildings; the exact dates of the individual buildings in the surviving group are unknown.
lede: Seen from the street, the three-bay gatehouse is flanked by the bell and drum towers; its upper storey is the theatre stage, which faces north into the courtyard where the audience filled the open ground. The Shanxi-Shaanxi Guild Hall of Jiaxian was founded in 1693 (Kangxi 32) by merchants from Shanxi and Shaanxi as a way-station and guild house where the old Nanyang-Luoyang and Xuchang-Luoyang roads crossed. Shown here are the gatehouse and the two towers: each tower stands on a 4 m base, with twelve round timber columns carrying a cross-beamed roof under two tiers of flaring eaves, rising above the ridge of the gatehouse.
facts: Form: the gatehouse is three bays wide, the central bay for passage and the side bays for gatekeepers and reception; the open three-bay upper storey faces north as the stage, its brick-carved ridge crowned at the centre by a qilin bearing a treasure vase. The bell and drum towers on either side stand on bases 4 m high, each with twelve round timber columns supporting cross beams, double tiers of flaring eaves and solid bracket sets.

History: the guild hall was founded in 1693 (Kangxi 32) with funds from Shanxi and Shaanxi merchants and is also called the Shan-Shaan Temple or Guandi Temple. It faces south over a watercourse on a site of 6,300 square metres; the river-guarding screen wall before the gate is 8 m wide, 7 m high and 1 m thick, with a brick-carved coiled dragon on a red-sandstone base.

Comparison: the east and west galleries have eleven bays each, the courtyard could hold a thousand spectators, and to the north stand the five-bay Guan Gong Hall and, behind it, the Spring-and-Autumn Pavilion. Jiaxian lay where the Nanyang-Luoyang and Xuchang-Luoyang roads met; the tea route north from Nanyang branched here toward Shanxi, and the hall is regarded as a surviving relic of the Qing 'Ten-Thousand-Li Tea Road' in Henan.

name: Linfeng Fortified Village
sub: West Gate and connected red-stone wall
era: Red-stone walls rebuilt in the 1st year of Tongzhi
yearNote: Red-stone walls rebuilt in the 1st year of Tongzhi.
lede: The red-stone plaque above the gate is cut with the two characters 'Linfeng', and the iron sheathing of the doors is chiselled 'first year of Tongzhi, the year renxu': this wall wears its own birthday on its face. Linfeng Fort was originally a late-Ming earthen stockade; in 1862 (Tongzhi 1) the villager Zhu Zifeng led its rebuilding in purplish-red ashlar, an oval ring 1,100 m around and 6.6 m high, with five watch-towers and eight hundred merlons, and three gates set by the trigram directions to the north-west, south-west and south-east. Shown here are the west-facing Linfeng Gate and the wall joined to it.
facts: Form: the wall is stone outside and earth within, built of purplish-red ashlar on an oval plan 1,100 m around and 6.6 m high, with five watch-towers and 800 merlons. Each gate is a barrel-vaulted opening fitted with a pair of elm doors sheathed in 10 cm iron plate, with flood gates and drainage culverts outside; a moat 13 m wide circles the fort.

History: the Zhu clan is said to have moved here from Hongtong, Shanxi, in the Wanli reign of Ming and first raised an earthen stockade. In 1862 (Tongzhi 1) Zhu Zifeng, a native holding a purchased magistrate's rank, led the building of the red-stone fort; the words 'first year of Tongzhi, the year renxu' chiselled on the iron of the north-west gate are still legible. Inside survive one Ming courtyard house and more than a hundred Qing buildings with over four hundred bays.

Comparison: after 1949 village walls were pulled down across the region, but Linfeng's low-lying site and the need for flood defence saved it; Luo Zhewen called it 'the first red-stone fort of the Central Plains'. It was listed as a Chinese Historic and Cultural Village in 2005, among the first batch of Traditional Chinese Villages in 2012, and from 2014 the National Cultural Heritage Administration funded its overall restoration.

name: Gaoge Temple
sub: Pavilion and upper part of the high platform
era: Ming building with later repairs; approximate timeline placement
yearNote: Ming building with later repairs; approximate timeline placement.
lede: The one pavilion-hall left from a Ming princely palace. In 1404 (Yongle 2) the Yongle emperor enfeoffed his third son Zhu Gaosui as Prince of Zhao; the prince took up residence at Zhangde (Anyang) in 1425 (Hongxi 1) and turned the prefectural offices into his palace. The palace was abolished with the fall of the Ming in 1644, and by the Republican era only this Dashi Pavilion remained; because it stands on a brick platform about 8 m high it is known as Gaoge Si, the 'High Pavilion Temple'. The existing pavilion was rebuilt in 1470 (Chenghua 6), with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof of glazed tile; shown here are the pavilion body and its two tiers of eaves above the stone balustrade of the platform.
facts: Form: a pavilion on a high platform, more than 20 m in total height. The square brick platform is about 8 m high and 13 m on a side, with a flight of 32 stone steps on the south; white marble balustrades with carved lions line the steps and the platform top. The pavilion is three bays square, about 9 m each way, under a double-eaved nine-ridge hip-and-gable roof of glazed tile, with four round timber through-columns rising inside to the top beams.

History: Zhu Gaosui was made Prince of Zhao in 1404 (Yongle 2), took up residence at Zhangde in 1425 (Hongxi 1) and converted the prefectural offices into the Prince of Zhao's palace, of which the Dashi Pavilion was one hall; the existing building was rebuilt in 1470 (Chenghua 6). The Zhao line passed through eleven generations until the palace was abolished in 1644 (Chongzhen 17); by the Republican era its buildings had collapsed, leaving only this pavilion.

Comparison: most Ming princely palaces were demolished after the dynasty fell, and what survives elsewhere, such as the gate of the Jingjiang palace in Guilin, the Longting of the Zhou palace in Kaifeng or the Wangjing Tower of the Lu palace in Xinxiang, are fragments; Gaoge Si is the only building left of the Zhao palace. Twenty-five dragons carved in stone, interspersed with Sanskrit script, run around the outer walls of the pavilion, a rare decoration for a princely hall.

name: Wenzhi Pavilion, Xun County
sub: Surviving crossroads bell and drum tower
era: Surviving pavilion rebuilt in the Kangxi period according to research, approximately placed on the timeline; the Ming date in the national list is for the city wall and Wenzhi Pavilion as a whole
yearNote: According to research, the surviving pavilion was rebuilt in the Kangxi period, and its timeline placement is approximate; the Ming date in the national protected site list refers to the city wall and Wenzhi Pavilion as a whole.
lede: The east-west and north-south main streets of old Junxian cross here; the base is pierced by vaulted openings on all four sides, and carts and pedestrians pass beneath the pavilion. It is at once the bell-and-drum tower at the heart of the town and a gate-tower over the street. Originally called the Central Pavilion, of unknown founding date, it received the town bell after 1615 (Wanli 43) and has been known as the Bell-and-Drum Tower ever since; it burned in 1649 (Shunzhi 6) and was rebuilt in 1709 (Kangxi 48) by magistrate Liang Tongluo, who renamed it Wenzhi Ge, 'Pavilion of Civil Rule'. Shown here are the brick base and the two-storey, double-eaved pyramidal-roofed pavilion that make up the surviving structure.
facts: Form: about 20 m high in all, in two parts, base and pavilion. The square brick base is about 12 m on a side, with an arched vault through the middle of each face so that the four openings align east-west and north-south. On top stands a two-storey square pavilion about 10 m high, with a double-eaved four-sided pyramidal roof, upturned corners and ornamental ridges trimmed with glazed tile; the lower storey opens on all four sides, and the platform is ringed by a gallery and a 1 m parapet with square openings.

History: the Jiaqing-era Junxian Gazetteer records that 'after the yimao year of Wanli (1615) the bell was moved to the Central Pavilion'. It was destroyed by fire in 1649 (Shunzhi 6) and rebuilt in 1709 (Kangxi 48) by magistrate Liang Tongluo, who renamed it Wenzhi Ge after the idea of 'ruling by civil virtue'; Zhang Xi wrote a 'Record of the Rebuilding of Wenzhi Ge'. The present pavilion is the structure left by that rebuilding, with later repairs.

Comparison: above the four vaults are Qing bluestone horizontal tablets, 'Red glow streams from the eastern wall' and 'Jade pours from the western hills' by Zhao Sulu on the east and west, 'Clear waters ring the Li' and 'Dark mist guards the Pi' by Zhang Zhe on the south and north. The pavilion is listed together with the surviving stretch of city wall on the Wei River, first built in 1370 (Hongwu 3), and is one of the heritage points of the Junxian section of the Grand Canal.

name: Angkor Wat
sub: Five central towers and adjoining terrace galleries
yearNote: Reign of Suryavarman II; 1125 is only an approximate timeline placement within the first half of the 12th century, and later conservation and restoration are recorded separately.
lede: Angkor Wat’s central tower and four corner towers rise from stepped terraces, organising stone architecture as a sacred mountain. The central towers and adjacent galleries form an inner area of worship within the larger temple grounds. Built under Suryavarman II in the first half of the twelfth century for Vishnu, it later continued as a Buddhist place of worship.
facts: A central tower and four corner towers form a five-tower plan above ascending terraces and galleries. From an oblique viewpoint towers overlap; the visible count differs from the complete plan.

APSARA dates construction to Suryavarman II’s reign in the first half of the twelfth century and records original dedication to Vishnu. Approximate dating distinguishes construction, later Buddhist use and conservation, without asserting one completion year.

Terraces and five towers express a sacred centre, while continuing Buddhist devotion keeps the former Hindu temple a living religious place. This continuity is more accurate than a story of complete abandonment and rediscovery.

name: Bayon
sub: Central face towers and their supporting terraces
yearNote: Angkor period; 1200 is an approximate placement at the turn of the 12th and 13th centuries, and since the surviving towers have been repaired, they are not regarded as complete original fabric of a single year.
lede: Great stone faces turn towards different directions above Bayon’s clustered towers, appearing and disappearing as visitors move. The central group developed around the late twelfth and early thirteenth centuries in connection with Jayavarman VII’s Buddhist kingship. Conserved towers and their supporting platform create a shifting experience unlike Angkor Wat’s ordered five-tower plan.
facts: The central group combines towers of differing heights with their supporting platform. Monumental faces look in different directions, and nearby towers overlap; spatial relationships matter more than a theoretical total tower count.

APSARA places foundation under Jayavarman VII in the late twelfth century. Subsequent construction and changes support approximate dating around the turn of the thirteenth century, distinct from later conservation.

The faces turn architecture into sculpture, changing their relationships with each movement of the viewer. Their precise identity remains debated; they are not all asserted to be literal portraits of the king.

name: Banteay Srei
sub: Three central shrine towers and shared platform
yearNote: 967 is the dedication year recorded in inscriptions and is not the same as the completion date of every stone component; the surviving form also includes conservation and restoration.
lede: Fine carving interlaces the pink sandstone of Banteay Srei’s three central sanctuaries. Their modest scale concentrates elaborate door lintels and wall ornament on one platform. Towers overlap from an oblique view, rewarding close attention rather than sheer height. Dedication in 967 provides the date, not a claim that every stone was installed that year.
facts: Three central sanctuaries share a platform, with carved sandstone doorframes, walls and stepped superstructures. They form the core; libraries and gateways are separate, and this group is not the whole temple plan.
APSARA records dedication on 22 April 967 and inscriptions on central-group door jambs concerning the founder and his family. Dedication, construction stages and later conservation are distinguished.

A high official, rather than a royal foundation alone, sponsored the temple. Fine carving reveals the spread of courtly art to other patrons; the familiar name does not establish a queen’s residential palace.

name: Borobudur
sub: Surviving main structure and complete base
yearNote: UNESCO gives the 8th–9th century; 825 is only an approximate timeline position within this period. The surviving stonework underwent conservation and restoration in the 20th century.
lede: Square terraces and carved galleries lead upwards to three circular platforms, where perforated stupas surround a great central stupa. Borobudur turns circumambulation into an expression of Buddhist cosmology. Built in the eighth and ninth centuries and conserved in the twentieth, its complete outline combines ancient design with continuing preservation.
facts: Five square terraces support three circular platforms and a central stupa. Seventy-two perforated stupas on the circular platforms contain Buddha images; relief galleries and the complete base frame the ascending route.
UNESCO dates building to the eighth and ninth centuries under the Syailendra dynasty, without one exact completion year. Major twentieth-century conservation restored and repositioned stonework.

Base, square terraces and circular platforms correspond to different Buddhist cosmic realms. Narrative reliefs give way to simpler upper stupas, turning movement through the monument into a passage towards open space.

name: Shiva Temple of Prambanan
sub: Single main Shiva temple and steps
yearNote: On the same UNESCO page, the brief description gives the 10th century and the detailed description the 9th century; 900 is only for approximate ordering. The surviving main temple has undergone modern reconstruction and restoration.
lede: A narrowing superstructure raises Prambanan’s Shiva temple about forty-seven metres above the central precinct. Entrance steps lead into concentrated stone ornament. The main temple and its base express the hierarchy of this sacred centre. Ninth-to-tenth-century dating is retained, and modern reconstruction forms part of the surviving structure.
facts: The central Shiva temple is the tallest principal shrine, about forty-seven metres high. Body, stepped crown and entrance stair form a vertical profile; Brahma and Vishnu temples beside it are separate buildings.

UNESCO’s summary uses the tenth century while its detailed account also refers to the ninth. A ninth-to-tenth-century range remains appropriate without an exact year, with restored stonework distinguished from the inherited design.

The group organises worship around Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma, with the main shrine’s height emphasising Shiva’s central position. Its steep outline creates a different religious space from Borobudur’s spreading terraces.
