name: Main Chedi of Wat Mahathat, Sukhothai
sub: Lotus-bud main chedi and its supporting base
yearNote: Reliable sources confirm the Sukhothai period and the lotus-bud form of the main chedi, but the precise year of its remodeling is unknown; 1350 is used only for timeline ordering, and the temple's founding year is not substituted for the age of the surviving main chedi.
lede: A lotus-bud crown narrows into a fine spire above Wat Mahathat’s stepped base, expressing a distinctive Sukhothai form. Surviving masonry and stucco reveal the tower itself rather than lost hall roofs. The central chedi and its supporting base form the core of worship; the exact rebuilding year remains unconfirmed.
facts: The central chedi rises from a stepped base to a lotus-bud crown and slender spire, characteristic of Sukhothai art. Nearby hall columns and separate towers belong to the wider layout, not its direct body.

The Fine Arts Department suggests the tower may have been converted from an earlier Sri Lankan form. An exact rebuilding year is not established; approximate Sukhothai dating is separated from temple foundation and later repairs.

Stucco disciples on the base walk with hands joined in reverence, bringing devotional movement onto the building surface. Together with the lotus-bud crown, they show a local interpretation of external stupa traditions.

name: Wat Chaiwatthanaram
sub: Central prang, four corner prangs and shared base
yearNote: 1630 is the temple's founding year recorded in historical sources; the plate shows the surviving group of the central prang and four corner prangs, and given the discussion of earlier construction and the modern restoration, not all the brickwork is taken as built in the same year.
lede: A tall central prang and four corner towers share a broad brick platform at Wat Chaiwatthanaram, arranging a sacred centre as a temple-mountain. Chronicles record foundation in 1630, while modern conservation also shapes the surviving masonry. The central group shows how Ayutthaya Buddhism adopted Khmer tower forms to express cosmology.
facts: A high main prang and four smaller corner prangs rise from one platform, their narrowing bodies emphasising the centre. The outer gallery and eight tower-shaped chapels form a separate surrounding zone.

The anthropology centre cites several Ayutthaya chronicles for foundation in 1630 and records archaeology and restoration in 1987–1992. Foundation does not establish that all surviving bricks were laid simultaneously.

The study interprets the main prang as Mount Sumeru and its corner towers and gallery as the surrounding world. This shared Buddhist and Hindu cosmological pattern is expressed through the group, not height alone.

name: Ananda Temple, Bagan
sub: Whole temple body, central spire and projecting entrances
yearNote: The Indian government's conservation project description gives the early 12th century; 1110 is only an approximate placement within that period, and none of the unverified exact years 1090, 1091 or 1105 is chosen. The surviving form includes later restoration.
lede: Ananda’s broad body projects entrances in four directions, while terraces lift a golden central crown. This early-twelfth-century Bagan temple links interior devotion with an ascending exterior profile. Later repairs remain part of its walls and roofs; the whole body explains a shrine containing images and circulation better than a view of its crown alone.
facts: The cruciform body projects entrances in four directions, with terraces rising to the central crown. Four standing Buddhas face the cardinal directions within; the crown belongs to the temple body, rather than a separate stupa.

India’s conservation account dates building to the early twelfth century. Approximate dating is retained without choosing an unverified exact year; conservation after the 2016 earthquake contributes to the present appearance.
Unlike a solid stupa worshipped externally, Ananda contains images and circumambulation space inside its broad body. Four entrances and standing Buddhas connect devotional movement with orientation.

name: Sim of Wat Xieng Thong
sub: The sim (main hall) and its supporting platform
yearNote: Official sources record its founding in about 1560; the main hall was repaired in 1928, in 1952–1960 and at other times, so not all the surviving decoration can be regarded as original 16th-century work.
lede: Three sweeping roof tiers descend over Wat Xieng Thong’s main sim, with gilding and glass mosaic adding close detail. Founded around 1560, it has been repeatedly repaired, so present ornament is not all sixteenth-century work. The hall and platform reveal Luang Prabang form through the relationship between low roofs and interior space.
facts: The sim has a central hall and side spaces beneath a low, three-tiered sweeping roof, with four decorated entrance columns. Its supporting platform belongs to the hall; the royal funeral-chariot building is separate.
The official tourism account gives foundation around 1560 and repairs including 1928 and 1952–1960. The founding period is distinguished from the age of present glass mosaic and gilded surfaces.

Low eaves and upturned finials define Luang Prabang hall architecture. Glass mosaics introduce daily and religious imagery, while inherited roof forms and later ornament sustain the building’s devotional use.

name: Main Tower of Po Klong Garai
sub: Surviving main shrine tower with entrance and base
yearNote: Official Khánh Hòa Province sources give the late 13th–early 14th century; 1300 is only for approximate ordering, and the construction date of the tower is not inferred from the life dates of the king worshipped there.
place: Khánh Hòa Province · Phan Rang–Tháp Chàm
lede: Red-brick pilasters rhythmically divide Po Klong Garai’s main tower, whose narrowing superstructure rises above the hill. Its entrance and base form a central worship space, distinct from the gate and fire towers. Built around the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries and later associated with a revered ruler, it remains part of Cham ceremonial life.
facts: The central main shrine combines a square exterior with four diminishing levels and an east-facing entrance. Pilasters and niches articulate brick walls; the gate tower and elongated-roof fire tower are separate structures.
Khanh Hoa cultural and tourism sources date construction to the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries. The revered ruler lived earlier, so his lifespan is not used to date the brick tower.

Worship combines Shiva belief with the memory of a local ruler. Tower-opening, rain-prayer and Kate ceremonies continue, making both historic masonry and ongoing ritual essential to its community significance.

name: Meridian Gate (Ngọ Môn) of the Huế Imperial City
sub: Complete gate platform and Five Phoenix Pavilion
yearNote: 1833 is the construction date of the Meridian Gate; the surviving timber pavilion, roofs and platform have undergone later repairs, and there are also records of modern repairs.
lede: Ngo Mon is the imperial entrance to Hue’s royal enclosure, formed by a substantial masonry platform and the Five Phoenix Pavilion above it. Five passages and layered roofs express a strict order of access. Built in 1833 under Emperor Minh Mang, the gate belongs to the ceremonial heart of the Nguyen capital. It combines the scale of a fortified entrance with separate routes for emperor, officials and attendants.
facts: The brick-and-stone platform has a recessed, U-shaped plan with five passages. Above it, the two-level timber Five Phoenix Pavilion has multiple roofs covered with yellow and green glazed tiles. Heavy masonry and lighter timber create clearly distinct lower and upper parts.

The present gate was built in 1833 under Minh Mang, replacing the earlier Nam Khuyet Dai. This date describes Ngo Mon’s construction phase, not the foundation of the entire imperial enclosure. The building has also undergone later restoration.

The central passage was reserved for the emperor; the others served civil and military officials, soldiers and attendants with animals. Used for access and royal ceremonies, the gate made Nguyen court hierarchy visible through its circulation routes.

name: San Agustin Church, Manila
sub: Surviving church facade and bell tower
yearNote: 1607 is the completion date of the surviving stone church, as distinct from the earlier wooden churches. The bell tower and later repairs have their own histories, and the present building as a whole is not dated as original fabric of a single year.
lede: Tiered orders of columns divide the doors and windows of the stone facade, a round window and a cross mark the triangular pediment, and the surviving bell tower adjoins it on the right. San Agustin Church preserves another architectural tradition of old Manila.
facts: The plate shows the surviving main facade and the single bell tower on the right; the low remnant of the lost left tower is kept and not reconstructed as symmetrical twin towers.

The National Museum of the Philippines records that the surviving stone church was completed in 1607; the original wooden church and later repairs are described separately, and the monastery as a whole is not drawn.

name: Sudeoksa Daeungjeon
sub: Single Daeungjeon hall and stone platform
era: Hall built 1308; the temple's founding is dated separately.
yearNote: Hall built in 1308; the temple's founding is dated separately.
lede: Sudeoksa’s Daeungjeon is a restrained timber hall with a three-bay front in a mountain monastery courtyard. Column-top brackets and the side framing are clearly exposed beneath its gabled roof. An ink inscription discovered during repairs dates its construction to 1308, giving this Koryo-period timber building unusually firm chronological evidence. Its columns, beams and roof invite close attention to construction rather than ornament.
facts: The hall is three bays across and four deep, with a gabled roof. Brackets are concentrated above the columns, while the side elevation exposes successive framing members. The load-bearing relationship between columns, beams and roof is readily visible.

An ink inscription found during repairs in 1937 establishes the hall’s construction date as 1308. This firm date belongs to the surviving hall; traditions about the monastery’s foundation and later repairs must be considered separately.

The restrained column-top brackets and open framing retain characteristics of Koryo timber construction. Its secure date makes it important for comparing early buildings. A view from the side reveals more of the builders’ methods than the front alone.

name: Buseoksa Muryangsujeon
era: Surviving Muryangsujeon rebuilt in 1376; the temple was founded in 676.
yearNote: The surviving Muryangsujeon was rebuilt in 1376; the temple was founded in 676.
lede: Muryangsujeon at Buseoksa is known for its broad five-bay front, gently swelling columns and restrained column-top brackets. A wide hip-and-gable roof covers the hall dedicated to Amitabha Buddha, creating a composed yet supple silhouette. Records describe rebuilding in 1376, while structural forms preserve earlier traditions. The surviving building and repeated later repairs together make up its historical layers.
facts: The hall is five bays wide and three deep, with a single hip-and-gable roof and column-top brackets. Columns swell gently at mid-height; their shape and generous spacing make the substantial roof appear both supple and stable.

Records describe damage in the fourteenth century and repair in 1376, followed by later repairs and dismantling restoration. Some structural forms continue earlier traditions, so every surviving component cannot be assigned to the same rebuilding year.

The hall houses Amitabha Buddha and is Buseoksa’s principal Buddhist sanctuary. The coordination of column shape, brackets and roof helps visitors understand Koryo timber traditions and the long continuity of monastery space through visible components.

name: Dabotap of Bulguksa
sub: Complete Dabotap stone pagoda with stairways on four sides
era: Officially dated to the 8th century, Unified Silla; 751 is a date associated with the building of Bulguksa, and the pagoda's ordering year is approximately taken as 751.
yearNote: Officially dated to the 8th century, Unified Silla; 751 is a date associated with the building of Bulguksa, and the pagoda's ordering year is approximately taken as 751.
lede: Square stone pillars support a pagoda body whose tiers keep changing form, while balustrades and an octagonal canopy shift its scale in the upper part. Carved from granite into a complex outline close to timber construction, Dabotap is entirely different from the common multi-roofed stone pagodas.
facts: Korean authorities officially date Dabotap to the 8th century, Unified Silla; 751 is a date associated with the building of Bulguksa, the ordering uses an approximate value, and no precise completion year is claimed for the pagoda.

Square stone pillars and stairways on four sides below combine with octagonal elements above, and official sources explain that its number of stories is hard to count in the way used for an ordinary pavilion-style pagoda.
Following its present state, the single surviving stone lion is kept, the lost lions are not added back, and the neighboring Seokgatap is not drawn.

name: Changdeokgung Injeongjeon
era: The surviving Injeongjeon shown here was rebuilt in 1804; the palace's founding and successive fires are dated separately.
yearNote: The surviving Injeongjeon shown here was rebuilt in 1804; the palace's founding and successive fires are dated separately.
lede: Injeongjeon at Changdeokgung stands on two stone terraces. Its five-bay front and two-tier roof command the ceremonial court, while the interior rises uninterrupted through both levels. The present timber hall was rebuilt in 1804 after a fire, and its interior retains early twentieth-century alterations. It records both Joseon court ceremony and the palace’s adaptation through successive building phases.
facts: The hall is five bays across and four deep, with a two-tier hip-and-gable roof and dense brackets above two terraces. There is no intermediate floor inside: tall columns and upper framing enclose a single lofty ceremonial space.

The hall burned in 1803 and was rebuilt the following year, reusing the existing stone terraces. The timber structure is principally dated to 1804, while its flooring and some interior decoration reflect early twentieth-century alterations.

Injeongjeon hosted court congratulations, investitures and important political ceremonies; rank stones organized officials in the courtyard. A low hill behind and corridors adjusted to the slope show how ceremonial order was reconciled with the terrain.
captions: Changdeokgung Injeongjeon · Injeongjeon hall and terrace

name: Namdaemun of Kaesong
sub: Stone gate platform and postwar rebuilt gate tower
era: Inner-city gate first built 1391–1393; the gate tower was destroyed in war in 1950 and rebuilt from 1954, a caption in the World Heritage nomination file records its restoration in 1955, and the timeline is placed by the surviving gate tower.
yearNote: The inner-city gate was first built in 1391–1393; the gate tower was destroyed in war in 1950 and rebuilt from 1954, a caption in the World Heritage nomination file records its restoration in 1955, and the timeline is placed by the surviving gate tower.
lede: Kaesong’s Namdae Gate has a granite base with a central arch supporting a single-storey wooden pavilion. It survives from the former southern entrance to the inner city. The gate originated in the late fourteenth century, but its pavilion was destroyed during the Korean War and reconstructed in 1955 using earlier images and architectural records. Old masonry and rebuilt timber together preserve its form and record destruction and recovery.
facts: The granite platform contains a central arched passage. Above it stands a timber pavilion three bays across and two deep. Its broad roof contrasts with the low, substantial masonry, making passage, platform and pavilion easy to distinguish.

The gate was first built in 1391–1393. Its timber pavilion burned during the Korean War and was reconstructed in 1955 using old photographs, drawings and surviving foundations. The present timberwork and earlier masonry belong to different phases.

The gate records the urban layout of Kaesong, capital of Koryo, and the postwar effort to preserve monuments. Distinguishing the early base from the reconstructed upper part shows how continuity can depend on reliable records as well as surviving fabric.

name: Pyongyang Pothong Gate
sub: Gate platform and double-eaved gate tower of Pothong Gate
era: According to Kim Il Sung University sources, the surviving Pothong Gate was extensively repaired in 1473, with further repairs and extensions later; the Goguryeo origins of the city site are not used as the date of the surviving gate tower.
yearNote: According to Kim Il Sung University sources, the surviving Pothong Gate was extensively repaired in 1473, with further repairs and extensions later; the Goguryeo origins of the city site are not used as the date of the surviving gate tower.
lede: Pothong Gate in Pyongyang combines an arched stone platform with a two-level wooden pavilion. Its broad double eaves once marked the city’s western entrance. The gate’s origins reach back to Koguryo, but its surviving form is chiefly associated with major repairs in 1473 and subsequent enlargement. Now standing apart from its former walls, it condenses memories of defence, travel and farewells in its masonry and timber silhouette.
facts: The granite base contains a central arched passage. Above it rises a wooden pavilion three bays wide and three deep, with two levels of eaves. Substantial stonework and the spreading timber roof create distinct layers.

The gate’s foundation is traditionally traced to the mid-sixth century under Koguryo. Its surviving form reflects major repairs in 1473 and later enlargement. The ancient origin of the entrance does not date every component of the present timber pavilion.

Pothong Gate was an important western route out of Pyongyang, serving defence, journeys and farewells. Although the city-wall layout has changed, the surviving gate still evokes the old urban boundary and the everyday movement of its inhabitants.
captions: Pyongyang Pothong Gate · Gate platform and double-eaved gate tower

name: Lecture Hall of Sungyang Academy
sub: Five-bay lecture hall of the academy
era: The academy was established in 1573, and the lecture hall was repaired in the 17th and 19th centuries; the exact construction year of the surviving timberwork is undetermined, and about 1600 is only a timeline position within the Joseon period.
yearNote: The academy was established in 1573, and the lecture hall was repaired in the 17th and 19th centuries; the exact construction year of the surviving timberwork is undetermined, and about 1600 is only a timeline position within the Joseon period.
lede: The lecture hall of Sungyang Academy stands on the highest of its stepped terraces, with a broad five-bay front facing the teaching courtyard and a shrine precinct behind. Established in the sixteenth century on the site of Jong Mong Ju’s former home, the academy combined Confucian education and commemoration. Repeated repairs complicate the hall’s precise construction date; its layout explains its use more clearly than a single year.
facts: The teaching precinct has three terraces. The lecture hall occupies the highest and is five bays wide by three deep; east and west student dormitories stand on a lower terrace. Walls and gates separate the shrine precinct behind.

The academy was established in 1573 on the site of Jong Mong Ju’s former home. Records describe repairs to the lecture hall in 1633 and to the whole academy in 1823. Its foundation date does not date every component of the surviving hall.

Teaching in front and worship behind combined Confucian learning with remembrance of Jong Mong Ju. Moving up the terraces reveals how courtyards, dormitories and the hall organized the academy’s educational and ceremonial life.

name: Sonjuk Bridge, Kaesong
sub: Old stone beam bridge and 1780 stone balustrades
era: The nomination file says the bridge has been in use since the early Goryeo, exact year unknown; about 1100 is an ordering position, 1392 is the year Jeong Mong-ju was killed, and the stone balustrades were added in 1780.
yearNote: The nomination file says the bridge has been in use since the early Goryeo, exact year unknown; about 1100 is an ordering position, 1392 is the year Jeong Mong-ju was killed, and the stone balustrades were added in 1780.
lede: A short granite beam bridge spans a shallow stream, its deck enclosed by round-topped stone posts and rails. Sonjuk Bridge became a memorial site because Jeong Mong-ju was killed there, and the later balustrades also record its withdrawal from everyday traffic.
facts: The nomination file says the stone bridge has been in use since the early Goryeo, and its exact construction year has not been confirmed; about 1100 is an ordering position, and 1392 is the year of the killing.
The bridge is 8.35 m long and 3.36 m wide, with stone piers carrying stone beams topped by stone slabs; it is not an arch bridge. The surviving stone balustrades on both sides were added in 1780.
Only the old Sonjuk Bridge and its later balustrades are drawn; the separate bridge built alongside for traffic, the stele pavilion and the inscribed steles are not part of the subject.

name: Karamon of Ueno Tōshō-gū
yearNote: The timeline follows the 1651 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the shrine's founding.
lede: Ueno Toshogu’s Karamon concentrates splendour into a small entrance: a curved gable crowns its doors, with gilding and dense carving around the frame. The surviving gate belongs to the 1651 rebuilding. Only one bay across and deep, it creates a strong ceremonial boundary through elaborate curves. Roof and frame can be read before the dragon and bird decoration; repaired surfaces are not all original.
facts: The gate is one bay across and one bay deep, with a curved karahafu facing the approach and copper roof tiles. Its small structure supports dense ornament, contrasting the curved gable with upright posts and doors.

Heritage records date the surviving gate to 1651, and the shrine connects it with that rebuilding campaign. Subsequent repairs and surface maintenance mean that today’s gilding and paint cannot all be treated as original fabric.

Dragons by the posts and surrounding birds and flowers make the entrance a visual focus and express the sanctuary’s ceremonial status. The density of ornament shows how a small gate can acquire significance through detail rather than width.

name: Rōmon of Nezu Shrine
yearNote: The timeline follows the 1706 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the shrine's founding.
lede: Nezu Shrine’s gate concentrates entry into one central passage. Solid side bays give it gravity, while the upper balustrade draws a lighter line below the roof. This three-bay, single-passage romon has two storeys beneath one principal roof, unlike a gate with two large tiers of eaves. Built in 1706, its red frame and tiled roof make an Edo shrine entrance’s order easy to read.
facts: Three bays and one passage mean that only the central bay allows entry. The upper storey has a balustrade beneath a tiled hip-and-gable roof. Two storeys share one principal eaves line; storeys and roof tiers are different counts.

Heritage records date the surviving gate to 1706 as part of Nezu Shrine’s Edo-period buildings. This date applies to the gate itself; earlier shrine traditions and subsequent repairs form separate historical layers.

A central passage, enclosed side bays and an upper balustrade create a boundary between outside and inside, unlike a route through successive torii. Bay proportions and roof form show how a gate’s mass organises shrine space.

name: Asakusa Shrine
yearNote: The timeline follows the 1649 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the shrine's founding.
lede: Asakusa Shrine’s low, broad timber worship hall contrasts with neighbouring Senso-ji’s postwar main hall. Tokugawa Iemitsu donated the surviving shrine buildings in 1649; they retained their early Edo form through fires, earthquakes and war. Painted mythical creatures and the red frame reward close attention. The shrine’s three deities also connect it with Senso-ji’s Kannon foundation legend.
facts: The shrine comprises a main sanctuary, offering hall and worship hall linked by corridors. The worship hall’s front faces approaching worshippers. Low eaves, doors and painted details establish the entrance, while corridors connect deeper ritual spaces.

The shrine records that Tokugawa Iemitsu established and donated the surviving buildings in 1649, and that they escaped subsequent disasters and war. Painted and lacquered surfaces were later repaired, so building dates and present coating dates should be distinguished.

The three people enshrined here belong to Senso-ji’s Kannon origin legend, linking neighbouring Buddhist and Shinto traditions. Mythical-creature decoration conveys auspicious wishes, serving both ritual and close visual inspection.

name: Sangedatsumon of Zōjō-ji
yearNote: The timeline follows the 1622 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding.
lede: Sangedatsumon makes entry solemn through two deep eaves and a five-bay frontage. Three central passages occupy the ground floor, while the upper level houses Buddhist images. Zojo-ji dates the surviving rebuilding to 1622. Its early Edo scale gives passage the Pure Land meaning of leaving greed, anger and ignorance behind. Its complete outline also carries a conservation history; work began in 2025.
facts: This five-bay, three-passage gate has two storeys and two tiers of eaves beneath a hip-and-gable roof. An upper balustrade encircles it. The eaves distinguish lower circulation from the image-housing space above.

The temple records the earlier gate’s collapse in a storm in 1621 and rebuilding the following year; the heritage database separately lists 1621. The temple date and official record coexist; the discrepancy and ongoing conservation should be distinguished.

The name refers to release from greed, anger and ignorance, making passage a symbolic transition from ordinary life into the temple. Images above and entry routes below give the same gate both circulation and devotional functions.

name: Kiyomizu Kannon-dō of Kan'ei-ji
sub: Kannon Hall and the stage in front
yearNote: The timeline follows the 1631 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding. It was moved to its present site in 1694, and conservation repairs were completed in 1996.
lede: Kiyomizu Kannondo’s timber platform projects towards the Ueno slope, bringing worship and viewing together. Modelled on Kyoto’s Kiyomizu-dera, the hall has its own Edo history: Tenkai founded it in 1631, and later Kanei-ji construction prompted relocation. Red columns and the platform form one building. Its conserved appearance should not be confused with Kyoto’s much larger raised stage.
facts: A timber platform extends the hall towards the slope. Railings and supporting timbers join the red-columned hip-and-gable hall to an open viewing area, bringing the worship entrance close to the outlook.

Tenkai established the hall in 1631; it moved to its present site in 1694 for Kanei-ji’s main-hall project. Conservation finished in 1996, restoring its relocation-period appearance according to the temple. Foundation, relocation and conservation are distinct.

The hall adapted an image of Kyoto’s Kiyomizu-dera for Edo, adjusting its platform to local terrain. It shows how celebrated places could inspire another city while retaining each building’s own structure and history.

name: Main Hall of Gokoku-ji
yearNote: The timeline follows the 1697 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding.
lede: Gokoku-ji’s broad copper roof has turned green above a timber Kannon Hall from the Genroku period. The temple was founded in 1681, but this seven-by-seven-bay hall was built in 1697. A three-bay worship porch projects centrally. Approaching its steps and galleries reveals the scale of an Edo prayer temple through its nearly square mass and sweeping roof.
facts: The single-storey hall measures seven bays across and deep, with a hip-and-gable roof, a projecting three-bay worship porch and batten-seam copper roofing. Its square plan and broad eaves frame an emphatically central worship entrance.

The temple dates from 1681; the surviving Kannon Hall was completed in 1697, the tenth Genroku year. Temple foundation and hall construction are separate, and later roof and timber repairs cannot be attributed to the original foundation.

The broad hall accommodates collective Kannon worship and services, showing another scale of timber architecture beyond small refined structures. Its seven-bay body and three-bay porch reveal how a large mass focuses the direction of worship.

name: Five-Story Pagoda of Ikegami Honmon-ji
yearNote: The timeline follows the 1608 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding.
lede: Ikegami Honmon-ji’s pagoda tapers through five dark tiled roofs beneath a finial. The temple records topping-out in 1607 and a dedication the following year, placing it in early Edo construction. Relocation and modern dismantling repairs are also part of its history: an intact outline does not mean every component is unchanged, and the temple’s earlier origins do not date this tower.
facts: Five progressively smaller roofs crown the timber pagoda beneath its finial, with a platform supporting the lowest level. Broad eaves alternate with a narrower body. Five roof tiers should not be assumed to mean five accessible internal floors.

The temple records topping-out in 1607 and dedication in 1608. The pagoda moved to its present location during the Genroku period and later underwent modern dismantling conservation. Its construction date differs from relocation and repair dates.

Japanese timber pagodas and Chinese brick towers both form layered vertical markers, but this tower emphasises deep eaves and intricate framing. Comparing its broad roofs with shorter brick cornices reveals how materials change related religious forms.

name: Jizō Hall of Shōfuku-ji
sub: Single-story Zen Buddhist hall with mokoshi
yearNote: The timeline follows the 1407 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding.
lede: Shofuku-ji’s Jizo Hall seems to have two roofs stacked above two storeys, but it is a single-storey hall surrounded by a lower mokoshi aisle. A 1407 ink inscription found during repairs gives this Kanto Zen hall a secure date. Wooden shingles on the main roof contrast with copper over the aisle; refined interior framing directs the eye upwards, inviting both exterior and interior readings.
facts: The three-by-three-bay hall has one storey and a surrounding mokoshi aisle. The main hip-and-gable roof is wood-shingled, while copper covers the lower aisle roof. Two eaves lines do not indicate two floors.

Repairs revealed an inscription for Oei 14, or 1407, on a support for the tail rafters. Heritage documentation uses it to establish the construction date. This physical inscription dates the hall more directly than temple foundation legends.

Heritage research compares it with Engaku-ji’s reliquary hall in Kamakura, showing the standardised design of Muromachi Zen halls. Dense brackets and framing rising towards the centre give a modest space a highly refined order.
